pieces.label: The Spring That Talks Back
pieces.text: Thirsty after walking in the hills all morning, (seeker) kneels at a little spring under a rock, and before (seeker.he/she) can drink, the water clears its throat. "Ask me anything. But only one thing. I'm busy."

pieces.label: Ask What to Be Good At
pieces.text: (Seeker) clears (seeker.his/her) own throat, feeling very silly. "What am I meant to be good at?" (seeker.he/she) asks. The spring bubbles thoughtfully for a long moment, the way a person drums their fingers on a table...

pieces.label: Ask Nothing and Just Drink
pieces.text: (Seeker) decides that talking water is none of (seeker.his/her) business. (seeker.He/She) says "No thank you," politely, and drinks. The spring goes very quiet, as if it is deciding whether to be offended...

pieces.label: Argue with the Spring
pieces.text: Argue with the Spring.

pieces.label: Run Back Down the Hill
pieces.text: Run Back Down the Hill.
"Plants," says the spring. "You've always liked plants. You just never noticed." By the end of the week (seeker) has dirt under every fingernail and can't stop talking about soil.
"Not swimming, that's for sure. You swim like a coconut with ambitions." (Seeker) stomps off red to the ears, and nobody can talk (seeker.him/her) into so much as wading.
The spring seems almost insulted to be treated like a spring. The water is cold, sweet and perfectly ordinary, and (seeker) walks home very refreshed.

The water tastes faintly of honey, and a knot (seeker) didn't know (seeker.he/she) had comes undone. The next morning (seeker.he/she) does the job (seeker.he/she) always grumbled about, or never had the knack for, and does it well.
(Seeker) tells the spring it's only an echo. The spring answers by telling (seeker.him/her) exactly what (seeker.he/she) had for breakfast, and (seeker) leaves at a run.
"Patience," says the spring. "You're good at waiting for people." (Seeker) goes home and is suddenly wonderful with the little ones.
(Seeker) bolts, trips on a root and skins both knees. Behind (seeker.him/her), the spring gurgles with laughter.
A single blue dragonfly keeps guard on a reed, as if it has heard all this before.
The spring's voice is like a very old aunt who has been interrupted in the middle of something.
Ferns lean over the water.
When (seeker) tells the story at supper, half the village laughs and the other half asks exactly which rock it was.

pieces.label: A Face in the Tide Pool
pieces.text: At low tide, looking for crabs among the warm pools, (looker) leans over a perfectly round pool, and (looker.his/her) reflection smiles a moment too late. Then it waves.

pieces.label: Wave Back
pieces.text: Slowly, feeling very foolish, (looker) lifts a hand and waves. The reflection's smile grows wider. The water in the pool begins to tremble, though there is no wind at all...

pieces.label: Throw a Pebble In
pieces.text: (Looker) picks up a pebble and, before (looker.he/she) can think better of it, tosses it straight at the smiling face. Plop...

pieces.label: Call Someone Over
pieces.text: Call Someone Over.

pieces.label: Walk Away Without Looking Back
pieces.text: Walk Away Without Looking Back.

The reflection climbs out, dripping, with (looker)'s face and hair and knobbly knees, but not (looker)'s opinions. "Is that how you wear your hair? On purpose?" It takes the name (made1) and all the jobs (looker) never liked.
The reflection gives a slow, kind little wave and sinks back into the dark of the pool. (Looker) walks home feeling politely turned down by (looker.himself/herself).
The ripples break the face into a hundred wobbling pieces, and a small striped fish swims out and looks at (looker) with deep reproach. Just a pool after all.
The pebble hits the reflection right on the nose. It flinches, and the pool goes dark and cold. (Looker) never swims near the tide pools again.
By the time a friend comes running, only one face looks up from the pool. The friend thinks (looker) has had too much sun.
(Looker) walks away fast, and that night finds wet footprints on the floor of (looker.his/her) hut, leading in and back out.
A single hermit crab is the only one watching.
The tide pool is perfectly round, as if someone measured it.
The air smells of salt and sun-dried seaweed.
The reflection keeps waving, friendly and patient.

pieces.label: The Very Long Nap
pieces.text: On the hottest afternoon of the year, (sleeper) lies down "for five minutes" in the cool shade of a strange tree with sky-blue leaves, and wakes with an aching back, creaking knees and little white flowers rooted in (sleeper.his/her) hair.

pieces.label: Hurry Home
pieces.text: (Sleeper) scrambles up, groaning, brushing at the flowers, and hobbles towards the village as fast as (sleeper.his/her) complaining knees will go. Behind (sleeper.him/her), the blue leaves rustle, though there is no wind...

pieces.label: Lie Back Down
pieces.text: (Sleeper) is very comfortable, and very tired, and the shade is very cool. (sleeper.He/She) remembers something the elders once said about blue trees, though not quite what. (sleeper.He/She) closes (sleeper.his/her) eyes to think about it...

pieces.label: Pull the Flowers Out
pieces.text: Pull the Flowers Out.

pieces.label: Ask the Tree to Give Them Back
pieces.text: Ask the Tree to Give Them Back.
Only one night has passed, but the tree's roots drank twenty years and pushed them out as flowers. "At least I'm well rested," says (sleeper). "Somebody else can do the afternoon work."
The flowers drop out on the path home and wither, leaving a streak of grey and a few new lines. "You look distinguished," everyone says, very kindly.

(Sleeper) remembers: whoever eats the blue tree's flowers gets back what it drank. They taste like chewing a sandal, but (sleeper.he/she) wakes with (sleeper.his/her) own knees, back and luscious hair. Nobody believes a word of it.
The second nap is longer, the roots drink more, and (sleeper) wakes an elder with a white crown of flowers. "Well. That's that, then." Two strong young people carry (sleeper.him/her) home for dinner.
(Sleeper) pleads with the tree. A single blue leaf drops onto (sleeper.his/her) chest, and the years seep back in with the evening dew.
Each flower comes out with a sting like a plucked hair, and a year comes back with each one, all but a handful.
The cicadas are whirring like a hundred tiny saws.
Even the chickens have given up and lain down in the dust.
The blue leaves rustle, though there is no wind.
A child points and asks if a visitor has come.

pieces.label: Two Hammocks, One Storm
pieces.text: (Sleeper1) and (sleeper2) string their hammocks between the same two palms on the beach on a stormy summer night, lightning strikes the sand between them at midnight, and in the morning each wakes up in the other's body.

pieces.label: Try to Switch Back
pieces.text: The healers have never heard of anything like it. The elders say lightning took them, so lightning must give them back. That evening (sleeper1) and (sleeper2) sit back to back on the sand between the two palms, under a sky that is, very annoyingly, clear...

pieces.label: Make the Best of It
pieces.text: "Well," says (sleeper2), in (sleeper1)'s voice. "We can't go anywhere like this. Could be worse. I've always wondered what you actually do all day." (Sleeper1) looks down at (sleeper2)'s hands, and has to admit (sleeper1.he/she) has wondered the same...

pieces.label: Go to the Healers
pieces.text: Go to the Healers.

pieces.label: Wait for the Next Storm
pieces.text: Wait for the Next Storm.
On the third night the lightning strikes almost exactly where it struck before, and they wake in their own bodies. "Your knees are terrible." "Your stomach is worse. What do you even eat?"
The lightning never strikes the beach again, and they learn to live each other's lives. By the end of the season they argue less than they used to, which their families find very strange.

They try each other's jobs, with a great deal of shouting for advice. "Which end of this do I hold?" "The END THAT ISN'T SHARP!" They never swap back, and end up better at each other's work than their own.
The healers make them drink something thick, grey and bubbling that tastes like a swamp. It works, and neither of them will go near the healers' hut again unless they're carried.
The healers try everything and nothing works. They send the two of them home with a pat on the shoulder each, the wrong shoulder.
A storm comes, but the bolt strikes the palm instead, and both hammocks catch fire. They tumble out swapped back, singed and shaking.
The storm smells of hot stone and green rain.
The palms bend and whip like dancers who have had too much to drink.
The lightning strikes with a crack that shakes every hut on the island.
(Sleeper2) wakes up and screams in (sleeper1)'s voice.

pieces.label: The Wind That Took a Name
pieces.text: A warm, cinnamon-scented wind blows through the village from no direction in particular, snatches (nameless)'s good morning, name and all, into a seed pod rolling down the path, and nobody can remember what (nameless.he/she) is called.

pieces.label: Chase the Wind
pieces.text: (Nameless) takes off after the seed pod, barefoot, past the huts, through the gardens, scattering chickens in every direction. The pod bounces ahead along the path towards the cliffs, never quite close enough to grab...

pieces.label: Pick a New One
pieces.text: "Well, there's no use running after the wind," says one of the elders. "Nobody's ever caught it yet. Somebody fetch the drum." In no time at all, half the village has gathered around (nameless) in a ring...

pieces.label: Ask the Elders
pieces.text: Ask the Elders.

pieces.label: Wait for the Wind to Turn
pieces.text: Wait for the Wind to Turn.

At the cliff edge the wind runs out of island and drops everything it took. (Nameless) cracks open the seed pod and hears (nameless.his/her) own name whispered inside. (nameless.He/She) also returns the hat.
The wind swings the pod out to sea. No name the villagers try is right, and none of them sticks, so (nameless) is left as "?". On windy days (nameless.he/she) stands at the cliff edge and listens.
A drum, a ring of villagers and a hundred shouted suggestions, some lovely, some rude, one the name of a fish. The one that sticks is (renamed).
Every time the village agrees on a name, the cinnamon wind gusts back and snatches that one too, until (nameless) is left with none at all: "?".
The elders say a name taken by the wind comes back with the evening breeze. It does, in through the doorway, at supper.
(Nameless) waits a day, and a different name blows in on the turning wind. Nobody is sure whose it was before.
All the chickens turn to face the same way, which chickens never do.
The wind smells faintly of cinnamon bark.
A feather, somebody's hat and a long tangle of string go bowling down the path.
The neighbour scratches their head. Neither can they.

pieces.label: The Basket on the Beach
pieces.text: At a pink, flat dawn, (finder) comes down to check the fish traps and nearly steps on a woven basket tangled in the seaweed, with a baby fast asleep inside, and no boat, no footprints and no note anywhere.

pieces.label: Take the Baby Home
pieces.text: (Finder) scoops up the basket, blanket and all, and hurries back to the village with the baby tucked against (finder.his/her) chest. By the time (finder.he/she) reaches the huts, there is a small crowd following (finder.him/her), and everyone has an opinion about what should be done...

pieces.label: Wait for Its Parents
pieces.text: Someone, somewhere, must be missing this baby. (Finder) sits down on the warm sand beside the basket, facing the sea, and settles in to wait. The sun climbs. The gulls lose interest. The baby wakes, and is hungry, and says so...

pieces.label: Search the Coast
pieces.text: Search the Coast.

pieces.label: Ask the Elders
pieces.text: Ask the Elders.
Plenty of people offer to take the baby. "I found the basket," says (finder), holding on tight, "so I'm the one who gets up at night." And (finder.he/she) does, every night.

(Friend) holds out (friend.his/her) arms, and the baby goes into them as if it had been waiting for exactly that pair. By evening the whole village has brought blankets, a carved rattle and advice nobody asked for.
Nobody comes. By evening the baby has a name, a favourite song about a turtle, and a village. Every year, on the same morning, someone leaves a flower at the tideline.
Around noon a small boat skids in, rowed by a frantic young couple. The basket slipped off the side in last night's swell. They hug the baby, then (finder), then the baby again. They decide to stay.
Around the point, (finder) finds the couple's wrecked canoe and the two of them clinging to a rock, cold and frightened. (finder.He/She) brings all three home.
The elders say the sea sometimes gives back what it takes. Nobody ever claims the baby, and the whole village raises (finder.him/her).
The sea is very calm and very quiet, as if it has done nothing and would rather not discuss it.
The baby yawns, opens one eye, looks at (finder) and goes back to sleep.
Gulls are squabbling over something along the tideline.
The sea is pink and flat as a plate.

pieces.label: The Granary Gets Wet
pieces.text: The food store roof has leaked for weeks, from one drip to a large mushy mess on the wall that everyone noticed and everyone thought someone had reported. Nobody did. After a night of the hardest rain all year, the store is ankle-deep in water.

pieces.label: Dry What's Left
pieces.text: The whole village forms a chain, passing dripping baskets hand to hand out of the store and into the open air. Every flat rock, every roof and every mat is covered with soggy food spread out in hopes the sun will dry it out...

pieces.label: Blame Someone
pieces.text: "Who was supposed to fix it?" someone asks, and the whole village turns to look at someone else. Within moments everyone is pointing, and everyone is pointing at a different person...

pieces.label: Fix the Roof First
pieces.text: Fix the Roof First.

pieces.label: Eat the Soggy Food Now
pieces.text: Eat the Soggy Food Now.
The sun takes its time, and by evening most of the food is just a smell, then a pile, then the pigs' problem. The builders find eleven holes. "You should have said something when there was one."
The clouds tear open and the sun blazes down like it's trying to make up for last night. Almost everything dries, and somebody patches over the mushy parts.
The builders say nobody told them. The farmers say they told the builders, sort of, once. While they argue, a great flock of birds eats the soaked baskets left outside the door.
Everyone blames everyone, then everyone feels bad, because they all knew about the mess. By evening the roof is mended and it has all ended with a picnic of the food that wouldn't keep anyway.
The roof is mended in an hour, but by the time anyone turns to the baskets, they've gone sour.
The village eats soggy food for three days straight. Nobody is happy, but very little is wasted.
The stain on the inside wall has turned into a large mushy mess.
The store is ankle-deep in water and the baskets are sagging.
The village forms a chain, passing dripping baskets hand to hand.
By noon the village smells like a wet dog that has rolled in fruit.

pieces.label: The Coconut Bonanza
pieces.text: Every palm on the island has decided, all at once, that this is the year to sprout coconuts, and ripe, tasty coconuts fall day and night, thudding into the sand, bouncing off roofs and rolling into the cooking pots.

pieces.label: Gather Them All
pieces.text: The village puts down every other job and turns out with baskets. Children race each other to the fallen nuts, adults haul full baskets on their shoulders, and the elders sit in the open sand well away from the trees, shouting directions...

pieces.label: Throw a Coconut Festival
pieces.text: "We'll never eat all these anyway," someone says, "so let's not try. Let's celebrate!" The idea catches like fire in dry grass. Within an hour there are cooking fires lit all over the village and the first drums are going...

pieces.label: Trade the Extras Away
pieces.text: Trade the Extras Away.

pieces.label: Leave Them to Sprout
pieces.text: Leave Them to Sprout.
Every basket, pot, bowl and hat in the village is filled, and then a great pyramid of coconuts that the children climb and refuse to come down from.
(Unlucky) stops under a palm to tie a sandal and forgets to look up. A loud, hollow thunk, a bump the size of a hen's egg, and two of everything, including two healers.
Coconut milk, coconut bread, coconut-rolling races, and a band of coconut-shell drummers who are terrible and loud and wonderful. The leftovers alone fill the stores.
The festival goes on for three days, and half the coconuts are eaten on the spot by people lying in the sand with their eyes closed. Nobody minds.
Passing canoes trade carved tools and strange seeds for boatloads of coconuts.
The sprouted nuts become a young grove that feeds the village for years to come.
The chickens have learned to run in zigzags.
The whole village smells of split husks and sweet milk.
Babies have stopped flinching at the thuds.
The elders sit in the open sand well away from the trees, shouting directions.

pieces.label: The Elder Who Forgot to Get Old
pieces.text: (Elder), the elder whose sitting stone by the fire is worn smooth in exactly (elder.his/her) shape, wakes up able to touch (elder.his/her) toes, with smooth hands and full, luscious hair, because (grandchild) tried out a spell far too old and strong for a youngster.

pieces.label: Enjoy It
pieces.text: (Elder) does not waste a moment wondering. (elder.He/She) walks straight out of (elder.his/her) hut, past the sitting stone, past (elder.his/her) astonished neighbours, and up to the tallest climbing tree in the village...

pieces.label: Ask the Healers
pieces.text: (Elder) walks, very quickly and with no pain at all, to the healers' hut. "Something has happened to me," (elder.he/she) says, "and I'd like to know if it's going to un-happen." The healers stare at (elder.him/her) for a long time...

pieces.label: Keep It a Secret
pieces.text: Keep It a Secret.

pieces.label: Go Back to Bed
pieces.text: Go Back to Bed.
(Elder) climbs the tallest tree in the village for the first time in forty years. The magic holds, and the children start using the empty sitting stone to crack nuts.
The healers poke and prod and learn a great deal about how bodies change with age, and the magic settles halfway. "Fifty," says (elder). "I'll take it."
The healers admit they have no idea what to do, so, wisely, they do nothing. (Elder) stays forty and finds forty-year-old knees just as tired by evening.
(Elder) tries to hide it under a big hat and a pretend limp. Nobody is fooled for a moment, but the spell holds anyway.
(Elder) decides it's a dream and goes back to sleep. (elder.He/She) wakes up old, and (grandchild) never dares to try that spell again.
The sitting stone by the fire is worn smooth in exactly (elder.his/her) shape.
(Elder) touches (elder.his/her) toes. There is no creak.
(grandchild) clutches a little bundle of feathers and crushed herbs.
"Well," says (elder). "That's odd. How'd I get so limber?"

pieces.label: The Bee Hat
pieces.text: Golden drips run down a fallen log by the stream where a wild hive hums, and (subject), disguised in a leaf hat so big it comes down past (subject.his/her) shoulders, reaches in. The bees pour out and start circling the hat, closer with every turn.

pieces.label: Move Very Slowly
pieces.text: (Subject) freezes. Then, slowly, so slowly it hurts, (subject.he/she) starts drawing (subject.his/her) hand out of the log, honeycomb and all. The humming gets louder. A bee lands on (subject.his/her) nose and walks across it, considering (subject.him/her) with its stinger...

pieces.label: Forget It and Run
pieces.text: No honey is worth some nasty stings. (Subject) flings the hat at the bees and runs for (subject.his/her) life, crashing through the bushes towards the stream with a roaring golden cloud right behind (subject.him/her)...

pieces.label: Smoke Them Out
pieces.text: Smoke Them Out.

pieces.label: Hum to the Bees
pieces.text: Hum to the Bees.

The bees decide (subject) is an unusually tall bush, and a not very interesting one. (subject.He/She) comes home with a full pot of honey and combs, and the children call (subject.him/her) "the walking bee-bush."
The leaves of the hat tickle (subject.his/her) nose. "AHCHOO!" Every bee takes it personally, and the healers stop counting stingers at thirty.
(Subject) jumps in the river and holds (subject.his/her) breath. When (subject.he/she) comes up, the bees are stinging the hat on the bank instead. The hat is never recovered.
(Subject) trips headfirst into a patch of bushes covered in ripe wild berries. It's not honey, but it's something, and (subject.he/she) comes home stained purple.
A smoky fire of green leaves makes the bees drowsy, and (subject) takes a big slab of comb.
(Subject) hums, and the bees hum back, and settle all over (subject.his/her) arms without stinging. (subject.He/She) has a way with bees after that.
The air around the log hums like a whispered song.
A bee lands on (subject)'s nose and considers (subject.him/her) with its stinger.
The humming gets louder.
The hat comes down past (subject.his/her) shoulders.

pieces.label: The Second (Name)
pieces.text: As the fireflies come out, (original) walks back from the jungle with a basket of mushrooms and goes to wash. Ten minutes later another (original) walks in with the same basket, the same broken handle and the same scratch on the same elbow, and both of them turn to (cook): "Who are YOU?"

pieces.label: Ask Them Questions Only (Name) Would Know
pieces.text: (Original)'s oldest friend is fetched, and sits both of them down on opposite sides of the fire. "Right," the friend says, cracking (original.his/her) knuckles. "What did you hide under my mat when we were nine?" Both of them answer at the same time, and both of them go red...

pieces.label: Let Them Sort It Out
pieces.text: "Well, I'm not getting in the middle of that," says (cook), the head cook, and goes back to stirring. The rest of the village quietly drifts away and leaves the two of them alone by the fire, staring at each other...

pieces.label: Call the Elders
pieces.text: Call the Elders.

pieces.label: Feed Them Both
pieces.text: Feed Them Both.

Both of them get every answer right, and blush at the same story with the same hand. "You're both (original)," says the oldest friend. The second one chooses the name (made1) "so it's less confusing." It is not less confusing.
"What's your favourite food?" "Mashed taro," says (original). "Moonlight," says the other, and comes apart into a little cloud of grey moths. The second basket of mushrooms is delicious.
"Well, I'm not getting in the middle of that," says (cook). The two of them talk by the fire all night, and by morning they are best friends and one of them is (made1).
They argue long into the night until the elders send them both to bed in the same hut. In the morning there is only one (original), who asks, "What other one?"
(cook) gives them three bowls each. Only one of them is still there when the bowls are cleared, and nobody saw the other leave.
The elders say the jungle sometimes sends back an echo. They name the echo (made1) and give it a hut.
The fireflies are just coming out and the cooking pots are bubbling.
The cooks drop their spoons and do a double-take.
Same basket, same broken handle, same scratch on the same elbow.
"Who are YOU?" they both say, at once.

pieces.label: The Biggest Fish in the Bay
pieces.text: (Fisher) paddles out alone, with a brand new spear and a very small canoe, after the giant fish of the bay that the old fishers say once swallowed a person, and something very large and very slow rolls up beside (fisher.him/her), its lightning scar gleaming.

pieces.label: Throw the Spear
pieces.text: (Fisher) stands up in the rocking canoe, braces (fisher.his/her) feet, and draws back the spear. (fisher.His/her) heart is pounding so hard (fisher.he/she) can hear it. The great fish turns one huge, round eye up towards (fisher.him/her), as if it knows exactly what (fisher.he/she) is about to do...

pieces.label: Let It Go
pieces.text: (Fisher) holds the spear for a long, long time. The great fish just lies there in the dark water, breathing, watching (fisher.him/her) with its old round eye. Very slowly, (fisher) lowers the spear...

pieces.label: Follow It Out
pieces.text: Follow It Out.

pieces.label: Paddle Home for Help
pieces.text: Paddle Home for Help.

(Fisher) strikes true. The fish drags (fisher.him/her) halfway round the bay while the village screams advice from the shore, and at sunset (fisher.he/she) comes home with enough fish for a week. "Well done," says the oldest fisher.
The spear glances off the scar as if it were rock. The fish's tail lifts the canoe clean out of the water and brings it down on top of (fisher). (fisher.His/her) back is never quite right again.
(Fisher) lowers the spear and lets the old fish go. "It has earned its old age." The oldest fisher nods and gives (fisher.him/her) the best seat by the fire.
(Fisher) sits too long watching it go, and the storm comes up faster than anyone can remember. (Fisher)'s half-eaten body washes up with the broken canoe, and is laid to rest on the headland.
The fish leads (fisher) to a cove so full of smaller fish that the water boils with them.
Five canoes come back with (fisher), and together they bring the old fish in, but most of the meat spoils before it's smoked.
As long as two canoes, older than anyone alive, the old fishers say.
Its teeth could crack a boulder.
The great fish turns one huge, round eye up towards (fisher).
Out in the middle of the bay, the water goes dark and still.

pieces.label: The Researchers' Bonfire
pieces.text: On a cold night in the research hut, (researcher) has been drying some priceless old scrolls by the hearth, and they have become maybe a bit too dry: a fat orange spark lands on the pile and the whole pile catches fire. (Researcher) has only a few seconds to act.

pieces.label: Attempt to Salvage the Scrolls
pieces.text: (Researcher) doesn't think. (researcher.He/She) tears off (researcher.his/her) cloak and throws (researcher.himself/herself) at the flames, beating at them with both hands while the other researchers shout and scramble for water...

pieces.label: It Is Too Late
pieces.text: (Researcher) drags the other researchers outside, away from the smoke. "Let it burn," (researcher.he/she) says, through gritted teeth. "It's too late now. Luckily I've read every one of those scrolls a hundred times. I can rewrite them." (researcher.He/She) sits down on a log, picks up a fresh sheet of bark, and starts to write...

pieces.label: Throw Water on Everything
pieces.text: Throw Water on Everything.

pieces.label: Run for Help
pieces.text: Run for Help.

(Researcher) beats out the flames with (researcher.his/her) own cloak and drags the oldest, most important scrolls out first. Half the rest are ash, and the healers call (researcher.him/her) very brave and very stupid, in that order.
The fire is too fast and too hungry. Every scroll burns, and the grey flakes drift up the chimney like snow. Nobody blames (researcher), out loud, but inside they are seething.
"It's too late now. I can rewrite them." (Researcher) writes all night and all the next day, and finds three mistakes in the old scrolls that nobody ever noticed.
What (researcher) remembers best is the margins: a doodle of a grumpy fish, somebody's goat, a very good nimbus cloud. The researchers pin the grumpy fish on the wall.
The fire goes out at once. So does the ink. Every scroll is a soggy grey smear.
By the time help comes running, (researcher) has already stamped it out, and only the top few scrolls are lost.
The research hut smells of smoke and old ink.
Everyone has crowded close to the hearth against the cold.
A fat orange spark sits on the pile, glowing.
The blaze is burning fast.

pieces.label: The Fog Walker
pieces.text: On the third night of a thick sea fog, with huts vanishing ten steps away, (listener) lies awake and hears someone singing far off in the white mist, a tune (listener.he/she) almost remembers from when (listener.he/she) was very small.

pieces.label: Follow the Song
pieces.text: (Listener) steps out into the fog. It closes behind (listener.him/her) like a curtain. (listener.He/She) walks towards the singing, one hand out in front, and the singing moves too, always a little ahead, never any closer...

pieces.label: Stay Inside and Hum Along
pieces.text: (Listener) stays in the doorway, one hand on the post. Something about the fog feels like a held breath. But (listener.he/she) can't stop listening to the song, so quietly, very quietly, (listener.he/she) begins to hum along...

pieces.label: Wake Someone Up
pieces.text: Wake Someone Up.

pieces.label: Call Out to the Singer
pieces.text: Call Out to the Singer.

(Listener) walks and walks, and never comes back. (listener.His/her) footprints stop in the middle of an open field, as if (listener.he/she) simply flew up into the air. On misty nights there are two voices singing.
The song stops in a sheltered grove (listener) has never seen, with branches so heavy with fruit they touch the ground. Nobody can ever find it again.
(Listener) wakes knowing all the words: a song about the sea coming home. By the end of the week the whole village is singing it.
The singing stops the moment (listener) hums, as if someone has been caught out. (listener.He/She) is grumpy with everybody for a week.
By the time a sleepy neighbour comes to the door, there's nothing to hear. The neighbour is not pleased.
The two of them listen together until dawn, and the next morning both of them can play it on the flute.
Huts vanish ten steps away. Voices come from nowhere.
Everyone's hair is beaded with tiny condensation drops.
The fires hiss and smoke and won't burn properly.
The singing moves too, always a little ahead, never any closer.

pieces.label: The Visitor with the Enormous Hat
pieces.text: A friendly traveller arrives by canoe in the biggest hat anyone has ever seen, with feathers, shells, small living ferns and something on the brim that might be a nest, and at dawn (host) walks (host.him/her) down to the beach, curious about this peculiar traveller.

pieces.label: Trade Something for the Hat
pieces.text: "I'll give you anything for that hat," (host) blurts out, before (host.he/she) can stop (host.himself/herself). The traveller straightens up slowly, one hand on the brim, and gives (host) a long, measuring look...

pieces.label: Ask Where (He/She) Is Going
pieces.text: "Where are you going, anyway?" asks (host). The traveller stops, the canoe halfway into the water, and looks out at the horizon for a long moment, as if (host.he/she) has never really thought about it...

pieces.label: Ask (Him/Her) to Stay
pieces.text: Ask (host.Him/Her) to Stay.

pieces.label: Pack (Him/Her) Some Food
pieces.text: Pack (host.Him/Her) Some Food.
"Your best basket." The hat is wonderful, enormous and surprisingly heavy, and the nest is occupied by a very small, very cross bird, which (host) names "Sweetie".
"Oh no. I can't part with this." Instead the traveller hands over clever little tools of bone and shell, and a thing with a spiral in it that the researchers take a week to work out.
"Somewhere else," says the traveller, and drops a heavy bag of strange dried food at (host)'s feet. "For the road you aren't taking."
"I've been to a great many somewhere elses." The traveller pulls the canoe back up the sand and stays, tipping (host.his/her) hat to (host).
The traveller laughs, says no, and paddles off. The hat bobs on the horizon for a very long time.
The traveller accepts the food and gives back a fistful of seeds "that grow anywhere." They do.
Small living ferns grow out of the top of the hat.
Something in the nest cheeps.
The children run along the shore beside the canoe, just to stare.
Something in the hat waves goodbye on its own.

pieces.label: The Fertility Stone
pieces.text: At the edge of the jungle stands an old carved stone, half covered in moss, with lichen grown into a little green smile; the elders say anyone who leaves a flower on it will be blessed with a baby. (Carrier) has always called it nonsense, and this morning finds a fresh red flower on it while (friend) looks very hard at a tree and whistles.

pieces.label: Laugh It Off
pieces.text: (Carrier) laughs out loud. "You didn't!" (Friend) goes pink and says (friend.he/she) was just passing, and the flower just happened to be in (friend.his/her) hand. (Carrier) laughs all the way home, and teases (friend) about it for days...

pieces.label: Leave a Flower Too
pieces.text: (Carrier) rolls (carrier.his/her) eyes. Then, without a word, (carrier.he/she) picks a white flower from the bush beside the path and sets it on the stone, right beside (friend)'s red one. "Just so it's fair," (carrier.he/she) says. The mossy face seems to smile a little wider...

pieces.label: Sit with the Stone a While
pieces.text: Sit with the Stone a While.

pieces.label: Pretend Not to Notice
pieces.text: Pretend Not to Notice.

"It's just a stone," (carrier) says, every time it comes up. A few weeks later the healers take one look at (carrier.him/her) and smile, and (carrier) gives the mossy smile a little pat when nobody is watching.
It really is just a stone, this time at least. (Carrier) catches (friend) slipping off with another flower, and walks along too, and they sit in the green shade without saying anything.

Two flowers seem to do the trick, and then some. The healers hear {#babies:one strong heartbeat|two heartbeats|two heartbeats, maybe even three}. (Friend) has to sit down, and the next morning the stone is buried in flowers.
The stone is unmoved, but the slow walk home hand in hand is lovely, and each of them starts helping with the other's favourite job, and comes to like it.
They sit with the stone until dusk, and a soft rain starts that smells of flowers. Weeks later, (carrier) is pregnant.
Lichen has grown into a little green smile across the front of it.
There are always flowers on it, fresh and wilted, in every colour.
(Friend) is looking very hard at a nearby tree and whistling.
The mossy face seems to smile a little wider.

pieces.label: The Name Nobody Can Say
pieces.text: A gracious visiting elder from very far away, with a carved walking stick taller than (named.him/her) and a basket of strange red nuts, has learned everyone's name except (named)'s, and has tried it eleven times while the children roll in the dust.

pieces.label: Teach (Him/Her) to Say It
pieces.text: (Named) sits down beside the visitor and says (named.his/her) name very slowly, one sound at a time, while the visitor watches (named.his/her) mouth with great concentration and repeats each syllable under (named.his/her) breath...

pieces.label: Answer to Whatever (He/She) Says
pieces.text: "Don't worry about it," (named) says kindly. "Call me whatever you like. I'll know you mean me." The visitor looks enormously relieved, and from then on calls (named.him/her) something completely different every time...

pieces.label: Write It Down
pieces.text: Write It Down.

pieces.label: Offer a Nickname
pieces.text: Offer a Nickname.
(Named) says it one syllable at a time, and on the twelfth try the visitor gets it perfectly. The children cheer loudest, and (named) feels unexpectedly proud of (named.his/her) own name.
The twelfth try is wrong in a brand new way, like water running over stones, and (named) likes it much better than (named.his/her) own. From then on (named.he/she) is (renamed).
One of the visitor's versions catches on, first with the children, then their parents, then (named). The visitor waves goodbye shouting the new name, perfectly.

Laughing at the twentieth try, (named) topples off the log and cracks (named.his/her) head on the visitor's walking stick. When (named.he/she) comes round, (named.his/her) own name is simply gone, and (named.he/she) is "?" from then on.
The visitor can't read the marks either, and holds the bark upside down, but says the name perfectly by guessing.
The ninth try sounds like a sneeze. The tenth sounds like a goat.
On the eleventh, the visitor's ears go red.
A basket of strange red nuts is passed around.
The carved walking stick is taller than its owner.

pieces.label: The Pig Who Knew Better
pieces.text: (Farmer) has fought soil baked as hard as a rock for an hour, while a big mud-coloured pig watches from the shade with deep and patient pity, until the pig shoves (farmer.him/her) aside, roots up the whole row in three snorts and lies down where (farmer) was standing.

pieces.label: Do It the Pig's Way
pieces.text: (Farmer) looks at the pig. The pig does not look at (farmer). With great dignity, (farmer) kneels down, digs (farmer.his/her) fingers into the loose soil the way the pig's snout went in, and plants the seeds...

pieces.label: Shoo the Pig
pieces.text: "Thank you," says (farmer), stiffly, "but I know what I'm doing." (farmer.He/She) flaps (farmer.his/her) arms. The pig opens one eye, looks at (farmer.him/her) for a long moment, then gets up and walks off with its nose in the air...

pieces.label: Thank the Pig
pieces.text: Thank the Pig.

pieces.label: Bribe the Pig to Do Another Row
pieces.text: Bribe the Pig to Do Another Row.
The seeds come up in four days, faster and greener than any in the village. (Farmer) calls it "a new method," and never, ever admits where (farmer.he/she) learned it.
(Farmer) follows the pig all season, planting where it digs. It is very undignified, but by harvest (farmer.he/she) is the best farmer in the village, and leaves the best scraps under a certain bush.
The seeds don't come up. Not one. Across the field the pig watches, and (farmer) is absolutely certain it knew. (farmer.He/She) comes to dread the fields.
Deeply offended, the pig walks straight into the vegetable store and eats a basket of the best roots, looking at (farmer) the entire time. It's a very big pig.
The pig accepts a bribe of fruit and roots up the whole field. It is a very good field.
The soil is baked as hard as a rock.
The pig chews something, with an expression of deep and patient pity.
(Farmer) has broken one digging stick and is working on a second.
The pig opens one eye.

pieces.label: The Glowing Berries
pieces.text: At dusk, on the way home from the far gardens, (finder) finds a low bush covered in berries that glow softly from the inside, like coals in a fire that's nearly out, and smell of honey and rain. Nobody knows if they're safe.

pieces.label: Eat One
pieces.text: (Finder) picks the biggest, brightest berry. It's warm in (finder.his/her) fingers. (finder.He/She) sniffs it, shrugs, and pops it into (finder.his/her) mouth. It bursts on (finder.his/her) tongue like a little star...

pieces.label: Take Some to the Healers
pieces.text: (Finder) wraps a few clusters carefully in a leaf, trying not to squash them, and carries them home like something precious. The healers unwrap them by the fire and all lean in at once, faces lit green-gold...

pieces.label: Feed One to a Pig First
pieces.text: Feed One to a Pig First.

pieces.label: Leave Them for the Moths
pieces.text: Leave Them for the Moths.

It bursts on (finder.his/her) tongue like a little star. For two days (finder) glows softly in the dark and feels fantastic, followed at night by a long giggling line of children and a few very determined moths.
By midnight (finder) is burning with fever and seeing colours that don't have names, crawling on the roof, singing. A week in the healers' hut, and a drawing of the bush with a big cross through it.
Three days of boiling, drying and crushing give a thick golden paste that eases stiff joints better than anything. The healers make sure everybody knows (finder) found it.

"Just a small taste. For science." (Healer) ends up talking to the roof beams with a roaring fever, and (finder) nurses (finder.him/her) for a week and learns more healing than (finder.he/she) ever expected.
The pig eats one, glows all night, and seems perfectly happy. (Finder) decides that's proof enough and gathers a basketful.
The moths settle on the bush until it's covered in soft wings, and the glow goes out. Nobody can find the bush again.
The berries hang in heavy clusters like tiny paper lanterns.
Moths circle them in slow, dizzy loops.
They smell sweet and sharp, a little like honey, a little like rain.
The healers' faces are lit green-gold.

pieces.label: The Grumpy Morning
pieces.text: Elder (grump) has woken up on the wrong side of the mat. The fire smoked, the water was warm, the birds are too loud, and now (grump.he/she) is standing in the middle of the path with (grump.his/her) arms folded, telling everyone what (grump.he/she) thinks of birds, water, fires, whistling and young people today. "You whippersnappers nowadays..."

pieces.label: Leave (Him/Her) Alone
pieces.text: The village decides that some storms are best waited out. Everyone keeps their heads down, their whistling to themselves, and a good distance between them and (grump), and goes about their day...

pieces.label: Bring (Him/Her) Breakfast
pieces.text: One brave young villager fills a bowl with warm mash, adds a spoonful of honey on top, and walks straight up to (grump) with it, holding it out at arm's length like someone offering fruit to a crocodile...

pieces.label: Stop the Whistling
pieces.text: Stop the Whistling.

pieces.label: Send the Children to Cheer (Him/Her) Up
pieces.text: Send the Children to Cheer (grump.Him/Her) Up.

By evening (grump) has grumbled (grump.himself/herself) right out, and is back in (grump.his/her) usual seat by the fire, telling the children the story about the turtle who wanted to fly. Nobody mentions the morning.
The grumpiness settles in, like damp in a wall. (Grump) decides the noisiest thing in the village is the children, and waves them off like flies from then on.

(Grump) glares at the bowl of warm mash with honey on top. Then (grump.he/she) takes a spoonful, and stops glaring, and declares it the best breakfast of (grump.his/her) entire life. An old grudge melts away too.
"Too warm. And too sweet. And too lumpy." (Grump) complains all the way through the bowl, says "More," and complains through the second and the third.
The whistler is found, and it turns out to be a bird. (Grump) argues with the bird for an hour and feels much better.
The children bring (grump) a crown of flowers, and (grump.he/she) can't stay cross while wearing it.
Even the fat little lizard in (grump.his/her) roof thatch is keeping well out of the way.
People are taking the long way round to the well.
The same three whistled notes, over and over.
A bowl held out at arm's length, like fruit offered to a crocodile.

pieces.label: The Spring of Small Years
pieces.text: Hot and sore from cutting wood in the hills, (bather) wades into a kingfisher-blue spring that the elders say "gives back what you spent," and the years start to wash off (bather.his/her) skin like grey silt, until (bather.his/her) clothes are far too big.

pieces.label: Run Home
pieces.text: (Bather) grabs (bather.his/her) things, holds (bather.his/her) trousers up with one hand, and pelts down the hill towards the village as fast as (bather.his/her) new, springy legs will carry (bather.him/her)...

pieces.label: Climb Back In
pieces.text: (Bather) looks down at (bather.his/her) smooth hands, then back at the cool blue water. If one dip did all this, what could another do? (bather.He/She) takes a deep breath and wades back in, all the way up to (bather.his/her) chin...

pieces.label: Bottle Some Water
pieces.text: Bottle Some Water.

pieces.label: Ask the Elders What It Means
pieces.text: Ask the Elders What It Means.
(Bather) bursts into the village all elbows and knees, voice cracking halfway through "HELP." Sixteen again, and it's much harder the second time, because now (bather.he/she) knows how it ends.
Just eighteen, fresh-faced and bright-eyed. Then at dinner (bather.he/she) remembers the awkwardness, the bad decisions, the haircut. "This time I'll do it properly."

The second dip washes off great clouds of silt, and (bather) climbs out a child of about ten, with an adult's memories and a child's enormous appetite. "The spring," say the elders, in the same tired voice.
This time the water stays perfectly clear. The few years from the first dip have already drifted away downstream, and (bather) decides five years younger is plenty.
The water in the gourd turns to plain water by the bottom of the hill. The years stay off, though.
The elders only say "it gives back what you spent," and that's no help at all. (Bather) stays as the spring made (bather.him/her): twenty, and very confused.
The water is the blue of a kingfisher's wing.
Nothing grows on its banks but soft white moss.
The years come off like grey silt, clouding the water in soft swirls.
(Bather) holds (bather.his/her) trousers up with one hand.

pieces.label: The Echo Cave
pieces.text: (Shouter) shouts (shouter.his/her) name into the echo cave, the one the elders say has heard every voice on the island. The cave shouts it back, fainter each time, and then footsteps crunch on the gravel and someone wearing (shouter)'s face walks into the light.

pieces.label: Shout Hello
pieces.text: (Shouter)'s knees are shaking, but (shouter.he/she) stands (shouter.his/her) ground. "Hello?" (shouter.he/she) calls out. The figure in the cave mouth stops. It tilts its head, exactly the way (shouter) does when (shouter.he/she) is thinking...

pieces.label: Run
pieces.text: (Shouter) doesn't wait to find out. (shouter.He/She) turns and runs, as fast as (shouter.he/she) can, not looking back, with the sound of the cave's breathing all around (shouter.him/her)...

pieces.label: Shout Someone Else's Name
pieces.text: Shout Someone Else's Name.

pieces.label: Throw a Stone into the Dark
pieces.text: Throw a Stone into the Dark.
"Hello," says the stranger, in (shouter)'s own voice, then, deeper and warmer: "Sorry. I'm (made1)." It loves the jobs (shouter) hates, and has strong opinions about how to cook beans.
"Hello. Hello. Hello." Each one quieter, like an echo, until the light shines straight through the figure and it's gone. (Shouter) only ever shouts other people's names at the cave after that.

An hour after (shouter) hides in (shouter.his/her) hut, the stranger walks in, out of breath. "You run fast. Is there any dinner?" It decides to be called (made1), and nobody can think of a reason to send it away.
In (shouter.his/her) panic (shouter) runs the wrong way, deeper into the cave and straight into the wall. (shouter.He/She) is never quite sure afterwards whether (shouter.he/she) saw anything at all.
(Shouter) shouts a friend's name, and the friend's voice answers from inside, though the friend is back in the village. (Shouter) runs.
The stone clatters away, and the figure is gone. Something in the dark goes "Ow."
The cave mouth breathes out cool air that smells of wet stone and old bats.
Children go there to shout rude words and run away giggling.
The figure tilts its head, exactly the way (shouter) does when (shouter.he/she) is thinking.
Footsteps, slow and careful, crunching on the gravel.

pieces.label: Lightning on the Research Hut
pieces.text: Just before dawn, lightning strikes the research hut. Flames lick up through the thatch, and out of the smoke comes a researcher, blackened from head to foot, hair standing straight up, shouting that something "ABSOLUTELY FASCINATING" has happened.

pieces.label: Go and See
pieces.text: The researcher is so excited that a small crowd follows (rescuer.him/her) right back into the smoking hut, ducking under the burning edge of the thatch and coughing, to see what all the fuss is about...

pieces.label: Put Out the Fire First
pieces.text: "Fascinating later! Water now!" someone bellows. In moments the whole village is lined up from the river to the hut, passing buckets, pots and bowls hand over hand, while the smoke rolls overhead...

pieces.label: Save the Notes
pieces.text: Save the Notes.

pieces.label: Ask the Researcher What Happened
pieces.text: Ask the Researcher What Happened.
Where the lightning came down, the sand has melted into glass shapes like frozen flowers, like roots made of ice. The researchers will have new questions for a year.
The fascinating thing is that the roof is gone, and has landed, still burning, on the shelf where the notes were kept. The researcher stops being excited quite suddenly.
"Fascinating later! Water now!" The bucket chain works like a dream, and the fascinating thing turns out to be a scorch mark in the shape of a fish.
Half the notes are ash, but the bucket chain was so well run that the builders learn from it, and everyone who carried a bucket helps rebuild the hut stronger.
(Rescuer) dashes in and saves every scroll, but comes out with burnt arms.
Everyone grabs an armful of notes and runs. Nothing is lost except, somehow, all the researcher's left sandals.
The storm grumbles like a hungry belly and flashes white behind the hills.
Smoke pours out of the door in a thick grey column.
The researcher's hair is standing straight up on end.
Buckets, pots and bowls pass hand over hand from the river.

pieces.label: The Sleepwalkers
pieces.text: Under a huge orange full moon, sleepwalkers (sleepwalker1) and (sleepwalker2) walk up to the old carved stones, which the elders say let two souls trade places for a night, bow to each other very formally, and walk home into each other's huts. In the morning they are in the wrong bodies, and it hasn't worn off.

pieces.label: Sleepwalk Back
pieces.text: The elders say whatever happened at the stones can only be undone at the stones. So on the next full moon, (sleepwalker1) and (sleepwalker2) go to bed very early, in their own huts, lie down very still, and hope with all their hearts...

pieces.label: Tie Their Ankles to Their Beds
pieces.text: "No more wandering," says one of the healers firmly, and ties a length of soft rope around each of their ankles, with the other end tied to the posts of their sleeping mats. "Nobody goes anywhere until we've worked this out." (Sleepwalker1) and (sleepwalker2) look at the knots and then at each other...

pieces.label: Take Them to the Stones Awake
pieces.text: Take Them to the Stones Awake.

pieces.label: Leave Them Be
pieces.text: Leave Them Be.
They wake at the stones, wet with dew. Without a word, without knowing why, they both stand up and bow, and something shifts, like stepping off a boat onto land. Neither has sleepwalked since.
The clouds roll in thick and grey and the moon never shows its face. After three cloudy full moons they give up. "I suppose it's an adventure."
Nobody sleepwalks, nobody goes near the stones, and nobody swaps back either. Every morning they wake tied to their beds, in each other's bodies, with stiff ankles.
The ropes slip loose in the night, and they wake in the middle of the circle as themselves, holding the same bit of rope, one at each end.
Awake, at the stones, they bow, and feel foolish, and nothing happens at all.
Left alone, they swap back the next full moon in their sleep, without ever leaving their beds, which nobody can explain.
Once (sleepwalker1) was found fast asleep in a fishing net hanging from a tree.
Once (sleepwalker2) woke at dawn in the goat pen, holding a goat, which did not seem to mind.
The full moon hangs huge and orange over the sea.
They bow to each other, very formally.

pieces.label: A Quiet Afternoon
pieces.text: Nothing is happening at all. The work is done, the breeze smells of warm grass, and (watcher) sits in the shade of a big rock watching a very small crab try to climb a very large rock, slip, tumble down, right itself, and start again.

pieces.label: Help the Crab
pieces.text: (Watcher) watches the crab fall off for the seventh time. That's enough. (watcher.He/She) leans over and, very gently, holds out one finger behind the crab, so it has something to push against...

pieces.label: Keep Watching
pieces.text: (Watcher) settles back against the warm rock. This is none of (watcher.his/her) business. The crab gets halfway, slips, falls, rights itself, and starts again. And again. And again...

pieces.label: Cheer It On
pieces.text: Cheer It On.

pieces.label: Build It a Ramp
pieces.text: Build It a Ramp.
With a little nudge the crab reaches the very top, looks around as if it has conquered a mountain, then climbs straight down the other side without a backward look. It was worth it anyway.
The crab does not want help. It pinches (watcher)'s finger, hard, for interfering, and starts climbing again on its own. "Fair enough," says (watcher).
On the eleventh try the crab finds a little crack and hauls itself over the top. "YES!" shouts (watcher), punching the air, while villagers walking past stare at (watcher) cheering at a rock.
(Watcher)'s eyes close. When (watcher.he/she) wakes, the shadows are long and gold, and the crab is asleep too, tucked right up against (watcher.his/her) foot.
(Watcher)'s cheering draws a crowd, and soon half the village is cheering at the crab.
The crab ignores the ramp entirely and climbs the steepest side instead.
Somewhere a woodpecker is knocking, slow and lazy.
It is a very small crab, and a very large rock.
The crab rights itself and starts again, with what (watcher) can only describe as determination.
The shadows are long and gold.

pieces.label: The Chief's Bad Idea
pieces.text: Chief (chief) has had an idea in the night, and climbs onto a stool at breakfast to announce that tomorrow everyone will swap jobs for a day. "So we can understand one another! Farmers will build! Builders will research! Researchers will farm!" Somewhere at the back, a baby starts clapping.

pieces.label: Do as the Chief Says
pieces.text: The Chief has spoken. The next morning, the village sets off to its new jobs with great reluctance, and the sound of a lot of people asking "which end do I hold?"...

pieces.label: Gently Talk the Chief Out of It
pieces.text: The village elders take Chief (chief) aside after breakfast and explain, very kindly and very carefully, that the harvest is nearly due, the fences need mending, and perhaps this wonderful idea could wait for a quieter time...

pieces.label: Try It for Just One Hour
pieces.text: Try It for Just One Hour.

pieces.label: Let the Chief Go First
pieces.text: Let the Chief Go First.

A builder plants a field of seedlings upside down, a researcher knocks down three fences, and a farmer uses a research scroll to start a fire. But at supper everyone has a new respect for everyone else's work.

(Builder) sits down at the researchers' table for the first time, doesn't look up until dark, and solves a problem the researchers have been stuck on for a month. Chief (chief) says this was the plan all along.
Chief (chief) sighs the sigh of a great leader not understood in (chief.his/her) own time. "Next year, then." Everyone hopes (chief.he/she) will forget. (chief.He/She) has written it down.

The Chief sulks, and does everyone's job (chief.himself/herself) for a week "to understand." (chief.He/She) gets chased by the pig, comes to hate the feel of soil, and turns out to be a decent fence-builder and a much humbler Chief.
The hour is so awful that nobody ever mentions the idea again, including the Chief.
The Chief tries the healers' work first, is very good at it, and spends a happy season helping the sick.
The farmers look at the builders. The builders look at the researchers. The researchers look at their breakfast.
Chief (chief) is practically bouncing on (chief.his/her) toes by the cooking fire.
"Which end do I hold?"
A baby at the back starts clapping.

pieces.label: The Tree Remembers
pieces.text: (Dreamer) falls asleep against the warm roots of the Tree of Life, and in (dreamer.his/her) dream the Tree shows (dreamer.him/her) every season it has ever lived through: storms and droughts, the first people coming up the beach, a thousand harvests. (dreamer.He/She) wakes with a gasp and a head full of things (dreamer.he/she) never knew.

pieces.label: Write It All Down
pieces.text: (Dreamer) leaps up and runs for the research hut, holding (dreamer.his/her) head with both hands as if it might spill. Everything is fading already, like a dream does, and (dreamer.he/she) has to get it down before it's gone...

pieces.label: Thank the Tree
pieces.text: (Dreamer) doesn't move. (dreamer.He/She) turns round, very slowly, presses both hands flat against the warm bark and bows (dreamer.his/her) head. "Thank you," (dreamer.he/she) says. The whole Tree seems to shiver, from the roots to the topmost leaves...

pieces.label: Tell the Elders
pieces.text: Tell the Elders.

pieces.label: Go Back to Sleep
pieces.text: Go Back to Sleep.

(Dreamer) fills scroll after scroll, faster than the researchers can bring them: rainfall over a thousand years, where the river used to run. They understand almost half of it, which is still more than they've learned in years.
Most of it goes the way dreams go. All that's left is one thing, very clear and very strong: an opinion about soil. The farmers are delighted with it.
"Thank you." A single fruit drops into (dreamer)'s lap, and that season the Tree's fruit is so sweet and plentiful the branches bend. (Dreamer) doesn't say anything, but (dreamer.he/she) knows.

A drop of the Tree's dark, old sap falls on (dreamer)'s lips, tasting of earth and rain and time. (dreamer.He/She) wakes ten years older, with a great calm in (dreamer.his/her) heart and a steadiness in (dreamer.his/her) hands.
The elders listen, and say the Tree used to speak to their grandparents too. They write down what they can.
The dream doesn't come back. (Dreamer) wakes up with a stiff neck and a beetle in (dreamer.his/her) ear.
The bark against (dreamer.his/her) back is warm, warm as skin.
The leaves whisper like a crowd waiting for a story to start.
A thousand harvests, a thousand winters.
There are leaves in (dreamer.his/her) hair.

pieces.label: The Wrong Step at the Falls
pieces.text: (Subject) has carried water from the top of the falls for years, but today, with both jars full, the third flat rock wobbles for the first time ever, slides out from under (subject.his/her) foot, and (subject) goes over the edge.

pieces.label: Grab the Vine
pieces.text: (Subject) twists in the air and lunges for the vine with both hands. (subject.His/her) fingers close round it. It burns through (subject.his/her) palms as (subject.he/she) slides, and then catches, and holds, and (subject) swings out over the white water like a weight on a string...

pieces.label: Let Go and Hope for the Pool
pieces.text: There's no time to reach the vine. (Subject) shuts (subject.his/her) eyes, pulls (subject.his/her) arms in tight, and falls, and falls, down through the rainbows and the spray and the roaring white...

pieces.label: Grab the Rock Edge
pieces.text: Grab the Rock Edge.

pieces.label: Shout for Help
pieces.text: Shout for Help.

The vine holds. (Subject) slams into the cliff, something in (subject.his/her) arm goes crack, and (subject.he/she) staggers home with one empty jar still hooked over (subject.his/her) shoulder. Off water duty for the season.
The vine holds. (subject.His/her) leg doesn't. (Subject) walks again in the end, slowly, with a stick, and the elders put up a carved post beside the third flat rock.
(Subject) hits the deep pool feet first and bursts back up, gasping, alive, somehow completely unhurt, and laughs at the sky. Someone else can carry water from now on.
(Subject) misses the pool. They find (subject.him/her) on the rocks in the spray, with the little rainbows still dancing over (subject.him/her), and carry (subject.him/her) home for the last time.
(Subject)'s fingers catch the lip of the falls, and (subject.he/she) hangs there until the others pull (subject.him/her) up, scraped raw.
Nobody can hear over the roar, but a fisher below happens to look up at the right moment. (Subject) lands in the fisher's net.
The spray throws little rainbows over the rocks.
The roar is so loud that nobody would hear a shout.
The jars fly.
A thick old vine hangs out over the water.

pieces.label: The Old Fisher's Last Tide
pieces.text: (Subject) has fished from the same rock every morning since (subject.he/she) was a child, always alone, with an old grey heron waiting nearby. This morning (subject.he/she) stops at (name2)'s door with two rods over (subject.his/her) shoulder. "Come along with me today. I want to show you where the big ones sleep."

pieces.label: Go with (Him/Her)
pieces.text: (Name2) pulls on a wrap and follows (subject) down to the rock in the grey dawn. They sit side by side in the cold, (subject) in (subject.his/her) worn dip, (name2) on the bare stone beside (subject.him/her), and cast their lines out into the water...

pieces.label: Say Not Today
pieces.text: "Not today," says (name2), rubbing (friend.his/her) eyes. "I've got the fields. Maybe another time?" (Subject) nods, slowly. "Another time," (subject.he/she) agrees, and walks off alone down the path towards the sea, the two rods still over (subject.his/her) shoulder...

pieces.label: Bring Breakfast Along
pieces.text: Bring Breakfast Along.

pieces.label: Ask Why Today
pieces.text: Ask Why Today.

(Subject) shows (name2) everything: where the big ones sleep, the knot that never slips, how to wait. On the walk home (subject.he/she) says quietly, "Good. Now I can rest," and that night dies peacefully in (subject.his/her) sleep. The next morning the heron is waiting for (name2).
Not a single fish all morning, so they talk: about (subject)'s mother, the person (subject.he/she) loved and lost, the heron's grandmother. (Name2) agrees that this was the real catch.
(Subject) goes alone, as always, and comes back at noon with a basket of fish, as always. When (name2) asks about the big ones, (subject) just smiles. "Another time."
(Name2) can't stop thinking about the two rods, and goes down to the rock before dawn. The second rod is lying ready on the stone, and (subject) just moves over a little.
They share warm breadfruit on the rock, and the heron gets most of it.
"Because I'm old, and you're not," says (subject), and that's all (subject.he/she) will say. They catch the biggest fish of the year.
There's a dip worn into the stone where (subject) always sits.
An old grey heron waits nearby for scraps, as patient as (subject) is.
The sky is just going pale.
"I want to show you where the big ones sleep."

pieces.label: The Mould That Made a Friend
pieces.text: (Subject)'s spare sleeping mat has sat rolled up in a damp corner so long that a row of tiny brown mirror-caps has sprouted along it, the mushrooms that grow into a copy of whoever sleeps nearest. This morning a perfect copy of (subject) is sitting up on the mat, yawning.

pieces.label: Introduce Yourself
pieces.text: (Subject)'s mouth is very dry. (subject.He/She) clears (subject.his/her) throat and holds out a slightly trembling hand towards the corner. "Hello," (subject.he/she) says. "I'm... well. I'm (subject)." The copy looks at the hand for a long moment...

pieces.label: Hang the Mat in the Sun
pieces.text: (Subject) doesn't trust anything that grows in a damp corner. Without a word, (subject.he/she) grabs the edge of the mat and drags it, copy and all, out of the hut and into the blazing sunshine, and throws it over a fence...

pieces.label: Fetch the Healers
pieces.text: Fetch the Healers.

pieces.label: Offer It Breakfast
pieces.text: Offer It Breakfast.

"Hello," says the copy, in exactly the same voice. Same likes, same dislikes, same terrible jokes, same need for breakfast. It settles on the name (made1), and the first thing it does is help (subject) throw out the mat.
The copy shakes (subject.his/her) hand and smiles (subject)'s exact smile, then crumbles, softly, like a sandcastle in the sun, into very clean dust. (Subject) finally washes the mat.

Drying on the fence, the copy firms up, and a second one tumbles out of the far end of the mat. "Harvest today, isn't it?" they say together, and {#made:only one comes back, calling itself (made1)|come back calling themselves (made1) and (made2)}.

The copy dries paler and thinner, like mist burning off a morning field. (Subject) is oddly sad, rebuilds the back wall of (subject.his/her) hut so the damp can never get in, and finds (subject.he/she) really likes working with wood.
The healers poke it, it giggles exactly like (subject), and they declare it perfectly healthy and send it home as (made1).
It eats breakfast, says thank you, and walks off into the jungle. A ring of mushrooms comes up where it sat.
The corner smells like a forest floor after rain.
A neat little row of tiny brown mushrooms grows along the edge of the mat.
A perfect copy, right down to the little scar on (subject.his/her) thumb.
The copy picks a mushroom out of (subject.his/her) hair.

pieces.label: The Shipwrecked Family
pieces.text: At a grey dawn, the fishers spot a battered outrigger drifting towards the bay, half its float torn away, with three people clinging to it: a tired, sunburnt adult, a teenager hooked round the mast, and a small child in a soaked cloth. "Anywhere dry," the adult calls.

pieces.label: Bring Them Ashore
pieces.text: Three canoes go out at once. The fishers paddle hard through the swell, lash the wreck to their own boats with rope, and tow it in, while the whole village gathers on the sand with blankets, shouting encouragement...

pieces.label: Send Food Out to Them
pieces.text: The reef is rough and the swell is high. Instead of risking more canoes, the fishers paddle out just far enough to throw a bundle of food and a gourd of water across to the wreck. The adult catches them, clumsily, and holds them up with a tired wave...

pieces.label: Swim Out with a Rope
pieces.text: Swim Out with a Rope.

pieces.label: Call to Them to Paddle In
pieces.text: Call to Them to Paddle In.
Wrapped in every blanket the village owns and fed soup until they stop shivering, they say the storm took them four days ago. The child is already playing in the sand. They decide to stay.
"The rest of our people will think we're lost." The adult and the child paddle off in the mended outrigger, but the teenager asks to stay. "I like it here. It's quiet."
The current carries them round the point. A week later the same outrigger comes back, mended, loaded to the brim with fresh fish. "You fed us when we were starving. Now we feed you."
They eat, then paddle straight for the shore, wrecked float and all. "We could smell the cooking," the child explains, very seriously. The adult and the child stay.
(Swimmer) swims out with a rope through the rough swell and tows them in, but comes back with a gashed leg from the reef.
They paddle in, too tired to argue, and all three stay.
The sky is still grey and heavy with last night's rain.
Half the outrigger's float has been torn away.
The whole village gathers on the sand with blankets, shouting encouragement.
The child is already playing with the village children in the sand.

pieces.label: The Monkey Raid
pieces.text: The monkeys have watched the food store for days, pretending very hard to be interested in anything else, and this morning, while everyone is in the fields, they make their move. There are monkeys everywhere, with yams in both hands, and one of them is wearing a bowl as a hat.

pieces.label: Chase Them Off
pieces.text: The alarm goes up. The whole village comes pelting back from the fields, shouting, waving their arms, banging pots and pans and digging sticks together. The monkeys look up. They do not look worried...

pieces.label: Leave Out a Decoy Basket
pieces.text: The cleverest of the farmers has an idea. Quietly, while the monkeys are busy, (subject.he/she) fills the biggest basket in the village with the rotten fruit from the compost heap, covers the top with a few good mangoes, and leaves it out in the open where the monkeys can't miss it...

pieces.label: Bang Every Pot in the Village
pieces.text: Bang Every Pot in the Village.

pieces.label: Bribe Them with Fruit
pieces.text: Bribe Them with Fruit.
The monkeys scatter, screeching and laughing, up into the trees with as much food as they can carry. One eats a mango slowly on a high branch, looking down. The one with the bowl hat keeps the bowl.
The chase goes round and round the huts all morning until half the village is collapsed in the shade, wheezing, and the monkeys come straight back for seconds.
The decoy basket is rotten fruit under a few good mangoes. The look on the monkeys' faces is pure betrayal. They throw some of the mush, and don't come back for a month.
Two monkeys carry the decoy carefully up into the trees while the rest of the troop quietly empties the real store from the other side. "They're cleverer than us," someone says. Nobody argues.
The racket is so loud that the monkeys flee empty-handed, and so does every bird for a mile.
A pile of fruit at the edge of the jungle keeps them happy. They leave the store alone, mostly.
One monkey has groomed the same patch of fur for an hour without taking its eyes off the door.
Another has been "sleeping" on the next roof since breakfast, with one eye open.
Fruit rains down on the villagers' heads.
One of them is wearing a bowl as a hat.

pieces.label: Something Has Been Eating the Scrolls
pieces.text: The research hut is full of tiny holes, in the walls, the scrolls, the maps and the chart of the moon that took a whole year to make, and (researcher) follows the trail to the most important scroll of all, where a very fat, very happy beetle is curled up asleep in a perfect round hole.

pieces.label: Evict the Beetle
pieces.text: (Researcher) picks the beetle up between (researcher.his/her) finger and thumb, carries it outside at arm's length, and flicks it off into the bushes as hard as (researcher.he/she) can. Then (researcher.he/she) comes back in, rolls up (researcher.his/her) sleeves, and starts going through the shelves...

pieces.label: Study the Beetle
pieces.text: (Researcher) doesn't touch it. (researcher.He/She) pulls up a stool, sits down, and watches. The beetle wakes up, yawns, if beetles can yawn, and starts eating again, slowly. (Researcher) gets out a fresh piece of bark and starts taking notes, keeping it well out of the beetle's reach...

pieces.label: Smoke Out the Hut
pieces.text: Smoke Out the Hut.

pieces.label: Feed It Something Else
pieces.text: Feed It Something Else.
(Researcher) flicks the beetle into the bushes, but it has eaten a whole season of notes, carefully and neatly, the way a person eats a good meal. Some of them have more hole than scroll.
The beetle goes. Its family stays: hundreds of them, all very fat and very happy. It takes a whole month to get rid of them, and a great many notes are gone for good.
After three days of offering it every bark on the island, (researcher) finds it eats only the pale bark of the paper tree. The researchers switch to darker bark and never lose another note.

While (researcher) watches one beetle eat one scroll, its whole family eats a basket of notes across the room. The researchers are furious. (Researcher) has fallen head over heels in love with learning.
The smoke clears the beetles and blackens half the scrolls.
The beetles love old fruit peel even more than scrolls, and move into the compost heap for good.
Daylight comes in through the walls in little dots, like stars at noon.
The chart of the moon took a whole year to make.
The beetle yawns, if beetles can yawn, and starts eating again.
Very fat, very happy, fast asleep.

pieces.label: A Gift from the Smoking Mountain
pieces.text: The mountain has rumbled all week like a giant snoring, and this morning a hot black stone the size of a fist comes bouncing all the way down the path, through the village, and stops dead at (finder)'s feet, orange light glowing in its cracks.

pieces.label: Pick It Up with Tongs
pieces.text: (Finder) fetches the long wooden tongs from the cooking fire, gets a grip on the glowing stone, and lifts it very, very carefully, holding it as far away from (finder.his/her) body as (finder.his/her) arms will go...

pieces.label: Leave It Alone
pieces.text: (Finder) steps back, carefully, and puts a ring of stones around it so nobody treads on it by accident. Then (finder.he/she) calls the others over. Everybody stands in a circle around it, at a respectful distance, and watches it glow...

pieces.label: Douse It with Water
pieces.text: Douse It with Water.

pieces.label: Give It to the Researchers
pieces.text: Give It to the Researchers.
In a bucket of water it hisses and spits and boils the water half away. When it cools, it breaks open like a nut, full of green crystals, clear ones, and some that change colour in the light.
Halfway to the research hut the tongs slip, and (finder) grabs for it bare-handed. Burned palms, weeks of not holding anything, and a few green crystals for the researchers.
By evening it cracks open on its own with a little pop. Just ordinary grey stone, all the way through. The children use it to crack nuts, and it's very good at it.
It glows warm all night like a little cooking fire that never needs feeding, and in the morning there's a great ring of perfectly roasted nuts around it.
It explodes in a cloud of steam and spatters (finder) with hot grit.
The researchers wait a day, then crack it, and the crystals inside ring like little bells.
The ground hums through bare feet like a giant snoring.
A thin grey plume leans across the sky from the peak.
Everything smells faintly of struck flint.
Everybody stands in a circle around it, at a respectful distance, and watches it glow.

pieces.label: The Weaver's New Pattern
pieces.text: (Weaver) boiled up a new blue dye from the shimmering vine over the old shrine stones and wove all night without meaning to. At breakfast (weaver.he/she) holds up a pattern of waves and flying birds, in deep blues and greens and white, that seems to move when anyone looks at it.

pieces.label: Wear It
pieces.text: (Weaver) sews it into a wrap that afternoon, and puts it on, and walks around the village in it. People turn to watch (weaver.him/her) go by. Children follow (weaver.him/her), trying to catch the birds...

pieces.label: Give It Away
pieces.text: (Weaver) looks at what (weaver.he/she) has made for a long time. It's the best thing (weaver.he/she) has ever made. Perhaps the best thing (weaver.he/she) will ever make. And somehow, that makes (weaver.him/her) want to give it to someone...

pieces.label: Hang It in the Meeting Hut
pieces.text: Hang It in the Meeting Hut.

pieces.label: Weave Another
pieces.text: Weave Another.

Half the village wants one, so (weaver) builds looms instead: wooden frames, pegs, a clever little bar to hold the threads. Twelve by the end of the season. Nobody else's pattern ever quite moves like (weaver.his/hers).

At the festival dance, the faster (weaver) spins, the more the pattern moves, until the birds are flying in great circles around (weaver.him/her) in the firelight. (Weaver) is first on and last off at every festival after.
(Elder), shivering all season in a blanket worn see-through, puts it on and never takes it off. "The birds keep me warm."
(Elder) twirls in it, sneezes, sneezes again, and breaks out in an angry red rash from the shimmering-vine dye. The wrap goes on the wall, admired from a safe distance.
Everyone who sits under it at the meeting hut seems to argue less. Nobody can say why.
The second one comes out perfectly ordinary. The vine dye has run out, and (weaver) can never make the pattern move again.
The waves roll. The birds fly.
Anyone who looks away, and looks back, finds the birds have gone a little further.
Someone's spoon hangs in mid-air, dripping, unnoticed.
Children follow (weaver), trying to catch the birds.

pieces.label: The Coughing Season
pieces.text: A cough that started with one sneeze at breakfast a week ago has gone round the whole village, and now at night it sounds as if a flock of geese has moved into every hut. The healers have run out of honey, and nobody will admit to sneezing first.

pieces.label: Send Everyone to the Healers
pieces.text: The healers set up mats all round the hospital, boil every pot of herbs they have, and line up the whole coughing, sneezing, sniffling village outside the door, one at a time...

pieces.label: Let It Run Its Course
pieces.text: "It's just a cough," say the elders. "We've all had coughs. It'll pass." So everyone keeps working, keeps sneezing, keeps coughing, and waits...

pieces.label: Keep the Sick Apart
pieces.text: Keep the Sick Apart.

pieces.label: Find the First Sneezer
pieces.text: Find the First Sneezer.
The healers make tea after tea, rub chests with strong-smelling ointment, and sleep in shifts. By the end of the week the last cough is gone, and they sleep for two whole days.
Crowding everyone together turns out to be the worst idea all year. For every villager cured, two more catch it in the line, and three end up properly sick.
Everyone gets better on their own, with a great deal of nose-blowing into leaves. The first sneezer finally owns up and fetches everyone's water for a week.

For (elder) it goes deep into (elder.his/her) chest and stays. (elder.He/She) gets better in the end, but never quite gets back (elder.his/her) strength. "The healers say I was lucky. I don't feel lucky."
The sick sleep in their own huts, away from the rest, and it's gone in a week.
Everyone blames a different person, and the arguing makes the coughing worse.
At night the village sounds as if a flock of geese has moved into every hut.
The healers have run out of honey.
The children have been sent to bed early three nights running.
Noses are blown into leaves.

pieces.label: The Prank Mirror
pieces.text: A passing trader left behind a polished bronze mirror in a frame of twisted copper vines. "It tells the truth," the trader said, with a wink. (Looker) finally looks in, sees (looker.himself/herself) but better, with much, much better posture, and the reflection steps out of the frame.

pieces.label: Shake Hands
pieces.text: The reflection holds out a hand. (Looker) looks at it, then at the reflection's confident smile, and then, very slowly, takes it. The hand is warm, warm as the mirror...

pieces.label: Smash the Mirror
pieces.text: (Looker) doesn't trust it. Not for a moment. (looker.He/She) grabs the nearest rock and swings it at the mirror with all (looker.his/her) strength...

pieces.label: Turn the Mirror Around
pieces.text: Turn the Mirror Around.

pieces.label: Ask It What It Wants
pieces.text: Ask It What It Wants.

A perfect likeness outside and a completely different person inside, with no idea how anyone could eat taro. (made1) moves in next door, and the two of them argue over the fence every morning and are secretly very fond of each other.
"It's lovely here," it says, in (looker)'s voice, but softer. "You're lucky." It climbs back into the mirror, which is never quite as shiny again, and (looker) starts standing up a little straighter.
The reflection hops out a moment before the rock hits. "That was extremely rude." It goes to live with the farmers as (made1), and won't sit next to (looker) at festivals.
The mirror cracks with a sound like a bell, and the reflection flickers and vanishes. Seven kinds of guilty: (looker) can't stand mirrors, or polished things, or the still surface of the lagoon.
