Turned to the wall, the mirror goes cold. In the morning there are two sets of footprints leading away from it.
The mirror is round as the moon, in a frame of twisted copper vines.
It is warm to the touch, even in the shade.
A little smile (looker) doesn't recognise.
The hand is warm, warm as the mirror.

pieces.label: The Sacred Pool
pieces.text: Deep in the hills, (bather1) and (bather2) reach the pool inside the ring of black standing stones just before midnight. The elders say two people who bathe in it together at midnight "will see through each other's eyes," and the water holds the stars so clearly anyone could count them.

pieces.label: Bathe at Midnight
pieces.text: They take a deep breath, grin at each other, and step down into the water together, right in the middle of the reflected stars. It's warmer than they expected. The moment the moon reaches the top of the sky, the stars in the water begin to swirl...

pieces.label: Bathe at Noon Instead
pieces.text: Standing there in the dark with the black stones all around them, they both lose their nerve at the same moment. "Maybe," whispers (bather2), "we could come back tomorrow. When it's light." They sleep under a tree nearby, and come back at noon...

pieces.label: Just Dip Their Feet
pieces.text: Just Dip Their Feet.

pieces.label: Turn Back
pieces.text: Turn Back.
They climb out and see themselves. "Well," says (bather1), in (bather2)'s voice. They walk home hand in hand, getting used to each other's legs, and decide it's very romantic. Nobody else agrees.
For exactly one breath they see through each other's eyes, then they're themselves again. They walk home very close together, and never tell anyone what they saw.
At noon the pool is just a pool, with little blue fish and a frog on a stone. They fall asleep on the bank and walk home red as crabs.
The pool keeps a different clock. That night at exactly midnight, asleep in their own beds, they swap anyway, and both sit bolt upright and scream.
Their feet tingle all the way home, and for a week each of them dreams the other's dreams.
They turn back, and talk the whole way home, and know each other better than any pool could have made them.
The black stones stand around the pool like people waiting.
The water holds the stars so clearly anyone could count them.
The water is warmer than they expected.
It is very, very quiet.

pieces.label: The Forgetful Morning
pieces.text: (Forgetful) wakes up feeling marvellous, knowing how to farm and build and cook and everyone's goats' names, except (forgetful.his/her) own, which is gone like a dream on waking. A forget-me-all moon-vine has crept in over the doorway in the night, and its sweet smell is drifting out over the village.

pieces.label: Ask Around
pieces.text: (Forgetful) wanders out into the village and starts asking people, as casually as (forgetful.he/she) can manage: "Morning! Remind me, what's my name again?" People look at (forgetful.him/her) very oddly...

pieces.label: Make One Up
pieces.text: (Forgetful) decides that if (forgetful.his/her) name can't be bothered to stay, (forgetful.he/she) can't be bothered to go looking for it. (forgetful.He/She) stands in the middle of the village, clears (forgetful.his/her) throat, and announces that from now on (forgetful.he/she) shall be called...

pieces.label: Retrace Yesterday
pieces.text: Retrace Yesterday.

pieces.label: Ask the Elders
pieces.text: Ask the Elders.

The moment (forgetful.he/she) asks, everyone realises they've forgotten it too, and each very confidently gives a different name. Nine names by lunchtime, none of them right, and (forgetful) is left with no name at all: "?".

A very small child tugs at (forgetful)'s wrap and says (forgetful.his/her) name as if it were the most obvious thing in the world. It all comes rushing back, and the child gets (forgetful)'s dessert two nights running.
"From now on I shall be called... (renamed)!" It fits so well that within a month even (forgetful.his/her) mother uses it without thinking.
(forgetful.He/She) can't think of a single name, so (forgetful.he/she) shrugs. The moon-vine isn't giving anything back, and (forgetful.he/she) is left as "?". "It's honest," (forgetful.he/she) says.
At the river where (forgetful.he/she) washed last night, away from the moon-vine's smell, (forgetful) remembers it the moment (forgetful.his/her) feet touch the water.
The elders say names come back on their own. (Forgetful)'s doesn't, but a different one turns up in a dream that night.
The smell of roasting breadfruit drifts in through the doorway.
The moon-vine's pale trumpets hang over the doorway.
"It's on the tip of my tongue."
Gone, like a dream on waking.

pieces.label: The Naming Shell
pieces.text: On the morning after the first storm of the season, (finder) finds the year's naming shell half buried by (finder.his/her) foot, pearly pink inside, with dark markings the elders say the sea itself writes. This year they clearly spell a name, and it is very clearly not (finder).

pieces.label: Take the New Name
pieces.text: (Finder) carries the shell up the beach to the elders with both hands, and holds it out. The elders read the markings, one after the other, and then they all look at (finder.him/her) with great solemnity...

pieces.label: Throw It Back
pieces.text: (Finder) doesn't want a new name. (finder.He/She) likes (finder.his/her) old one. Before anyone can stop (finder.him/her), (finder.he/she) winds up and throws the shell as far out to sea as (finder.he/she) can. It spins through the air, glinting pink, and splashes down past the breakers...

pieces.label: Hide the Shell
pieces.text: Hide the Shell.

pieces.label: Give It to Someone Else
pieces.text: Give It to Someone Else.

(Finder) takes it proudly: (renamed). The elders say it out loud three times, the village repeats it, and that evening there's a small feast where everybody uses the new name as many times as they can.
For a day or two it feels like wearing someone else's sandals. Then it fits so well that a child asks, "Was there an old one?" and nobody can quite remember.
The very next wave rolls the shell back up the beach and drops it, with a smack, on (finder)'s foot. "Fine." (finder.He/She) takes the hint, and the name: (renamed).
The shell sinks without a trace and nothing happens at all, except that next season's shell is never found, and everyone privately blames (finder).
(Finder) hides it under (finder.his/her) mat. In the morning the markings on it have changed to (finder.his/her) own name.
A friend takes it gladly, but the elders insist that the finder keeps the name. Now there are two (renamed)s arguing about it.
The shell is pearly pink inside, big as two cupped hands.
The dark markings look a little like writing.
Everybody still goes down to look.
The sea is doing its very best to look innocent.

pieces.label: The Midwife's Dream
pieces.text: Just after dawn, (healer), the village's best healer, walks barefoot through the village in (healer: his/her) sleeping wrap with a pillow feather still stuck in one ear, knocks on (carrier)'s doorpost and says, "I had a dream. A very clear one. You're going to have a baby." (Healer) does not laugh.

pieces.label: Believe the Healer
pieces.text: (Carrier) stops laughing. (carrier.He/She) looks at (friend), and (friend) looks back, and then they both look at the healer. "Are you sure?" (carrier) whispers. (Healer) just pulls the feather out of (healer: his/her) ear and nods...

pieces.label: Laugh It Off
pieces.text: (Carrier) laughs again, harder. "A dream! Go back to bed!" (Friend) laughs too, a bit nervously. (Healer) just shrugs, as if to say "we'll see," and turns round and walks back home...

pieces.label: Ask What Else the Dream Showed
pieces.text: Ask What Else the Dream Showed.

pieces.label: Tell No One and Wait
pieces.text: Tell No One and Wait.
(Healer) is right, as usual. Within a couple of weeks (carrier) is sick in the mornings and very, very hungry for pickled fish, and (healer) never once says "I told you so."

Months go by and (healer) starts avoiding (carrier)'s side of the village. Then, a whole season later, (carrier) suddenly wants pickled fish more than anything. It was just a season early. (Healer) is so relieved (healer: he/she) cries.

They laugh about the healer and the feather all week. Next month nobody is laughing, except for joy, and they bring (healer) a basket of the best fruit. (Healer) whispers whether it's a girl or a boy.
It really was just a dream. (Carrier) and (friend) find they're a tiny bit disappointed, and that evening talk, for the first time, about what it might be like.
"A red blanket and a storm," says (healer). When the baby comes, it storms, and someone has woven a red blanket.
A feather from (healer: his/her) pillow is still stuck in one ear.
(Healer) has delivered half the babies in the village and has a way of knowing things.
Behind (carrier), (friend) has gone very still.
Very, very hungry for pickled fish.

pieces.label: The Raft of Strangers
pieces.text: After a night of howling wind, (carer) finds a bamboo raft wedged in the rocks, with a young woman burning with fever and a baby screaming at the sea. "Please. Just while I rest. Just a little while." (Carer) takes the baby, it stops screaming at once, and the mother sleeps, and sleeps.

pieces.label: Take the Baby
pieces.text: The healers carry the mother to the hospital. (Carer) carries the baby home and sits up all night with (carer.him/her), rocking, walking, singing every song (carer.he/she) knows, while the healers come and go with cool water and bitter tea and worried faces...

pieces.label: Find a Nursing Mother in the Village
pieces.text: (Carer) knows nothing about babies. (carer.He/She) hurries up the beach to the village, holding the baby out in front of (carer.him/her) like a very fragile, very loud pot, calling for anyone who's nursing a little one of their own...

pieces.label: Carry Them Both to the Healers
pieces.text: Carry Them Both to the Healers.

pieces.label: Sing to the Baby
pieces.text: Sing to the Baby.

The fever breaks on the fifth day and the mother asks to stay, but by then the baby screams whenever (carer) leaves the hut. The mother laughs and says the baby has two parents now, and that's twice as lucky.

On the third night, without ever waking, the mother slips away. She is buried on the hill above the beach under a row of shells, though nobody ever learns her name, and (carer) raises the baby as (carer.his/her) own.
A young mother in the village tucks the baby in beside her own without a second thought. When the stranger wakes to find her child warm and fed, she weeps for a whole morning, and asks to stay.
The baby screams the roof off for everyone but (carer). After an hour of this, (carer) gives in. "Fine. You win."
The healers nurse the mother back to health in a week, and she takes her baby back with a hug for (carer), and stays.
The raft is lashed together from bamboo.
The baby stops screaming at once and stares up at (carer), very seriously.
"Just while I rest. Just a little while."
(Carer) carries the baby like a very fragile, very loud pot.

pieces.label: The Bitter Leaf
pieces.text: A wandering herbalist with a bag of tiny clay pots that smells so strongly of mint it makes eyes water calls out to (worker), loaded with firewood, and holds out a dark, glossy leaf. "Chew this. Makes hard work feel easy."

pieces.label: Chew It
pieces.text: (Worker) takes the leaf, sniffs it, and puts it in (worker.his/her) mouth. (worker.He/She) chews once. (worker.His/her) whole face screws up. It's the bitterest thing (worker.he/she) has ever tasted. The herbalist nods encouragingly. "Keep going," (worker.he/she) says...

pieces.label: Spit It Out
pieces.text: The moment it touches (worker.his/her) tongue, (worker) knows. (worker.He/She) spits it out onto the path, coughing and gagging, and wipes (worker.his/her) tongue on (worker.his/her) sleeve. The herbalist looks at the leaf in the dirt, then back at (worker)...

pieces.label: Ask What's in It
pieces.text: Ask What's in It.

pieces.label: Give It to Someone Lazier
pieces.text: Give It to Someone Lazier.

It's the bitterest thing (worker) has ever tasted, so awful that work feels like a relief. (worker.He/She) does the job (worker.he/she) always hated all afternoon. The taste wears off by morning. The not-minding doesn't.

It works too well. A fence, a weeded field, three scrolls, another fence around a tree. At midnight two friends find (worker) digging a ditch by moonlight, singing, and carry (worker.him/her) home. The herbalist has, very wisely, moved on.

The taste stays all day, and somewhere around the fifth cup of water (worker) decides (worker.he/she) hates herbs, roots, teas, anything that smells like mint, and anything to do with healing whatsoever.
"Ha! Good! You've got sense." The herbalist hands over a pale green leaf that tastes like honey and lime and summer. "What does this one do?" "Nothing at all. But it's delicious."
The herbalist explains every ingredient at great length. (Worker) learns a great deal, and never chews the leaf.
A friend chews it, works like a storm for a day, and then sleeps for two.
The bag clinks with tiny clay pots.
The smell of mint is so strong it makes eyes water.
A seed "for luck in love" has been very popular.
(worker.His/her) whole face screws up. "Keep going," says the herbalist.

pieces.label: The Master Builder's Last Lesson
pieces.text: (Master) has built half the huts in the village and can tell if a beam is straight just by tapping it, but (master.he/she) is old and slow now. This morning (master.he/she) knocks on (apprentice)'s door with (master.his/her) tool bag. "I'm going to teach you everything I know. All of it. In one week. Starting now."

pieces.label: Learn Everything
pieces.text: For seven days (apprentice) does exactly what (master) says. (friend.He/She) watches every movement of (master)'s hands, and copies them, and does them again, and again, until (friend.his/her) own hands are blistered and sore and doing it without thinking...

pieces.label: Ask Questions Instead
pieces.text: (Apprentice) doesn't just copy. On the very first morning, (friend.he/she) starts asking. Why this way and not that? Why this wood? Why does the knot go over and not under? Why, why, why. (Master) stops, blinks, and puts down (master.his/her) hammer...

pieces.label: Build Something Together
pieces.text: Build Something Together.

pieces.label: Ask for More Time
pieces.text: Ask for More Time.

On the seventh day (apprentice) builds a whole hut alone. (Master) walks round it twice, tapping the posts, and finds there is nothing left to say except "Good." It's the proudest word (apprentice) has ever heard.

(Apprentice) learns more than one head should hold in a week, then forgets about half of it. Half of everything (master) knows is still a very great deal. (Master) grumbles, then smiles when (apprentice) isn't looking.
The questions make (master) really think, and remember things (master.his/her) own teacher showed (master.him/her) sixty years ago. They argue happily all week, and both come out better builders.

"Just DO it," (master) snaps on the second day, and goes home for a lie-down. (Apprentice) teaches (friend.himself/herself) the rest, badly, with a lot of fallen-down beams, and can't stand the sight of a hammer.
Together they build a little shelter by the beach. It's crooked, and they both love it.
"I don't have more time," says (master), very gently. They start that afternoon.
(master.His/her) hands are rough as bark, scarred and knobbly.
(master.He/She) can still tell if a beam is straight just by tapping it and listening.
(Master) has built the meeting hut twice.
"All of it. In one week. Starting now."

pieces.label: The Shortcut over the Ridge
pieces.text: Coming home late from the far beach with a basket so heavy (gatherer.his/her) shoulders ache, (gatherer) stands at the start of the shortcut: a knife-edge of crumbling red rock no wider than a sleeping mat, with a long drop to the sea on one side. Every adult has taken it once, and quietly not mentioned it.

pieces.label: Take the Shortcut
pieces.text: (Gatherer) shifts the basket on (gatherer.his/her) back, takes a deep breath, and steps out onto the ridge. The wind comes up from the sea in gusts, tugging at (gatherer.him/her). Far below, the waves boom against the rocks. (gatherer.He/She) doesn't look down...

pieces.label: Take the Long Way
pieces.text: (Gatherer) looks at the ridge for a long time, at the red rock and the drop and the setting sun. Then (gatherer.he/she) sighs, shifts the heavy basket, and turns down the long, winding path through the jungle instead...

pieces.label: Leave the Basket and Cross
pieces.text: Leave the Basket and Cross.

pieces.label: Wait for Morning
pieces.text: Wait for Morning.

One foot in front of the other, quick and light. A gust nearly takes (gatherer.him/her) halfway, but (gatherer) jumps down onto the soft grass on the far side, laughing, and tells everyone (gatherer.he/she) took the long way.

It rained on the ridge in the afternoon, and the red rock is slick. The searchers find only (gatherer.his/her) basket on its side at the edge, with the fruit spilled over the rocks. The sea gives nothing back.

Down into a valley and back up, through mud and mosquitoes, stubbing every toe in the dark. (Gatherer) gets home long after dinner, tired, grumpy, filthy and safe, and swears off long gathering trips forever.
A wrong turn down an old overgrown path leads to a grove nobody has picked in years, the trees bent nearly double with fruit. The next day half the village goes back with baskets.
(Gatherer) crosses light and fast, and goes back for the basket at dawn, but the monkeys have got there first.
(Gatherer) sleeps under a rock and crosses in the dry dawn light, slowly, safely, and with a good view.
The ridge is no wider than a sleeping mat.
Far below, the waves boom against the rocks.
The wind comes up from the sea in gusts, tugging.
The sun is going down.

pieces.label: The Night of Falling Stars
pieces.text: For one whole night the stars fall over the island like rain, thousands of thin silver scratches, so bright the village is lit as if by a pale moon. In the morning little bright stones lie scattered along the beach, still faintly warm.

pieces.label: Collect the Star Stones
pieces.text: The whole village goes along the beach with baskets, picking up the stones one by one. They're heavy for their size, dark and pitted, with flecks of something bright inside that catches the light...

pieces.label: Leave Them Where They Fell
pieces.text: The elders say the stars came down on their own, and should be left where they chose to land. So nobody touches them. The children are told to walk around them. For days, the beach sparkles...

pieces.label: Make Wishes on Them
pieces.text: Make Wishes on Them.

pieces.label: Bury Them on the Hill
pieces.text: Bury Them on the Hill.

Inside every stone is strange metal, heavy and bright, that bends instead of breaking and doesn't rust in water. The researchers come out of months of study with more questions than answers, the best kind of discovery.

There are only enough stones for three necklaces, given to (wearers), (name2) and (name3), who watched every last star fall. On clear nights the stones still glimmer, as if they remember where they came from.
The stones sink a little deeper with every tide until they're gone, and the beach feels warmer, calmer, after that. Nobody can quite say why, and nobody wants to.
A big blue crab carries one off to its hole under a fallen tree, where the researchers find its hoard of lost tools, including somebody's grandfather's carving chisel.
Every child holds a stone and makes one more wish. Nobody tells what they wished, but the next morning everyone is in a very good mood.
Buried on the hill, the stones make the grass grow greener there than anywhere else on the island.
Thin silver scratches streak down the sky.
The babies stop crying to watch.
The children wish until they run out of things to wish for, then fall asleep in a heap.
The stones are heavy for their size, dark and pitted, with flecks of something bright inside.

pieces.label: The Elder on the Wet Rocks
pieces.text: (Elder) has gathered shellfish on the wet rocks at the point every morning for sixty years, but the rocks are slick with green seaweed after the rains and (elder.he/she) isn't as quick as (elder.he/she) used to be. Everyone has told (elder.him/her) to let someone younger do it, and (elder.he/she) is already halfway down the path.

pieces.label: Go with (Him/Her)
pieces.text: A young villager, (companion), grabs a basket and jogs after (elder), calling that (friend.he/she) has nothing better to do and could use the company. (Elder) snorts. "Company," (elder.he/she) says. "Is that what they're calling it." But (elder.he/she) doesn't send (companion) back...

pieces.label: Let (Him/Her) Go Alone
pieces.text: The village decides that (elder) has been doing this for sixty years, and knows the rocks better than any of them, and would never forgive them for fussing. So they let (elder.him/her) go. Several people find reasons to keep glancing towards the point all morning...

pieces.label: Offer to Carry the Basket
pieces.text: Offer to Carry the Basket.

pieces.label: Watch from the Cliff
pieces.text: Watch from the Cliff.

On the slipperiest rock (elder)'s foot goes out from under (elder.him/her), and (companion) catches (elder.his/her) arm just in time. Neither says anything. (Elder) grumbles all the way home, but holds (companion)'s hand the whole way.

(Elder) slips anyway, so fast nobody could have been quick enough, and lands in the rock pool with (elder.his/her) hip twisted under (elder.him/her). (elder.He/She) walks with a stick after that, and watches from the cliff, telling the young ones they're doing it wrong.

(Elder) comes back at noon, soaked to the knees, with the biggest basket of shellfish anyone has seen all year, drops it where everyone can see, and says nothing at all. (elder.He/She) doesn't need to.
A twisted ankle in a crack between two rocks, and a long, cold, furious wait on the highest rock until the tide goes out. (Elder) refuses to discuss it.
"Carry it? I'm not dead yet." But (elder.he/she) lets them, on the way back.
The rocks are slick with green seaweed.
The waves come in fast and white.
(Elder) has told everyone, in some detail, where they can put their advice.
Several people find reasons to keep glancing towards the point.

pieces.label: The Barnacle Beard
pieces.text: (Diver) has spent so long diving for shellfish at the old wreck reef, where the sea likes to claim things for its own, that one morning there's a barnacle on (diver.his/her) chin. By the next morning there's a grey-white, crusty, clicking barnacle beard, and a small crab has been seen sitting in it.

pieces.label: Keep It
pieces.text: (Diver) looks at (diver.himself/herself) in a bowl of still water for a long time, turning (diver.his/her) head this way and that. "Actually," (diver.he/she) says slowly, as the barnacles click, "I think I like it."...

pieces.label: Scrape Them Off
pieces.text: (Diver) has had enough. (diver.He/She) takes a flat shell, sharpens the edge on a rock, grits (diver.his/her) teeth, and starts to scrape...

pieces.label: Ask the Healers
pieces.text: Ask the Healers.

pieces.label: Wait for Them to Fall Off
pieces.text: Wait for Them to Fall Off.

The barnacles are oddly flattering: rugged, sea-weathered, like someone in an old story who came out of the waves. The children spend a week sitting in the shallows with their chins in the water, disappointed when nothing grows.

The beard makes (diver) feel more at home in the sea than ever. (diver.He/She) holds (diver.his/her) breath longer than anyone, the fish stop being afraid of (diver.him/her), and (diver.he/she) becomes the best diver in the village.
It hurts. A lot. Barnacles hold on very tightly, and take little bits of (diver) with them. The healers tell (diver.him/her) very firmly not to do that again.
Off they come, one at a time, with a very satisfying pop each. Thinking about how (diver.he/she) was slowly being turned into a rock, (diver) swears never to swim again.
The healers soak them in vinegar, and they drop off in a day without a mark.
They never fall off. (Diver) gets used to the clicking.
It clicks faintly when (diver.he/she) talks, and a lot when (diver.he/she) laughs.
A small crab has been seen sitting in it.
"You're turning into a fish," says (diver.his/her) family.
By evening there are four.

pieces.label: Grey Overnight
pieces.text: In the deepest part of the night (dreamer) sits bolt upright and screams, from a dream (dreamer.he/she) can't remember, and the frogs in the marsh all stop singing at once. In the morning (dreamer.his/her) hair is grey as ash and (dreamer.his/her) knees creak like someone much older; the elders whisper that the island's oldest spirit takes payment in years.

pieces.label: Go to the Healers
pieces.text: (Dreamer)'s family help (dreamer.him/her) across the village to the healers' hut, (dreamer.him/her) leaning on their arms, while the whole village stares. The healers sit (dreamer.him/her) down and look at (dreamer.him/her) for a long time without saying anything...

pieces.label: Ask What the Dream Was
pieces.text: The elders say that a dream that strong is a message, and it can't be ignored. They sit (dreamer) down by the fire and ask (dreamer.him/her) to close (dreamer.his/her) eyes and go back into it, slowly, piece by piece...

pieces.label: Go Back to Sleep
pieces.text: Go Back to Sleep.

pieces.label: Wash It Out in the River
pieces.text: Wash It Out in the River.

Teas, poultices, chants, cold baths: nothing changes the grey. "We can't undo it, but we can help you live with it." By the end of the week (dreamer) has made peace. "Fifty is a fine age to be. I'll just skip the bits in the middle."
A calming tea, the strongest they have, and over a few days the grey fades like ash washed off by rain, though not all the way. (Dreamer) sleeps with a light on for a while.

A voice, deep and old as the island: "You will need wisdom more than youth." (Dreamer) decides to believe it, grows into an elder over the week, calm and clear, and the other elders make room by the fire.
The dream won't come back. The grey stays, and the lines stay, but it suits (dreamer.him/her), and the children start bringing (dreamer) their troubles, the way they go to the elders.
(Dreamer) sleeps again and wakes with (dreamer.his/her) own luscious hair, and the memory of a voice saying "Not yet."
The river water turns grey around (dreamer.him/her), and (dreamer.he/she) comes out only a little older.
In the marsh, the frogs all stop singing at once.
Grey as ash. Not a few strands: all of it.
(dreamer.His/her) family come to check, and stop in the doorway.
The healers look at (dreamer.him/her) for a long time without saying anything.

pieces.label: The Parrot with Opinions
pieces.text: A big green parrot with a red patch over one eye has moved onto (owner)'s roof uninvited. It knows three words: (owner)'s name, twice, shouted at every dawn, and "No," which it says whenever (owner) starts a job.

pieces.label: Listen to the Parrot
pieces.text: (Owner) decides to try an experiment. For a whole week, (owner.he/she) picks up each tool in turn, holds it up towards the roof, and waits to see what the parrot says. The neighbours think (owner.he/she) has lost (owner.his/her) mind...

pieces.label: Ignore the Parrot
pieces.text: (Owner) refuses to be bossed about by a bird. (owner.He/She) picks up (owner.his/her) tools, walks right past the hut, and gets on with the day. "No," says the parrot. "No. NO." (Owner) doesn't look up...

pieces.label: Teach It a New Word
pieces.text: Teach It a New Word.

pieces.label: Bribe It with Fruit
pieces.text: Bribe It with Fruit.

It screams "NO NO NO" at every building tool until (owner) puts the hammer down, but never once says no to the thing (owner) used to hate most. (Owner) finds (owner.he/she) doesn't mind that thing any more.

It says "No" to everything, until (owner) picks up a cooking pot, and the parrot goes silent and hops onto the rim, hopefully. (Owner) turns out wonderful at cooking. The parrot gets the first taste of everything.

The parrot sulks off to shout someone else's name on {someone else's roof|the meeting hut|the chief's doorway}. (Owner) is very relieved, and then, rather to (owner.his/her) surprise, misses it. A little.

Every "No" makes (owner) work harder, out of pure stubbornness. By the end of the month (owner.he/she) is far better at (owner.his/her) work, and the parrot's "No" sounds, perhaps, a little impressed.
After a week of patient lessons, the parrot learns "Yes." It uses it only for naps.
The parrot eats the fruit, says "No," and eats more fruit.
When it's bored it pulls bits out of the thatch and drops them on (owner)'s head.
"No," quietly, almost sadly, as if it's disappointed.
The red patch sits over its eye like a little cap worn at an angle.
The neighbours think (owner) has lost (owner.his/her) mind.

pieces.label: The Old Wanderer
pieces.text: An old traveller walks slowly into the village, leaning on a stick worn smooth by years of hands, with sandals tied with vine and a white beard so full of twigs a small bird could live in it. "I've walked every path on this island. This is the last. I'd like to sit down now. For a few years."

pieces.label: Give (Him/Her) a Hut
pieces.text: The elders look at each other, and then at the old traveller, and nod. There's an empty hut at the edge of the village, with a good view of the sea. The children carry (subject.his/her) bag. The builders patch the roof. Someone brings a mat...

pieces.label: Give (Him/Her) a Meal and Send (Him/Her) On
pieces.text: The village is kind, but cautious. They bring the old traveller a big bowl of stew, a cup of water and a fresh pair of sandals, and sit with (subject.him/her) while (subject.he/she) eats, and wait to see what (subject.he/she) does next...

pieces.label: Ask About the Paths
pieces.text: Ask About the Paths.

pieces.label: Let the Children Decide
pieces.text: Let the Children Decide.

Every night at the fire (subject.he/she) tells stories about {the waterfall that runs uphill|the village where everyone speaks in whispers|the lizard (subject.he/she) once shared a cave with}. The children pick twigs out of (subject.his/her) beard when (subject.he/she) dozes off.

On the first morning (subject.he/she) walks the gardens. This one wants more shade. That one is planted too deep. This weed is good to eat if it's boiled twice. The farmers follow (subject.him/her) around with their mouths open.

(subject.He/She) eats every bit of the stew, ties on the new sandals, and picks up the stick. "I thought this was the last one. But there's always one more path." (subject.He/She) walks off humming, and is never seen again.
(subject.He/She) sits by the fire "for a minute." On the third morning someone builds a little roof over the spot. Nobody ever says "you can stay." (subject.He/She) just never leaves.
(subject.He/She) draws a map of every path on the island in the dirt, and the researchers copy it before the rain comes.
The bag over one shoulder smells of every forest on the island.
The sandals are tied together with vine.
A small bird could live in that beard, and possibly does.
A long, contented sigh.

pieces.label: The Child from the Forest
pieces.text: Gathering deep in the forest, (finder) feels watched, and finds a thin, quiet child behind a tree, in a cloak of big green leaves stitched with grass, with a tiny brown bird on one shoulder; perhaps from the canoe wrecked on the far shore two seasons ago.

pieces.label: Bring the Child Home
pieces.text: (Finder) crouches down, so (finder.he/she) isn't so tall, and holds out (finder.his/her) hand instead of the fruit. The child looks at it for a very long time. The little bird on (finder.his/her) shoulder chirps, once...

pieces.label: Leave Food and Walk Away Slowly
pieces.text: (Finder) doesn't want to frighten the child. (finder.He/She) sets the fruit down on a flat stone, and a bundle of bread beside it, and backs away one slow step at a time, smiling, and then turns and walks off through the trees...

pieces.label: Sit Down and Wait
pieces.text: Sit Down and Wait.

pieces.label: Fetch Help from the Village
pieces.text: Fetch Help from the Village.

The child takes (finder)'s hand, very tightly, and doesn't let go for a whole month. Slowly the village takes the child in, and slowly the child lets go, just a little, to play with the others. The little brown bird stays too.
The child eats one bowl of mash, then another, then a third, and falls asleep by the fire, cloak of leaves and all. In the morning the child is still there, which everyone agrees is a very good sign.

Every week (finder) leaves food on the same flat stone, and every week it's gone. Once there's {a feather|a little carved stick|a perfect white shell} in its place. (Finder) never sees the child again, but never stops.
Little footsteps follow (finder) all the way through the forest, at a careful distance. At supper there's the child, on the other side of the fire, holding out an empty bowl.
By the time (finder) comes back with others, the child is gone, and only small footprints lead into the deep forest.
The cloak is made of big green leaves, stitched together with grass.
The tiny brown bird on the child's shoulder is perfectly calm.
Enormous dark eyes, watching.
One small step at a time.

pieces.label: The Moon's Mirror
pieces.text: On the one night a year the full moon sees itself perfectly in the lagoon, (wader) wades in up to (wader.his/her) waist to get closer to the moon in the water. When (wader.he/she) wades back out, there are two sets of footprints, two shadows, and a second (wader) standing dripping and smiling in the shallows.

pieces.label: Welcome the Second One
pieces.text: (Wader) takes a long breath. Then (wader.he/she) holds out (wader.his/her) hand. "Well," (wader.he/she) says, a little shakily. "You'd better come and get dry." The second one smiles (wader.his/her) own smile back...

pieces.label: Wait for Sunrise
pieces.text: (Wader) doesn't trust anything that comes out of the water by moonlight. (wader.He/She) sits down on the sand, arms round (wader.his/her) knees, and waits. The second one sits down too, a little way off, in exactly the same position. They wait together, in silence, for the dawn...

pieces.label: Ask It Where It Came From
pieces.text: Ask It Where It Came From.

pieces.label: Walk Back into the Water
pieces.text: Walk Back into the Water.

Same voice, same laugh, same habit of humming, same scar. The second one agrees to be called (made1) "to keep things simple," and goes straight to work doing exactly what (wader) would have done. It's very efficient, and slightly unsettling.
It takes (wader)'s hand, cool like the lagoon, then walks back into the water until it's over its head. When (wader) looks up, the moon in the water has gone.
At sunrise it's still there, complaining about the cold in exactly the same words as (wader), at exactly the same moment. They both burst out laughing, and the second one takes the name (made1).

As the first light touches the water, it gives (wader) a little wave and simply isn't there any more. (Wader) feels as if (wader.he/she) has done twice the work, or lived twice the night, and sleeps all the next day.
"From over there," it says, pointing at the moon in the water. It stays, and takes the name (made1).
(Wader) wades back in, and the second one wades out past (wader.him/her) without a glance, and is gone.
Two moons, one in the sky and one in the water, both exactly as bright.
Little silver fish leap through both moons at once, sending out rings of light.
The water is still and warm as a bath.
Two sets of footprints in the wet sand.

pieces.label: The Fire Spirit's Joke
pieces.text: (Arguer1) and (arguer2) have argued since supper about whose turn it is to keep the cooking fire going. "That was a NAP." The mischievous spirit in the fire has been listening. It bursts into blue sparks with a smoky little laugh, and when the smoke clears they are looking at each other's faces from the wrong side.

pieces.label: Apologise to the Fire
pieces.text: The two of them, in each other's bodies, kneel down in front of the embers together. "We're sorry," says (arguer1), in (arguer2)'s voice. "We'll take turns," says (arguer2), in (arguer1)'s. "Fairly." They put a fresh log on, together. The fire crackles, thinking about it...

pieces.label: Let It Burn Out
pieces.text: "Fine," says (arguer1), in the wrong voice. "Let it go out, then." "Fine," says (arguer2). "See if I care." They both fold their arms. And the fire, very slowly, dies down to embers, and to ash...

pieces.label: Feed It a Big Log
pieces.text: Feed It a Big Log.

pieces.label: Keep Arguing
pieces.text: Keep Arguing.

"We're sorry. We'll take turns. Fairly." The fire flares up warm and gold, and with a puff of blue smoke they are themselves again. They scratch a rota into the cooking hut doorpost and stick to it for life.
The fire seems satisfied. Mostly. A single blue spark pops, and nothing changes. They never quite learn to share, so they stay swapped, and now each argues the other one's side.
The last ember winks out with a cold little puff of grey smoke, and the magic goes out with it. Neither of them ever argues about the fire again, and both keep sneaking out at night to check on it.
The fire burns out. The magic doesn't. From that night on, both of them keep the fire going all night, every night, out of guilt. It's the best-kept fire in the village's history.
The log roars up, the fire laughs again, and they're themselves, with singed eyebrows.
"I did it yesterday." "You did it HALF of yesterday."
The fire sinks to a low, sulky orange glow.
A smoky, crackly, delighted little laugh.
An enormous crackle and a great burst of blue sparks.

pieces.label: The Blank Morning
pieces.text: (Yawner) wakes up to find a blank where (yawner.his/her) name should be. It must have slipped out in a yawn in the night, in the season of the thieving breeze, and blown away through the doorway. Outside, a rooster crows three times, as if it's trying to help.

pieces.label: Go Ask the Elders
pieces.text: (Yawner) goes to the elders' hut and explains, feeling very foolish. The elders don't laugh. They look at each other, and nod slowly, and one of them says, "Ah. A yawner."...

pieces.label: Carry On Without It
pieces.text: (Yawner) decides a name is not that important, really. (yawner.He/She) still knows how to farm and cook and build. So (yawner.he/she) gets up, eats breakfast, and goes off to work as if nothing has happened. People wave and open their mouths to say hello, and then look confused...

pieces.label: Follow the Breeze
pieces.text: Follow the Breeze.

pieces.label: Ask the Rooster
pieces.text: Ask the Rooster.

"Ah. A yawner." The elders have seen it before: once the wind's had a name, there's no getting it back, and it has taken the name out of every head in the village. (Yawner) is left with none at all: "?".
"Which way was the breeze blowing? Then go to the beach. Quickly." On the wet sand the breeze has traced the name in long, curling letters, and (yawner) reads it just as a wave washes it away.
(Yawner) gets along fine without one. The breeze took it out of everyone's head, so (yawner.he/she) is simply "?" now, and answers to a shrug and a smile.

At lunchtime the breeze turns round and blows the name back in through the doorway, past (yawner.his/her) ear. (yawner.He/She) says it out loud three times, and shuts the door every night for a month.
The breeze leads (yawner) up the hill to a tree full of rustling leaves, and the name (yawner.he/she) hears in them isn't quite the old one.
The rooster crows three times, very meaningfully. It does not help, and the breeze keeps the name.
(yawner.He/She) checks under the mat. It isn't there.
(yawner.He/She) checks behind the water jar, which is silly, but checks anyway.
Like a word on the tip of the tongue that won't come.
A rooster crows three times, as if trying to help.

pieces.label: The Elder's Gift of Years
pieces.text: The very old, very tired (giver) remembers a charm from (giver.his/her) grandmother for giving years to a loved one: one knot in a cord for every year, worn round the wrist until the knots untie themselves. (Beloved), the one (giver) loves best in all the world, has been sick for weeks, and (giver) is tying knots.

pieces.label: Let (Name1) Do It
pieces.text: (Giver) finishes the last knot, and holds the cord out with both shaking hands. (Beloved) lets (giver) tie it round (friend.his/her) wrist. That night they both lie awake, in their separate huts, listening...

pieces.label: Refuse the Gift
pieces.text: (Beloved) looks at the knotted cord in (giver)'s hands, and understands what it is. (friend.He/She) reaches out and closes (giver)'s fingers gently over it. "No," (beloved) says...

pieces.label: Tie Only One Knot
pieces.text: Tie Only One Knot.

pieces.label: Take It to the Healers
pieces.text: Take It to the Healers.

In the night the knots untie themselves with tiny soft sounds like a sigh. (Giver) wakes a little older and more silver, and (beloved) wakes stronger, the fever gone. (Beloved) holds (giver)'s hand all evening, and (giver) says "There, there."
In the morning every knot is still tied. "Well. I tried. It's the trying that counts." (Beloved) gets better slowly, with time and soup and rest, and never takes the cord off.
"Keep your years. Every single one. I want you around." (Giver) puts the cord away, and teaches (beloved) to shell beans properly. (Beloved) gets better the ordinary way.
The cord is already round (beloved)'s wrist from the measuring, and the knots untie the wrong way round. Both wake five years younger, and (giver) laughs so hard (giver.he/she) has to sit down.
One knot, one year, and (beloved)'s fever breaks by morning.
The healers don't believe in charms, but keep the cord by (beloved)'s bed anyway. (Beloved) recovers within the week.
Shelling beans in the shade, watching the children chase crabs on the sand.
One knot for every year.
The knots untie with tiny soft sounds, like a sigh.
"There, there."

pieces.label: Old Friends Again
pieces.text: Years ago (sweetheart1) and (sweetheart2) were sweethearts, until they drifted apart over different work, different friends and a quarrel nobody can remember. Tonight, at the harvest dance, with torches in the sand and the air smelling of roasted corn and frangipani, they end up standing side by side, and neither moves away.

pieces.label: Dance Together
pieces.text: (Sweetheart2) holds out a hand, a little awkwardly, the way (friend.he/she) used to all those years ago. (Sweetheart1) looks at it, and laughs, and takes it. The drums pick up. They step out into the torchlight together...

pieces.label: Just Talk
pieces.text: Neither of them is quite brave enough to dance. So instead, they drift away from the drums together, down to the quiet end of the beach, and sit on an upturned canoe, and (sweetheart1) says, "So. How have you been?"...

pieces.label: Walk on the Beach
pieces.text: Walk on the Beach.

pieces.label: Pretend Not to Notice
pieces.text: Pretend Not to Notice.

They dance until the drummers' arms give out, as if the years in between never happened. A few weeks later, at dawn on the beach, (sweetheart1) tells (sweetheart2) (sweetheart1.he/she) is pregnant, and (sweetheart2) spins (sweetheart1.him/her) round in the surf.
Sitting on the sand with their feet in the water, they both say it at the same time: they're better as friends. It's a relief, actually, and they dance together at every festival after.

On an upturned canoe they talk all night, and the old quarrel turns out to have been about {a fish|a goat|whose turn it was to fetch water}. They move in together that week, and a few weeks later the whole village says it's about time.
They talk about the old days, and it's lovely, but it's the past. (Sweetheart2) squeezes (sweetheart1)'s hand once, and they go home to their own huts, smiling.
Pretending works for one song. On the second, someone bumps them together, and they laugh, and dance after all.
The air smells of roasted corn and frangipani.
Torches are stuck in the sand all along the beach.
(Sweetheart2) holds out a hand, a little awkwardly, the way (friend.he/she) used to.
Neither of them moves away.

pieces.label: The Magic Seed
pieces.text: A bright blue bird with a long gold tail flies over the cooking fire at lunchtime and drops a tiny shimmering seed, plop, into (eater)'s soup. (Eater), talking to (friend), eats it without noticing, and that night dreams of a little green sprout growing in the middle of (eater.his/her) heart.

pieces.label: Ask the Healers
pieces.text: In the morning, (eater) tells (friend) about the dream, and the seed that somebody saw drop into the soup. (Friend) insists they go to the healers right away. The healers listen, very seriously, and then put their ears to (eater)'s chest, and then lower...

pieces.label: Wait and See
pieces.text: (Eater) decides not to make a fuss over a dream. (eater.He/She) and (friend) wait, and go about their days, and say nothing to anyone. But every night, the dream comes back: the little green sprout, a little bigger each time...

pieces.label: Plant Another Seed
pieces.text: Plant Another Seed.

pieces.label: Look for the Bird
pieces.text: Look for the Bird.
The oldest healer listens for a long time and sits back. "Well. I've heard of it. I never thought I'd see it." (Eater) is going to have a baby, and (friend) has to sit down on the floor.
Just a seed, the healers say. Probably a nice one. (Eater) and (friend) are a little disappointed, and that evening both keep looking up for a flash of blue.

Something grows, slowly, quietly, like the sprout in the dream. The baby arrives with a tiny green birthmark shaped like a leaf, and that morning the blue bird sits on the roof, and is never seen again.
No baby, no magic. Except that (eater) suddenly, very much, wants to garden, and starts a little garden behind the hut. (Friend) brings (eater.him/her) lunch.
A strange blue-leaved vine comes up overnight, heavy with sweet fruit.
(Eater) and (friend) follow the bird for three days, and come back with nothing but sunburn and a very good story.
The gold tail streams out behind it like a ribbon.
The seed glints like a drop of water in the sun.
Plop, right into the soup.
A little green sprout, curling up out of the earth.

pieces.label: The Swarm
pieces.text: At noon the sky goes dark with no clouds. A dry, rattling hiss rises, as if the whole island were being shaken in a giant gourd of seeds, and a brown cloud of millions of grasshoppers strips the fields in moments and turns towards the food store.

pieces.label: Light Smoky Fires
pieces.text: "Smoke! They hate smoke!" one of the elders shouts. Everyone runs for wet leaves, green branches, damp thatch, anything that will burn badly, and piles it on fires all round the food store. Thick grey smoke billows up...

pieces.label: Catch Them
pieces.text: "Catch them?!" "Catch them! They're FOOD!" Every basket, net, pot, cloth and bare hand in the village is pressed into service, and everyone runs out into the whirring cloud, scooping, grabbing, shrieking, laughing...

pieces.label: Cover the Store
pieces.text: Cover the Store.

pieces.label: Bang Drums and Shout
pieces.text: Bang Drums and Shout.

Wet leaves, green branches and damp thatch on every fire. The cloud wavers, whirring angrily, and pours away over the hills. Most of them. The rest eat a little of everything before they're swept out.
For a moment it works. Then the wind turns, blows the smoke back into the villagers' eyes, and drives the grasshoppers straight into the food store in a great whirring wave.
"Catch them! They're FOOD!" Roasted by the potful, they taste a lot like crunchy nuts, and with a bit of salt they're delicious. The fields are bare, but the stores are full to bursting.
Basket after basket, until their arms ache. But there are millions, and while everyone is catching them in the fields, the rest of the cloud settles on the food store and eats its way through it.
Every spare mat and cloth goes over the store, and the swarm passes over it hungry.
They chew through the mats. They chew through the thatch. They chew through {a sandal|a hat|most of a fishing net}.
The island sounds as if it is being shaken in a giant gourd full of seeds.
A brown, whirring cloud so thick the sun can't be seen through it.
The crops vanish under them in moments.
A dry, rattling hiss, louder and louder.

pieces.label: The Soft Yams
pieces.text: Somebody opens the yam store and slams the door shut again: rain has been seeping in under the back wall for days, and the yams have gone soft, black and wet, with flies crawling over every one.

pieces.label: Throw Them Out
pieces.text: Nobody wants to do it. In the end, the whole village draws straws, ties wet cloths over their faces, and goes in together in a long chain, passing out the slimy black yams hand over hand to be dumped far away beyond the gardens...

pieces.label: Try to Save Some
pieces.text: "Wait," say the researchers. "Not all of it's gone. If we cut out the bad parts..." Everyone looks at them as if they're mad. The researchers tie cloths over their faces, take their sharpest knives, and go in...
Every yam is thrown out, even the ones that look all right, and the store is scrubbed with sand and seawater. Nobody eats a yam for a month, and, rather surprisingly, nobody complains.
Right at the very bottom, packed down in cool sand, the last yams are dry, firm and perfect. It isn't much, but it's something.
The researchers slice the good parts thin and dry them on hot rocks until they're hard as bark. Not tasty, but food, and it keeps for months.
(Taster) takes a bite of one of the soft ones to check. "Seems all right." By evening (taster.he/she) is very, very sick, and everything is thrown out after all.
The smell drifts out under the door and across the village.
Rainwater has been seeping in under the back wall for days.
Everyone ties wet cloths over their faces.
The whole village draws straws.

pieces.label: The Flood
pieces.text: After nine days of rain, the river comes over its banks with a deep, groaning roar and pours through the village, and there's only time to save the food store or the research notes.

pieces.label: Save the Food
pieces.text: "The store! The store!" Everyone wades for the food store, waist-deep in the brown water now, forming a chain to pass the baskets up the hill to the high ground, one after another, while the water climbs...

pieces.label: Save the Research Notes
pieces.text: "The notes! Years of work!" The researchers and half the village wade for the research hut and carry out armful after armful of scrolls, holding them high above their heads, struggling up the hill with the water pulling at their legs...
The food is carried up to the hilltop, dry and safe, but the river goes in through the research hut door and out through the window, and the notes end up as a brown, soggy paste on the floor.
The food is saved, and at the last moment the water turns round the research hut instead of through it. It leaves rich black mud on the fields, and everything planted in it comes up twice as fast.
The notes are saved, but the walls of the food store give way with a long, wet groan, and baskets and pots go sailing off downstream towards the sea. It's a very hungry season afterwards.

By some miracle everything is saved: the notes, the food, the tools, the babies, the goats. The only casualty is one villager's favourite hat, last seen floating out to sea the right way up, as if it's going on a holiday.
Frogs sit on every doorstep, looking very pleased with themselves.
A canoe floats by, upside down.
Nothing anybody owns is dry.
A deep, groaning roar that everybody hears at once.

pieces.label: The Library in the Wreck
pieces.text: A great storm uncovers an old shipwreck crusted with orange coral on the reef, and wedged inside it (diver) finds a chest sealed with black tar, full of flat bundles of thin leaves covered in tiny marks.

pieces.label: Bring It Ashore
pieces.text: It takes (diver) and three of the strongest swimmers all morning to haul the heavy chest up out of the wreck and tow it back across the reef to the beach. The whole village crowds round as the researchers lift the lid...

pieces.label: Leave It
pieces.text: (Diver) looks at the chest for a long time, hanging there in the cold water among the coral. Somebody put this here. Somebody sealed it, carefully, against the sea. (diver.He/She) closes the lid, gently, and swims back up to the light...
Nobody can read the marks, but there are hundreds of drawings: tools, boats, plants, stars, the insides of things. The drawings alone teach the researchers more than a whole year of study.
The moment the bundles touch the sun they crumble and blow away along the beach. But (diver) looked at the first few pages for a long time underwater, and draws a few of them again in the sand.
"Whoever owned it might come back for it. It's not ours." Nobody ever does. The coral grows over the lid, and the wreck sinks back into the sand.
A week later another storm washes the chest up on the beach, lid closed, as if it's waiting for someone. "All right," (diver) sighs. "If you insist."
The ribs stick up out of the water like the bones of a great fish.
Little striped fish dart away through the broken hull.
Black tar seals the lid.
(Diver) prises the lid open underwater with (diver.his/her) knife.

pieces.label: A Stranger's Recipe
pieces.text: A passing trader wraps a fresh fish in big green leaves and buries it on glowing-hot stones under sand, "how we do it at home," and the smoke smells so good that half the village is pretending to pass by.

pieces.label: Try It Right Away
pieces.text: When the trader finally digs the fish out and unwraps the steaming leaves, the smell rolls out over everyone like a warm wave. (Learner) takes the first bite. Then (learner.he/she) asks to try making one (learner.himself/herself), right now...

pieces.label: Write It Down for Later
pieces.text: (Learner) fetches a piece of bark and a burnt stick and asks the trader to go through it all again, slowly, every step, while (learner.he/she) writes it all down: how hot the stones, which leaves, how long to wait...

The fish falls apart like butter and tastes of green and smoke. (Learner) learns it on the spot, with the trader laughing and correcting (learner.him/her), and that night makes a whole row of it for the village.

(Learner) gets bored of waiting, digs it up early, puts it on the fire and gets distracted. The fish becomes a small black lump that smokes when poked. The trader laughs, then shows (learner.him/her) again, slower.
Copied neatly onto good bark and pinned to the cooking hut wall, it becomes the village's favourite dish for weddings and festivals. Nobody remembers it came from a stranger, except (learner).
(Learner) tucks the bark into a pocket and can't find it anywhere. A year later it turns up in an old wrap, smudged and faded. All (learner.he/she) can still read is "...then you wait."
"Slow. You wait. Then you eat."
Smoke curls up out of the sand.
Several people have been "just passing" for quite some time.
Stones heated in the fire until they glow.

pieces.label: The Coral Reef Dive
pieces.text: (Diver) has gone a little deeper on the reef every day, and today (diver.he/she) wants to touch the bottom, where the water fades from green, to blue, to a cold dark blue that seems to go on forever.

pieces.label: Dive Deep
pieces.text: (Diver) jack-knifes and kicks down, hard, along the coral wall. Ten strokes. Twenty. The light fades. The water turns cold, then colder. (diver.His/her) ears ache. (diver.His/her) chest starts to burn. The bottom is right there, pale sand in the dark blue...

pieces.label: Stay Near the Surface
pieces.text: (Diver) looks down into the dark blue for a long, long time. Then (diver.he/she) lets the breath out slowly, and shakes (diver.his/her) head, and decides the bottom will still be there tomorrow. (diver.He/She) dives along the bright, sunny top of the reef instead...
(Diver)'s fingers sink into cold, soft sand. (diver.He/She) grabs two handfuls of shells and kicks for the light, bursting out into the sunshine gasping and grinning so wide it hurts.

A shell is stuck, and (diver) pulls a moment too long. The others dive in and find (diver.him/her) halfway up the coral wall, but it is too late. The village mourns a fearless diver who loved the deep blue more than anyone.

There's plenty near the surface for anyone who looks carefully: fat shellfish in the coral, crabs under ledges, little silver fish for the net. (Diver) comes home sunburnt and safe with a full basket.

Halfway back to the canoe, (diver)'s leg cramps, knotting up like a fist. (diver.He/She) swallows what feels like half the sea and only just makes it to shore. After that, no deeper than (diver.his/her) ankles.
Fish like scattered jewels.
Slow green turtles drift past.
(diver.His/her) ears ache and (diver.his/her) chest burns.
Ten strokes. Twenty. The light fades.

pieces.label: The Sinking Sand
pieces.text: (Sinker) has forgotten which patch of grey sand by the river mouth is the sinking one, and is now standing right in the middle of it, up to (sinker.his/her) knees, cold and thick and sucking, and going down fast.

pieces.label: Lie Flat and Wriggle
pieces.text: (Sinker) remembers what the elders always said: don't fight it, spread out, lie down. Every part of (sinker.him/her) wants to struggle, but (sinker.he/she) forces (sinker.himself/herself) to lean back, slowly, and spread (sinker.his/her) arms wide across the surface of the sand...

pieces.label: Shout for Help
pieces.text: (Sinker) shouts. (sinker.He/She) shouts as loud as (sinker.he/she) has ever shouted in (sinker.his/her) life, again and again, while the sand creeps up to (sinker.his/her) thighs, then (sinker.his/her) waist. Up on the bank, a fisher turns round, drops (sinker.his/her) net, and starts to run...
Lying flat on (sinker.his/her) back like a starfish, (sinker) wriggles out a finger's width at a time. It takes most of the afternoon, and (sinker.he/she) washes in the river for an hour.

The sand is deeper and softer than (sinker.he/she) thought. By the time help comes running, the grey sand is smooth and still, with only a few reeds lying on top. The village puts a ring of white stones around it, so no one forgets again.
A long branch, a rope, everyone pulling together, and (sinker) comes out with a great wet sucking sound, like a cork out of a gourd, minus one sandal. The sandal is never seen again.

In (sinker.his/her) panic (sinker) twists to climb out too fast, and something deep in (sinker.his/her) leg wrenches and gives. (sinker.He/She) walks with a limp from then on, and running hurts too much to bear.
It smells, very faintly, of rotten eggs.
It looks just like the sand around it, which is the whole problem.
Children are warned about it from the time they can walk.
Every move pulls (sinker.him/her) a little further down.

pieces.label: The Whispering Cave
pieces.text: Deep in the hills there's a cave curtained with long pale roots that sighs out cold air, where the elders say the island keeps the voices of those it has lost, and today (listener) hears (listener.his/her) own name in it, like someone (listener.he/she) loved long ago calling (listener.him/her) in for supper.

pieces.label: Go In
pieces.text: (Listener) pushes the roots aside. They're cold and damp against (listener.his/her) arms. The whisper grows a little louder, and a little closer, and (listener) follows it into the dark, one hand on the wall...

pieces.label: Stay Out
pieces.text: (Listener) stands there at the mouth for a long time, (listener.his/her) heart thumping, with the voice saying (listener.his/her) name over and over. Then (listener.he/she) turns away, and makes (listener.himself/herself) walk home without looking back...
Where the cave opens out, a thin beam of light falls on an ancient painting of the village: every hut in its place, even (listener)'s crooked doorpost, painted long before the village was ever built.
(Listener) follows the voice until the light from the mouth is gone, and never comes out. That night, for the first time anyone can remember, the cave stops whispering.

The whisper follows (listener.him/her) home, every night: from just outside the door, from under the mat, from right beside (listener.his/her) ear. Nobody else hears it. It stops after a week, but (listener) never trusts the dark again.

Four researchers go up with torches, ropes and a lot of nervous jokes, hear nothing at all, and find a hidden store behind a fall of rocks: wax-sealed clay jars full of very old dried fruit, still good.
Long pale roots hang over the mouth like a curtain.
Cold air sighs out even on the hottest day.
The elders say it holds the voices of people the island has lost.
A thin beam of light falls from a crack in the roof.

pieces.label: The Long Illness
pieces.text: (Patient) has been ill for weeks with a fever that comes and goes like the tide, and (healer), the oldest healer, offers a very strong old remedy that nobody has used in years, or rest.

pieces.label: Try the Old Remedy
pieces.text: (healer) spends a whole day making it, grinding roots and boiling bark and muttering over the pot. It's thick and black and smells like a swamp. (Patient) drinks it, one bitter spoonful at a time, and then lies back, and the whole village waits...

pieces.label: Rest and Wait
pieces.text: The village decides not to risk it. They keep (patient) warm and quiet. They take turns sitting with (patient.him/her), day and night, holding (patient.his/her) hand, wiping (patient.his/her) face with cool cloths, and singing soft songs when (patient.he/she) can't sleep...

Thick and black and smelling like a swamp, the old remedy works. On the fifth day (patient) sits up and asks, in a perfectly ordinary voice, whether there's anything to eat, and everybody who hears it bursts into tears.

The remedy breaks the fever, but it's a hard, cruel thing to drink. (Patient) is never as strong again: (patient.his/her) hands shake when (patient.he/she) lifts anything heavy, and work that used to be easy becomes too hard.
One morning, with no warning at all, (patient) wakes up well. "How long was I asleep?" Nearly a month. (patient.He/She) eats every bowl of soup in the hut.
The fever goes, but takes something with it. (Patient) is left weak and tired for good, and (patient.his/her) quick mind gets foggy whenever (patient.he/she) tries to learn anything new.
The hut smells of bitter tea and burnt herbs.
Bowls of soup are left by the door.
The fever comes and goes like the tide.
The villagers take turns sitting with (patient.him/her), day and night.

pieces.label: The Snake in the Basket
pieces.text: In the dim, cool storehouse, (gatherer) hums to (gatherer.himself/herself), reaches into the big basket in the corner for a yam without looking, and touches something smooth, cool and moving.

pieces.label: Pull Your Hand Out Fast
pieces.text: (Gatherer) doesn't think. (gatherer.He/She) yanks (gatherer.his/her) arm out of the basket as hard and as fast as (gatherer.he/she) can, staggering backwards across the storehouse, and yams go flying everywhere...

pieces.label: Stay Very Still
pieces.text: (Gatherer) remembers what the elders say about snakes: they only bite if they're frightened. So (gatherer.he/she) doesn't move. Not a finger. (gatherer.He/She) stands there, arm deep in the basket, barely breathing, while the snake decides what to do...

Fast enough. Yams fly everywhere, and a long brown snake pokes its head over the basket, looks at (gatherer) with deep offence, and slithers out into the sunshine. (Gatherer) never reaches into a basket without looking again.
Not fast enough. The snake strikes, quick as a thought, and by evening (gatherer)'s hand is red and hot and the size of a coconut.

The snake coils round (gatherer.his/her) wrist, heavy and cool, and lifts its head to look at (gatherer.him/her) for a very long moment. Then it slips away. (Gatherer) doesn't move for another hour, just in case.
The snake bites anyway: just two small marks, and an hour later the poison starts. The world goes swimmy and strange, and it's a week with the healers before (gatherer) is well.
Dust floats lazily in the single beam of light.
Smooth, and cool, and moving.
A soft, dry rustle among the yams.
Then a quiet hiss.

pieces.label: The Robe That Shrank
pieces.text: Somebody, and nobody will say who, has washed the Chief's robe in boiling hot water with the cooking pots, and now it's steaming, smells overpoweringly of wet feathers and fish stew, and would fit a child.

pieces.label: Make a New Robe
pieces.text: Chief (chief) takes a long, deep breath, folds the tiny robe very neatly, and hands it to the weavers. "I'd like," (chief.he/she) says, with enormous dignity, "a new one." The weavers bow very low and hurry away...

pieces.label: Wear It Anyway
pieces.text: Chief (chief) looks at the tiny steaming robe for a long, long moment. Then (chief.he/she) sets (chief.his/her) jaw. "Nobody," (chief.he/she) says, "tells the Chief what to wear." And (chief.he/she) starts to put it on...

The weavers outdo themselves: longer, richer, more feathers, and a pattern of waves along the hem. Chief (chief) is delighted, and announces that the Chief's robe is to be washed by the Chief, personally, in cold water.
Terrified of making it too small, the weavers make it quite a lot too big. Chief (chief) trips over it at every ceremony for the rest of the year, and the children walk behind holding up the hem.

It takes three people pulling, but Chief (chief) squeezes into it and announces that this is the new style, from far away. By the end of the week, two of the younger villagers have shrunk their own clothes on purpose.

Halfway through a long and serious speech, the robe splits all the way down the back with a long, loud RRRRIP. Chief (chief) laughs louder than anyone, and the village loves (chief.him/her) for it, more than ever.
It smells overpoweringly of wet feathers and fish stew.
The builders are very interested in a fence.
The farmers are examining a cloud.
Steam is still rising off it.

pieces.label: The Tree Blossoms Early
pieces.text: The Tree of Life bursts into blossom a whole season early, after unusually warm rains, petals the colour of sunrise drift into every soup pot, and bees come from all over the island in a great humming golden cloud.

pieces.label: Gather the Blossoms
pieces.text: Out come the baskets and the long poles. The villagers spread cloths under the Tree and shake the lower branches, very gently, and the blossoms come tumbling down like warm snow, while the bees grumble overhead...

pieces.label: Leave Them on the Tree
pieces.text: The elders say that something this rare should be left alone. So nobody picks a single blossom. They let them be. The village just stops and looks at them, every morning and every evening, for as long as they last...
A handful dropped into hot water turns it the colour of a sunrise, sweet and soft and a little bit like honey. There's sunrise tea at every meal for the whole season, and a sweet blossom bread.
The blossoms are too delicate, and by lunchtime the baskets are full of soggy brown petals. The Tree, still covered in flowers, doesn't seem to mind, and the petals sink into its roots.
Where every blossom was, there's a tiny green bud of fruit, and it ripens much earlier than ever before. The Tree gives the village a whole harvest, heavy and sweet.
Camped under the Tree for a week, the researchers notice the blossoms open at sunrise and close at sunset, all at once, every single one, and that the Tree is warm to the touch.
The smell is like walking into a wall of honey.
Petals drift into every soup pot.
The children are running about trying to catch them.
The bees come in a great humming golden cloud.

pieces.label: The Sculptor
pieces.text: After months of tapping, with stone chips in (sculptor.his/her) hair, bed and sandals, (sculptor) finishes a small stone figure of a sitting elder so lifelike that people keep saying hello to it as they walk past.

pieces.label: Carve Another
pieces.text: (Sculptor) looks at the finished figure for a long time, with a little frown. It's good. But (sculptor.he/she) can already see how it could be better. The very next morning, (sculptor.he/she) is out by the quarry, choosing another stone...

pieces.label: Give It Away
pieces.text: (Sculptor) didn't carve it to keep. (sculptor.He/She) picks it up carefully, wraps it in a soft cloth, and carries it through the village, trying to decide who should have it...

The second figure takes half as long and is twice as good: a woman holding a baby, so real that people swear they can see the baby breathing. By the end of the season (sculptor) is carving the posts for every new hut, a true master.

(Sculptor) taps the chisel once too hard, and with a little dry crack, the head falls off and lands on (sculptor.his/her) foot. (sculptor.He/She) throws the chisel into the bushes, and gives up carving for good.
The elders put it in the place of honour by their fire, and ask (sculptor) to carve the posts for the new huts. Soon the whole village is full of carved faces and birds and waves.

A little child who has been staring at it for weeks is overjoyed, carries it everywhere, and loses it within a week. A long time later it turns up in the river shallows, watching the fish go by, and (sculptor) decides to leave it there.
Tap, tap, tap.
Stone chips in (sculptor.his/her) hair, in (sculptor.his/her) bed, in (sculptor.his/her) sandals.
People keep saying hello to it as they walk past.
A gentle, sleepy face.

pieces.label: The Clay Copy
pieces.text: The clay figure of (potter.himself/herself) that (potter) made for fun, from clay dug below the old spirit tree, is such a good likeness that in the middle of the night it sits up on the shelf, stretches its little arms, and starts to grow.

pieces.label: Say Hello
pieces.text: By the time it climbs down off the shelf, it's as tall as (potter), and its clay skin is turning soft and warm in the moonlight. (Potter) sits up on (potter.his/her) mat, swallows hard, and says, "...Hello?"...

pieces.label: Pretend It's Not Happening
pieces.text: (Potter) decides that this is a dream, and the best thing to do with a dream is to ignore it. (potter.He/She) lies back down, pulls the blanket over (potter.his/her) head, squeezes (potter.his/her) eyes tight shut, and does not look...

"Hello," it says, in a voice a little lower and a little dustier than (potter)'s. By morning it's a real person who looks exactly like (potter) but likes completely different things. It picks the name (made1), and its bowls are much better than (potter)'s.

It smiles (potter)'s own crooked smile, sits down very carefully, and shrinks back like a sandcastle in a rising tide, until it crumbles into a little heap of dry grey clay. (Potter) doesn't make another figure.
In the morning it's full-size, real, humming to itself, stirring a pot of mash with exactly the right amount of honey. "You're awake. Sit down." It decides to be called (made1), and stays.
In the morning it's back on the shelf, small again, its eyes closed, its little clay face peaceful and hard as stone. It never moves again. (Potter) never quite trusts it, all the same.
A row of lopsided bowls and wonky cups.
The nose is just right, and so is the little crease between the eyebrows.
A soft, dry, scraping sound.
Its clay skin turns soft and warm in the moonlight.

pieces.label: Too Many Cooks
pieces.text: Twelve villagers have all decided to help with tonight's stew at the same time, nobody agrees on anything, someone has added fruit "to balance out the fish," and there may be a sandal in it.

pieces.label: Let Them Carry On
pieces.text: Nobody wants to be the one to tell twelve people with spoons to stop. So the cooking goes on. And on. More things go in. Some things come out. One of them is definitely a sandal. The pot bubbles ominously...

pieces.label: Pick One Cook
pieces.text: (elder), one of the elders, bangs a spoon on the side of the pot. "ENOUGH! One cook!" Everyone falls silent. Then everyone points at everyone else. In the end the elders pick (cook), who was standing on the log, and everyone else is sent to sit down...

It's brown. And purple. And green in places. But everybody made it, so everybody eats it, pulling faces and laughing until they cry. Years later, "it's a twelve-cook stew" still means anything that's gone horribly wrong.
Somehow it's the best stew anyone has ever eaten. Everyone asks for the recipe, the twelve cooks all give completely different answers, and nobody can ever make it again.

(Cook) fishes out the sandal, tips out half the pot, adds fresh water and roots and a few careful herbs, and lets it simmer while eleven people watch with their arms folded. A fine stew. They all have seconds.
With eleven people saying "I'd add a bit more...", (cook) argues about salt until the bottom of the stew burns black and sticks to the pot. They eat bread for supper.
The smallest stirrer is standing on a log to reach.
Someone has added fruit "to balance out the fish."
There may be a sandal in it.
The pot bubbles ominously.

pieces.label: The Goat That Followed (Name) Home
pieces.text: A wild goat with one bent horn, a beard like a paintbrush and a voice like a rusty hinge has decided that (friend) is its best friend in all the world, follows (friend.him/her) everywhere, and has eaten (friend.his/her) hat.

pieces.label: Keep the Goat
pieces.text: (Friend) looks down at the goat. The goat looks up at (friend), chewing what remains of (friend.his/her) second-best sandal. "Fine," (friend) says. "Fine. But you sleep outside." The goat bleats like a rusty door, and comes inside anyway...

pieces.label: Walk It Back to the Hills
pieces.text: (Friend) ties a bit of vine round the goat's neck and leads it up the hill path, out past the last of the gardens, all the way up into the high grass where the wild goats live. The goat trots along beside (friend.him/her) happily the whole way...

(Friend), never known for patience, turns out to have an endless supply of it. (friend.He/She) teaches the goat not to eat the thatch, mostly, and soon finds (friend.himself/herself) minding the village children too. Goats and children are not so different.

The goat eats the seedlings, the thatch off the research hut, one of the research scrolls, and then the replacement seedlings. After a week of replanting, (friend) can't look at a seed without groaning.

(Friend) takes off the vine at the top of the hill, says goodbye, and walks back down. The goat walks back down with (friend.him/her), step for step, in time for supper, and eats (friend.his/her) supper.

At the top of the hill, the goat sees a small herd of wild goats, pulls its head out of the vine, and trots off without one single backward look. (Friend) walks home alone, surprised to find (friend.he/she) is a little bit hurt.
A beard like a paintbrush.
A voice like a rusty hinge.
Strange yellow eyes full of deep and complete love.
It tried to eat (friend.his/her) hair.

pieces.label: The Mask Seller
pieces.text: A traveller lays out rows of carved, painted masks from a lightning-struck tree on a ribboned cloth, "Anyone can be anything, for a little while," and (wearer) can't choose between a bird mask with blue and green feathers and a big, round, painted laughing face.

pieces.label: Try the Bird Mask
pieces.text: The seller lifts the bird mask and ties it on (wearer)'s face with a soft cord. It's light as a leaf. The feathers brush (wearer.his/her) cheeks. Through the eye holes the world looks somehow higher, and brighter, and very far away...

pieces.label: Try the Laughing Face
pieces.text: The seller ties on the big round laughing face. It's heavy and warm, and smells of old wood and paint. For a moment nothing happens. Then (wearer) feels a giggle coming up from somewhere very deep...

(Wearer) loves it so much that (wearer.he/she) trades (wearer.his/her) very best basket, the one (wearer.his/her) grandmother made, on the spot, and wears it to every festival, dancing with (wearer.his/her) arms out like wings. The children call (wearer.him/her) "the bird."

(Wearer) opens (wearer.his/her) mouth, and what comes out is "CAW." Then "Kreeee." Then "Hoo hoo." The children are absolutely delighted. (Wearer) is not, and tears the mask off, and the words come back.
(Wearer) laughs for an hour, at the crowd, at the sky, at the very idea of feet, and gets up feeling lighter than in years. Some old grudge has simply been laughed away.

In the seller's bronze mirror, somehow it fits. "Keep it. It suits you." (Wearer) starts painting (wearer.his/her) own face to match on festival days, and the whole village learns to look forward to it.
Bird faces with long beaks, fish faces with round staring eyes.
Bright ribbons tied to the corners of the cloth flutter in the wind.
"Anyone can be anything, for a little while."
"Lightning always leaves a little of itself behind."

pieces.label: The Second Name Day
pieces.text: (Builder) has built a proper bridge over the stream, with a handrail, in one afternoon, all alone, and the elders are gathering in their best cloaks with their tall feather staffs and the big carved drum to give (builder.him/her) a second name.

pieces.label: Accept the New Name
pieces.text: (Builder) steps forward and kneels on the new bridge, while the drum beats slowly. (elder), the oldest elder, lifts the feather staff high over (builder.his/her) head, and the whole village holds its breath...

pieces.label: Keep Your Own Name
pieces.text: (Builder) steps forward and bows low to the elders. "Thank you," (builder.he/she) says. "But I like the name I have. My mother gave it to me." The drum stops. The elders look at each other...

The drum booms three times, and (builder) becomes (renamed). From then on, whenever a bridge is needed anywhere on the island, (renamed) is the one they ask, and the bridges get longer and stronger and finer.

The elders argue all night about which name to give, and at dawn, tired and cross, settle on (renamed). Nobody likes it, and certainly not (builder). It sticks anyway. Names given by the drum always do.
"Then the bridge shall have the name instead." The elders bless the bridge and carve its new name into the handrail, and children who cross it are told (builder)'s name, and remember it.
(Builder) keeps (builder.his/her) own name. Officially. From that day on, nobody calls (builder.him/her) anything but "the bridge one." "The bridge one's in the river again."
Strong enough to carry a goat.
Everyone has been walking across it and back, just for fun.
The big carved drum only comes out on very special days.
Tall feather staffs.

pieces.label: The Mirror Twins
pieces.text: On the rare night of a double moonbow, when the elders say still water becomes a doorway, (bather) bathes in a still forest pool ringed with white lilies, and someone with (bather.his/her) face and scars climbs out after (bather.him/her).

pieces.label: Bring (Him/Her) Home
