pieces.text: (Bather) doesn't know what else to do. (bather.He/She) holds out (bather.his/her) spare wrap, and the newcomer takes it with (bather)'s own hands, and puts it on exactly the way (bather) would, and they set off through the trees together...

pieces.label: Ask Who (He/She) Is
pieces.text: (Bather) stands very still on the bank, dripping, (bather.his/her) heart racing, and looks the newcomer right in the eye. "Who are you?" (bather.he/she) asks. The newcomer opens its mouth...

They walk home side by side, in step, in silence, and in the firelight it is a perfect copy of (bather) in every way. When the elders ask what it would like to be called, it thinks, head on one side, exactly the way (bather) thinks. "(made1). If that's all right." It is.

It follows (bather) halfway home, its bare feet making no sound. Where the path bends, it stops at the edge of the trees, smiles (bather)'s own smile, raises one hand, and steps back into the trees as the moonbow fades.
"I'm you," it says, simply, in (bather)'s own voice. Then it wrinkles its nose, exactly the way (bather) does. "But you'd better call me (made1). It's less confusing."

It just smiles, warm and a little sad, and as the double moonbow fades, so does the newcomer, like a reflection in water when a cloud goes over the moon. (Bather) is left alone among the white lilies.
A double moonbow, pale and silver.
Every drop rings like a tiny bell.
Twisting (bather.his/her) hair to the left, exactly the way (bather) does.
The elders say it's a night when the island is thin.

pieces.label: The Child Who Grew Up Overnight
pieces.text: After weeks of complaining that (child.he/she) is too small, too small, too small, (child) wishes on a falling star, and wakes with (child.his/her) feet sticking a long way out of the end of (child.his/her) sleeping mat.

pieces.label: Go to Work
pieces.text: (Child) leaps up, banging (child.his/her) head on the roof beam, and runs out into the village. "I'm big!" (child.he/she) shouts to everyone. "I can help now! Give me something to do!" The adults look at each other...

pieces.label: Wish It Back
pieces.text: (Child) looks down at (child.his/her) long new legs, and (child.his/her) big new hands, and at (child.his/her) parents' faces, and suddenly doesn't feel so sure about any of this. That night (child.he/she) goes back out to the beach and lies on the sand, watching the sky, waiting for another falling star...
Long-legged, gangly and very keen, (child) carries water, hauls firewood, digs and fishes, and at lunch falls asleep sitting up, spoon still in hand. Being big is a lot harder than it looks.

A real grown-up overnight, who still holds the hoe upside down and ties knots that fall apart. The adults show (child.him/her) everything, one thing at a time, and (child) learns much faster than anyone expected.

Very late in the night, a star streaks across the sky over the sea, and (child) wishes on it as hard as (child.he/she) has ever wished. In the morning (child.his/her) feet fit, and (child.he/she) runs around the village hugging everyone.
The next falling star never comes, not for weeks. (Child) stays a teenager, and (child.his/her) old friends decide they're still allowed to play with (child.him/her), sometimes.
Too small, too small, too small.
(child.His/her) feet stick out a long way past the mat.
The breakfast bowl looks far too small.
(child.He/She) bangs (child.his/her) head on the roof beam.

pieces.label: The Feast for the Elders
pieces.text: The village has decided the elders have done quite enough work for one lifetime and deserve a huge feast under the great banyan tree; the elders protest they're not even hungry, until they see the food, and the children chase them with flower crowns.

pieces.label: Spare No Expense
pieces.text: Out comes everything: the best fish, the sweetest fruit, the special bread, the honey cakes that are only made at weddings. Platter after platter after platter, until the mats under the banyan tree can't hold any more...

pieces.label: Keep It Simple
pieces.text: The stores are not what they could be this season, so the village keeps it simple: a good warm meal under the banyan tree, flower crowns, and everyone sitting together...
The feast lasts all night, and then the elders tell stories nobody under fifty has ever heard, until the sun comes up. The whole village walks home in the dawn feeling closer than it has in years.

When the drums start, the elders get up and dance, all of them. (elder), one of the oldest, dances longest, crown slipping over one eye, then collapses, happy and exhausted, into a hammock and falls asleep with a smile.

Fish and taro and fruit, nothing fancy. But the children bring the elders their bowls with great ceremony, and keep refilling the water whether they want it or not, and the elders love it just as much as any feast.

The elders announce that if this is a feast for them, they'll cook it themselves, thank you very much, and get to work with the old recipes nobody else remembers. It's the best meal anyone has had in years.
Long mats in the shade of the great banyan tree.
The elders say they're not even hungry. Then they see the food.
A flower crown slipping over one eye.
Honey cakes that are only made at weddings.

pieces.label: The Healer's Mistake
pieces.text: All the jars on the healers' shelf are the same brown clay, the same size, none of them labelled, and (healer) has given (patient), who came in with a bad cough, a big spoonful of the remedy for a sore foot. (Patient) is coughing, and also hopping.

pieces.label: Admit the Mistake
pieces.text: (Healer) takes a deep breath. "I'm so sorry," (healer.he/she) says. "That was the wrong jar. That was for feet." (Patient) stops hopping, mid-hop, and stares at (healer.him/her). Then at (friend.his/her) foot. Then back at (healer.him/her)...

pieces.label: Hope Nobody Notices
pieces.text: (Healer) puts the jar back on the shelf, quickly, and gives (patient) a big smile. "That's normal," (healer.he/she) says. "The tingling. It means it's working." (Patient) looks at (healer.his/her) face for a long time...

(Healer) owns up at once and mixes the right remedy, checking every ingredient twice. That very afternoon the healers test every jar on the shelf, and paint a little picture on the side of each to show what it's for.

The foot remedy doesn't agree with (patient) at all, and the cough turns deep and rattling, with a fever behind it. (Healer) sits up with (friend.him/her) every night for a week, and is forgiven long before then.
(Patient) notices straight away, because the foot is still tingling and the cough is not one bit better, and tells everyone. Every time (healer) walks past, someone hops.

The cough gets better on its own over the next few days, as coughs do, and (patient) tells everyone the healers are wonderful. Nobody ever finds out. (Healer) quietly scratches a little mark on the bottom of every jar.
The same brown clay, the same size, none of them labelled.
Coughing, and also hopping.
"That's normal. The tingling. It means it's working."
It was the remedy for a sore foot.

pieces.label: The Rock Slide
pieces.text: After a week of heavy rain, (gatherer) is pulling wild roots on the soaking hillside when the ground gives a long, low groan, every bird on the hill takes off at once, and the whole slope above (gatherer.him/her) starts to move.

pieces.label: Run Downhill
pieces.text: (Gatherer) drops the basket and runs, down the slope, as fast as (gatherer.his/her) legs will go, leaping over roots and rocks, with the roar growing louder and louder behind (gatherer.him/her), and stones whizzing past on both sides...

pieces.label: Hide Behind a Boulder
pieces.text: There's no time to run. Just below (gatherer.him/her) is a great old boulder, half buried in the hillside, as big as a hut. (Gatherer) throws (gatherer.himself/herself) down behind it, curls up tight, and covers (gatherer.his/her) head with (gatherer.his/her) arms. The roar comes down over (gatherer.him/her) like a wave...

(Gatherer) reaches the flat ground just as the slide comes to a stop behind (gatherer.him/her), and a rock the size of a hut rolls to a halt a few steps from (gatherer.his/her) heels. (gatherer.He/She) sits down very suddenly, laughing and crying at the same time.

The slide is faster. The villagers dig with sticks and bare hands until dark, calling (gatherer.his/her) name, and lay (gatherer.him/her) to rest in the garden (gatherer.he/she) loved, at the foot of the hill.
The boulder holds, and the slide parts around it like a river round a rock. (Gatherer) climbs out plastered with mud and completely unhurt, pats the boulder, and thanks it, out loud.
The boulder holds. Mostly. A big rock bounces off the top and comes down hard on (gatherer)'s foot. (gatherer.He/She) walks with a limp for the rest of (gatherer.his/her) life, and never runs again.
The ground gives a long, low groan.
Every bird on the hill takes off at once in a great clattering cloud.
The smell of torn earth.
A few last pebbles trickle down.

pieces.label: The Riptide
pieces.text: Floating on (swimmer.his/her) back past the breakers on a bright, lazy afternoon, strong swimmer (swimmer) turns over to swim back and finds the beach very, very small: a riptide, a hidden river in the sea, is pulling (swimmer.him/her) straight out.

pieces.label: Swim Straight Back
pieces.text: (Swimmer) puts (swimmer.his/her) head down and swims straight for the beach, as hard as (swimmer.he/she) has ever swum, kicking and pulling and gasping, fighting the water with everything (swimmer.he/she) has...

pieces.label: Swim Sideways
pieces.text: Every part of (swimmer) wants to swim straight for the shore. But (swimmer.he/she) remembers what the old fishers always say: never fight a rip. Swim along the beach, not towards it. So (swimmer.he/she) turns, and swims sideways, parallel to the sand...

For a long, terrible time the beach stays exactly where it is. Then, a stroke at a time, (swimmer) starts to gain, until (swimmer.his/her) feet touch sand. (swimmer.He/She) sleeps for a whole day and night.

The current is stronger. By the time the canoes reach the tiny dark dot far out past the reef, there's nothing. Every evening for a long time, someone from (swimmer.his/her) family goes down to the beach and watches the horizon until dark.

Just like the old fishers say, after a few dozen strokes along the beach the current lets go, like a hand opening. (Swimmer) walks straight to the oldest fisher in the village and hugs (swimmer.him/her) without a word.

(Swimmer) has already spent too much strength fighting the water. The current lets go far out past the reef, where the waves are big and grey, and two days later (swimmer.his/her) body washes up on the far side of the island.
The sea glitters like a cloth scattered with beads.
It always looks calm, right before it isn't.
The beach looks very, very small.
Never fight a rip. Swim along the beach, not towards it.

pieces.label: The Elder from the Sea
pieces.text: A leaky little canoe with faded eyes painted on the prow and a small grey crab riding on the paddle comes onto the beach, and a small, very old person with a face as wrinkled as a dried fig climbs out: "Ah. This must be the place."

pieces.label: Ask Where (He/She) Came From
pieces.text: The elders come down the beach and greet the visitor politely, and ask where (subject.he/she) has come from, and where (subject.he/she) is going. The old one sits down on the edge of the canoe, crab and all, to answer...

pieces.label: Offer Food First
pieces.text: Questions can wait. The village brings the old one a warm bowl of stew and a cup of fresh water, and sits (subject.him/her) down by the fire, and lets (subject.him/her) eat in peace...

"Far away. Very far. And I'm not going back." (subject.He/She) walks straight up to the little empty hut at the top of the sand and puts (subject.his/her) bag down on the mat as though (subject.he/she) has always lived there. The crab moves in too.

"Oh, where to begin." Islands made of black glass, islands where the trees walk, islands where the fish talk and the people don't. The researchers are still writing a month later, because the old one, of course, has stayed.
The old one eats every bit, has seconds, looks round again, and says, "Hm. No. Wrong place." Then paddles off slowly, the crab still riding on the paddle. "Lovely though!"

The old one nods off by the fire, bowl in lap, and nobody wakes (subject.him/her). A year later (subject.he/she) is still there, in the best spot, and the crab lives in the canoe rotting slowly on the beach.
A face as wrinkled as a dried fig.
A small grey crab is riding on the paddle.
A pair of faded eyes painted on the prow.
Nobody knows what place. The old one seems quite sure.

pieces.label: The Two (Name)s Problem
pieces.text: In the dry season, near the old carved stones the elders say keep the island's spirits company, (sneezer) sneezes a huge thunderclap of a sneeze, and something sneezes back: another (sneezer), dusty from head to foot, already complaining about the dust.

pieces.label: Make the Best of It
pieces.text: (Sneezer) is too surprised to be frightened. "Bless you," (sneezer.he/she) says, automatically. "Thanks," says the other one. "Awful, isn't it? The dust." They look at each other. Then, because there's nothing else to do, they walk back down to the village together...

pieces.label: Ask the Elders
pieces.text: (Sneezer) marches the newcomer straight down the hill to the elders' hut, and stands the two of them side by side in front of the oldest elder. "This," (sneezer.he/she) says, "happened at the stones." The elder looks from one to the other, slowly...

"Bless you." "Thanks. Awful, isn't it? The dust." By the time they reach the village, (sneezer) has worked out that the newcomer looks exactly like (sneezer.him/her) and is nothing like (sneezer.him/her) inside. It takes the name (made1), and fits in surprisingly well.

Halfway down the hill, the dust gets up the newcomer's nose. "Ah... ahh... AHCHOO!" And with the sneeze, it's gone, in a little puff of yellow dust. (Sneezer) walks the rest of the way home trying very hard not to sneeze.

"It happens," says the oldest elder, as if it's no more surprising than rain. "The stones do that sometimes, in the dry season. My grandmother had one." The newcomer is named (made1) on the spot and found a mat to sleep on.
One stern, steady, ancient look from the oldest elder, and the newcomer shuffles back up the hill, behind the old stones, and never comes out again. "You just have to be firm with them."
Dust gets in everything: eyes, food, teeth, dreams.
The faces that nobody remembers carving.
A thunderclap of a sneeze that echoes off the stones.
It's already complaining, loudly, about the dust.

pieces.label: The Swapping Mango
pieces.text: After years of searching, (eater1) and (eater2) find the once-in-a-lifetime mango glowing like a little lamp on a wind-twisted tree on a cliff, share it half each, and with the very first bite their minds slip and trade places.

pieces.label: Finish the Mango
pieces.text: (Eater1) looks down at (eater2)'s hands holding (eater1)'s half of the mango. (Eater2) looks down at (eater1)'s. They look at each other's faces. Then, because it is, after all, the best mango either of them has ever tasted, they both take another bite...

pieces.label: Spit It Out
pieces.text: "Spit it out!" shouts (eater1), in (eater2)'s voice, and they both do, at once, spitting the mouthfuls of sweet gold mango over the edge of the cliff...
They eat their halves down to the stone, sticky to the elbows, and stay swapped. "I suppose I'm you now." "Make the most of it." Years later they agree it was worth it, for that mango.

With the very last sweet scrap from around the stone, their minds slip again and swap back. They plant the stone on the cliff, side by side, and promise to come back in a lifetime to see if it's grown.
The magic stops the moment the mango leaves their mouths. They walk home themselves again, wondering for the rest of their lives what the second bite would have tasted like.
Too late. The first bite was enough. They walk all the way home swapped, and sticky, and cross, and stay swapped for good. The stickiness wears off by morning.
One perfect mango glows red and gold like a little lamp.
The tree is twisted almost flat by the wind.
Like stepping onto a wet rock.
Juice runs down their chins.

pieces.label: The Stranger Who Took a Name
pieces.text: A charming stranger in a cloak of patchwork bark cloth asks (named) to say (named.his/her) name into a little spiral shell, plugs it with a blob of wax, says "I'll have that," and walks off, and (named) can't remember what (named.he/she) is called.

pieces.label: Chase After (Him/Her)
pieces.text: (Named) runs after the stranger, down the path, round the bend, through the palms, shouting "Hey! HEY! You!" because that's all (named.he/she) can shout. The patchwork cloak is always just disappearing round the next corner...

pieces.label: Let It Go
pieces.text: (Named) stands in the middle of the path, watching the patchwork cloak disappear round the bend. (named.He/She) could run. But somehow (named.he/she) doesn't. "Well," (named.he/she) says. "I suppose (named.he/she) needed it more than I did."...

On the beach the stranger is sitting on a rock, waiting, as if (named.he/she) expected it. "You're fast. Good." The wax comes out, and (named)'s name comes out of the shell in (named.his/her) own voice. "Just borrowing."
The stranger is gone: no footprints on the beach, no canoe on the water, and the shell gone too, with (named)'s name sealed up inside it. Nobody can remember the name. (Named) is "?" now.
At the fire, everyone suggests something: a lot of laughing, some very bad ideas, and one quite good one, from a child, which (named) likes at once: (renamed). Everyone toasts it with coconut milk.

Every new name the village tries slides out of everyone's heads by morning, as if the stranger's shell is still drinking them up. (Named) is "?" from then on, through no choice of (named.his/her) own. "At least nobody can take this one."
A cloak of patchwork bark cloth in every shade of brown.
"What a name. Say it once more?"
A blob of wax plugs the end of the shell.
Wanderers who collect names the way children collect shells.

pieces.label: The Beach Wedding
pieces.text: (Bride) and (friend) are getting married barefoot on the frangipani-strewn beach at sunset, the children throwing petals at everyone, the elders pretending they've got sand in their eyes, and the tide creeping up as if the sea wants a better view.

pieces.label: Have a Big Feast
pieces.text: As soon as the words are said and the elders have tied the cord round their joined hands, the drums start, and the cooks bring out everything: roast fish, honey bread, fruit piled in towers, the special sweet wine...

pieces.label: Keep It Small
pieces.text: (Bride) and (friend) don't want a fuss. When the words are said, they thank everyone, hug everyone, and then slip away down the beach, just the two of them and their families, to watch the rest of the sunset...
Roast fish, honey bread, fruit piled in towers, and dancing on the sand by torchlight until the sun comes up. A few weeks later, there's more good news: (bride) is pregnant.
So much food, and so much dancing, that nobody can manage to walk home. The whole village wakes up on the beach together, sandy and stiff and smiling, with gulls stealing the leftovers.

Just the two of them, their families, a few flowers and the sunset. (Bride)'s mother sings a song from when she was married, (friend)'s father tells a terrible joke, and the tide washes over their feet, warm as a bath. It's perfect.

A quiet walk home along the beach under the first stars, and a little later, a happy surprise. (Bride) tells (friend) at the exact spot where they were married, and (friend) sits down in the wet sand without even noticing.
The elders pretend they've got sand in their eyes.
The tide creeps up as if it wants a better view.
Grinning like fools.
The children throw petals at everyone, married or not.

pieces.label: The Baby in the Ferns
pieces.text: On a steaming late afternoon, (finder) hears thin, high, very cross crying from a patch of ferns, and finds a baby wrapped tightly in a woven mat, with no footprints, no basket and no sign of anyone in any direction.

pieces.label: Take the Baby Home
pieces.text: (Finder) picks the baby up, mat and all, very carefully, the way someone would pick up a bird's nest. The baby grabs a fistful of (finder.his/her) hair and holds on tight. "All right," (finder) says. "All right. Let's go home."...

pieces.label: Search for the Parents
pieces.text: Somebody must be looking for this baby. (Finder) ties the baby to (finder.his/her) chest with (finder.his/her) wrap and goes into the jungle, calling, searching, following every path, every broken twig, every bent fern (finder.he/she) can find...
(Finder) raises the baby alone, walking up and down at night singing the same three songs. Nobody in the village has ever seen (finder.him/her) so tired. Or so happy.

(Friend) takes one look at the little red furious face and falls in love, there and then. "Is it... can we...?" They raise the baby together, and it turns out to be the most smiling baby in the village.
(Finder) searches for days and finds no one. By the end of the week the baby has slept every night to the sound of (finder.his/her) heartbeat, and (finder) can't imagine giving the baby to anyone.

On the second day, (finder) finds a frightened young couple huddled under a rock. A storm caught them, they set the baby down safe in the ferns, and then they couldn't find the ferns again. They come back with (finder), and the baby, and stay.
Every leaf is dripping.
The baby grabs a fistful of hair and holds on tight.
Red-faced, furious, and very much alive.
No footprints, no basket, no sign of anyone.

pieces.label: The Fever Dream
pieces.text: After three days of a fever so high that (dreamer.he/she) talked to spirits nobody else could see, (dreamer) sits up remembering everything they told (dreamer.him/her): a lizard wearing a crown, a song about rain that falls upwards, a door in the sea, and a number.

pieces.label: Tell the Researchers
pieces.text: The researchers come and sit by (dreamer)'s mat with bark and charcoal, and (dreamer) tells them everything, from the beginning, while they write it all down as fast as they can...

pieces.label: Rest
pieces.text: The healers won't hear of anything else. They lay (dreamer) back down, cover (dreamer.him/her) with a blanket, give (dreamer.him/her) a cup of honey tea, and sit with (dreamer.him/her) while (dreamer.he/she) sleeps, and sleeps...

Most of it is nonsense. But the number turns out to be exactly how many days there are between one big tide and the next, the lizard in the crown matches an old carving, and the upward rain describes water rising from the sea into the clouds.

The researchers listen very politely, nodding, holding their charcoal very still over the bark, then thank (dreamer.him/her) warmly and leave. They haven't written down a single word. (Dreamer) is sure, for the rest of (dreamer.his/her) life, that it all meant something.

(Dreamer) sleeps for two days straight, deep and dreamless, and the strange memories fade like a dream after waking. Within a fortnight (dreamer.he/she) is back at work. Sometimes, when it rains, (dreamer.he/she) looks up, just in case.

The fever breaks, but it was too high for too long. (Dreamer) is left weak, for good, (dreamer.his/her) hair grey at the front, and (dreamer.his/her) mind gets tired and foggy whenever (dreamer.he/she) tries to learn anything new.
A lizard wearing a crown.
A song about rain that falls upwards.
A door in the sea.
(dreamer.He/She) repeats the number over and over, very urgently.

pieces.label: The Big Wind
pieces.text: A great wind howls round the huts all night like something trying to get in, and at dawn three huts have lost their roofs, the fences are flat, the cooking pots are halfway down the beach, and somebody's hammock is swinging from the top of the tallest palm.

pieces.label: Rebuild Right Away
pieces.text: The builders don't wait. Before breakfast they're up on the walls with fresh thatch and new poles and rope, and soon everyone who can carry anything is carrying it to them, while the children are sent to fetch the cooking pots back from the beach...

pieces.label: Clean Up First
pieces.text: Before anyone can build anything, the village has to be cleared. Everyone starts at one end and works to the other, hauling away the fallen branches, the broken poles, the torn thatch, the smashed baskets and the goats that have got into places goats shouldn't be...

The builders work day and night, eating on the roofs, sleeping in turns. By the end of the week the village looks better than before the wind, and the builders have learned how to lash a roof pole so it holds and set a fence post so the wind can't pull it.

Cursing at a roof pole that keeps slipping, one builder comes up with a clever double knot round the rafters, pinned with a wooden peg, that the wind just can't pull loose. The researchers draw it and write it up very carefully.

The cleanup turns up piles of good wood: straight poles, solid branches, planks from a fence, all stacked and ready for the builders. The roofs still have to be mended. The hammock comes down on the third day, and nobody will admit to having climbed up for it.

Under one of the biggest fallen branches is a nest of big speckled eggs, somehow still whole, and the wind has shaken every coconut off every palm on the island. By evening the store is full of eggs and coconuts.
The wind howls round the huts like something trying to get in.
Torn leaves are plastered over every wall like green paint.
The cooking pots are halfway down the beach.
The hammock swings gently, as if it's been put there on purpose.

pieces.label: The Wise Old Tortoise
pieces.text: A huge old tortoise with a small yellow flower growing from a crack in its shell walks up from the sea all morning, sits down in the middle of the main path, and looks only at (chosen).

pieces.label: Sit with It
pieces.text: (Chosen) sits down cross-legged in the dust in front of the tortoise, and looks back at it. The tortoise blinks, very slowly. (Chosen) blinks back. People walk round them, carefully, and the afternoon goes on...

pieces.label: Follow It
pieces.text: At last, the tortoise turns, very slowly, all the way round, and starts to walk away, and looks back over its shell at (chosen). Clearly, unmistakably, it wants (chosen.him/her) to come. So (chosen) follows. Very, very slowly...

The tortoise says nothing all afternoon. Once, it slowly stretches out its neck, and slowly draws it back in. But (chosen) comes to understand waiting, and listening, and letting things take the time they take, and becomes the most patient person with the little ones in the whole village.
(Chosen) sits so long that (chosen.he/she) completely forgets about work, and the fruit sits unpicked, and the birds get at it. The farmers are very annoyed. The tortoise is not sorry at all.

The tortoise leads (chosen) along a stream and through a gap in the rocks to a hidden grove full of herbs. (Chosen) watches what it eats, picks a little of everything, and comes home knowing more about healing plants than anyone in the village.

The tortoise leads (chosen), very, very slowly, all afternoon, straight to the edge of the water, walks into the sea and swims away. That's where it was going. The little yellow flower is the last thing to disappear under the waves.
Its shell is scratched with marks that look older than the village.
A small yellow flower grows from a crack near the top.
Deep, slow, ancient eyes.
People walk round them, carefully.

pieces.label: The Spilled Dye
pieces.text: Carrying a pot of dark purple dye across the research hut, only going to the weavers, (researcher) catches a foot on a stool, and the dye pours across every research note on the table, including the big river chart that took four researchers a whole year.

pieces.label: Try to Wash It Off
pieces.text: (Researcher) grabs an armful of dripping purple notes and runs for the river, and the other researchers grab the rest and run after (researcher.him/her), and they all kneel in the shallows together, dipping and rinsing and scrubbing...

pieces.label: Start Again
pieces.text: (Researcher) looks at the purple ruin for a long time. Then (researcher.he/she) takes a deep breath, wipes (researcher.his/her) hands on (researcher.his/her) wrap (making it purple too), sits down at a clean corner of the table with fresh bark, and starts writing everything out again, from memory...
Some of the notes come clean enough to show the faint charcoal marks underneath. Most of them don't. The river runs purple for three days, and the fish look worried.

The water makes the dye spread and soak deeper, the soft wet bark falls apart, and the charcoal washes away completely. (Researcher) sits in the river with purple water up to (researcher.his/her) waist and purple hands over (researcher.his/her) purple face.

(Researcher) remembers far more than (researcher.he/she) expected, and finds that a lot of the old notes were muddled, and some were simply wrong. The new notes are better than the old ones ever were.

Halfway through, (researcher) comes to the big chart of the river and can't remember one measurement. (researcher.He/She) puts the charcoal down, walks out, and can't stand being in the research hut after that.
Purple to the wrists, and somehow the nose.
It was only going to the weavers.
Very pretty, and completely unreadable.
The fish look worried.

pieces.label: The Lucky Harvest
pieces.text: After long rains and a hot dry spell, every field, tree, vine and garden on the island ripens on the very same morning, and the bees are so busy and happy that they can't even be bothered to sting anyone.

pieces.label: Harvest Everything
pieces.text: Every single villager who can walk heads for the fields with a basket. Children, elders, healers, researchers, the chief. They pick from dawn to dark, and carry, and pick again, singing to keep going...

pieces.label: Share with the Island
pieces.text: The elders say that a gift this big should be shared. So the village harvests what it needs, and then, on purpose, leaves the rest: whole rows in the fields, whole trees in the orchards, left standing, untouched...

It takes a whole week, and every basket, pot, bowl, net, cloth and hat in the village, and the harvest ends up in heaps on the meeting hut floor. The children lie on top of the pile of melons and refuse to get off.
The baskets fill up faster than anyone can carry them, and the birds come in great happy flocks and help themselves. Even so, it's the biggest harvest the village has ever had.

The rest is left for the animals, and at sunset birds, pigs, goats and little striped forest creatures eat side by side in the fields. The pigs turn the soil, the birds leave their droppings, and the next harvest is just as good.

Bowls of the best fruit are left for the spirits, the way the old stories say. In the morning they're empty, and in each one lies {a smooth river stone with a hole in it|a carved bone hook, finer than anyone in the village can make|a shell full of seeds nobody recognises}. Everybody agrees not to ask.
Fat gourds roll into the doorways.
The fruit trees are bent so low their branches touch the ground.
The bees can't even be bothered to sting anyone.
Children, elders, healers, researchers, the chief: everyone has a basket.

pieces.label: The Peaceful Passing
pieces.text: Very old (elder) asks everyone to come to the fire one evening, looks round at every face, and tells them, simply, how much (elder.he/she) has loved being part of the village. Every day of it. Even the hard ones.

pieces.label: Stay with (Him/Her)
pieces.text: Nobody leaves. One by one, the villagers settle down around the fire, close to (elder), and the night comes on, and the stars come out, and they stay...

pieces.label: Let (Him/Her) Rest
pieces.text: "You need to rest," someone says gently, and they help (elder) up, and walk (elder.him/her) slowly to (elder.his/her) hut, and lay (elder.him/her) down on (elder.his/her) mat with the blanket tucked round (elder.him/her), and let (elder.him/her) sleep...

The village sits with (elder) all night, telling stories about (elder.him/her), and (elder.he/she) listens, and smiles, and sometimes corrects them. Somewhere in the darkest part of the night, (elder) stops correcting them. In the morning (elder.he/she) is gone, with a smile on (elder.his/her) face.

At dawn, (elder) yawns, stretches, and looks round at the whole village sitting there, red-eyed and exhausted. "What," (elder.he/she) says, "is all the fuss about?" Then (elder.he/she) goes off to make breakfast.

(Elder) sleeps a long, deep sleep and wakes up feeling much, much better than (elder.he/she) has in weeks. "Hm. Not today, then." (elder.He/She) asks what's for breakfast, and lives on for a good while yet.

(Elder) sleeps peacefully, with the sound of the village settling down for the night all around (elder.him/her), and in the morning, (elder.he/she) doesn't wake. The village gathers at the fire again and tells every story about (elder.him/her) they can remember, until dawn.
Someone tucks a blanket round (elder.his/her) shoulders.
Even the children are quiet.
The fire crackles softly.
(elder.He/She) looks round at every face.

pieces.label: The Ghost Light
pieces.text: For three nights a soft pale green light has bobbed among the trees as if walking, and the elders say it's a spirit searching for someone; on the fourth night (seeker) slips out to the forest's edge, and the light bobs once, as if it's nodding.

pieces.label: Follow the Light
pieces.text: (Seeker) steps into the trees. The light drifts ahead of (seeker.him/her), never too fast, never too far, waiting whenever (seeker.he/she) stumbles, glowing softly on the trunks and the ferns and the ground...

pieces.label: Call Out to It
pieces.text: (Seeker) doesn't step into the trees. (seeker.He/She) stays right at the edge, where the grass ends and the forest begins, and calls out, quietly, into the dark: "Hello? Who are you? What do you want?"...

The light leads (seeker) to a clearing covered in thousands of mushrooms that glow the same soft green, hangs there a moment, and fades away. (Seeker) finds (seeker.his/her) way home by their light with a basketful, and the researchers are absolutely thrilled.

The light leads (seeker) deeper and deeper, through forest that gets older and darker and quieter, until (seeker.he/she) can't remember which way the village is, and doesn't seem to care. (seeker.His/her) footprints lead into the trees and stop.

The light stops, perfectly still, as if it's listening, then slowly drifts away, fading. (Seeker) feels oddly comforted, as if somebody (seeker.he/she) once knew has just said goodbye. The light never comes back.

The light rushes towards (seeker), silently, faster than anything should move, and wraps (seeker.him/her) in a soft, cool green glow, like being underwater in sunlight. When it fades, (seeker) is gone. The village keeps a fire burning at the edge of the trees for a whole season, in case.
Pale green, about the size of a cooking pot.
It moves almost as if it were walking.
It's best not to be the one it finds.
It waits whenever (seeker) stumbles.

pieces.label: The Grand Copy
pieces.text: A travelling magician in a cloak sewn all over with tiny white shells, who claims to have learned every trick from the spirits of the deep sea, announces "the trick of tricks," and ignoring every child's raised hand, picks (volunteer) as the volunteer.

pieces.label: Let the Magician Do the Trick
pieces.text: The magician stands (volunteer) in the middle of a circle drawn in the sand, sweeps the shell cloak up and round in a great clattering arc, and shouts a word that nobody understands...

pieces.label: Back Out
pieces.text: (Volunteer) looks at the magician's slow smile, and at the circle in the sand, and suddenly gets cold feet. "Actually," (volunteer.he/she) says, "I think I'll let one of the children have a go." (volunteer.He/She) steps back into the crowd. The magician's smile flickers...

A flash of white light so bright everyone covers their eyes, and there are three of (volunteer) standing in the circle, down to the last eyelash and the stain on the left sandal. {#made:One new one walks off; the other stays|The two new ones stay}, {#made:as (made1)|as (made1) and (made2)}, and nobody, not even the magician, knows how to undo it.

A flash, a great puff of thick grey smoke, and when it clears (volunteer) is still alone in the circle, and the magician is gone, shell cloak and all, with a very large basket of food, somebody's good knife and the chief's other sandal.
A cheerful farmer who volunteers for everything goes instead. A puff of smoke, a lot of coughing, and when it clears the farmer is standing there holding a live chicken. That's the trick.

"No matter. I can do it from here." A flash, and (volunteer) is standing in the crowd, and so is (volunteer), right beside (volunteer.him/her), blinking in surprise. The second one grins (volunteer)'s grin, and picks the name (made1).
The shell cloak clatters and shimmers whenever the magician moves.
The chief's sandal from the chief's own mouth.
Every child's hand shoots up.
A slow smile.

pieces.label: Back to Childhood
pieces.text: Worn out from working too hard for too long, (wisher) wishes out loud to be a child again, "just for a little while," and a warm breeze that smells of sand and sugarcane swirls round (wisher.him/her), and (wisher.his/her) feet start to shrink.

pieces.label: Enjoy Being Little
pieces.text: By the time the breeze has passed, (wisher) is sitting on the doorstep in a grown-up's wrap that's suddenly far too big, with small hands and small feet and a small, delighted face. (wisher.He/She) looks down at the beach, where the children are playing. Then (wisher.he/she) runs...

pieces.label: Wish to Grow Up Again
pieces.text: (Wisher) looks down at (wisher.his/her) shrinking hands in horror. "No, no, no! Not like that! I didn't mean it! I take it back!" (wisher.He/She) jumps up, grown-up wrap trailing, and runs after the breeze down the path, shouting...

(Wisher) spends the whole of the next day as a child: tag on the beach, a sandcastle with a moat and three bridges, fruit until (wisher.his/her) belly hurts. At sunset the same warm breeze comes back, and (wisher.he/she) is (wisher.himself/herself) once more, with a very big grin. It was exactly what (wisher.he/she) needed.

The breeze doesn't come back, and (wisher) doesn't mind one bit. (wisher.He/She) plays tag every day and asks a thousand questions, and seems happier than (wisher.he/she) has been in years. (wisher.He/She) just doesn't want the grown-up life back yet.

The breeze stops, turns round, seems to sigh a little, and swirls round (wisher.him/her) once more. (Wisher) is (wisher.himself/herself) again, and somehow more rested, as if (wisher.he/she) had a whole long summer holiday in that one moment.

The breeze has moved on over the hills, and the more (wisher) runs, the smaller (wisher.he/she) gets, until (wisher.he/she) is about six years old, alone on the path in the dusk with a grown-up's memories. The village helps (wisher.him/her) grow up all over again.
The breeze smells of sand and sugarcane.
The children play tag on the beach and shriek with laughter.
A grown-up's wrap, suddenly far too big.
"Just for a little while."

pieces.label: The Last Sunset of the Year
pieces.text: The whole village climbs the hill together to watch the last sunset of the year, the elders on sticks, helped by the young ones, and the sky turns orange, then pink, then a purple deep enough to swim in.

pieces.label: Watch in Silence
pieces.text: Nobody says a word. Nobody needs to. The whole village sits on the hill together, quiet, watching the colours change, while the sun slides down, slowly, into the sea...

pieces.label: Sing Together
pieces.text: One of the elders starts it, softly, the old song for the end of the year. Then another voice joins, and another, and another, until the whole hillside is singing...

Nobody says a single word. The stars come out, one by one and then all at once, and the village helps each other up and walks home together down the hill in the starlight, feeling peaceful, every single one of them.

As the very last sliver of sun slips under the sea, a very small child asks, in a worried little voice that carries across the whole hillside, "Will it come back?" Everybody laughs and says "Yes!", all together.

The songs the elders learned from their grandparents, the ones the children made up last week, and the one about the turtle that everybody knows, roll down the hill and out over the dark sea until the moon is high. A night nobody ever forgets.

Somebody starts singing, very badly, then somebody else joins in just as badly, on purpose, and then the whole village is howling at the purple sky, and the goats in the valley start bleating along. The perfect way to end the year.
A purple deep enough to swim in.
The elders on sticks, helped by the young ones.
The first star comes out over the water.
The sky saying goodbye to the old year properly.

pieces.label: The Spring That Reflected Tomorrow
pieces.text: (Seer) kneels to drink at the little spring behind the waterfall rocks, and the face looking back is (seer.his/hers)... but older, grey at the temples, with a long scar across the cheek that (seer) has not earned yet.

pieces.label: Sketch the Older Face
pieces.text: (Seer) runs for bark and charcoal, telling (seer.himself/herself) that this is science and not at all because (seer.he/she) wants to know how (seer.he/she) gets that scar. (seer.He/She) settles at the edge of the spring, notes the hour, the angle of the sun, the way the light slants through the waterfall spray...

pieces.label: Let Someone Take a Long Look
pieces.text: Nobody wants to go first. Finally (name2) rolls up (seer.his/her) sleeves. "If it shows me with no teeth, I don't want to hear about it." (seer.He/She) leans out over the water, and the whole crowd leans with (seer.him/her)...

pieces.label: Ask the Oldest Villager
pieces.text: (elder) listens to the whole story without interrupting, then laughs a creaky laugh. "Ah. That spring. My grandmother used to talk about a pool that remembers forward..."

(Seer) draws until the light fails, and with the researchers works out that still water under that rock bends light in strange ways, and that some of the "age" may be shadow. Some. The scar is a problem for later. Much later.
A breeze wrinkles the water, and the older face breaks into a hundred wobbling pieces and never comes back together. (Seer) feels oddly as if (seer.he/she) missed an appointment.
(Name2) stares down for a long, long moment and straightens up with a new face and hair, changed for good, as if the water lent (seer.him/her) a little of whoever was looking back.
Just as (name2) bends over the spring, (seer.he/she) remembers an urgent net that needs mending. So does everyone else, all at once, and the crowd melts away into the trees.
"My grandmother used to talk about a pool that remembers forward... although she mostly said it to keep us children from falling in. It worked."
(elder) shows (seer) how to visit the spring at dawn and dusk and tie a knot in a cord for every change seen in the water, an old way of keeping records the researchers are delighted to have back.
A leaf lands on the surface, and the water does not even ripple.
Half the village goes to "fetch water" and comes back with none.
The older face looks patient, as if it has been waiting a long time.

pieces.label: The Second Shadow
pieces.text: At sunset on the beach, (subject) notices (subject.he/she) has two shadows; the second copies every move a heartbeat late, like a shy dancer trying to keep up with the music, and waves back at the children, a little late.

pieces.label: Time the Delay
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that if (subject.he/she) is going to be haunted, (subject.he/she) might as well be haunted precisely. (subject.He/She) claps once, then counts heartbeats until the shadow claps back. One... two...

pieces.label: Let the Shadow Step Forward
pieces.text: (Subject) takes a deep breath and steps aside, leaving room on the sand. "Well? Go on then." The second shadow hesitates... and then peels up off the beach like a wet leaf lifting from a rock...

pieces.label: Question the Keeper of Tales
pieces.text: (elder) hears the whole thing with (subject.his/her) eyes closed, nodding slowly. "Shadows that ran off to be people. Yes. I know that one..."

pieces.label: Walk Home Before Dark
pieces.text: (Subject) decides this is not (subject.his/her) problem and walks briskly up the beach without looking back. (subject.He/She) can hear the children giggling behind (subject.him/her)...
Every clap comes back after exactly the same count, as steady as a drum, and the fishers later borrow the trick for timing when to haul their nets.

Halfway through the count the sun slips into the sea, and the second shadow goes down with it like someone sinking into deep water. (Subject) is surprised to find (subject.he/she) is a little sad about that.

It peels up off the beach like a wet leaf lifting from a rock and stands up as a whole person with (subject)'s exact face, politely asks to be called by a different name, and then asks where supper is.
The shadow rises halfway, and (subject) loses (subject.his/her) nerve completely. "No. No, sorry, I changed my mind!" The shape slumps back down onto the sand.
"Shadows that ran off to be people... but I could never tell you if it is a true story or just a very good way to get children inside at dusk. Is it working?" It is.

(elder) shows (subject) how to push sticks into the sand at the tip of a shadow through the day, an old method for telling the hour and the seasons, and the researchers measure the arc with great excitement.

By the time (subject) reaches the fire, (subject.he/she) has turned it into a pretty good story, and the village decides it's something to tell tales about. (Subject) still checks the sand behind (subject.him/her) every sunset.
The next evening (subject) casts only one shadow, and the few who saw it tell it so often and so loudly that nobody quite believes them anymore.
When (subject) turns to run, it stumbles after (subject.him/her).
A child waves; the shadow waves back, a little late.
If (subject.he/she) is going to be haunted, (subject.he/she) might as well be haunted precisely.

pieces.label: The Twin in the Mist
pieces.text: Thick white morning mist rolls up from the lagoon, and out of it walks (original), same face, same hair, same scratch behind one ear, while the real (original) stands a few steps away holding a basket of fish.

pieces.label: Study the Double from Afar
pieces.text: (Original) puts the fish basket down very slowly and crouches behind a palm, watching. The double crouches behind the next palm and watches (original.him/her) back...

pieces.label: Offer the Double a Seat by the Fire
pieces.text: "Well," says (original) weakly, "you'd better come and have breakfast, I suppose." The double beams and follows (original.him/her) up the path. The whole village stops what it is doing to stare...

pieces.label: Bar the Doors Until It Lifts
pieces.text: (Original) runs. The whole village, hearing (original.his/her) shouting, decides that running is a fine idea, and every door flap is tied shut. Then the long wait begins...

For an hour they copy each other from behind two palms, and (original) notices the double wobbles and stretches whenever the fog gets thicker, the way the far shore wobbles on hot days. A small piece of new knowledge, and a large piece of new nightmares.
The double thins with the mist, gives one last friendly wave, and leaves a single, perfectly ordinary footprint. (Original) puts (original.his/her) own foot next to it. It is an exact match.
The double eats two bowls of porridge and simply... stays. By midday it is a real, solid person, and picks a different name so nobody mixes the two of them up at dinner.
"No. I'm sorry. I can't share a fire with my own face." The double looks only a little hurt, bows, and drifts back down the path into the mist, scratching behind one ear.

Crammed into one hut, (elder) shows (original) how to tell when fog will lift from the way the reeds bend. "Mist walkers never stay past the reeds standing up." The trick saves the fishers many wasted mornings.
When the doors open, the double is gone. By the end of the season the witnesses say it juggled fish and sang a song. It did neither.
The double scratches behind one ear, just the same.
A fish basket sits forgotten in the wet grass.
Every door flap in the village is tied shut.

pieces.label: The Charm That Forgot
pieces.text: The memory charm, a braid of hair and little shell beads made to help forgetful villagers remember their chores, made (wearer) forget (wearer.his/her) own name for one horrible breath, and one of its beads now shows a tiny carved name nobody recognizes.

pieces.label: Unpick the Charm's Knots
pieces.text: (Wearer) takes the charm to the brightest spot in the village and begins, very carefully, to untangle the braid, counting each knot under (wearer.his/her) breath. Seventeen... eighteen...

pieces.label: Let Someone Wear It Overnight
pieces.text: (Name2) volunteers. "What's the worst that happens? I forget to do the dishes?" (wearer.He/She) ties the charm around (wearer.his/her) wrist and goes to bed, while (wearer.his/her) family watches (wearer.him/her) a little too closely...

pieces.label: Show It to the Weaving Elder
pieces.text: (elder) turns the charm over in (wearer.his/her) knobbly fingers, frowning at the carved bead. "Hmm. The old charm makers... they made things that sometimes got ideas."

Knot by knot, (wearer) maps out which strands cross, which hold the beads, and which do nothing at all except look nice, and scratches it down for the researchers, remembering (wearer.his/her) own name the whole time.

At knot twenty-three the whole braid slips loose, and the odd carved bead rolls across the floor and drops neatly into a crack, never to be seen again. (Wearer) keeps checking that (wearer.he/she) still knows (wearer.his/her) name.

(Name2) wakes remembering everything, but the charm seems to have "forgotten" (wearer.his/her) old face and given (wearer.him/her) a new one, changed for good. After a long silence over a bowl of water, (name2) laughs.
"Actually, I quite like knowing who I am." The charm is hung on a peg by the door, and people walk around it the way people walk around a sleeping dog.
"The old charm makers made things that sometimes got ideas. Or so my mother said. She also said the cooking pot was haunted, and that was just my father."
(elder) soaks a strand in seawater to show how they tested a weave: tight weaves curl, loose ones sag, and good ones dry straight as an arrow. (Wearer) writes it down, and checks the bark twice.
One bead shows a tiny carved name nobody recognizes.
Someone keeps saying their own name under their breath, just to check.
The charm sits on its cord looking completely innocent.

pieces.label: The Night of Exchanged Voices
pieces.text: (Voice_a) and (name2) step out of neighbouring huts, wish each other good morning, and each hears the other's voice come out of (voice_a.his/her) own mouth: the rumbling drum now squeaks like a startled bird, and the soft speaker BOOMS across the clearing.

pieces.label: Record How Each Voice Sounds
pieces.text: A researcher sits the two of them down and has them sing the same chant over and over, marking each high and low note on a stick. (Voice_a) squeaks. (Name2) booms. The children gather to watch, giggling into their hands...

pieces.label: Have Someone Sleep Where They Slept
pieces.text: (Name3) is curious, and possibly a little bored. "If something swapped them in the night, I want to see it." (voice_a.He/She) drags a sleeping mat to the spot between the two huts and lies down, grinning at the stars...

pieces.label: Ask the Elder Who Hears Spirits
pieces.text: (elder) listens to (voice_a) squeak the story and (name2) boom the ending, and manages to keep a straight face for almost the whole thing...

Singing the same chant over and over while a researcher marks each note on a stick, the pair help show why a booming voice reaches the far huts while a squeaky one gets lost in the trees. Nobody asks them if they found it useful.
Halfway through the third chant, both voices slip back to their owners mid-note, and there is nothing left to study. The children are very disappointed. (Voice_a) and (name2) are not.
(Name3) sleeps on the spot between the two huts and wakes in (voice_a.his/her) own voice, but with a new face and new hair, changed for good. (Name3) seems rather pleased about it.
(Name3) lies there for about as long as it takes to hear an owl hoot twice, then picks up the mat and goes home. "I like my voice."

"Spirits sometimes play trading games with sleepers. Or so I'm told." Eating something they dislike "to show the spirits you mean business" does not help, and by night the voices drift home on their own anyway.

(elder) teaches an old way of tapping and listening for echoes through the floor. They find no spirits, but they do find two hollow, rotting floor posts, and the builders start using the trick everywhere. The voices come home that night.
A squeak and a boom try to say "what" at the same time.
The babies cry every time the soft-spoken one opens their mouth.
Breakfast is very, very funny for everyone who is not them.

pieces.label: The Blessing of the Old Tree
pieces.text: (Hopeful_parent_1) and (name2), who have hoped for a child for a long time, sit beneath the oldest tree on the island, the one with roots like folded arms, and a single leaf drifts down into their joined hands, glowing soft gold and as warm as a hearthstone.

pieces.label: Keep Notes on the Leaf
pieces.text: (Hopeful_parent_1) decides that before anyone gets their hopes up, someone should watch this leaf very carefully. (hopeful_parent_1.He/She) sets it on a flat stone and checks it every hour, scratching notes into bark...

pieces.label: Accept the Tree's Blessing
pieces.text: (Hopeful_parent_1) and (name2) look at each other. Then, together, they close their hands around the leaf and say thank you to the tree, out loud, feeling a little silly and very hopeful. The glow sinks slowly into their hands, warm all the way up to their elbows...

pieces.label: Ask the Tree's Keeper
pieces.text: (elder), who has tended the old tree's roots for decades, listens with (hopeful_parent_1.his/her) hand resting on the bark, as if checking the tree's side of the story...

The leaf glows brightest at dawn, dimmest at noon, and pulses gently whenever it rains, and the researchers learn a good deal about the old tree from watching it. (Name2) keeps the notes in a safe place.
By evening the glow has faded, leaving an ordinary dry leaf that crumbles a little at the edges. (Name2) quietly presses it between two pieces of bark to keep, and takes (hopeful_parent_1)'s hand.

They say thank you to the tree, out loud, the glow sinks warm into their hands, and within the month one of them is expecting a baby. They leave a basket of the best fruit in the village among the roots.
"If it happens, I want it to happen because it happens. Not because a tree said so." They set the leaf among the roots with a word of thanks, and the nosier aunts are very disappointed.
"It has blessed families before, or so my aunt swore. She also swore she once saw it walk, so." The couple decide to just enjoy the warm leaf while it lasts.

(elder) shows (hopeful_parent_1) how to judge the tree's health from the colour of its bark and the pattern of its fallen leaves, and (hopeful_parent_1) becomes one of the few who can listen to the tree properly.
The leaf stays as warm as a hearthstone all night.
The roots look like folded arms.
Everyone in the village has an opinion by sundown.

pieces.label: The Mirror of Other Years
pieces.text: In the rubble of the old healer's collapsed hut, builders find a disc of polished black stone, and in it (looker) sees (looker.himself/herself) much younger, gap teeth and all, and the longer (looker.he/she) looks, the less (looker.his/her) knees and back ache.

pieces.label: Compare the Reflection
pieces.text: (Looker) sits down with a few old friends and the stone, and goes through it carefully: old scars, the missing tooth, the shape of that bruise. "Was it the left knee or the right one?" "The right. You cried for a day."...

pieces.label: Gaze Into It Willingly
pieces.text: (Looker) sits cross-legged in the shade and stares into the stone, deeper and deeper, ignoring the voices around (looker.him/her). The young face in the stone stares back, and slowly begins to grin...

pieces.label: Wrap It and Set It Aside
pieces.text: (Looker) wraps the stone in bark cloth without looking at it again and carries it to (elder), who unwraps one corner, peers inside, and quickly wraps it up again...

(Looker)'s old friends check every scar, the missing tooth, the shape of that bruise, and they match far too well. The researchers learn a little about how the strange black rock was polished. Nobody can explain the knees.

The stone clouds over like breath on a cold morning, and shows only (looker)'s face as it is today, wrinkles and all. The young face never comes back. Neither does the feeling in (looker.his/her) knees.

The stone flashes white, and (looker)'s body is five years younger, with a little less grey and a lot more spring in (looker.his/her) step, memories exactly the same. (looker.He/She) runs up the hill to the fields, just because (looker.he/she) can.

(Looker) turns the stone face down. "I've earned every one of my years. I'd like to keep them." The aches start again almost at once. (looker.He/She) does not seem to mind as much as everyone expected.
(elder) refuses to look into it, but teaches the old way of polishing stone with wet sand and coconut oil, and the village's stone tools get noticeably shinier.
The stone goes on a high shelf, still wrapped. The next morning the bark cloth is empty and neatly folded, and nobody, as far as anyone can tell, looks a day younger.
The reflection has the haircut from the year of the big storm.
"Was it the left knee or the right one?" "The right. You cried for a day."
Someone runs up the hill just because (looker.he/she) can.

pieces.label: The Spirit's Unfinished Song
pieces.text: For three nights a slow, sweet, sad melody has drifted out of the empty hut at the edge of the village, always stopping one note short of the end, and (singer), who has the best voice in the village, cannot stop humming it.

pieces.label: Scratch the Tune Onto a Board
pieces.text: That night (singer) sits outside the empty hut with a board and a sharp shell. As the song drifts out, (singer.he/she) scratches it down: a mark high for high notes, low for low ones, long for long ones...

pieces.label: Sing the Missing Note
pieces.text: On the fourth night (singer) stands in the doorway of the empty hut, waits for the song to reach its unfinished end, takes a deep breath... and sings the note (singer.he/she) has been imagining for days...

pieces.label: Ask Who Lived There
pieces.text: (elder) stops what (singer.he/she) is doing when (singer) hums the tune. "Where did you hear that?" (singer.He/She) sits down heavily. "There was a singer who lived in that hut, when I was a child..."

By dawn (singer) has the whole melody on the board, every note except the last, and other singers start copying the method. (Singer)'s family is less thrilled, because now (singer.he/she) can hum it while reading it.
Halfway through the copying the song stops, in the middle, and never returns. (Singer) is left with half a song scratched on a board and a strange feeling of having interrupted someone.
The note rings out, clear and true, and the whole hut seems to sigh. When (singer) turns around, (singer.his/her) face and hair have changed for good, and the hut is silent from then on.
At the last moment, (singer) closes (singer.his/her) mouth. It does not feel like (singer.his/her) song to finish. The melody stops one note short, as always, and drifts away.

"There was a singer who lived in that hut, when I was a child... but whether it's truly her, or only the wind playing in the old thatch, I can't tell you. She never finished that one either." (Singer) leaves flowers on the doorstep that evening, and keeps doing it.

(elder) shows (singer) the old breathing method the hut's owner used to hold long notes: breathe low, into the belly, and let it out like a slow tide. (Singer)'s chants grow steadier, and somehow the song from the hut sounds happier.
"Just FINISH it!" "I CAN'T."
(Singer) hums it while asleep, according to (singer.his/her) family.
Nobody has lived there for years.

pieces.label: The Blue Flame
pieces.text: On a flat stone beside the volcano path, a little blue flame has been burning all day on bare rock, with no wood under it, the moss around it not even singed, and cool enough to hold a hand over. Three children have already tested this. There was shouting.

pieces.label: Sit Up with the Flame
pieces.text: (Observer) sends the children home with someone else, wraps (observer.himself/herself) in a blanket, and settles in for the night beside the blue flame, scratching notes onto bark by its strange cold light...

pieces.label: Pass a Hand Through the Fire
pieces.text: (Name2) shoulders through the crowd. "Children did it. How bad can it be?" Before anyone can stop (observer.him/her), (observer.he/she) holds out a hand and passes it straight through the blue flame...

pieces.label: Fetch the Fire Keeper
pieces.text: (elder), who has kept the village fire burning for longer than most villagers have been alive, hobbles up the path, takes one look at the flame, and makes a noise like an annoyed pigeon...

All night the flame leans away from the wind, brightens just before the rain, and smells faintly of rotten eggs whenever it flares. By morning (observer) has learned a good deal about the volcano's breath seeping through the rocks.
Around midnight the flame gutters, shrinks to a blue speck, and goes out, and (observer) walks home stiff and cold, and has to explain why (observer.he/she) spent the night talking to a rock.

Blue light runs up (name2)'s arm like water up a reed and across (observer.his/her) face. (observer.He/She) is completely unhurt, but (observer.his/her) look has changed for good: new hair, new features, same grin. "That was AMAZING."

The flame flares up tall and bright at (name2)'s fingertips, and (observer.he/she) yanks back with a yelp. It felt like plunging into cold sea water. Nobody wants to test the "cool" fire any further, and the children are firmly walked home.
"The volcano sometimes breathes blue. My father told me so. Or maybe he said it to keep us off this path. Either way, keep off this path." The flame is gone by morning.
(elder) teaches how to judge a fire's heat by its colour: red is lazy, yellow is working, white is fierce, blue is hottest of all. It helps with cooking and firing pots.
Three children tested it. There was shouting.
The flame flickers politely, the colour of the sky right before dark.
A faint smell like rotten eggs whenever it flares.

pieces.label: The Dream of Two Selves
pieces.text: (Dreamer_1) and (name2), who barely speak to each other, both describe the same dream at breakfast: they woke up in each other's bodies and spent the whole day faking it, right down to the cracked water jar by the door.

pieces.label: Compare the Two Accounts
pieces.text: A researcher takes (dreamer_1) to one side and (name2) to the other, and has each tell the dream in every detail, without the other listening. The two lists get longer, and longer...

pieces.label: Sleep Side by Side Tonight
pieces.text: Against all common sense, and mostly because the whole village is dying to know, (dreamer_1) and (name2) agree to sleep in the same hut, mats side by side. They lie there in the dark, very stiff, very polite. "Good night." "Good night."...

pieces.label: Ask the Dream Reader
pieces.text: (elder), who reads dreams for anyone who brings (dreamer_1.him/her) a fish, listens to both of them very gravely, chewing on the fish...

Told separately, the two accounts match down to what was for lunch, and the researchers come up with a careful way of questioning witnesses separately. (Dreamer_1) and (name2) start nodding to each other at the well. It is a start.
The dreams stop the next night, and the details fade, the way dreams do. Was the jar cracked on the left or the right? The matter is dropped, but they keep giving each other odd, thoughtful looks.

In the morning (dreamer_1) looks down at hands that are not (dreamer_1.his/hers), and (dreamer_1.his/her) own face is staring back across the hut in horror. Each keeps (dreamer_1.his/her) own mind, and they will have to talk to each other a great deal more from now on.

Halfway through the night, (name2) grabs (dreamer_1.his/her) mat and walks out. "I'm not risking it." (Dreamer_1) follows, going the other way. Neither sleeps a wink, but both wake up in their own bodies.
"A shared dream means two paths crossing. I say that about most dreams. It's usually true enough." They laugh together for the first time, and the cracked jar turns out to be perfectly whole.

(elder) teaches the old dream tally: a notch for each dream, a different notch for each place, a cross for each face. Over many nights it shows things no single dream could, and the dream reader gets a lot more fish.
"Good night." "Good night." Very stiff, very polite.
Neither of them is eating anymore.
The dream reader accepts payment in fish.

pieces.label: The Fishing Line Dispute
pieces.text: Two households both say the rocky stretch past the reef is theirs to fish, both marker stones look exactly alike, nets have been moved in the night twice, and yesterday somebody threw a fish. Not AT anyone. Near them. Pointedly.

pieces.label: Let Both Households Speak
pieces.text: (leader) calls everyone to the fire and lays down one rule: no interrupting, and absolutely no fish-throwing. (Leader) goes first, arms folded...

pieces.label: Walk the Reef at Low Tide
pieces.text: At dawn, (leader), (leader) and (name2) wade out along the reef together, picking their way between the rock pools in an extremely awkward silence...

pieces.label: Split the Day Between Them
pieces.text: (leader) decides to stop the arguing with a plain rule: (leader)'s family fishes the stretch in the mornings, (name2)'s in the evenings. Both families grumble. Then, for a week, they try it...

(Leader) explains, more quietly than anyone expected, that (leader.his/her) nets need the calm water at dawn to feed four hungry children. Even (name2) uncrosses (leader.his/her) arms, and the two families walk home side by side.

(Name3), who mends nets for both families, goes bright red and blurts it out: the stretch was always shared, until a storm rolled one of the marker stones two summers ago. (Leader) and (name2) stare at each other, and then both start to laugh.

The fish gather on the north side of the rocks at dawn and on the south side by evening. Neither family has been fishing the best spot at the best time, and the fishers start keeping track of where the fish go by the hour.

In a crevice near the end of the reef are tatters of both families' net ropes, where the tide has been dragging anything left loose. The sea moved the nets. (Leader) awkwardly offers (name2) a hand back over the slippery rocks.
(Leader)'s family fishes the mornings, (name2)'s the evenings, and the nets stay exactly where they were left. The fish-throwing is never mentioned again, except as a joke.

Both families spend half of every day standing on the beach glaring at the other family fishing. "This is worse!" "For once I agree!" The split is called off, and they go back to arguing, a little more cheerfully.
Somebody threw a fish. Not AT anyone. Near them. Pointedly.
Both marker stones look exactly alike.
One net was found floating halfway to the horizon.

pieces.label: The Watch at Night
pieces.text: Nobody wants the watch between midnight and dawn, when the fire burns low, the insects bite their hardest and the jungle goes "hoo" in a way that sounds personal, and three villagers have already loudly "volunteered" each other.

pieces.label: Hear the Night Guards Out
pieces.text: (leader) holds up a hand for quiet and turns to (leader). "You've sat it more than anyone. Tell us."...

pieces.label: Count the Notches on the Watch Post
pieces.text: Every guard cuts a notch into the old watch post at the end of a shift, and a different mark each time the fire is fed. (leader) has the whole post hauled into the firelight and starts counting...

pieces.label: Rotate the Worst Watch Each Moon
pieces.text: (leader) announces that the worst watch will pass from household to household, one each moon, so nobody gets stuck with it. It sounds simple. It sounds fair...

(Leader) tells them how the late watch wrecks (leader.his/her) sleep for days, and how (leader.he/she) snapped at (leader.his/her) own children last week over nothing. Afterwards, two of the loud "volunteers" offer to take (leader.his/her) next turns without being asked.
(Name2) raises a hand, lowers it, then raises it again. "I never sleep well anyway. I like the night. I'd take it, if nobody minds." Nobody minds. Several people want to hug (leader.him/her).

The notches show the fire only ever needs feeding twice a night, at the same two times, if it is banked properly before midnight. The late watch can be cut in half, and the cooks start banking their fires the same way.

The notches show everyone HAS been taking their turn, more or less fairly. It only felt unfair because the late watch is so miserable, and the three loud "volunteers" find something very interesting to look at in the fire.
Each household grumbles when its moon comes round, and grumbles a lot less when it passes. (Leader) sleeps through the whole night for the first time in a season.

On the first night two people turn up, both sure it is their turn. On the second, nobody comes, the fire goes out, and a curious pig wanders straight through the village. (Leader) sighs and picks up the watch stick again.
Something in the jungle goes "hoo" in a way that sounds personal.
"(leader.He/She) has the best ears!"
The insects bite their hardest.

pieces.label: The Lost Public Tools
pieces.text: On the morning the storehouse roof repair was finally meant to begin, the tool shelter is empty: the big stone adze, the long rope and both of the good digging sticks have vanished, and fingers are starting to point.

pieces.label: Ask the Builders What It Costs Them
pieces.text: (leader) sits everyone down before the finger-pointing turns into shoving. "Before we hunt for anyone, tell me why it matters so much."...

pieces.label: Follow the Drag Marks
pieces.text: (Leader) spots two long scrapes in the dirt leading away from the shelter, the kind a heavy adze makes when someone drags it instead of carrying it. The builders set off following them like hunters on a trail...

pieces.label: Lend Tools by Tally Stick
pieces.text: (leader) has an idea. From now on, anyone borrowing a shared tool must take a carved tally stick with their mark on it and hang it in the tool's place, so everyone can see who has what...

(Leader) explains that without the adze and rope the roof won't be finished before the rains, and the rains will soak every basket in the storehouse. Half the village helps search, and the tools turn up by evening.
Little (name2) tugs on (leader)'s arm. "I saw the long rope! It's tying a canoe down at the lagoon!" The rope is there. So is the adze, holding down the canoe's sail.

The marks lead to a tidy lean-to by the fields, where the tools are simply handier, right next to where the work happens most. Nobody stole anything, and the builders work out a smarter layout for every tool in the village.

The marks lead to (name3), happily digging away with both good digging sticks. "Oh! Was someone using these?" There was no theft, and no one is punished, though (name3) has to carry the adze all the way back.
The tally sticks hang neatly where the tools should be, the builders always know whose door to knock on, and the storehouse roof is finished two days before the rains.
The tally sticks go missing faster than the tools ever did. Children use them as swords. A goat eats two. The builders go back to shouting "WHO HAS THE ADZE?" across the village.
"WHO HAS THE ADZE?"
Somebody was "acting strange" last night. They always act strange.
The builders stand around with empty hands.

pieces.label: The Council's Empty Seat
pieces.text: The gathering is about to vote on moving the fish drying racks onto a nice flat patch of ground, which happens to be (leader)'s garden, and (leader) is out fishing, blissfully unaware.

pieces.label: Fetch the Gardener from the Beach
pieces.text: A runner sprints down to the beach. Some time later, (leader) is hauled into the gathering still dripping, still holding a fish, and extremely confused. "What about my garden?!"...

pieces.label: Pace Out the Ground
pieces.text: (leader) decides that before anyone votes on anything, they should actually go and look. The whole gathering troops out to the garden in the late afternoon sun...

pieces.label: Tell the Gardener First
pieces.text: (leader) calls off the vote and walks down to the beach alone, sits on the sand beside (leader), and explains what was being decided, before anyone else does...
Hauled in still dripping and still holding a fish, (leader) explains that the plot feeds three households, including two elders who can't farm anymore. The racks stay where they are.

(Name2) speaks at a gathering for the first time, voice shaking: there's an unused clearing just behind the current racks, if somebody would only cut back the vines. The racks move there, and (leader) gives (name2) the fish.

Pacing the ground shows the flat patch is shaded by palms half the day, while the slope above catches sun from dawn to dusk. The racks go on the slope, the garden stays a garden, and the fish dry faster than ever.

Someone claimed (leader) had let the plot go to weeds. Standing in it, everyone can see the taro is the healthiest on the island, and the person who said it suddenly remembers urgent business elsewhere.

(Leader) does not love it, and says so, at length, while gutting a fish with unnecessary force. But (leader.he/she) is grateful to hear it first, face to face, and chooses which one corner of the garden to give up.
Halfway through explaining, (leader) hears how it sounds and stops. "We were wrong to decide this without you. I'm sorry." (Leader) blinks, and offers half of today's catch.
Someone points at the empty mat. "Er. Shouldn't we wait?"
The gardener is still holding a fish.
A fish is gutted with unnecessary force.

pieces.label: The Water Jar Rule
pieces.text: A new rule lets water jars be filled only at the morning spring call, so the spring isn't churned into mud, and by noon the parents with babies and the villagers nursing the sick are standing in their huts with empty jars.

pieces.label: Listen to the Caregivers
pieces.text: (leader) takes one look at (leader)'s face and calls a gathering right then and there, before lunch...

pieces.label: Watch the Spring for a Day
pieces.text: (leader) sits beside the spring from dawn to dusk with (leader), watching every single villager who comes to fill a jar...

pieces.label: Allow Caregivers a Midday Fill
pieces.text: (leader) announces a compromise: caregivers may make one extra fill at midday...

(Leader) explains that the sick need fresh water all day long, for drinking, for washing, for cooling fevers. Several people who voted for the rule look at their feet, and by evening it has a sensible exception.
(elder), who rarely speaks at gatherings, remembers a second, smaller spring behind the rocks that nobody's used in years. By sunset it's cleared, and the caregivers have water of their own.

The spring only muddies when people wade into the shallows; filled from the big flat rock at the edge, it stays clear. Now anyone can fill a jar at any time from the rock, and a second flat stone step means there's never a queue.

Nobody muddies the spring all day, until a light rain sends muddy water trickling straight down the hill into it. The mud came from the rain all along, nobody is scolded, and the rule is quietly dropped.
The midday fill is quiet and quick, the spring stays clear, and (leader) stops looking as if (leader.he/she) wants to curdle anything.
By the third day the midday fill draws nearly everyone, each with a very creative reason for being a caregiver. ("I'm caring for my thirst!") A squabble, a broken jar, and the rule is withdrawn.
An empty jar under each arm, and an expression that could curdle milk.
A crying baby, and a long wait until tomorrow morning.
The spring is perfectly clear at noon. So far.

pieces.label: The Refused Duty
pieces.text: (Leader) was asked to climb the cliff behind the village and cut fresh vines for rope, and said no, flatly, and walked away; by evening the word "lazy" is drifting round the cooking fires, getting a little louder every time.

pieces.label: Hear Why They Refused
pieces.text: (leader) brings two bowls of stew and sits down beside (leader) without a word. After a while, (leader) starts eating. After a longer while, (leader.he/she) starts talking...

pieces.label: Inspect the Cliff Face
pieces.text: At first light, (leader) and a few climbers walk to the foot of the cliff to see what (leader) was so afraid of...

pieces.label: Pair Them with a Climber
pieces.text: (leader) suggests a compromise: (name3) climbs, while (leader) holds the ropes at the bottom and hauls the vines down...

Over two bowls of stew, (leader) explains that an old shoulder injury gives out without warning on hard climbs, and (leader.he/she) was too proud to say it in front of everyone. When (leader) repeats it at the fire, the word "lazy" stops going around very quickly.

(Name2) hurries over. "Did you tell them about the rockfall?" Last week the two of them watched a slab of that cliff smash onto the path below. Suddenly the talk is about the cliff, not about (leader).
At the shady base of the cliff, the climbers find thick, strong vines growing in the damp, every bit as good for rope and much easier to reach. The risky climb is no longer necessary at all.

Loose stones, fresh cracks, a rock that wobbles when a climber touches it: the cliff is crumbling exactly as (leader) feared. Nobody is punished, and the cliff is marked off-limits with a row of white stones.

(Name3) climbs fast and light, (leader) is strong and steady on the ropes below, and by midday they have more vines than anyone has ever brought back in one trip. They do the job together every season.

(Name3) shouts instructions (leader) can't hear, (leader) pulls when (leader.he/she) should let go, and by noon three ropes are so tangled they have to be cut apart. Nobody is hurt, but the plan is dropped.
The word "lazy" gets a little louder every time it passes from one fire to the next.
Two bowls of stew, and a long silence.
A rock wobbles when a climber touches it.
