pieces.label: The Storehouse Key
pieces.text: On feast day, (leader), the storehouse keeper, who has never once refused to open the door, stands in front of it with (leader.his/her) hand closed tight round the carved wooden peg, refusing to hand it over, and refusing to say why.

pieces.label: Ask the Keeper Privately
pieces.text: (leader) sends the cooks off to "check the fire" and takes (leader) behind the storehouse, where no one can hear...

pieces.label: Count Every Basket
pieces.text: (leader) suggests that everyone go in together, the keeper included, and count every basket in the storehouse, out loud...

pieces.label: Release One Basket at a Time
pieces.text: (leader) proposes that (leader) open the door, but let out only one basket at a time, and only when the cooks bring the last one back empty...

Behind the storehouse, (leader)'s shoulders slump: the stores are much lower than anyone realizes, and (leader.he/she) didn't want to be the one to ruin the celebration. The feast goes ahead, smaller, with fish from the morning's catch.

(Name2), the young helper who sweeps out the storehouse, peeks round the corner. "Is this about the rats?" They got into the yams last week. Within an hour the trap-setters are at work, and the feast goes ahead.

Counting together, they find the newest food stacked at the front and the oldest pushed to the back, going soft, and work out a way to stack it so the oldest is always eaten first. (Leader) finally hands over the peg, smiling.

The count matches (leader)'s tally exactly, down to the last coconut. (leader.He/She) simply forgot to tell the cooks that half the feast food was already set aside in a different hut. A lot of embarrassed laughter.
Nothing is wasted, (leader) can see exactly what is being used, and the cooks discover they needed far less than they thought. There is still plenty in the storehouse in the morning.
A slow, shuffling line of grumbling cooks: the fish is cold before the yams are hot, and the moon is high before dinner is served. The rule is dropped the next day, to loud cheers.
Somebody's stomach growls loudly. Nobody laughs.
(Leader)'s hand closes tight round the peg.
The feast cooks are lined up with empty baskets.

pieces.label: The Stranger's Complaint
pieces.text: A visiting trader with a canoe full of shells, dyes and carved combs says, very politely, that the rule letting outsiders trade only on the beach treats people like the trader unfairly, and has started packing the beautiful dyes back into their pots.

pieces.label: Hear the Trader Out
pieces.text: (leader) asks the trader to sit, offers a cup of coconut water, and listens...

pieces.label: Study the Tide Marks
pieces.text: (leader) walks the beach with the trader, looking at the old lines of seaweed and shell left behind by high tides...

pieces.label: Open the Edge Huts to Trade
pieces.text: (leader) agrees to try letting traders set up beside the first row of huts, just for this visit...

The beach floods at high tide, the trader explains, and twice a sudden wave has taken a whole pot of costly dye, a season's work. The trader stays one more day, trading from a dry spot above the high-tide line that the villagers clear especially.

(Leader), who travelled with traders when young, describes how other villages handle it: a special hut for visitors' goods at the edge of the village, with a roof and a door. The trader unpacks the dyes again to hear the end of it.

The old lines of seaweed and shell show the beach floods badly mostly around the new moon, and hardly at all in between. The village sets proper trading days, and the fishers use the same knowledge to plan when to pull canoes higher.

The trader suspects someone kicked over a pot of dye, but the tracks round it are crab tracks, hundreds of tiny ones, and a very blue crab is hiding under the next rock. The trader laughs until the tears come.
The dyes stay dry, the villagers browse in the shade beside the first row of huts, and the trader sells out by evening. "I'll be back, and I'll tell the others."

The stalls crowd the path, children run between them shrieking, and the families in the edge huts can't get out of their own doors without buying a comb. The trial ends at midday, though at least the village tried.
The beautiful dyes go back into their pots.
A very blue crab.
The children are thrilled. The trader is not.

pieces.label: The Broken Promise
pieces.text: Two moons ago, (leader) promised a family past the swamp a basket of dried fish and a new sleeping mat after their hard season, and nothing ever arrived; now their eldest has walked all the way in on bad feet, mud to the knees, not angry exactly, just very, very tired.

pieces.label: Hear the Distant Family
pieces.text: (leader) gives the visitor (leader.his/her) own seat by the fire, a bowl of hot stew, and the whole village's attention...

pieces.label: Retrace the Delivery Route
pieces.text: (leader) and a few villagers walk the route the basket was supposed to take, step by squelching step, looking for what went wrong...

pieces.label: Send Half Now and Half Later
pieces.text: The stores are a little thin right now. (leader) proposes sending half the fish at once with the eldest, and the rest, with the mat, next moon...

The eldest explains, without raising (leader.his/her) voice, that the family has been living on coconut alone for weeks, and the children are thin. Before the night is over, three households have filled baskets of their own.

(Leader), who carries messages for the village, goes pale: the swamp path flooded weeks ago, and (leader.he/she) turned back with the basket and never told anyone. (leader.He/She) apologizes in front of everyone, and offers to carry it personally.
Halfway round the swamp's edge they find a ridge of firm, dry ground curving neatly round the worst of the mud. The runners mark it with stakes, and the fish and the mat arrive two days later, dry.

In a little shelter on the path is the basket, still packed, the mat rolled beside it. The runner carrying it fell ill on the way and was too feverish to remember it. No one is punished, and it goes the rest of the way that afternoon.

The eldest goes home with a full basket and a promise, and next moon the rest arrives exactly when it should. The family sends back a carved bowl in thanks, which (leader) keeps on (leader.his/her) shelf as a reminder.
The second runner sprains an ankle in the swamp, and the mat falls in the mud. In the end (leader) walks the last delivery out personally, which is the least (leader.he/she) could do.
Mud to the knees, leaning on a stick.
Not angry exactly. Just tired. Very, very tired.
(leader) feels (leader.his/her) face go hot.

pieces.label: The Vote That Tied
pieces.text: After an evening of speeches so long a cook fell asleep and had to be poked, the vote between a new fishing canoe and a second cooking hut comes out exactly half and half, and the only one who hasn't voted, (elder), is snoring by the fire with a small lizard on (leader.his/her) knee.

pieces.label: Ask Who Each Choice Helps
pieces.text: (leader) asks for no more speeches. Just one plain answer from each side: who does it help, and how?...

pieces.label: Tally the Logs and Thatch
pieces.text: (leader) sends everyone off to count logs, thatch and willing workers, and they gather again at dawn with knotted cords and scratched boards...

pieces.label: Wake the Elder and Explain
pieces.text: (leader) gently shakes (elder) awake. The lizard leaves in a huff. (elder) blinks around at the whole silent village staring at (leader.him/her). "What? What did I miss?"...

(Leader) explains that the old canoe leaks so badly now that last week (leader.he/she) bailed water the whole way home, and one big wave could have sunk it. A second vote is taken, and the canoe wins easily.

(Name2), the cook's young helper, stands up at a gathering for the first time. "I can see the stars through the cooking hut roof. It's quite nice, but the rain gets in the soup." The cooks win the second vote.
The canoe can be carved from a single big trunk already lying by the beach, which frees up all the thatch and most of the workers for the hut. They can build both!

Someone accuses the other side of counting a child's raised hand. A recount shows the "child" was a very short adult, now deeply offended, who is given the first bowl of stew in apology. The vote is still a tie.

The lizard leaves in a huff, and after many questions about the fisher's very long speech, (elder) votes for the canoe, "because I like fish more than I like waiting for fish." The cooks are promised the next big project.
"You're not going to let one old person who was asleep decide this. Vote again tomorrow when you've all slept as well as I have." The gathering agrees to vote again next evening.
A cook fell asleep in the middle of a speech and had to be poked.
The lizard leaves in a huff.
Exactly half and half. Counted twice.

pieces.label: The Little Scientist
pieces.text: Little (little_scientist) has lined up a banana, a mango and a breadfruit on a ledge, and marks how ripe each one is every morning on a board covered in tiny fruit faces; by day four the banana looks deeply worried and the mango looks smug.

pieces.label: Ask About the Fruit Faces
pieces.text: (adult) crouches down to (little_scientist)'s height and asks, very seriously, what the faces mean. (Little_scientist)'s eyes light up...

pieces.label: Help Count the Marks
pieces.text: (adult) offers to help, and after a long, hard, suspicious look, (little_scientist) allows (little_scientist.him/her) to sit on the other end of the ledge. But not to touch the fruit...

pieces.label: Let the Child Find the Pattern
pieces.text: (adult) decides not to say anything at all, and just watches over the next few days to see what (little_scientist) figures out alone...

The happy faces mean "nice and hard", the worried faces mean "getting soft", and the sad faces mean "too squishy, do not eat, bad." (Little_scientist) beams at being taken seriously, and explains the faces to anyone who will stand still.
Halfway through, (little_scientist) gasps. "The mango faces are all WRONG!" and wanders off to redraw every single one, muttering. The redrawn mango looks even more smug.

(adult) shows (little_scientist) how to group the marks in fives with a line across, each fruit in its own neat row, and by the end of the day (little_scientist) has redone the whole board properly, very proud of it.

After about three marks, (little_scientist) asks politely to do the counting alone, and (adult) pretends to be very busy whittling a stick nearby. Everything is counted twice, with the same answer both times.

(Little_scientist) moved one banana into the shade "for fairness", and the one in the sun went squishy twice as fast. That afternoon the store's fruit baskets are moved out of their sunny corner into the shade, and (little_scientist) supervises.
On day five a bird lands on the ledge and eats the whole banana. For a moment (little_scientist) might cry. Then: "Tomorrow I'm doing a new row. And a bird net."
The breadfruit has no expression at all, "because breadfruit is like that."
The fierce suspicion of a scientist guarding (little_scientist.his/her) work.
The mango looks smug.

pieces.label: The Secret Fort
pieces.text: Behind the gardens, (fort_leader) and some of the other children have built a fort of fallen branches, palm fronds, a great deal of string and one sleeping mat nobody will admit to borrowing, with a password adults are not told, and its roof is sagging right over three children eating mangoes.

pieces.label: Ask to Hear the Fort's Rules
pieces.text: (adult) stops at a respectful distance outside the fort and asks if (fort_leader.he/she) may please hear the rules. (Fort_leader) pokes (fort_leader.his/her) head out, narrows (fort_leader.his/her) eyes, and considers this...

pieces.label: Help Brace the Roof
pieces.text: (adult) mentions, casually, that the roof looks a bit tired, and asks if the fort's builders would like any help. After a whispered meeting, (fort_leader) agrees, "just this once"...

pieces.label: Let the Wind Teach Them
pieces.text: (adult) bites (fort_leader.his/her) tongue and says nothing. That night, a strong breeze comes up off the sea and rattles through the gardens...
No grown-ups, no crabs, snacks must be shared, and anyone who knocks the wall down has to fix it. As a special honour, (adult) is allowed to sit on the doorstep. Not inside. On the doorstep.
(adult) has now heard too much, so the password has to be changed. After a long consultation inside the fort, the new password turns out to be "banana", which the old password also was.

(adult) shows (fort_leader) how to lash two sticks into a triangle under the sagging middle: push a square and it squashes flat, push a triangle and it stays a triangle. (Fort_leader) tests this on everything, and the roof holds beautifully.
After one knot, (fort_leader) takes the string firmly. "I can do the rest." (Fort_leader) braces the roof alone, slowly, tongue sticking out in concentration. It holds. Mostly.

After a windy night, (fort_leader) notices the walls tied to living trees are still standing, and only the loose ones fell over. The builders start tying the windward sides of their own frames to living trunks.
The whole fort is a heap of fronds and string, with the mystery sleeping mat on top. (Fort_leader) draws a new fort in the dirt, twice as big, with a tower. "Tomorrow we build THIS."
Nobody will admit to borrowing the sleeping mat.
Adults who guess the password are told they are wrong, even when they are right.
A tongue sticking out in concentration.

pieces.label: The First Fish
pieces.text: Using a bit of line and a bent bone hook, little (young_fisher) has caught (young_fisher.his/her) very first fish, by (young_fisher.himself/herself), and stands frozen at the water's edge, torn between showing everyone and letting it go, while the fish wriggles furiously.

pieces.label: Ask What the Child Wants
pieces.text: (adult) kneels in the shallow water beside (young_fisher). "That's a fine fish. What do you want to do with it?"...

pieces.label: Show How to Hold It Gently
pieces.text: (adult) shows (young_fisher) how to wet (young_fisher.his/her) hands in the sea before holding a fish, and how to cup it gently instead of squeezing...

pieces.label: Let the Child Watch the Reef
pieces.text: (adult) suggests that before deciding anything, (young_fisher) should look at where (young_fisher.he/she) caught it. They wade out a little, and (young_fisher) stares down into the clear water...

(Young_fisher)'s lip wobbles: it's (young_fisher.his/her) very first fish, it's so little, and it's looking at (young_fisher.him/her). Together they let it go, and (young_fisher) runs up the beach to tell everyone anyway: "I caught one AND I let it go!"
(Young_fisher) decides the fish's name is Bubbles. This settles nothing. Bubbles, who does not like being named, flips out of (young_fisher.his/her) hands and back into the sea. "Bye, Bubbles!"

"Fish don't breathe air like we do. They breathe the water. Dry hands hurt them." (Young_fisher) asks about fifty questions, learns how fish breathe, and keeps the fish for dinner, now that (young_fisher.he/she) knows how to be gentle about it.
(Young_fisher) wets (young_fisher.his/her) hands and asks to decide on (young_fisher.his/her) own. After a long think, (young_fisher.he/she) lets the fish go, then immediately casts the line again.

(Young_fisher) notices the fish all gather where the reef shades the water, and hardly any in the bright parts. The fishers are genuinely impressed, and start casting into the shady spots, with better catches.
While (young_fisher) watches the reef, the fish makes a heroic leap and vanishes. (Young_fisher) grins. "That's okay. I know where they live now. I'm coming back tomorrow."
The fish has strong opinions about the situation.
"I caught one AND I let it go!"
A bit of line and a bent bone hook.

pieces.label: The Teacher Who Listened
pieces.text: In the middle of a lesson about the tides, (pupil), a quiet pupil who almost never speaks, raises a hand: "I think you have the time of the high tide wrong." Someone drops a shell, and everyone turns to see what the teacher will do.

pieces.label: Let the Pupil Explain
pieces.text: "Go on," says (teacher), and sits down cross-legged in the sand with the others. "Teach us."...

pieces.label: Check the Tide Together
pieces.text: (teacher) packs up the lesson early, and walks down to the beach with (pupil), to see for themselves...

pieces.label: Let the Shore Settle It
pieces.text: (teacher) proposes a deal: the whole class will mark the high tide in the sand every day for a week, and whoever is right, is right...

Haltingly at first, then faster, (pupil) explains that the tide comes in a little later every single day. (teacher) thanks (pupil.him/her) in front of everyone, and (pupil) goes pink to the ears, but sits up a little straighter.
(Pupil) looks at all the faces staring and goes completely red. "...I'll say it tomorrow." Nobody pushes, and the next morning (pupil) explains it all, very quietly, just to (teacher).

For a few days they mark the waterline at the same time each morning, count the days on a knotted cord and line the marks up against a big rock. (Pupil) learns how to keep track of the tide, and the marks prove (pupil.him/her) right.
"I want to be sure it's really true. Not just because you helped." (Pupil) does the marking alone, and (teacher) waits further up the beach every morning, pretending to look for shells.

After a week of marks, the pattern is impossible to argue with: the tide arrives later each day, by about the same amount. The fishers start using the marks to plan their trips, and (teacher) puts (pupil)'s name on the corrected lesson.
On the fifth night a storm wipes every mark off the beach. (Pupil) is the first to pick up a stick. "We'll just start again tomorrow," (pupil.he/she) says, loud enough for everyone to hear.
Someone drops a shell.
The teacher slowly puts down the pointing stick.
Pink to the ears, but sitting up a little straighter.

pieces.label: The Broken Toy Boat
pieces.text: Little (child)'s favourite toy canoe, carved by (child.his/her) grandparent, has survived storms, younger siblings and one very curious pig, but this morning it sank in the lagoon, and there's a crack running right down the hull.

pieces.label: Let the Child Talk About the Boat
pieces.text: (adult) sits on the sand next to (child), says nothing for a while, and then asks the boat's name...

pieces.label: Mend It Side by Side
pieces.text: (adult) fetches a little pot of sticky sap and a bundle of plant fibre, and sits down with (child) to mend Swift together...

pieces.label: Let the Child Test the Patches
pieces.text: (adult) gives (child) a few different things to try: plain sap, sap mixed with sand, sap mixed with ash from the fire, and lets (child.him/her) test each one on bits of old wood in a bucket of water...

Between sniffles, (child) explains everything: the boat is called Swift, and it is the fastest boat on the whole island, probably the whole world. By the end (child) is smiling, and (adult) has promised to help fix Swift tomorrow.
(Child) announces that Swift wants to be a shipwreck now. A brave, famous shipwreck. It is buried in the sand with a shell on top, and the legend of the great storm that sank it grows every day.

Fibre pressed into the crack and sealed with warm sap, and why wood splits: it dries out faster on the outside than the inside, and pulls itself apart along the grain. Swift sails again by evening, slightly crooked and better than ever.
(Child) does the mending alone, because Swift is (child.his/hers). It takes a long time and a lot of sap. The patch is enormous and lumpy, and (child) thinks it is the most beautiful patch ever made.

Plain sap, sap with sand, sap with ash: the ash mix holds best by far, stays hard and watertight, and works on a real canoe with a leaky seam too. Soon every canoe in the village is patched with "(child)'s mix."
None of the patches hold, and Swift sinks again with a sad little glug. "Okay. Tomorrow I'm trying sap and mud. And maybe banana." (adult) is quietly very impressed.
It survived storms, younger siblings and one very curious pig.
A tiny sail made from a leaf.
"(Child)'s mix."

pieces.label: The Child Who Feared Thunder
pieces.text: A huge storm rolls over the island in the middle of the night, and little (frightened_child) sits bolt upright on (frightened_child.his/her) mat with a blanket over (frightened_child.his/her) head, jumping at every crash of thunder, so nobody else in the hut is getting any sleep either.

pieces.label: Ask What Scares Them
pieces.text: (adult) shuffles over and sits beside the blanket-shaped lump. "Hey. What's the matter?" A small voice comes out from under the blanket...

pieces.label: Count the Thunder Together
pieces.text: (adult) lifts a corner of the blanket. "Want to know a secret? You can tell how far away a storm is. Watch for the next flash..."

pieces.label: Let the Child Watch from the Doorway
pieces.text: (adult) wraps (frightened_child) in an extra blanket and sits with (frightened_child.him/her) in the doorway, where they can watch the storm out over the sea, safe and dry under the overhang...

"The thunder sounds like the mountain is angry. What if it's angry at us?" (adult) explains that the mountain probably doesn't even know their little hut is there, and (frightened_child) falls asleep against (adult)'s arm, which then cannot move for the rest of the night.

"Actually... it's the drip." A leak in the roof is dripping onto the end of the mat, plip, plip, plip, which is somehow much more frightening in the dark than the thunder. Someone fetches a bowl, and (frightened_child) is asleep within minutes.

One... two... three... four... five... BOOM. "Five. That means it's far away, out over the sea." (Frightened_child) learns how to tell the storm's distance, and by the end is more interested than scared.

(Frightened_child) wants to keep counting alone, so (adult) sits nearby in the dark listening to a small voice counting, very seriously. Somewhere around "eleven," the voice turns into gentle snoring.

Watching the flashes over the water, (frightened_child) notices the counts getting longer and longer. "It's going away!" In the morning (frightened_child.he/she) tells the fishers, and they start using the same trick before they set out.

They watch the lightning dance over the sea for a long time, and it is actually quite beautiful. (Frightened_child) falls asleep in the doorway, and in the morning asks if they can watch the next storm too.
CRASH. "Eep."
Rain hammers the thatch.
The wind howls through the palms.

pieces.label: The Two Best Friends
pieces.text: (Friend_1) and (name2), best friends since before they could walk, are building a bird feeder together, and it has become the most serious argument of their lives: (friend_1) insists it must be ROUND, and (name2) insists it must be SQUARE.

pieces.label: Hear Each Friend Out
pieces.text: (adult) sits down between them. "All right. One at a time. Tell me about your feeder." (Friend_1) goes first, with diagrams drawn in the dirt...

pieces.label: Help Without Picking a Side
pieces.text: (adult) suggests they build both, a round one and a square one, and offers to help with the tricky parts...

pieces.label: Let the Birds Decide
pieces.text: (adult) suggests a test. Build both, hang them side by side in the same tree, and see which one the birds choose. The two friends shake on it, very solemnly...

Each child explains their design in enormous detail, with a great deal of pointing. By the end the two of them feel properly heard, and are sitting side by side again, arguing more quietly about where the perch should go.

Halfway through, (name2) looks at (friend_1)'s drawing and says, "Actually, round is nice." (Friend_1) is so surprised (friend_1.he/she) says, "Actually, square is nice." They stare at each other, then burst out laughing.
While they build both, (adult) explains that birds need somewhere thin to grip before they eat, like a twig. (Friend_1) learns how birds land, perch and feed, and explains it to (name2) at length.
Both children finish it themselves, together. The feeder is round on one side and square on the other. It is the strangest feeder anyone has ever seen.

For three days the birds always go to the one with a perch, whichever shape it is. The adults are interested enough to put perches on the bird-scarers in the fields, so the birds land there instead of on the crops.
No birds come to either feeder. Not one. Then (name2) says, "Want to try again tomorrow?" and (friend_1) says, "Together?" and that seems to settle everything that mattered.
"Never speaking again" lasts about as long as it takes to say it.
Birds are round and nests are round and the sun is round.
Back to back in the dirt, arms folded.

pieces.label: The Lost Shell Collection
pieces.text: Little (collector)'s shell collection, sorted for weeks along the ledge from biggest to smallest, pink to white, spiky to smooth, has nearly all vanished overnight, leaving tiny sandy tracks across the floor, up the wall and out the door. "Somebody is a THIEF."

pieces.label: Ask About the Special Shells
pieces.text: (adult) asks which shells were the most special. (Collector) sniffs and starts counting them off on (collector.his/her) fingers...

pieces.label: Help Follow the Tracks
pieces.text: (adult) crouches to look at the little tracks. "Shall we find your thief?" (Collector) nods fiercely. They follow the trail out the door, across the path and down toward the beach...

pieces.label: Let the Child Watch the Crabs
pieces.text: (adult) suggests (collector) puts a few spare shells back on the ledge tonight, hides, and watches to see who comes...

The pink one shaped like an ear, the one with a hole that whistles, the stripy one from the far beach... (Collector) feels taken seriously, and somehow that helps. That afternoon, (adult) quietly leaves a new pink shell on the ledge.
"Actually, I was getting bored of those. I want to start a NEW collection. Of rocks." By evening the ledge is covered in rocks, and it is somehow much heavier.

The tracks lead to a burrow where a hermit crab is sitting proudly in the whistling shell. (Collector) learns that hermit crabs move into bigger shells as they grow, and lets it keep the whistler, "because it looks happy."
(Collector) follows the tracks alone, like a real tracker, and returns triumphantly with an armful of shells and a very indignant crab, which (collector.he/she) is persuaded to put back.

By moonlight two hermit crabs climb the wall and take only the shells of one particular size. The adults, who have been losing small shell tools and beads for years, finally know why, and start storing them high up.
The crabs refuse to show themselves, and (collector) falls asleep watching. "They KNEW I was watching. I'll catch them tomorrow."
"Somebody is a THIEF."
A shell with a hole that whistles.
A very indignant crab.

pieces.label: The Very Serious Play
pieces.text: The children have invented a game with sticks, a coconut, three circles drawn in the sand and rules so complicated that two adults gave up learning it, and it has stopped dead over whether the coconut was in the moon circle or the sun circle. The referee is very small.

pieces.label: Ask for the Rules
pieces.text: (Inventor) draws (inventor.himself/herself) up to (inventor.his/her) full height and begins to explain the rules...

pieces.label: Keep Score for Them
pieces.text: (adult) offers to keep score, since there seems to be a lot of arguing about it. (Inventor) considers this offer very seriously...

pieces.label: Let Them Fix Their Own Rules
pieces.text: (adult) suggests that if the game keeps stopping for arguments, maybe the players should sit down together and fix the rules themselves...

(Inventor) explains the rules with enormous dignity. There are seventeen of them. Rule nine is "no biting." Rule fourteen is "the coconut is always right." (adult) understands almost none of it, is made to play, and loses, badly.

Halfway through, (inventor) realizes the rules mean (inventor.he/she) loses, so (inventor.he/she) changes them. Then changes them again. Nobody minds, and (referee) blows a whistle made of a leaf, for no clear reason.

One knot for a point, a big knot for every five. (Inventor) takes over the cord almost at once and becomes very bossy about it. There are no more arguments about the score. There are a lot of arguments about everything else.
(Inventor) keeps score alone, since it's (inventor.his/her) game, and at the end declares that both teams won, which everyone agrees is fair.

The children argue in a circle for a long time and work out the game only feels fair when the teams are even and everyone gets the same number of turns. Soon the adults are using "even teams, same turns" for the fishing rota.

The rules meeting collapses into happy chaos within a minute: someone chases someone else, the coconut rolls into the sea, and the referee falls asleep. They vow to fix the rules properly tomorrow. They will not.
"The coconut is always right."
The referee blows a whistle made of a leaf, for no clear reason.
The moon circle or the sun circle? It matters enormously.

pieces.label: The Young Helper
pieces.text: The builders are working on a new hut, and little (young_helper) has decided to help by dragging one of the big logs, about three times (young_helper.his/her) own size, across the clearing inch by inch, refusing every offer of help with a furious "I CAN DO IT."

pieces.label: Ask Why It Matters to Them
pieces.text: (adult) crouches down beside the log and the very sweaty child. "That's a big log. Why this one?"...

pieces.label: Lift the Other End
pieces.text: Without asking, (adult) quietly picks up the other end of the log. (Young_helper) glares at (young_helper.him/her), but doesn't tell (young_helper.him/her) to put it down...

pieces.label: Let the Child Try Rollers
pieces.text: (adult) doesn't help. Instead, (young_helper.he/she) leaves a row of short, round sticks lying on the ground near the log, and walks away whistling...

Between gasps, (young_helper) explains that (young_helper.he/she) wants to be useful like the builders, but everybody's always too busy to let (young_helper.him/her) help with anything real. (Young_helper) ends the day carrying bindings and fetching water, feeling very much part of the crew.

(Young_helper) looks at the log, then at the enormous pile of thatch bundles waiting by the hut. "Actually, can I carry THOSE?" They're exactly what the builders need, and far more help than the log ever was.

A smaller round log laid underneath, a push, and the big log rolls along on top almost by itself. (Young_helper) is astonished, and spends the rest of the day rolling everything (young_helper.he/she) can find.
After a few steps, (young_helper) asks to finish alone. The log reaches the hut at sunset. Every builder cheers. (Young_helper) collapses on the grass and sleeps right there.

(Young_helper) looks at the short round sticks, looks at the log, lays them out in a row, heaves the end of the log onto them, and pushes. It rolls! The builders use it for the rest of the hut, and it is "(young_helper)'s trick" forever after.

The sticks all roll out sideways, and the log won't budge an inch more. (Young_helper) flops down on it: "I'm going to move it tomorrow," with such confidence that the builders leave the log exactly where it is.
"I CAN DO IT."
So far the log has moved about the length of (young_helper.his/her) own foot.
The builders have stopped working to watch.

pieces.label: The Elder's Last Garden
pieces.text: An elderly gardener wants to plant a breadfruit sapling that will take many years to give its best fruit, and has done the counting. "Somebody will eat from it."

pieces.label: Let the Gardener Choose
pieces.text: (young) closes (elder_gardener.his/her) mouth again, and asks only, "How do you want to do it?" (Elder_gardener) looks at (elder_gardener.him/her) for a long moment, surprised...

pieces.label: Learn the Planting Lore
pieces.text: (young) asks if (elder_gardener.he/she) can watch and learn how (elder_gardener) does it. (Elder_gardener) snorts, but (elder_gardener.his/her) eyes light up. "Well, first, you don't just stick it in any old dirt..."

pieces.label: Bring a Stool to the Garden
pieces.text: (young) fetches a low stool and a long-handled digging stick, so (elder_gardener) can sit and dig without bending...
The gardener plants it alone at dawn, at their own pace, and sits beside it drinking coconut water, looking very satisfied.
The gardener gruffly asks for help with the digging, and three of the family grab digging sticks at once.
The gardener teaches how to judge soil by its smell, its colour and the way it crumbles in the hand.
The gardener can't remember the third verse of the old planting chant; three elders piece most of it back together and sing it, badly.
With the stool and the long stick, the gardener plants in comfort, calls the stool "a fine invention" and refuses to give it back.
The gardener naps under the palm instead. "It can wait a day. It's going to be around a long time."
Everyone can see the gardener doing the counting in their head.
A glossy-leaved, sturdy sapling.
A ring of stones around something small and new.

pieces.label: The Forgotten Path
pieces.text: An elder insists there is a shortcut through the bamboo to the far beach, a path they ran along every day as a child; none of the younger villagers have ever seen it.

pieces.label: Ask Where They Want to Walk
pieces.text: (young) doesn't argue. (elder.He/She) just asks (elder) to show (elder.him/her)...

pieces.label: Map the Old Way
pieces.text: (young) asks (elder) how (elder.he/she) would find an old path that's grown over. (Elder) brightens immediately. "Ah. Now THAT is a skill..."

pieces.label: Clear the Bamboo Ahead of Them
pieces.text: (young) fetches a cutting blade and a couple of friends, and they start hacking back the bamboo wherever (elder) points...
The elder walks the path alone, slowly, poking the bamboo aside with a stick, and comes out on the far beach. "TOLD you."
The elder holds out an arm to lean on, surprising everyone, and tells stories about every bend.
The elder teaches how to find old paths by the lean of the trees and the little stacks of stones at every turn.
At a fork the elder can't remember the way; the other elders are fetched and choose right. It was left.
The cleared path leads to the far beach, and the elder kicks off their sandals and walks into the sea, the way they did as a child.
The walk is too much for today, and the young villagers promise to finish clearing the path. They do.
Very dense, very tall bamboo, and a lot of spiders.
"It's THERE. You're just not looking properly."
A path worn deep into the ground under all the growth.

pieces.label: The Old Fisher's Hands
pieces.text: An old fisher who tied half the nets on the island now fumbles the knots, and hides the knotting work under a mat whenever anyone walks past.

pieces.label: Ask How They Want to Fish
pieces.text: (young) sits down beside (old_fisher) and asks, very simply, "What would you like to keep doing?"...

pieces.label: Record the Knots
pieces.text: (young) asks if (old_fisher) would teach (old_fisher.him/her) the knots, all of them, before they're forgotten. (Old_fisher) frowns, then cracks (old_fisher.his/her) aching knuckles. "Sit down. Watch my hands. Not my face, my HANDS."...

pieces.label: Build a Knotting Frame
pieces.text: (young) has an idea, and spends the afternoon building a wooden frame that can hold a net steady at just the right height, so (old_fisher) doesn't have to grip it...
The fisher decides to keep fishing by hand line from the rocks, and comes back with three fish and a smug expression.
The fisher slides the mat off the half-finished net and asks for help, and everyone sits down at once.
The fisher teaches seven net knots and the reason behind each one. Saying nothing is the highest praise.
The old "crab claw" knot is forgotten, and the old fishers spend the whole evening, and a lot of string, puzzling it out.
A knotting frame holds the net steady, and the fisher ties knots in comfort again. "Huh. Not bad."
The hands hurt too much today, so they soak in warm water while the two of them talk about the sea.
"Watch my hands. Not my face, my HANDS."
Knuckles that ache in the mornings and swell in the damp.
A half-finished net hidden under a mat.

pieces.label: The Birthday No One Counted
pieces.text: Nobody knows how old one elder is. Guesses range from "younger than me" to "older than the volcano", and the elder claims a different age every time someone asks.

pieces.label: Ask How They Would Celebrate
pieces.text: "Well," says (young), "if nobody knows your birthday, you might as well pick one. What would you like to do on it?"...

pieces.label: Work Out Their Age
pieces.text: (young) is determined to solve the mystery properly. (Elder) chuckles. "If you want to count years, you don't count them. You count storms."...

pieces.label: Swap Stories of the Years
pieces.text: That evening, (elder)'s family and friends gather around the fire to share memories of all the years they've known (elder.him/her)...
The elder plans a swim at sunrise, the biggest meal anyone can cook and a long nap in the best hammock, and calls it the best birthday in "at least eighty years. Or sixty. Or a hundred."
The elder asks for help planning a proper feast, with drums, and dances, badly and with great joy, until the moon is high.
The elder teaches how the old people counted years by the great storms, comets and dry seasons everyone remembered.
The elder can't remember which great storm came first, and the whole elders' circle shouts about storms. They never settle it.
Swapped memories fill the evening, and nobody needs an exact number after all. "However old I am, it's been worth it."
An old disagreement about whose idea the first cooking hut was comes up, and is left unsettled, which is how both of them like it.
"Already old when I was a baby." Deeply offensive.
A different age every time someone asks.
"If you want to count years, you don't count them. You count storms."

pieces.label: The Teacher Who Retired
pieces.text: The teacher who has taught every child in the village for years announces that the daily lessons have become too exhausting, and the children are horrified.

pieces.label: Ask What They Would Like Now
pieces.text: (young) finds (teacher) sitting alone on the beach, looking at the sea, and sits down beside (teacher.him/her). "What would you like to do now?"...

pieces.label: Learn Their Teaching Ways
pieces.text: (young) asks if (teacher) would show (teacher.him/her) how to teach, so someone can carry on. (Teacher) gives (teacher.him/her) a long, measuring look, the same look (teacher.he/she) gave (teacher.him/her) when (teacher.he/she) was six and hadn't done (teacher.his/her) counting...

pieces.label: Move Lessons Into the Shade
pieces.text: (young) suggests moving the lessons out of the stuffy hut, under the big shade tree, with a cushion and a water jar for (teacher)...
The teacher decides to teach one long, good lesson a week and go fishing the rest of the time; it becomes the most popular event in the village.
The teacher asks for an assistant, and the younger villager volunteers on the spot. Two teachers instead of one.
The teacher shows how to teach counting with pebbles for ones, shells for tens and a coconut for a hundred.
The counting rhyme is forgotten after "seven fishes in a net", and half the adults chant it back together.
Under the big shade tree, with a cushion and a jar of water, the teacher decides they aren't quite ready to stop after all.
The children get a surprise day off and run off shrieking before the teacher can change their mind.
Some adults still sit up straight when the teacher walks past.
Which berries can kill, and why nobody should ever poke a pufferfish.
"Seven fishes in a net..."

pieces.label: The Letter Never Sent
pieces.text: Clearing an old shelf, an elder finds an apology letter written long ago to a dear friend, who fell ill and died before it could be given. The elder can still recite almost every word.

pieces.label: Ask What They Want to Do with It
pieces.text: (young) sits down quietly on the floor beside (elder), and waits. After a while, (elder.he/she) asks gently what (elder) would like to do with the letter...

pieces.label: Copy the Old Writing
pieces.text: (young) gently suggests copying the letter onto fresh bark, before it fades away completely. (Elder) agrees, and fetches charcoal and a little pot of sap...

pieces.label: Read It at the Friend's Grave
pieces.text: (young) offers to walk with (elder) to (elder.his/her) friend's grave, and builds a small bench there so (elder.he/she) can sit...
The elder reads it alone by the sea at sunset, and comes back after dark, eyes red, but somehow lighter.
"Will you sit and read it with me?" The elder says the faded words along, then talks about the friend for hours.
The elder teaches the old way of writing on bark with charcoal and thin sap, so the words last for years.
Some words have faded too far, and others who knew the friend gather to remember them, telling stories all evening.
On a little bench by the grave, the elder reads the letter aloud, at last, and tucks the bark into the earth.
At the grave it is too much for today, and the letter is put away for another time.
An argument so small nobody can remember what it was about.
The charcoal has faded almost to nothing.
Was it "I'm sorry I said" or "I'm sorry I didn't say"?

pieces.label: The Last Dance
pieces.text: The festival drums have started, and an elder whose legs have been unsteady for a while announces they are dancing tonight, whatever anyone says.

pieces.label: Ask How They Want to Dance
pieces.text: (young) steps forward before anyone can argue. "How do you want to dance?"...

pieces.label: Learn the Old Steps
pieces.text: (young) asks (elder) to teach (elder.him/her) the dances from (elder.his/her) youth, the ones nobody does anymore. (Elder)'s eyes sparkle. "The harvest dance? Nobody remembers the harvest dance!"...

pieces.label: Dance from a Stool
pieces.text: (young) fetches a sturdy stool and sets it at the edge of the dancing circle, right where the drums are loudest...
The elder dances slowly, carefully and very proudly in the middle of the circle, until the whole circle is dancing their way.
"I'd like a partner. To steady me." The elder picks the smallest grandchild, and everyone watching gets a bit misty-eyed.
The elder teaches the old harvest dance and what each step once meant: planting, the rain coming, chasing birds from the crops.
A step is forgotten, and six elders stand in the firelight arguing about feet.
Dancing from a stool with arms and shoulders, the elder starts a whole row of seated dancers.
The elder would rather watch tonight, and calls out compliments and insults to the dancers in equal measure from the best seat at the festival.
A glare that could stop a charging boar.
The old people complain that the young people dance wrong.
One foot already tapping.

pieces.label: The Grandparent's Story
pieces.text: Around the fire, a grandparent changes the ending of the story every child knows by heart: the village's first canoe wasn't found at all. It was a GIFT. From whom, they aren't saying.

pieces.label: Ask Which Ending They Want
pieces.text: (young) asks (grandparent) quietly, once the children have calmed down, which ending is the real one...

pieces.label: Memorize Both Endings
pieces.text: (young) asks how storytellers keep long tales straight, so (grandparent.he/she) can remember both endings. (Grandparent) pulls a knotted cord out of (grandparent.his/her) pocket. "With this."...

pieces.label: Tell It Over Several Nights
pieces.text: (young) suggests (grandparent) tell the new version a little each night, so (grandparent.he/she) doesn't get too tired...
"The one I tell." The grandparent reveals the gift came from "someone who lived on the island before any of us", and won't say any more.
The grandparent and the children build the new ending around the fire together. It ends with a talking turtle. Nobody minds.
The grandparent teaches how storytellers keep long tales straight with knotted cords: a big knot for each part, a twist for each surprise.
"Was it the turtle people or the fish people?" Five different versions later, the children have decided on all of them.
Told a little each night, the story turns the whole village into eager listeners begging for "just one more bit."
On the second night the grandparent is too tired, and a child who sneaks in to ask "WHO WAS IT FROM?" gets a sleepy "Tomorrow."
The children mouth along with every word.
"From WHO?"
A knotted cord pulled out of a pocket.

pieces.label: The Old Scar
pieces.text: A young villager finally asks an elder about the long, pale scar on their forearm, and this time the elder doesn't joke about wrestling a shark. They go quiet.

pieces.label: Let the Elder Decide What to Share
pieces.text: (young) says, "You don't have to tell me," and means it. (Elder) looks up at (elder.him/her)...

pieces.label: Learn from the Old Accident
pieces.text: (Elder) traces the scar with one finger. "I broke it. Badly. And there was nobody to help, so I had to set it myself..."

pieces.label: Talk Somewhere Quiet
pieces.text: (young) suggests they go somewhere quieter, away from the fire and all the listening ears...
The elder tells only part of it: a fall, someone they loved, a very bad day. Nothing more, and that is respected.
"I think I'd like to tell someone." The elder tells the whole story for the first time in decades, while relatives listen from the shadows in tears.
The elder teaches how they set and splinted their own broken arm that day, and the younger villager shares it with the healers.
Old friends help fill in the gaps of that day. They argue about the rain, but they all remember who found the elder.
By the lagoon, with only the frogs to hear, it becomes one of their longest talks, and they are friends from then on.
The elder is too tired to go into it today. "Another time," they promise at the door.
Crooked, like a river on a map.
"Oh, that old thing."
Only the frogs to hear.

pieces.label: The Bench in the Sun
pieces.text: An elder asks for a bench on the steep bluff above the shore to watch the fishing canoes come home each evening, and points out they will not be asking for many more things.

pieces.label: Ask Where Exactly It Should Go
pieces.text: (young) asks (elder) exactly where the bench should go. (Elder)'s face lights up...

pieces.label: Learn What They Watch For
pieces.text: (young) sits with (elder) on the beach and asks what (elder.he/she) used to watch for from up there...

pieces.label: Build Steps Up the Bluff
pieces.text: (young) and some friends haul flat stones up the bluff, setting them into the slope one by one to make a gentle stair...
The elder describes the exact spot, down to the angle of the sunset, and sits on the new bench without a word for an hour.
The elder asks for help up the bluff, catches their breath at the top, and points. "There."
The elder teaches how to read the coming weather from the clouds over the sea: fluffy is safe, long and flat means wind, dark and piled means get the canoes in now.
The old cloud names are half forgotten, and the elders spend a lively afternoon pointing at the sky and arguing.
Flat stone steps let the elder reach the bench every evening; it becomes "(elder)'s bench", guarded fiercely from young couples.
The climb is too much today, so the elder watches the canoes from a mat on the beach. "I'll go up tomorrow."
Watching for a canoe that used to be their family's.
A very uncomfortable silence, and a hand reaching for a hammer.
Fish-scale clouds, old-woman's-hair clouds, the angry ones.

pieces.label: The Trader with No Goods
pieces.text: A trader's storm-cracked canoe limps onto the beach at dawn, stuffed with moss to slow the leak. All that is left of the cargo is one sack of dried fish and a dripping bolt of dyed cloth.

pieces.label: Offer Them a Hot Meal
pieces.text: (Finder) helps the trader haul the canoe up the sand and leads (finder.him/her) straight to the cooking fire...

pieces.label: Ask What the Storm Was Like
pieces.text: Once the trader has dried off, the fishers gather around, eager to hear about the storm...

pieces.label: Offer Them a Place Here
pieces.text: (Finder) asks, gently, whether the trader has anything to go back to. The trader looks down at (finder.his/her) cracked canoe, and the dripping cloth...

pieces.label: Trade Field Work for Repairs
pieces.text: (Finder) suggests a fair trade: the village will mend the canoe, and while it dries, the trader can help out in the fields...
The trader falls asleep before finishing the stew, sleeps half a day, and wakes asking whether there's more. There is.
"You fed me. I'm not taking it back out to sea." The trader insists on giving the village the last sack of dried fish.
The trader explains reading the long, slow waves that come before the wind, and the fishers start watching for them before every trip.
The trader goes quiet at the night the cargo went over the side. "Another day." Someone hands them more stew.
With nothing left to go back to, the trader joins the village for good, and the dried cloth becomes the brightest curtain in the village.
The trader wants to rebuild their trade, and paddles away once the canoe is sound, promising the first and best of the new cargo.
While the canoe's patches dry, the trader throws themselves into the taro harvest, singing sea songs the whole time.
The trader is hopeless at farming and pulls up three taro plants by mistake, but leaves with a sound canoe.
"Would you like to buy a very wet blanket?"
Moss stuffed into a crack to slow the leak.
Sea songs in the taro field.

pieces.label: The Sailor Who Stayed
pieces.text: A sailor from another settlement's fishing crew stopped in for one night, five nights ago, and has found a new excuse to stay every morning since. On the fifth night they admit it: "I don't want to go back. I'd rather live here."

pieces.label: Make Room at the Fire
pieces.text: (Host) just shifts over on the log and passes the sailor another bowl...

pieces.label: Ask About Their Crew
pieces.text: (Host) asks about the crew the sailor came with. The sailor thinks for a while before answering...

pieces.label: Offer the Sailor a Hut
pieces.text: (Host) tells the sailor there's an empty sleeping spot in one of the huts, if (host.he/she) means it...

pieces.label: Put the Sailor in the Fields
pieces.text: (Host) decides that if the sailor is staying another day, (host.he/she) can earn (host.his/her) stew. "Grab a digging stick."...
Host and sailor swap stories of storms and sea monsters that turned out to be logs until the coals go grey.
The sailor brings a basket of smoked fish from the crew's stores. "They won't miss it. Probably."
The sailor shows how the crew lashes an outrigger with a double-wrapped knot so it never works loose.
The sailor doesn't want to talk about why they are leaving the crew, and the host changes the subject to stew, which is always safe.
The sailor makes a home here, sea legs and all, and walks around for a week as if the ground is rocking.
After a long night of thinking, the sailor goes back to the crew that still needs them, and asks the host to save some stew.
The sailor digs yams, complaining cheerfully that dry land "doesn't MOVE", and turns out to be a surprisingly hard worker.
The sailor's heart is out at sea, so the villagers mend the torn sail and send them home with fruit and an open invitation.
A sore foot. A cloudy sky. A stew too good to leave.
"It doesn't MOVE, how do you stand it?"
Walking as if the ground is rocking.

pieces.label: The Letter Across the Sea
pieces.text: A courier brings a roll of bark tied with braided hair: a letter for a villager from someone who sailed away years ago. The courier is still standing on the beach, salt-stiff and very hopeful about dinner.

pieces.label: Feed the Courier
pieces.text: Before (recipient.he/she) can even think about opening the letter, (recipient) takes the courier by the arm and leads (recipient.him/her) up to the fire...

pieces.label: Ask How the Letter Travelled
pieces.text: (Recipient) can't stop wondering how this little roll of bark crossed so much water. (recipient.He/She) asks the courier to explain...

pieces.label: Ask Whether They Would Settle
pieces.text: Over dinner, the courier mentions how tired (recipient.he/she) is of the sea. (Recipient) asks, half joking, whether (recipient.he/she) would ever settle down somewhere...

pieces.label: Trade a Reply for an Afternoon's Work
pieces.text: (Recipient) wants to send a reply. The courier agrees to carry it, and while (recipient) works on it, offers to help out around the village...
The courier is snoring in a hammock within minutes, while the recipient reads the letter three times and looks out at the sea, smiling.
"Payment for the best meal I've had in a moon." The courier shares their dried fruit, and the children immediately try to steal it.
Letters are passed boat to boat, with a knot in the braided hair for every hand. This one has eleven knots.
"That's for the letter to tell, not me." The recipient finally unrolls it, and goes very quiet for a long time.
Tired of the sea and of sleeping on other people's boats, the courier stays for good. "Somebody else can carry the letters for a while."
The courier pats a bag full of letters for people all over the sea, and sails on in the morning.
While the reply is carved, the courier climbs the breadfruit trees with alarming speed.
The villagers stitch up the courier's torn satchel, which has been losing letters for weeks, and add a stern warning to check it more often.
Bark tied with braided hair.
Salt-stiff and hopeful about the smell of dinner.
Eleven knots, eleven hands.

pieces.label: The Farmhand from the West
pieces.text: A farmhand from a settlement in the west shows the village their way of digging taro with a curved stick, always leaving a piece of each plant in the ground. The village farmers are fascinated, and a little offended.

pieces.label: Welcome Them with Fresh Fruit
pieces.text: (Village_farmer) unfolds (village_farmer.his/her) arms with some effort, and offers the farmhand a ripe mango...

pieces.label: Ask About Western Farming
pieces.text: (Village_farmer) finally gives in to curiosity, and asks how they farm in the west...

pieces.label: Offer a Plot of Their Own
pieces.text: To everyone's surprise, it's (village_farmer) who offers. "There's a spare plot by the stream. If you want to show us properly."...

pieces.label: Harvest Side by Side
pieces.text: (Village_farmer) issues a challenge: one row each, the village way and the western way, and see whose basket fills first...
A ripe mango in the shadiest spot leads to an hour of talking about soil, and suspicion turns into curiosity, which is much more dangerous.
The farmhand shares a pouch of smoky, sweet roasted nuts from home, and the farmer eats far more than their share.
The farmhand explains resting each field every third season, and the farmer rests their tiredest field the next season.
The farmhand taps their nose: the curved stick's secret stays private. The farmer's own curved stick breaks.
The farmhand settles for good; the two of them argue about farming every day and grow the best taro on the island.
The farmhand's own fields are waiting back home, and they head west, leaving one curved digging stick as a gift.
A furious row-against-row contest brings in a fine harvest. Nobody can agree who won.
The curved stick cracks clean in two, and the villagers carve the farmhand a new one from good hard wood.
"Why dig a new hole when the old one is already there?"
Arms folded, watching a curved stick with deep suspicion.
Nobody can agree who won.

pieces.label: The Returning Exile
pieces.text: Years ago, a villager left after a bitter fight over a broken promise. Now they are standing at the edge of the village, thinner and greyer, asking very quietly whether they may come back.

pieces.label: Meet Them at the Village Edge
pieces.text: (Rememberer) walks out to the edge of the village alone. For a long moment the two of them just look at each other...

pieces.label: Ask Where They Have Been
pieces.text: Later, by the fire, (rememberer) asks where they have been all these years...

pieces.label: Let Them Decide About Staying
pieces.text: (Rememberer) tells the returnee plainly that the choice is theirs, and that (rememberer.he/she), at least, won't stand in the way...

pieces.label: Rebuild Trust Through Work
pieces.text: The returnee asks to help, any way they can. (Rememberer) hands them a digging stick and points at the fields...
"Come and eat." Old friends sit with the returnee by the fire in silence, which is more welcome than any words.
The returnee's bundle is a peace offering of smoked fish wrapped in leaves. "I didn't know what else to bring."
The returnee describes the coastline they followed: which beaches have fresh water, which coves shelter from storms, which reefs to avoid.
The returnee is not ready to talk about the old fight. "Another day," and it is meant kindly.
The returnee comes home for good, and one evening the person they fought with passes them a bowl, and that is the end of it.
They didn't come back to stay. They only needed to make peace, and leave with a lighter step.
The returnee works the harvest dawn to dusk, until the village starts saving them a seat.
Mending the returnee's leaky canoe side by side wears the old anger away, and they are seen off with more warmth than anyone expected.
A door flap ripped right off its hut, years ago.
A few tears into the stew.
Nobody spoke their name for a long time.

pieces.label: The Mapmaker's Apprentice
pieces.text: A young traveller walks in with a half-finished map on a stretched hide. The inland is blank except for one word, "?", and a villager's hut is labelled "goat?"

pieces.label: Offer Them Water and Shade
pieces.text: (Host) decides that, before anything else, this sunburned person needs a drink...

pieces.label: Ask About Their Map
pieces.text: (Host) asks how the apprentice is making the map. The apprentice brightens immediately and pulls out a long knotted cord...

pieces.label: Ask If They Want to Stay On
pieces.text: Seeing how happy the apprentice is walking the trails, (host) asks whether (host.he/she) might want to stay a while...

pieces.label: Swap Trail Walks for Harvest Help
pieces.text: (Host) agrees to the deal: help with the work in the mornings, walk the trails in the afternoons...
The apprentice falls asleep with the map clutched like a baby, and "goat?" is gently corrected to "hut".
The apprentice shares chewy, strange, delicious smoked eel, and the children dare each other to eat it.
Counting paces and tying a knot every hundred steps, the apprentice shows how to measure distance. The builders start using it for new huts.
The apprentice won't say who taught them. "Someone very good, who didn't want to be found."
The apprentice finishes the map from here and stays for good. The host's hut is correctly labelled. Mostly.
There is so much inland left to map; the apprentice walks on, promising to bring back a copy.
Between trail walks, the apprentice helps with the harvest and maps every field, which the farmers use for arguing about who owns what.
Rain warps the hide map, and the villagers restretch it on a frame by the fire until it's flat again.
"I'm a mapmaker. Well. An apprentice. Well. I'm trying."
One word in the middle of the map: "?"
Mostly correctly labelled.

pieces.label: The Injured Visitor
pieces.text: A traveller limps in from the volcanic side of the island, sandals shredded to ribbons and feet cut by the sharp black rock. "I'm so sorry. I didn't mean to bleed on your path."

pieces.label: Bring Them to the Healer's Mat
pieces.text: (Finder) half-carries the traveller to the healers, who take one look at the feet and send for warm water...

pieces.label: Ask How They Crossed the Black Rock
pieces.text: Once (finder.his/her) feet are wrapped, (finder) asks how anyone crosses that rock at all...

pieces.label: Let Them Heal Here for Good
pieces.text: As the days go by and the feet slowly heal, (finder) notices the traveller looking around the village with something like longing...

pieces.label: Trade Rest for Light Work
pieces.text: The traveller hates being waited on, so (finder) finds (finder.him/her) jobs that can be done sitting down, and later, once (finder.he/she) can stand, a few more...
The traveller's feet are washed, salved and wrapped in clean leaves, and they fall asleep mid-apology.
"Please. I'll feel better." The traveller insists on sharing the nuts carried all the way across the lava.
The traveller explains which black rock is safe: smooth and rope-like is safe, jagged and glassy is not, and brittle crust over hollows is worst of all.
The traveller looks away and would rather not say why they risked the crossing. Nobody asks again.
Healed, the traveller stays for good, never goes near the volcano side again, and becomes the village's loudest advocate for good sandals.
As soon as they can walk without wincing, the traveller heads home. By the long way. Not across the rock.
Once healed, the traveller works the harvest harder than anyone asked, and apologizes for not working faster.
The villagers weave thick bark-soled sandals, and the traveller is so moved they can't speak, the first time all week they haven't apologized.
"I didn't mean to bleed on your path."
A trail of small red footprints toward the volcano.
Grateful, embarrassed and very hungry, in that order.

pieces.label: The Stranger at the Well
pieces.text: A stranger at the spring asks very politely for water, drinks three bowls in a row, won't say where they have come from, and keeps glancing back toward the trees.

pieces.label: Fill Their Water Skin
pieces.text: (Villager_at_the_spring) doesn't ask again. (villager_at_the_spring.He/She) just fills the stranger's water skin to the top, and points to a patch of shade...

pieces.label: Ask Gently About the Road
pieces.text: Later, (villager_at_the_spring) asks again, more gently, not where the stranger came from, but how the road was...

pieces.label: Offer Them a Place Among Us
pieces.text: As dusk falls, (villager_at_the_spring) notices the stranger has nowhere to go. (villager_at_the_spring.He/She) offers a place by the fire, and more than that, if (villager_at_the_spring.he/she) wants it...

pieces.label: Swap Water for a Day's Help
pieces.text: The stranger asks if there's any work (villager_at_the_spring.he/she) could do to pay for the water and a meal...
The stranger rests in the shade, stops watching the trees quite so often, and by evening is laughing at something a child said.
The stranger shares a handful of wild berries from the road. "They're safe," they add quickly. They are.
The stranger points out a faster trail to fresh water through a gap in the rocks on the far side of the ridge.
The stranger still won't say where they came from. Some things are not anyone else's business.
The stranger stays, works hard and is kind to the children, but never walks near the trees alone, and nobody ever asks why.
The stranger moves on before nightfall, walking quickly down the beach, away from the trees.
The stranger carries harvest baskets without stopping, as if staying busy is the only thing keeping them together.
The stranger's water skin leaks badly, which explains the three bowls. The villagers patch it with sap and fill it.
Three bowls in a row.
A glance back toward the trees. Then another.
Nothing follows them out.

pieces.label: The Child from the Raft
pieces.text: On the morning tide, a little raft of lashed bamboo drifts into the lagoon with a silent, salt-crusted child gripping it, and a gourd of water and a leaf bundle tied on with neat, tight knots.

pieces.label: Wrap the Child in a Blanket
pieces.text: (Finder) wraps the child in the first blanket (finder.he/she) can find, and carries (finder.him/her) straight up to the healers...

pieces.label: Ask Gently About the Raft
pieces.text: Over the next few days, (finder) sits with the child often, never pushing, just talking about small things. Slowly, the child begins to talk back...

pieces.label: Let the Child Choose a Home
pieces.text: After a week, the child has started following (finder) everywhere, and the village begins to talk about what to do...

pieces.label: Give the Child Small Jobs
pieces.text: (Finder) notices the child is happiest when (finder.his/her) hands are busy. (finder.He/She) starts giving (finder.him/her) little jobs...
The child sleeps a full day and night, and wakes looking for the raft. It's safe on the beach, and the child relaxes, a little.
The leaf bundle holds dried fish packed by someone who loved the child, who shyly offers to share it.
The child proudly explains how their family lashed the raft, bamboo crossed and tied double at every crossing, so it could never tip.
The child talks about birds and shells and the colour of the sea, but not about the raft. No one presses.
The child stays, welcomed with more aunts and uncles than they can count, and keeps the raft's little pole by their sleeping mat.
A canoe arrives with the child's frantic relatives, and the reunion on the beach makes everyone cry.
Around the third breadfruit tree, the child starts chattering for the first time.
"Home is that way. Past the two rocks." Two fishers paddle the child home, and the family sends back a basket of shells.
Fingers pried loose from the bamboo one by one.
The knots are neat and tight.
The little pole kept beside a sleeping mat.

pieces.label: The Visitor's Farewell
pieces.text: For a whole season a visitor has lived among the villagers, mending nets and telling the funniest stories at the fire. Now they must return home, and the children have hidden their sandals. All of them.

pieces.label: Throw a Farewell Supper
pieces.text: If (friend.he/she) has to go, (friend) decides, then (friend.he/she) is going to go properly fed...

pieces.label: Ask About Their Way Home
pieces.text: As the fire burns low, (friend) asks how the visitor will find (friend.his/her) way home across all that water...

pieces.label: Ask Them to Stay After All
pieces.text: (Friend) finally says it: "You could stay, you know. We'd like you to."...

pieces.label: Help Them Pack
pieces.text: (Friend) decides the kindest thing is to help, even if (friend.he/she) doesn't want to...
A farewell meal of every dish the visitor ever liked, and the children sing the unapproved songs at the tops of their voices. Nobody stops them tonight.
The visitor shares the last of the honey saved since the start of the season, and the feast ends very sticky.
The visitor explains the stars they will steer by: the bright one that never moves, the three that rise over home, the curved line like a fish hook.
Some of the visitor's reasons for leaving stay private, and the two of them watch the stars instead.
The visitor changes their mind and stays, and the children solemnly return the sandals, all of them.
The visitor cries a little and goes home as planned; a very sulky child returns the sandals on the beach.
One last harvest, "so you'll remember me every time you eat." And they do.
The villagers tighten every lashing on the canoe, and the whole village comes down to wave. The friend waves the longest.
Songs nobody's parents approve of.
All the sandals are hidden. Someone knows where.
Watching a canoe until it is just a dot.

pieces.label: The First Rain After Drought
pieces.text: After weeks of cracked, grey ground, the sky finally opens and the farmers laugh like fools in the rain. Then the rain does not stop, and inside the brittle storehouse comes the sound: drip... drip... drip-drip-drip.

pieces.label: Cover the Storehouse
pieces.text: (Farmer) shouts for help, and a team of soaked villagers races to drag palm mats over the storehouse roof, while others run for the fields...

pieces.label: Run from Hut to Hut
pieces.text: (Farmer) runs through the village, splashing through puddles, checking that everyone is safe and dry...

pieces.label: Mark How Fast the Ground Drinks
pieces.text: While everyone else panics, (farmer) stands in the rain with a bundle of sticks, pushing them into the ground in different fields to see where the water soaks in and where it pools...

pieces.label: Patch the Dripping Roofs
pieces.text: (Farmer) gathers every pair of hands that isn't busy, and they set to work on the leaking roofs with fresh thatch and sap, in the pouring rain...
The mats go on just in time, and the ripe gourds are pulled in before the downpour can split them.
Water runs in under the mats anyway, and a basket of dried fish at the back is soaked through and swimming.
Families with leaking roofs squeeze into the driest huts, sharing blankets and complaining cheerfully about each other's feet.
Running back from the far huts, the farmer slips on the suddenly slick mud and twists their leg badly.
The terraced plots soak up the rain like a sponge while the flat ones flood, and the farmers start building terraces.
The sticks in different fields disagree completely. The farmer is very wet and has learned nothing, but doesn't seem to mind.
The worst roofs are patched before dark, and the village sleeps to the sound of rain on solid thatch.
The patching runs through dinner and into the night, and the shivering workers are fed twice from the stores. Nobody begrudges it.
Faces turned up to the rain, laughing like fools.
drip... drip... drip-drip-drip.
Rain on solid thatch: the most beautiful sound anyone has ever heard.

pieces.label: The Fog That Held
pieces.text: A fog rolls in from the sea so thick that nobody can see their own feet, and by the second morning it's still there. The fishing canoes can't find the reef markers, and one canoe hasn't come back at all.

pieces.label: Bring the Catch Inside
pieces.text: There's nothing to do for the missing canoe yet, so (fisher) does what (fisher.he/she) can: (fisher.he/she) rounds up the fishers who made it home, and they get to work on the catch...

pieces.label: Light Fires Along the Shore
pieces.text: (Fisher) has an idea: if the lost canoe can't see the reef markers, maybe it can see fire. The fishers build bonfires all along the beach and on the rocks...

pieces.label: Note Where the Fog Thins
pieces.text: (Fisher) walks the length of the shore, slowly, watching the fog, trying to work out if it's thinner anywhere...

pieces.label: Reset the Reef Markers
pieces.text: So this never happens again, (fisher) gathers workers to wade out at low tide and set new, bigger markers on the reef...
The catch is hurried into the smoke hut before the damp can spoil it, and late that afternoon the missing canoe bumps onto the beach, its crew safe.
A whole basket of dried food has gone furry with mould. The missing canoe paddles in at dusk, the only good news of the day.
Out of the fog comes a shout and the splash of paddles: the last canoe, following the shore fires home.
Groping along the wet rocks to tend the farthest fire, the fisher slips and cuts their leg badly.
The fog always lifts first over the warm, shallow lagoon, and the missing canoe comes in exactly there. In fog, head for the lagoon.
Everyone's notes about the fog disagree, and the lost canoe drifts home by luck, its crew sheepish and starving.
Tall new reef markers with bright cloth go up before nightfall, and the missing canoe follows them home.
Storehouse baskets are emptied and filled with stones to weight the markers, and their food is lost. The markers hold.
Not a paddle. Not a voice.
Orange smudges glowing in the grey.
The fog swallows every sound.

pieces.label: The Wind in the Granary
pieces.text: A howling wind in the night tears half the thatch off the grain shelter and scatters the seed and grain across the village like sand. Every bird on the island is arriving in flocks, looking very pleased.

pieces.label: Sweep Up the Spilled Grain
pieces.text: (Granary_keeper) grabs a broom and shouts for help. Half the village turns out with brooms, baskets and very loud voices for scaring birds...

pieces.label: Check on the Granary Keeper's Family
pieces.text: (Granary_keeper)'s family sleeps in the hut beside the granary. (granary_keeper.He/She) runs to check on them first...

pieces.label: Watch Which Way the Wind Tears
pieces.text: Before anyone fixes anything, (granary_keeper) walks slowly around the granary, studying exactly how the roof came apart...

pieces.label: Rethatch the Granary
pieces.text: (Granary_keeper) organizes a work crew, and they start on the roof straight away, while the birds watch hopefully from the trees...
Grain from the swept hut floors and the clean cooking stones is saved, a few forgotten baskets turn up, and the birds leave, disappointed.
The rain follows the wind, and a whole basket of stored grain is soaked, swells up and starts to sprout. The birds are delighted.
The keeper's family is fine, just shaken, and moves in with neighbours, bringing a lot of grain in their hair.
Tying down the last of the thatch in the gusting wind, the keeper is struck across the shoulder by a loose roof pole.
The wind always rips the thatch from the sea side first, so the builders tie the sea-facing edges down twice as tight.
Nobody can prove which side went first. The birds, meanwhile, keep eating.
The roof is rethatched before nightfall, tighter and thicker, and the next night's wind doesn't even rustle it.
The village runs out of rope, and some stored grain is traded to a passing trader for more. The roof gets finished properly.
Grain in people's hair.
The birds look very pleased.
Thatch peeled back like a banana skin.

pieces.label: The Heat in the Classroom
pieces.text: On a scorching afternoon the lesson hut is an oven. The children are wilting over their counting pebbles, nobody can remember what seven and five are, and the fruit on the drying racks is starting to blacken in the sun.

pieces.label: Shade the Drying Racks
pieces.text: (Teacher) abandons the lesson, and sends the children running to help move the drying racks under the trees, which is the most exciting thing that's happened all day...

pieces.label: Check on Every Child
pieces.text: (Teacher) goes along the rows checking every child, making sure everyone drinks water...

pieces.label: Track the Hottest Hours
pieces.text: (Teacher) turns the heat into a lesson: every hour, the children feel the hut walls and the sand outside, and mark how hot they are with pebbles...

pieces.label: Open Up the Hut Walls
pieces.text: (Teacher) gets the builders to come and open up the hut so the sea breeze can blow through...
The children move the fruit into the shade, and it counts as a counting lesson. Seven racks and five racks. Twelve.
A basket of fish in the storehouse spoils in the heat and smells so terrible the children run screaming.
Everyone drinks water, and the lesson moves under the trees by the stream, feet in the water. Seven and five are twelve.
The teacher makes sure every child drinks but forgets to drink, faints, and hits their head on a hut post.
The pebbles show the hut is coolest after dawn and hottest just after midday, and lessons and farm work move to the early mornings.
The children's guesses disagree wildly, and one child's pebbles are arranged in a pattern shaped like a fish.
Windows are cut and the lower walls raised, the sea breeze blows through, and the adults start sneaking in to nap.
The sweltering work crew drinks its way through a whole pile of stored coconuts.
Dogs lie flat in the shade like dropped blankets.
"What are seven and five?" Nobody knows.
The air wobbles.

pieces.label: The Flooded Path
pieces.text: After a night of heavy rain, the stream jumps its banks and flows across the main path between the huts and the fields, knee-deep, brown and fast. Half the village is on each side, and the harvest baskets are on the wrong side entirely.

pieces.label: Carry the Harvest Across
pieces.text: (Worker) and a team of workers hoist the harvest baskets onto their shoulders and wade into the brown water...

pieces.label: Check Both Banks
pieces.text: (Worker) wades back and forth across the flood, making sure everyone on both sides is accounted for...

pieces.label: Mark How High the Water Rose
pieces.text: (Worker) walks the length of the flood, marking with charcoal on every tree trunk how high the water has reached...

pieces.label: Lay Stepping Stones
pieces.text: (Worker) organizes a crew to haul big, flat stones from the stream bed and lay a raised crossing across the flood...
The baskets make it across, and a heap of good fruit is found washed up against the garden fence. The frog is rescued too.
Someone stumbles on a hidden root, and a basket tips into the brown water, ruined. Everyone holds their baskets a lot higher after that.
Everyone is accounted for, and the two halves of the village shout cheerful insults at each other across the water until bedtime.
On the third crossing, the worker steps on a sharp stick hidden under the muddy water.
The water always crosses the path at one low dip, and the builders raise it as soon as the water goes down.
The charcoal marks disagree, and one seems to have been made by a child at the wrong height entirely.
A raised crossing of flat stones goes in before nightfall, and the children run back and forth across it, shrieking.
Hauling stones is hungry work, and the extra meals come out of the stores. The crossing stays long after the flood.
One very confused frog.
How deep is "knee-deep", really?
The harvest is on the wrong side entirely.

pieces.label: The Lightning-Struck Tree
pieces.text: CRACK. Lightning splits the old mango tree beside the main trail, the one everyone has eaten from since they were children. Half of it leans out over the path, creaking, and smoke curls up from the blackened trunk.

pieces.label: Gather the Fallen Mangoes
pieces.text: Keeping well clear of the leaning half, (woodcutter) and a few others creep around the edges, gathering the mangoes knocked loose by the blast...

pieces.label: Warn Everyone Off the Trail
pieces.text: (Woodcutter) runs to the trail and starts turning people back, waving (woodcutter.his/her) arms and shouting...

pieces.label: Study the Burn Marks
pieces.text: Once the storm passes, (woodcutter) examines the burned trunk carefully, and then walks around the island looking at other old lightning scars...

pieces.label: Clear and Brace the Trunk
pieces.text: (Woodcutter) leads the workers in cutting away the dangerous half, and propping up what's left...
The mangoes are gathered before the birds and bats get them. The scorched ones taste "like mango, but braver."
The rain pours in through a storehouse corner the thunder shook loose, and a basket of stored food is ruined.
The trail is closed with a rope, and the next morning the leaning half falls on its own, harmlessly, onto an empty path.
Clearing the trail in the rain, the woodcutter is knocked flat by a big branch breaking free from the leaning half.
Lightning keeps choosing the tallest trees, especially near the water. In a storm, keep away from tall trees near the shore.
The burn marks point in no clear direction, and the woodcutter hopes the next evidence doesn't come soon.
