The leaning half is cut away and the rest braced with strong poles. Battered, lopsided, alive. Next season, it fruits a little.
The clean-up takes three days, all fed from the stores, and the leftover wood goes into the fires for a month.
CRACK.
The leaning half creaks and groans.
"Like mango, but braver."

pieces.label: The Sudden Cold
pieces.text: A run of strange, cold nights blows in off the sea. Not cool: COLD. Families shiver under thin mats, the dogs move into the huts, someone wears a basket as a hat, and the root crops are going soft in the wet ground.

pieces.label: Dig the Roots Before They Rot
pieces.text: (Subject) rounds up anyone with a digging stick and warm enough hands, and they head out into the cold fields...

pieces.label: Visit Every Hut
pieces.text: (Subject) goes from hut to hut in the frosty dark, checking on everyone, especially the elders and the babies...

pieces.label: Note Which Nights Turn Cold
pieces.text: (Subject) starts keeping track of each night: how cold it gets, what the sky looked like, which way the wind blew...

pieces.label: Weave Thicker Mats
pieces.text: (Subject) gathers the weavers, and they set to work on thick new mats and blankets for every family...
The root crops come up before the cold, wet ground can rot them, and the basket-hat turns out to be very good for carrying yams.
The roots are saved, but the cold damp creeps into the storehouse, and a basket of stored fruit goes soft and rotten.
Families share blankets around the fires until the cold breaks; several new friendships form, and at least one feud.
Carrying firewood across the dew-slick rocks in the dark, the villager slips and lands hard on their back.
The cold always follows a clear evening with a north wind; cloudy nights stay warm.
Everyone was too busy shivering to keep proper track. More evidence is needed. Ideally, much later.
Thick new mats for every family before nightfall, and the village sleeps warm. The dogs, sadly, are evicted.
The weavers run out of fibre, and some stored food is traded to a neighbouring settlement for more.
Not cool. COLD.
A basket worn as a hat.
The dogs refuse to leave the huts.

pieces.label: The Tide at the Door
pieces.text: An unusually high tide creeps up the beach in the night and laps over the doorsteps of the huts nearest the shore. Sandals are floating out to sea, and a crab sits in a cooking pot as if invited for dinner.

pieces.label: Lift the Stores Up High
pieces.text: (Beach_resident) splashes out and starts heaving baskets onto rafters and shelves, shouting for everyone else to do the same...

pieces.label: Check the Beach Huts
pieces.text: (Beach_resident) wades from hut to hut along the shore, making sure everyone is awake and moving...

pieces.label: Mark the Water Line
pieces.text: Once everyone is safe, (beach_resident) goes along the huts marking exactly how high the water reached on every post...

pieces.label: Build Up the Sand Banks
pieces.text: Before the next high tide, (beach_resident) gets everyone digging, piling sand and stones into a low wall in front of the beach huts...
The baskets are lifted out of reach, and stranded fish are scooped from the flooded hollows. The crab is released, with apologies.
One low basket in the corner is soaked in seawater before anyone can move it. The crab refuses to leave the pot.
The beach families sleep in higher huts until the water goes down, and wake to seaweed on every doorstep.
Carrying belongings to higher ground, the resident slips on the wet stones and twists an ankle until it swells up like a melon.
The highest tides always come with a full moon and a strong onshore wind.
The water marks disagree, because some floors slope and some don't. They will wait for the next high tide.
A low bank of sand and stones goes up before nightfall, and the next high tide laps against it, and stops.
The work runs so late that supper is cooked from food meant for later in the week. But the bank holds.
A crab in the cooking pot, looking completely at home.
A sleeping mat drifts gently toward the door.
Seaweed on every doorstep.

pieces.label: The Dusty Season
pieces.text: Dry winds have been blowing fine red dust into everything for days: the tools, the food baskets, the inside of everyone's ears. Every meal crunches, and the storehouse keeper stares at the storehouse door with deep foreboding.

pieces.label: Seal the Food Baskets
pieces.text: (Storehouse_keeper) gets to work sealing every basket in the storehouse with big leaves and sticky sap...

pieces.label: Check on the Coughing Neighbours
pieces.text: Half the village is coughing. (Storehouse_keeper) goes from hut to hut checking on everyone...

pieces.label: Track Where the Dust Comes From
pieces.text: (Storehouse_keeper) sets out bowls of water all around the village, and watches which ones get dusty first, and when...

pieces.label: Shake Out Every Mat and Tool
pieces.text: (Storehouse_keeper) declares a cleaning day. Everyone hauls everything out of the huts and starts shaking, beating and wiping...
Sealing the baskets, the keeper finds a forgotten bundle of dried fruit at the back, still perfectly clean, and feels like they found treasure.
Dust gets into one basket someone left unsealed and turns the food into red, gritty paste.
Families tie damp cloths over their faces, the coughing eases, and the village looks like a gathering of very polite bandits.
Half-blinded by a gust of dust, the keeper trips over a digging stick left on the path and gashes a knee open on a stone.
The dust only blows in when the wind comes from the volcano side of the island.
The dust fills every bowl equally, from everywhere at once, so everything stays covered all the time.
A cleaning day sends enormous red clouds up from every hut, and that night dinner doesn't crunch.
Every spare basket is emptied to use as a cover, and their food is eaten early or thrown out. The tools are spotless.
Every meal crunches.
Everyone's hair is the same shade of rusty red.
Words the children aren't supposed to hear.

pieces.label: The Calm Before the Storm
pieces.text: The sea goes flat and glassy all the way to the horizon, the birds and insects go quiet, and far offshore a dark wall of cloud builds, the colour of a bruise. The navigator has seen this exactly once before.

pieces.label: Bring in the Drying Fish
pieces.text: (Navigator) sends everyone running for the drying racks...

pieces.label: Count Heads Before It Hits
pieces.text: (Navigator) runs through the village, counting everyone, sending them indoors...

pieces.label: Watch the Clouds Build
pieces.text: (Navigator) climbs the bluff and watches the cloud wall grow, marking the sun's position, trying to remember everything about the last time...

pieces.label: Tie Down Everything That Moves
pieces.text: (Navigator) organizes every pair of hands in the village to lash down roofs, canoes, drying racks and anything else that might fly away...
The fish come in from the drying racks, and the last basket is under cover just as the first fat drops of rain hit the sand.
The storm howls in faster than anyone expected, before the racks are half cleared, and a basket of stored food is ruined.
Everyone is sheltering before the first gust, and in the morning every family thanks the navigator.
Dragging the canoes higher at the last moment, the navigator is struck by flying debris.
The strange calm always lasts about half a day before a storm like this, so whenever the sea goes glassy, the village has until dusk.
The cloud shapes change too fast to read, and the navigator runs down from the bluff to wait for more evidence. From somewhere safer.
Every roof and canoe is lashed down before nightfall; every hut stands, and the navigator sleeps for a whole day afterwards.
Full food baskets weigh down the roofs, and some are crushed by morning. Not a single roof blew away.
Even the babies go quiet.
The sea is flat as polished stone.
A wall of cloud the colour of a bruise.

pieces.label: The Second Courtship
pieces.text: A few years after losing their partner, a villager has been laughing again on sunset walks with (name2), a kind, quiet fisher. Then the guilt arrives, all at once, like a wave, and they stop coming to the fire.

pieces.label: Talk It Through in Private
pieces.text: On the fourth night, (widowed_villager) walks down to the beach. (Name2) is there, as always. (Widowed_villager) sits down on the sand a little way off, and takes a deep breath...

pieces.label: Let the Widow Set the Pace
pieces.text: Nobody in the village pushes. (Name2) sends one message, through a friend: "No hurry." And then waits...

pieces.label: Ask an Old Friend's Opinion
pieces.text: (Widowed_villager) goes to (name3), (widowed_villager.his/her) oldest friend, who knew (widowed_villager.his/her) late partner well...
The widowed villager tells the fisher everything: the guilt, the memories, how the happiness frightens them. "I'll be here at sunset. Whenever you're ready. Or not."
The fisher gently admits they only ever hoped for friendship, and the widowed villager is a little relieved. The sunset walks carry on, lighter.
After a week they decide for themselves how and when to carry on, and weeks later leave flowers at the late partner's grave together.
Nothing is decided. Sometimes they sit together, and sometimes they don't. Some things can't be hurried.
The old friend listens all evening without telling them what to do, and says only: "They would have wanted you to laugh."
The old friend's advice is mostly about their own very complicated love life, involving three people and a canoe, and the guilt is laughed away.
Waiting on the beach at sunset, alone, three nights in a row.
Laughing more than in a long, long time.
A little further apart than usual.

pieces.label: The Farmer's Shy Admirer
pieces.text: A farmer from another settlement has come to help with the harvest, and a shy villager has been finding excuses to weed the very same row for a week. They have rehearsed a greeting eleven times, to a coconut, and said it to the farmer zero times.

pieces.label: Finally Say Something
pieces.text: On the eighth day, (admirer) stands up, takes a deep breath, turns to the farmer, opens (admirer.his/her) mouth, and...

pieces.label: Let It Grow Slowly
pieces.text: (Admirer) decides not to rush. (admirer.He/She) just keeps working the same row, and starts, very slowly, to actually talk...

pieces.label: Consult the Matchmaking Aunt
pieces.text: In desperation, (admirer) goes to (aunt), the village's self-appointed matchmaker, who has been waiting for this moment all week...
The admirer blurts out a tumble of words about the farmer's laugh. "I wondered when you'd say something. That's a very well-weeded row."
"You're lovely. But my heart's back home." The admirer is mostly relieved, and they finish the row as friends.
Day by day the conversations get longer and the weeds get fewer, and the farmer promises to come back for next year's harvest. And the one after.
The harvest ends, the farmer goes home with the next boat, and the admirer can't leave the island. "Next harvest."
For once, the matchmaker doesn't decide anything for anyone. "Just talk to them. Like a person. Not a weed."
The matchmaker's advice is a love song, in front of the whole village, with drums. It is politely ignored for a quiet talk at sunset.
Rehearsed eleven times, out loud, to a coconut.
Suddenly, intensely interested in a weed.
Half the village has noticed.

pieces.label: The Unexpected Proposal
pieces.text: Every week for ten years, two friends have shared a pot of stew. Tonight, halfway through, one of them asks very quietly whether their friendship might become something more. The other drops the ladle.

pieces.label: Answer Honestly in Private
pieces.text: (Name2) fishes out the ladle, very slowly, buying time. Then (friend_1.he/she) sets it down and looks at (friend_1)...

pieces.label: Take a Long Walk Together
pieces.text: "I need to walk," (name2) says. "Come with me." They leave the stew to cool and walk to the far beach, not talking...

pieces.label: Seek a Trusted Ear
pieces.text: The next day, (name2) goes to (name3), who has known them both for years, and pours out the whole story...
"And there's no rush. None at all. I'll still be here next week, with the stew." They finish it in a warm, strange silence.
The other doesn't feel the same way and says so, gently. "Same time next week?" "Same time next week."
On the far beach under the stars they talk for hours, and agree to try, carefully, and to keep stew night whatever happens. The stew is cold. They eat it anyway.
They want very different things from life. It's a sad walk home, but next week the pot is waiting.
"Only you two know what's in that stew pot." That week, at stew night, the answer is given.
The trusted friend throws up their hands and shouts "FINALLY!", loud enough for the neighbours. This is not much help.
The ladle lands in the stew with a plop.
Same day, same fire, same pot.
The stew is cold. They eat it anyway.

pieces.label: The Love Letter Lost
pieces.text: A villager spent three nights carving a love poem onto a wooden board. The runner delivered it to the wrong hut, the chief's grandmother's, who has read it aloud twice, once with dramatic gestures to the entire cooking fire.

pieces.label: Explain the Mix-Up Quietly
pieces.text: Eventually, (writer) crawls out of hiding, finds (name2), and takes (writer.him/her) aside, face burning...

pieces.label: Spend an Afternoon at the Lagoon
pieces.text: (Name2) finds (writer) first, and suggests, with a perfectly straight face, that they go somewhere far away from (elder)...

pieces.label: Ask the Grandmother's Advice
pieces.text: In a moment of madness, (writer) goes to (elder) (writer.himself/herself), to explain, and maybe, just maybe, get the poem back...
"It was very good. The bit about the eyes. All four bits." Then a walk tomorrow is suggested.
The intended doesn't feel the same way, and the grandparent refuses to give the poem back. It hangs on their wall forever.
They laugh at the lagoon until they can't breathe, especially about the dramatic gestures. "Please write another poem."
They want very different things, and part as friends, which is better than hiding in a hut.
"Go and tell them yourself. And do it before I read it at the next feast."
"Very romantic. Four times about the eyes! In my day, we were lucky to get one." The poem is not returned.
It rhymes. It mentions their eyes four times.
The whole village knows the poem by heart.
Hiding in a hut, possibly forever.

pieces.label: The Couple Who Chose to Wait
pieces.text: A happy couple are building a new hut together, and disagree about when to have a child. Every time they try to talk about it, it turns into an argument about the hut: the roof angle, the door, whose idea the extra window was.

pieces.label: Talk It Out at Home
pieces.text: That night, (partner_1) sits (name2) down and makes one rule: they are not allowed to mention the hut...

pieces.label: Take a Day Off Together
pieces.text: (Partner_1) and (name2) walk away from the half-built hut for a whole day, and go to the far side of the island...

pieces.label: Ask a Parent They Trust
pieces.text: They go together to (parent), who has raised a whole hut full of children, and ask what (partner_1.he/she) thinks...
Without the hut to hide behind, one is afraid of waiting too long and one of not being ready. They're both just afraid, and somehow that helps.
It was never about the hut; one is simply not ready yet. "Then we'll wait. But we're still arguing about the window."
A quiet afternoon on the rocks becomes a habit, one day off a week, no hut allowed.
Away from the hut, they see clearly that they want different timing. They walk home holding hands, still not sure what comes next.
"There's never a perfect time. But there's a time that's right for you two. Only you know when."
The trusted parent's advice is a long list of how tired babies make a person. And the thing with the coconut. The couple go back to finishing the hut.
The half-built hut looks innocent.
An hour about the window, and not one word about children.
"And the thing with the coconut."

pieces.label: The Wedding Without a Feast
pieces.text: A couple want a quiet wedding, just the two of them on the beach at sunrise. Their relatives are planning a three-day feast with drums, dancers, forty garlands and a fish the size of a canoe.

pieces.label: Speak to the Relatives Alone
pieces.text: (Partner_1) and (name2) gather their families together, take a deep breath, and try to explain...

pieces.label: Slip Away for an Afternoon
pieces.text: The two of them escape the planning entirely, and spend an afternoon alone on the rocks above the sea...

pieces.label: Ask a Married Friend
pieces.text: (Partner_1) and (name2) go to (name3), who has been happily married for many years...
"Well, why didn't you say so?" A sunrise wedding, just the two of them, and THEN the feast. With the fish. The uncle is relieved.
One of them confesses they secretly want the feast after all. "Fine. But I'm not wearing forty garlands."
On the rocks, away from the garlands, they remember it only matters that they get married. The relatives think they've been kidnapped.
One dreams of quiet. One, it turns out, dreams of drums. They don't solve it, but they hold hands the whole way home.
"The wedding is one day. The marriage is the rest." A sunrise wedding, and then a feast. A small one.
The married friend's advice is simply "Elope," and a wink. They do think about it. Quite seriously.
There are already forty garlands. There are going to be more garlands.
An uncle refuses to come back without the fish.
Hiding on the beach at sunrise.

pieces.label: The Partners at Work
pieces.text: Two partners work in the same research hut, and every disagreement about the work follows them home to dinner. Last night they argued about the proper way to sort seeds until the fire went out, and then kept arguing in the dark.

pieces.label: Talk Away from the Hut
pieces.text: (Name2) takes (partner_1) by the hand and walks (partner_1.him/her) to the far end of the beach, as far from the research hut as they can get...

pieces.label: Spend a Day with No Work at All
pieces.text: The next morning, instead of going to the research hut, (partner_1) and (name2) go swimming. And fishing. And napping. They do not mention seeds once...

pieces.label: Ask the Head Researcher
pieces.text: Desperate, the two of them go together to (head), and lay out the seed question, from both sides, at great length...
On the beach they each explain how the work is wearing on them, and saying it takes the sting out. A rule: no seeds after sunset.
One is too tired and too cross to talk yet. They watch the waves in silence, which is exactly what they both needed.
Swimming, fishing, napping, and not one word about seeds. The next day they sort by size AND colour. It takes twice as long. Nobody minds.
One wants to study plants, the other the stars. Maybe they don't need to work in the same hut.
"Work it out between you. And please, please do it somewhere other than my hut." They do.
The head researcher says to sort by moon phase. United at last against a common enemy, the partners go home arm in arm, complaining.
"By SIZE."
The other researchers eat lunch somewhere else.
Arguing in the dark after the fire went out.

pieces.label: The Friendship After No
pieces.text: A villager kindly said no to a friend's invitation to the moonlight dance, and is now terrified the friendship is over. They have been avoiding each other for a week at the only well, hiding behind different trees.

pieces.label: Clear the Air in Private
pieces.text: (Friend_1) can't stand it anymore. (friend_1.He/She) walks up to (name2)'s hut, knocks on the door post, and asks if they can talk...

pieces.label: Go Fishing Like Old Times
pieces.text: (Friend_1) turns up at (name2)'s door with two fishing lines, and doesn't say anything at all. Just holds one out...

pieces.label: Talk to a Mutual Friend
pieces.text: (Friend_1) goes to (name3), who is friends with them both, and asks for help...
"I miss you too. I've been drinking out of the stream for a week." They walk to the well together.
The friend is still hurt and needs time apart. Weeks later, a nod at the well. Then hello. Then, one day, waiting for them.
A quiet afternoon fishing off the rocks like they used to, catching absolutely nothing. It's perfect.
It isn't the same; they want different things from each other now. Something has changed. But not everything.
The mutual friend invites them both to dinner on the same night without telling either. Very awkward for about a minute. Then it's all right.
The mutual friend's advice involves a goat, a misunderstanding from six years ago and a theory about the moon.
There is only one well.
Waiting behind a tree. The other is waiting behind a different tree.
Two fishing lines held out without a word.

pieces.label: The Old Couple's Walk
pieces.text: Every evening for forty years, an elderly couple have walked the same route along the shore, arguing about which rock is the halfway rock. Lately the walk has been getting slower, and they turn back a little earlier each week.

pieces.label: Let Them Talk on the Way
pieces.text: One evening, about halfway to either rock, (partner_1) stops walking...

pieces.label: Walk the Old Route Together
pieces.text: On a good evening, when neither of them is too stiff, they set off on the full route, slowly, taking all the time in the world...

pieces.label: Ask Their Grandchildren
pieces.text: The couple put the question of the walk to (grandchild), who is delighted to be asked anything by grown-ups...
"It's getting hard. The walk." "It's getting hard for me too." Somehow saying it makes the walk home easier.
They start turning back at a nearer rock, and immediately begin arguing about whether THAT is the new halfway rock.
A slow walk all the way to the halfway rock, whichever one it is, and the sunset, holding hands. "Same time tomorrow?"
One wants the long walk and one needs the short one; they walk separately part of the way and meet at the rock. Either rock.
The grandchild asks to come on the walk, and stops to look at every crab. Nobody minds at all.
The grandchild suggests settling the halfway rock once and for all with a race. It is, privately, considered.
The big flat one, or the pointy one with the barnacles?
The most romantic argument on the island.
"Same time tomorrow?" "Same time tomorrow."

pieces.label: The Newcomer's Choice
pieces.text: A newcomer arrived in the dry season with one bag and no plans, and has caught a local villager's eye. The feeling might be mutual. But the newcomer hasn't decided whether to stay on the island at all, and the bag is still packed by the door.

pieces.label: Speak Plainly by the Shore
pieces.text: One evening, on the beach, ($newest) stops and turns to (name2). "I need to say something. Before I lose my nerve."...

pieces.label: Show the Newcomer the Island
pieces.text: (Name2) decides that if ($newest) is going to make a choice about the island, ($newest.he/she) should at least see the best of it first...

pieces.label: Ask Someone Who Settled Here
pieces.text: ($newest) goes to (name3), who also arrived here once with nothing, and stayed...
"I just didn't want you to have to guess." "Unpack the bag." The newcomer doesn't say yes. But doesn't say no.
The local doesn't feel quite the same way. A week later the newcomer unpacks anyway. "Because of the island."
The waterfall pool, the cliff where the birds nest, the beach where the sand squeaks. The bag stays packed, but only just.
One will never leave the island, and one is not sure they can ever stay anywhere. Liking each other doesn't change the rest.
"I kept my bag packed for two years." That night, the newcomer takes one thing out of the bag.
The advice is an hour about the fishing. The dawn fishing is, in fact, very good.
One bag, still packed by the door.
Walking back the long way.
A beach where the sand squeaks.

pieces.label: The Record Washed Away
pieces.text: In the night, the roof of the record hut sprang a leak and dripped for hours onto the village's earliest harvest records. The charcoal marks are running down the bark sheets in long grey streaks, like tears.

pieces.label: Rescue the Driest Sheets
pieces.text: (Scholar) snatches up the sheets that are still mostly dry and spreads them out in the sun, then sits down with fresh bark and charcoal and starts copying as fast as (scholar.his/her) hand will go...

pieces.label: Ask the Oldest Farmers
pieces.text: The records may be ruined, but the people who lived through those harvests aren't. (Scholar) goes to find (elder) and the other oldest farmers...

pieces.label: Start a Fresh Harvest Record
pieces.text: (Scholar) decides that what's gone is gone. What matters is never letting this happen again...
The scholar copies the clearest sheets onto fresh bark until their hand cramps: planting times, crop rotations, which seeds failed in the dry years.
The last readable sheets dissolve into grey pulp, and generations of farming knowledge are lost for good.
Comparing the oldest farmers' memories turns up a forgotten trick: planting just before the rains, not just after. It works.
The old farmers disagree about nearly everything, including the year of the purple sky, and all three versions are written down.
A new harvest record carved into wooden boards under a sound roof, and this time they write down why.
The scholar leaves the famine year unwritten, and the families who remember are quietly grateful.
Charcoal running down the sheets like tears.
A handful of mush that used to be a hundred harvests.
The drip goes on dripping.

pieces.label: The Wrong Name
pieces.text: Years ago, a villager stopped using their childhood name and chose a new one. Half the village still uses the old one, especially (elder), who shouts it across the beach every morning as if it's a tradition.

pieces.label: Keep the Story of the Old Name
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that if people are going to remember the old name, they might as well know where it came from. (subject.He/She) gathers a few curious listeners and explains...

pieces.label: Ask Who Gave the Old Name
pieces.text: (Subject) goes to (subject.his/her) relatives, and to (elder), and asks who gave (subject.him/her) the old name in the first place, and why...

pieces.label: Announce the Chosen Name
pieces.text: (Subject) waits until the whole village is gathered for the evening meal, climbs onto a log, and clears (subject.his/her) throat. Loudly...
The old name came from an old word for a fishing knot. The knot is written down, and now that the name belongs to the knot, people use it less.
The only bark sheet explaining the old naming customs crumbles while it is being copied.
The old name began as a great-uncle's nickname, because the baby wouldn't let go of his fishing line. It was never meant to be permanent.
The relatives can't agree: a great-uncle's idea, a dream, or a mistake.
"I would like to be known as Lani. Only Lani. Thank you." The elder calls out "Lani!" from the back, and everyone cheers.
Standing on the log, the villager changes their mind. "What were you going to say?" "Pass the fish."
Four times before breakfast.
Very calm, the way a volcano is calm.
An elder shouts the old name like a tradition.

pieces.label: The Name Lost to Magic
pieces.text: Walking on the beach, a villager picked up an old charm half-buried in the sand, a carved shell disc on a braided cord, and wore it to bed. This morning they can't remember their own name. The charm feels heavier, and warm as skin.

pieces.label: Hold on to What Is Left
pieces.text: (friend) grabs bark and charcoal. "Say it. Whatever's left. Say it, and I'll write it down." (Subject) screws up (subject.his/her) face, concentrating...

pieces.label: Ask Their Friends to Remember
pieces.text: (friend) gathers everyone who knows (subject), and they sit in a circle around (subject.him/her), telling stories about (subject.him/her), saying (subject.his/her) name over and over...

pieces.label: Carve Every Name Somewhere Safe
pieces.text: Shaken, the village decides that no one should ever lose their name again without a way to find it...
While the first part of the name is still there, the friend writes it down, and everything about the charm. By evening, the name comes back in full.
A thin thread of light rises from the villager's mouth and sinks into the shell disc. The charm has taken the name, and every memory of it; whenever anyone tries to say it, only "?" comes out.
An old woman remembers: it is a name keeper, used long ago to hold names safe for sleeping children. Once it is taken away, the name drifts back.
A shipwreck, a spirit, a joke? Nobody knows where the charm came from, and the name comes back by morning on its own.
Every villager's name is carved onto a tall new name post. Seeing their name carved first, the villager reads it aloud, and remembers.
The name returns by itself, but that morning stays private. The charm is thrown back into the sea.
Warm as skin.
Only pieces. The first sound, maybe.
"What's your name?" Nothing comes.

pieces.label: The Family Recipe
pieces.text: For every feast anyone can remember, a cook's grandmother made her famous coconut and taro pudding. She died last season, and never taught anyone the recipe. The first attempt tasted like wet sand. The feast is in three days.

pieces.label: Write Down What Is Remembered
pieces.text: (Cook) gathers the whole family together, and asks everyone to say everything they remember about watching Grandmother cook...

pieces.label: Ask Her Old Friends
pieces.text: (Cook) goes to Grandmother's oldest friends, the women she cooked beside at every feast for fifty years...

pieces.label: Start a Recipe Board
pieces.text: (Cook) decides this must never happen to any family again. (cook.He/She) proposes a carved board of every family's recipes...
Bit by bit the steps come back: fresh coconut, taro wrapped in leaves, cooked in the ground. The fifth pudding tastes almost right.
Grandmother's marks beside her cooking spot were the recipe, and a well-meaning cousin has scrubbed the wall clean "to tidy up."
"You don't know about the ash?" A pinch from the cooking fire, right at the end. The first spoonful makes the cook cry.
Honey. No honey, never honey. The leaves. The love. The fifth pudding tastes like slightly sweeter sand.
A carved board of every family's recipes, with "Grandmother's Pudding (almost)" at the top.
Some of Grandmother's secrets stay in the family. Some things should only be learned standing beside someone at the fire.
Wet sand. Dry sand. It exploded. The dog ate it.
People walked from the far side of the island for a bowl.
The first spoonful makes them cry.

pieces.label: The Child's First Word
pieces.text: A proud parent's baby has said a first word, "fish", clear as anything, by the drying racks. Nobody else seems to have heard it, and the baby refuses to say it again, looking at everyone with enormous smugness.

pieces.label: Keep the Bark Safe
pieces.text: (Parent) decides that this bark strip is the most important document in the village, and must be preserved...

pieces.label: Ask Who Else Was There
pieces.text: Stung by the doubtful looks, (parent) goes around asking if anyone else heard it...

pieces.label: Begin a First Words Board
pieces.text: (Parent) proposes a village board where every family can carve their children's first words, and when they were spoken...
The word is copied onto a smooth board with the recipe for the long-lasting berry ink: crushed berries, a little ash, and sap. Soon everyone uses "first word ink."
A downpour soaks the bark strip, and the ink recipe on the back washes away. The baby watches the rain and says nothing.
A neighbour did hear it, and remembers the baby was pointing at the fish on the drying racks.
"Fish." "Fiss." A sneeze. The sneeze witness is no longer welcome at the parent's hut. The baby sneezes, and everyone gasps.
A carved board of first words: "mama", "no", "coconut", and one baby long ago whose first word was apparently "volcano."
The first word stays a family treasure. A few days later, the baby says "fish" again. Only the parent hears it. That's fine.
An expression of enormous smugness.
"Fish? Fish?"
The most important document in the village.

pieces.label: The Unfinished Portrait
pieces.text: Clearing out an old hut, an artist finds a roll of bark cloth in the rafters: a half-finished portrait of a villager who died long ago. The painter did the eyes, and one ear, and stopped. The eyes are very, very good.

pieces.label: Restore the Faded Paint
pieces.text: (Artist) sits with the portrait for days, studying every flake of paint under a magnifying shell, trying to work out how it was made...

pieces.label: Ask Those Who Knew the Sitter
pieces.text: (Artist) shows the portrait to the oldest villagers, to see if anyone remembers the sitter, or the painter...

pieces.label: Finish It for the Future
pieces.text: (Artist) decides that the portrait deserves to be finished. (artist.He/She) asks everyone who knew the sitter to describe them...
From the tiny flakes, the artist works out the old pigment mix: red earth, crushed shell, burnt coconut husk and something oily that might be fish.
The cloth tears right across the bottom while being cleaned, and the old brushwork is lost. The eyes survive, and look a little reproachful.
An old man remembers the painter, a strange, quiet woman who only worked at night, by firelight. That explains the colours.
The nose was big. It was small. That isn't the sitter at all, it's the painter's cousin. The eyes look on, amused.
Finished from the villagers' memories over a whole season, the portrait makes the sitter's great-grandchildren cry, and starts a whole hut of portraits.
The artist decides it should stay unfinished, as the painter left it. Only the eyes were ever meant to be seen.
The eyes look as if they are about to say something.
Several villagers have had to sit down.
Something oily that might be fish.

pieces.label: The Two Histories
pieces.text: For three days, two villagers have argued about the great fire of long ago. One says the records are right: lightning. The other says their grandfather swore, on his deathbed, it was a cooking pot left on the coals by someone who went for a swim.

pieces.label: Copy the Old Fire Record
pieces.text: (scholar) fetches the ancient bark record of the fire, and unrolls it very, very carefully, with (arguer_1) and (name2) breathing down (arguer_1.his/her) neck...

pieces.label: Gather the Grandparents' Stories
pieces.text: (scholar) visits every elder whose family lived through the fire, and writes down every version...

pieces.label: Record Both Versions
pieces.text: (scholar) declares that the village will keep both versions, side by side, and let the future decide...
The record does say lightning, and also how the village rebuilt: wider gaps between huts, fire breaks, water jars by every door.
The old record cracks apart as it is unrolled, losing, ironically, the part that said what started the fire. For the first time in three days, they're both quiet.
Lightning struck the cooking hut. Where, yes, someone had left a pot on the coals. Both sides were half right.
Lightning, a cooking pot, a dropped torch, an angry spirit, and a great-aunt who insists there was no fire at all. Now there are seven sides.
Both versions are written side by side, with who told each one and how they knew. Both arguers sign, with a flourish.
The parts about which families lost people, and who was blamed, stay private to the families. Hearing why, the arguers quietly stop.
Shouting across the village in the middle of the night.
"It's written down. It's official."
Now there are seven sides.

pieces.label: The Hidden Diary
pieces.text: Under the loose floorboards of an abandoned hut, a villager finds a diary kept for years: the weather, the wind, the tides, when the rains came. Along with some very, very honest opinions about the neighbours.

pieces.label: Copy the Weather Notes
pieces.text: (Finder) decides the weather notes, at least, are too valuable to lose. (finder.He/She) sits down with fresh bark and starts copying...

pieces.label: Ask Who Lived in That Hut
pieces.text: (Finder) takes the diary around the village, asking the oldest villagers whose it might have been...

pieces.label: Start a Village Weather Log
pieces.text: Inspired by the diary, (finder) proposes that the village keep its own weather log, every day, like the old writer did...
Years of weather notes are copied onto fresh bark, and the farmers and fishers pore over them. The bits about the neighbours are left out. Mostly.
The oldest pages crumble at the first touch, the first years of notes, before anyone else kept any.
The writer was a cranky old fisher who never missed a storm warning in forty years. "And he was always right."
A fisher, a healer, a lonely farmer, a spirit? Nobody knows, but three families find out unflattering things about their ancestors.
The village begins its own daily weather log. No opinions about the neighbours are allowed. Officially.
The personal pages were never meant to be read, so the bundle goes back under the floorboards. Only the weather is copied.
"They cannot sing. Nobody has ever told them. I will not be the one."
Bark pages tied with old fishing line.
Somebody's great-great-grandparents, singing badly.

pieces.label: The Old Songbook
pieces.text: At the bottom of a storage basket, under some old nets and a very surprised spider, a villager finds a songbook of damp bark pages covered in verses nobody has sung in years. One page has just one word, underlined three times: "LOUDER."

pieces.label: Dry and Copy the Pages
pieces.text: (Singer) lays the pages out carefully in the sun, one by one, and as they dry, starts copying...

pieces.label: Ask the Old Singers
pieces.text: (Singer) takes the songbook to (elder) and the other old singers, who crowd around it, squinting...

pieces.label: Teach the Songs to the Children
pieces.text: (Singer) decides songs that sit in a basket aren't songs at all. They need to be sung...
A working song for hauling nets, a verse for each heave, and the fishers haul twice as smoothly on the beat.
Two stuck pages tear apart. All that can be read is "...and the moon..." and "...never again."
The old singer remembers a rowing song, sung so every paddle hits the water together, and "LOUDER" is what the song leader shouted when the rowers got tired.
"No, it goes like THIS." The old singers sing four different versions at once, very badly, and have the time of their lives.
The children learn the old songs faster than anyone expected. Their favourite part is shouting "LOUDER!"
The sad songs, about lost canoes and people who never came home, stay private, sung only by those who need them.
A very surprised spider.
"LOUDER." Underlined three times.
A little drawing of a person dancing in the margin.

pieces.label: The Stone of Names
pieces.text: At the edge of the village stands the carved stone bearing the names of the ancestors. The weather has worn the oldest names to shallow scratches, moss hides whole lines, and a child searching it asks, "Are we not on it?"

pieces.label: Trace the Last Clear Names
pieces.text: (Carver) brings charcoal and thin bark, and begins, very carefully, to scrub the moss away and take rubbings of the names...

pieces.label: Ask the Families Who Remember
pieces.text: (Carver) invites every family to come to the stone, and share whatever they remember about the names...

pieces.label: Carve a New Stone Beside It
pieces.text: (Carver) proposes a new stone, carved fresh, beside the old one, with every name that can still be read or remembered...
Taking rubbings of every clear name, the carver learns how the old carvers cut their lines: deep and angled, so the rain runs off.
A crumbling corner chips away under the brush, and four names, maybe five, are gone.
The names were carved in order of arrival. The child finds their family near the bottom. "We were LATE!"
Two families claim the same name, and a third says it's a spelling mistake. Everyone goes home a little sad, still unsure.
A new stone with every name that can still be read or remembered, and room at the bottom for the names to come. Every family is on it.
Some names are left to the moss, and to the memories of their families. Flowers are planted at the stone's base.
"Are we not on it?"
Fingers tracing marks worn almost smooth.
Moss, soft and green, hiding whole lines.

pieces.label: The Apprentice's First Failure
pieces.text: An apprentice builder's first solo project, a fish drying rack, collapsed instantly when the first fish was hung on it at sunset. The fish is fine. The apprentice has been staring at the pile of sticks for an hour.

pieces.label: Look at the Fallen Rack Together
pieces.text: Someone crouches down beside the pile of sticks, picks up a crossbar, and turns it over in (apprentice.his/her) hands. "Let's see what happened."...

pieces.label: Give Them a Smaller Job
pieces.text: The builders suggest (apprentice) build something smaller for a while, something with less riding on it. Like stools...

pieces.label: Call in an Old Builder
pieces.text: (mentor) wanders over, looks at the pile, looks at (apprentice), and sits down on the ground beside (apprentice.him/her)...
Every lashing had slipped: neat, but not tight. A proper building knot is so tight it creaks. The second rack holds three dozen fish.
Nobody ever actually showed the apprentice how tight to pull the lashings. From then on, every apprentice gets shown properly.
Small stools for a while, getting better and better, until half the village is sitting on them.
The first stool wobbles so badly that the first person to sit on it ends up on the ground, laughing. The apprentice does not laugh.
The old builder shows the cross-lashing: over, under, around, pull. The next morning's new rack, the old builder doesn't touch a single lashing.
"My first rack fell on the chief. With the chief under it. He had a fish on his head for a week." The apprentice finally laughs.
The fish is fine. It looks unbothered.
A sound like dropping an armful of firewood.
People walk past pretending not to look.

pieces.label: The Overworked Healer
pieces.text: A fever is going around the village, and everyone needs the healer at once. The healer has not eaten a hot meal or slept a full night in four days, and this morning fell asleep standing up, grinding stone in hand.

pieces.label: Ask the Healer What Is Draining Them
pieces.text: Someone sits (healer) down, puts a bowl of hot stew in (healer.his/her) hands, and won't let (healer.him/her) get up until (healer.he/she) has eaten it and answered one question: what's the worst part?...

pieces.label: Share Out the Sick Calls
pieces.text: The village asks (healer)'s trainee healers to take over the night calls, so (healer) can sleep...

pieces.label: Bring a Builder to the Sick Hut
pieces.text: (builder) watches (healer) bending over a patient on a low floor mat, wincing, and has an idea...
Half the exhaustion is the walking between sick huts scattered across the village. The healer helps lash up one shelter for the sick, and sleeps six hours that night.
Nobody told the healer the herb gatherers were sick too. Within an hour, two healthy villagers volunteer to gather herbs.
The trainees take the night calls, nervous but careful. By the end of the week the fever has passed, and the healer has had three hot meals.
The trainees mix up two patients' teas. Nobody is harmed: both were for fever, one just tasted worse. A list goes up by the door.
The builder teaches how to lash a raised sickbed at waist height, so the healer doesn't have to kneel over every patient.
The builder fainted the one time they tried to help a healer. "Went down like a felled tree." The healer laughs for the first time all week.
Asleep standing up, grinding stone in hand.
Woken twice in the night, every night.
A bowl of stew they are not allowed to put down.

pieces.label: The Unwanted Promotion
pieces.text: The most talented builder in the village has been asked to lead the team building the new longhouse, and would rather go fishing, which they hate. The team is waiting. The builder is hiding behind the lumber pile.

pieces.label: Ask Why It Feels Wrong
pieces.text: Someone finds (builder) behind the lumber pile and sits down next to (builder.him/her). "Why does it feel so wrong?"...

pieces.label: Split the Lead Between Two
pieces.text: (Builder) suggests, desperately, that maybe (builder.he/she) and (friend) could lead together...

pieces.label: Pair Them with a Seasoned Leader
pieces.text: (mentor), who has led building teams for years, finds (builder) behind the lumber pile and sits down with (builder.him/her)...
The builder has always done every hard joint themselves; leading means letting others do it. They hand the first hard joint to someone else. It holds.
Nobody ever said what "leading" would mean. Once it's explained (plan the work, check the joints, keep people fed), the builder comes out from behind the lumber pile.
The friend handles the people, the builder handles the wood, and the longhouse turns out to be the finest building in the village.
Two completely different sets of orders on the first day, and by noon there are post holes everywhere.
The seasoned leader teaches the secret: break one big build into lots of small jobs. "Dig four holes." "Trim ten posts."
"This is my spot, you know. I still hide behind the lumber pile sometimes."
"I would rather go fishing." They hate fishing.
Seasick in the shallows.
The longhouse posts lie on the ground, waiting.

pieces.label: The Fisher Who Wanted to Farm
pieces.text: The best fisher in the village has announced they want to learn farming instead. "I'm just tired of being wet." The other fishers are deeply, personally offended on behalf of the sea.

pieces.label: Ask What the Fence Taught Them
pieces.text: (Fisher)'s very first farming job is to put up a fence around a new garden plot. The next morning, (fisher.he/she) comes to look at it. It is lying flat on the ground...

pieces.label: Split Their Days Between Sea and Field
pieces.text: The village suggests a compromise: fishing in the mornings, farming in the afternoons, so the village doesn't lose its best fisher entirely...

pieces.label: Find Them a Farming Mentor
pieces.text: (mentor) watches (fisher) holding the digging stick upside down for a while, then gently turns it the right way up...
The first fence was knocked over by the wind; its posts were barely in the ground. The second fence is still standing a year later.
The farmers only said "put up a fence." Not how. Not how deep. A little ashamed, they start explaining things properly.
Fishing mornings and farming afternoons: still wet in the mornings, but dry by sunset.
Wet in the morning, muddy in the afternoon, and by evening wet AND muddy. The worst of both worlds.
The mentor teaches how to build raised garden beds framed with logs. The first taro is the best in the village, and the fishers are even more offended.
The mentor used to be a fisher too, and switched for exactly the same reason. "I got tired of being wet."
Holding the digging stick upside down.
Offended on behalf of the sea.
"I'm just tired of being wet. All the time."

pieces.label: The Day Without Tasks
pieces.text: A villager finishes every job on their list by noon and is struck by a kind of horror: nothing to do, for the whole afternoon. They have reorganized the tool shelf twice and swept a hut that isn't theirs.

pieces.label: Ask What They Were Looking For
pieces.text: Someone gently takes the broom out of (restless_villager)'s hands, and asks what (restless_villager.he/she) is looking for...

pieces.label: Teach Them a Quiet Craft
pieces.text: (mentor), who has watched all this with some amusement, hands (restless_villager) a block of wood and a carving knife...

pieces.label: Insist on a Real Day Off
pieces.text: (Restless_villager)'s friends confiscate every tool, broom and basket in reach, lead (restless_villager.him/her) to a hammock, and refuse to let (restless_villager.him/her) out of it...
"Something to FIX!" A loose post, rotting at the base, takes all afternoon to reset, and the villager is blissfully happy.
Nobody ever told them resting was allowed. They don't quite believe it, but they sit down. For a minute.
The worker teaches how to carve and fit sturdy tool handles. By the end of the week every tool has a new one, and there is still nothing to do in the afternoons.
"All these years, and I still don't know what to do with an afternoon." They sit in companionable silence, carving nothing in particular.
A whole day in a hammock. They hate the first hour, love the rest, and ask to do it again next week.
They lie in the hammock, rigid, worrying about falling behind. On what, nobody can work out.
Tools sorted by size, then by colour.
Three offers of help, all nervously declined.
Wild eyes searching for something, anything, to do.

pieces.label: The Misunderstood Apprentice
pieces.text: A novice was told to "put a roof over the shed by the field", and put a roof over the shed and the field: a vast canopy of palm leaves over the entire taro patch. The taro looks very happy. The builders look very confused.

pieces.label: Ask How They Read the Order
pieces.text: The head builder clears (novice.his/her) throat, carefully, and asks (novice) to repeat the order (novice.he/she) was given...

pieces.label: Turn the Canopy Into a Project
pieces.text: The farmers come to look, and notice something interesting: the taro under the canopy hasn't wilted in the midday heat, the way it usually does...

pieces.label: Bring a Master Builder to Look
pieces.text: (master) is fetched. (novice.He/She) walks all the way around the canopy, slowly, in silence, looking up at it...
"Over the shed, by the field. Over the shed AND the... oh." Taking it down, the novice learns how to brace a wide roof properly.
The order really could mean either thing, said quickly, with a mouth full of breakfast. Orders get given more carefully from then on.
The taro under the canopy hasn't wilted, and the novice is put in charge of shade for the seedlings.
The first shade frame blows over in the next breeze, flattening a row of beans. The novice apologizes to the beans.
"It's good. But it'll come down in the first storm." The master teaches guy ropes, deep-set poles and angled bracing. It survives three storms.
The master once built a door on the wrong side of a hut, facing the cliff, and the family climbed in through the window for a year.
Every palm leaf on that side of the island.
The taro looks very happy.
Standing proudly beside it, waiting to be praised.

pieces.label: The Shared Harvest
pieces.text: The fields have given the best harvest in years, and the planting team and the watering team are at war. Both want the first bowl at the harvest feast, and someone is counting out loud how many seeds they personally planted.

pieces.label: Walk the Fields and See
pieces.text: (Farmer) suggests everyone walk the rows together and see for themselves what made the harvest so good...

pieces.label: Mix the Two Teams Together
pieces.text: (Farmer) suggests that next season, there shouldn't be two teams at all. Just one...

pieces.label: Ask the Channel Builder to Help
pieces.text: (Farmer) fetches (builder), who built the original watering channel years ago, to look at it...
The watering channel leaks half its water before the far rows, and the harvest was still the best in years. Imagine it with a channel that didn't leak!
Half the planters watered. Half the waterers planted. "So... who gets the first bowl?" "Whoever gets there first."
One mixed team, nobody counting who did more, and at the feast everyone gets their bowl at the same time.
The mixed team spends its entire first morning arguing about tools. Nobody plants anything.
The channel builder teaches how to line a watering channel with clay, and the next harvest is so huge both teams forget the argument.
"My first channel watered the chief's hut instead of the field. Flooded it. With the chief inside, asleep."
Someone is counting how many seeds they personally planted. They are not finished.
Overflowing baskets, and nobody happy.
Planted AND watered, and trying to stay out of it.

pieces.label: The Long Way Home
pieces.text: Every morning the workers cross the old log bridge over the gully to the fields. Every morning one worker refuses, takes the long way around, and arrives an hour late. Someone has called them a coward. The bridge, to be fair, creaks.

pieces.label: Inspect the Old Bridge
pieces.text: Someone finally does what nobody has done in years: crawls underneath the log bridge to have a proper look at it...

pieces.label: Start Their Day Later
pieces.text: The village suggests that (worker) simply start work an hour later than everyone else, so (worker.he/she) can take the long way without falling behind...

pieces.label: Ask a Bridge Builder for Help
pieces.text: (Worker) goes to (builder), and asks, quietly, whether (worker.he/she) thinks the old bridge is safe...
Underneath: soft, dark, crumbling rot at the joints where the logs rest on the banks. The bridge is closed that morning. Nobody calls the worker a coward again.
Nobody ever said the bridge was safe. Nobody checked it. The worker was being careful, not lazy, and a builder is asked to check it properly.
Starting an hour later and working an hour later in the cool evenings suits the worker very well. The comments stop.
The later start throws off the whole team's schedule, and the comments get a little louder.
The bridge builder and the worker tie a rope bridge across the gully together, and the old log bridge is left for the moss.
"I haven't trusted that log in years. I go around too. Early, before anyone sees."
"Taking the scenic route?"
The bridge creaks. Yesterday it made a new noise.
Muddy and scratched, an hour late.

pieces.label: The Night Shift
pieces.text: A villager volunteered to tend the village fires at night, and did not consider sleeping during the day. Children shriek, pots clatter, and a small brown bird with a voice like a squeaky door sings outside their hut from noon until dusk.

pieces.label: Look at the Sleeping Hut
pieces.text: Someone suggests the problem might be the hut itself, and (night_tender), bleary-eyed, takes a proper look at it, in the middle of the day...

pieces.label: Swap Every Other Night
pieces.text: Another villager offers to share the night shift, so (night_tender) can sleep at night every other day...

pieces.label: Ask an Old Night Watcher
pieces.text: (mentor) tended the night fires for twenty years. (Night_tender) goes to ask how (night_tender.he/she) ever managed to sleep...
Daylight streams in through dozens of gaps in the weave, like stars. A tighter, doubled wall makes the hut dark as night. The bird is muffled.
Nobody warned them how hard day sleeping would be. The village, a little guiltily, keeps the noise down near their hut.
Sharing the night shift, the stars are beautiful again. The bird is still annoying, but only half the time.
On the second night both fall asleep by the fire. On the third, both stay up. A marker stone will show whose turn it is.
The old watcher teaches how to build a thick, double-layered sleeping screen, and that afternoon the night tender sleeps six hours, through the bird.
"Sleep? I never slept well in the day. Not once in twenty years. I just got used to being tired."
A voice like a squeaky door.
Glaring at birds.
Daylight through the walls, like stars.

pieces.label: The Worker Who Said No
pieces.text: A respected worker has just spent a whole season building the new canoe shed. The next morning they are asked to start hauling stone for the new sea wall. "No. I'm spent." Some people think they have gone soft.

pieces.label: Ask What Makes It Exhausting
pieces.text: Instead of arguing, someone asks (worker) to show them what hauling stone is actually like...

pieces.label: Give Them Lighter Work for Now
pieces.text: The builders suggest (worker) take some lighter work for a while, like thatching...

pieces.label: Ask a Stone Hauler for Tricks
pieces.text: (mentor), who has hauled more stone than anyone in the village, comes over to help...
The stone sled's runners dig into the sand like a plough. Fitted with rollers, it moves three times as easily. The worker agrees to haul stone after all. Next week.
No one ever said how much stone was needed. When the builders actually count, it's forty stones, which sounds much more possible.
Lighter thatching work in the shade, and a moon later the worker turns up at the sea wall, unasked, and starts hauling.
The thatching team is already full, and the head thatcher keeps giving the worker things to hold.
The stone hauler teaches the long lever and log pivot. "Never lift with your back. Lift with the log."
The stone hauler once refused the very same job. "If I'd kept going, I'd have broken my back. You're not soft. You're sensible."
Those people have not hauled stone recently. Or ever.
Said at the fire, not quite quietly enough.
A stone that rolls over like a pebble.

pieces.label: The Water That Tasted Different
pieces.text: Water from the old well tastes sweet and cool. Water from the new well tastes faintly of metal, like licking a stone, and turns the stew grey. "Grey stew," the head cook announces, "is not stew." The diggers are taking this very personally.

pieces.label: Taste Both Wells Every Morning
pieces.text: (Scholar) decides to taste both wells, every morning, at the same time, for a whole week, and write down exactly what (scholar.he/she) tastes...

pieces.label: Weigh the Rock Against the Rain
pieces.text: (Scholar) has two ideas: the taste comes from the rock the well was dug through, or from rainwater seeping in. (scholar.He/She) sets up a test: a jar from each well, left to settle overnight...

pieces.label: Let the Cooks Poke Holes in It
pieces.text: (Scholar) invites the cooks to point out anything (scholar.he/she) might have got wrong...

pieces.label: Show a Novice How to Taste-Test
pieces.text: (Scholar) decides this is a good chance to teach (novice) how a proper test is done...
The metal taste is strongest the morning after rain and fades as the days go dry, so the cooks use the new well only on dry days. The diggers are mollified. Mostly.
Metal one day, sweet the next, "sort of fishy" the day after that. The diggers take it as a victory, and the cooks as proof of everything.
Red grit settles at the bottom of the new well's jar: the well was dug through a band of red stone. Settled overnight, the water makes stew almost the right colour.
Both jars look the same in the morning, and both explanations still fit. The scholar sighs, and fetches two more jars.
"Did anyone look at it before it went in the stew pot?" Nobody had. The grey might come from the old iron-stained pot.
Whose tongue to trust? A child is asked, because children are honest, and says both waters taste "like water."
The novice learns a fair taste test: the same cup, the same hour, rinse between wells, and never know which water is which until afterwards.
The novice notices the scholar always tastes the old well first, so the new one always tastes strange by comparison.
"Grey stew is not stew."
"Delicious!" with an increasingly strained smile.
Like licking a stone.

pieces.label: The Plant That Grew Sideways
pieces.text: Someone left a seedling in a pot in the dark storage shelter and forgot it for a week. It has grown almost completely flat, bending hard toward one thin stripe of sunlight through a crack in the wall. "It looks like it's trying to escape."

pieces.label: Watch the Seedling for a Week
pieces.text: (Gardener) leaves the plant where it is, but every morning, turns the pot around so the plant is facing away from the crack...

pieces.label: Test Light Against Wind
pieces.text: (Gardener) has two ideas: the plant is chasing the light, or it's chasing the fresh air that comes through the crack. (gardener.He/She) sets up a test...

pieces.label: Ask Whether It Is Sick
pieces.text: (Gardener) asks everyone to suggest what else might be going on...

pieces.label: Teach the Turning Trick
pieces.text: (Gardener) decides to show (novice) how to repeat the pot-turning test properly, with other seedlings...
Turned away from the crack every morning, the plant has bent itself back toward it by evening. Every time. Plants grow toward light.
Some days it bends back toward the crack, and some days it doesn't. The plant keeps growing, in several directions at once.
The pot with sun and air bends toward the crack; the pot with only a draught stands there, pale and confused. The plant chases light, not air.
The second plant bends a little toward the draught, but only a little. Both ideas still seem possible, and two more pots are set up.
"What if it's just sick? What if it's not clever at all, it's just droopy?" Everyone had assumed the bending meant something clever.
By eye? By the angle? By how sad it looks? A notched stick settles how to measure "bending." It takes all afternoon.
The novice learns to repeat the test with several pots, all turned and watered the same, and soon has a whole row of sideways plants.
One pot was always watered more, because it was nearer the door. The group starts over with equal water.
Thin and pale and determined.
One stripe of sunlight through a crack.
A whole row of sideways plants.

pieces.label: The Shells with Holes
pieces.text: A child staggers in with a basket of shells, every one with a tiny, perfectly round hole, and is absolutely convinced a very small person with a very small drill lives on the beach, drilling shells at night.

pieces.label: Sort the Shells by Hole
pieces.text: (adult) suggests that if there's a tiny driller, they might learn something from the holes. (Child) tips the basket out and begins sorting, very seriously...

pieces.label: Compare the Drill and the Snail
pieces.text: (adult) remembers something about snails, and takes (child) down to the rock pools to look...

pieces.label: Ask Whether Waves Could Do It
pieces.text: (adult) gathers a few curious villagers and asks: what else could make holes like this?...

pieces.label: Teach the Shell Count
pieces.text: (Child) decides that (novice) needs to learn how to properly count shells with holes, and takes on the job of teacher...
The holes are always in the same spot on the same kind of shell: near the hinge on the round ones, near the point on the long ones. The tiny driller is "very neat."
No pattern at all. The child writes, in big careful letters, "not sure", and draws the tiny driller looking confused.
A small snail is caught on a shell with a tiny round hole starting: it drills into other shells to eat what's inside. The child decides the snail IS the tiny driller, and names it.
No snails are caught drilling. The very small bowl of food is left out anyway, and is empty by morning. (A crab.) (Probably.)
Could waves grinding sand wear holes over a long time? Everyone had assumed something alive made them. The child refuses to believe it.
By eye? By finger? By grains of sand? A thorn, pushed in until it stops, is very slow, and the child goes to play.
The child teaches the novice, very seriously, a proper shell count: walk in a straight line, pick up every shell, don't skip the ugly ones.
Half the shells came from one single rock pool, and the child is sent back to collect from somewhere else.
A drawing of a very small person with a very small drill.
A very small bowl of food, left out at night.
Smooth-edged, perfectly round.

pieces.label: The Ant Trail Experiment
pieces.text: A long trail of ants runs from the jungle to the honey pot in the cooking hut, and the cooks have tried everything. A scholar places a flat stone across the trail and waits, and soon a small crowd sits in total silence, staring at a stone with ants walking into it.

pieces.label: Count the Ants Around the Stone
pieces.text: (Scholar) starts counting the ants, and timing how long it takes them to get around the stone...

pieces.label: Test Scent Against Sight
pieces.text: (Scholar) wonders: are the ants following the trail with their eyes, or by smell? (scholar.He/She) sets up a test...

pieces.label: Ask Why Honey Matters
pieces.text: (Scholar) asks the crowd if anyone has any other questions they think should be asked...

pieces.label: Teach the Ant Watch
pieces.text: (Scholar) decides (novice) should learn how to run this kind of test...
Every time the stone moves, the ants find the shortest way around within the hour, and the crowd cheers each time the trail reforms.
Left, right, over the top, give up and go home. The crowd is still enthralled.
A stretch of trail wiped with a damp cloth leaves the ants wandering in circles. Scent, not sight! The cooks wipe the honey shelf every morning, and the ants stop coming.
After wiping, the ants are only a little confused. Both explanations still fit. More ant-watching is needed, which nobody minds at all.
"Would they still march if there wasn't any honey?" Nobody had checked. The honey pot is moved, and the trail breaks up within a day.
Counting only the ants that cross one particular leaf goes surprisingly well, until the leaf blows away.
The novice learns the fair stone test: same stone, same place, same time of day, and write down what happens, not what should happen.
Every time the scholar leans over, their shadow falls across the trail and the ants scatter. They watch from a respectful distance from then on.
A small crowd, in total silence, staring at a stone.
Nobody will admit it is the most exciting thing all week.
The cooks have tried everything.

pieces.label: The Two Kinds of Ash
pieces.text: Ash from the coconut husk fire, stirred into water, turns it strangely slippery, like soap, and stings a little in small cuts. Ash from the driftwood fire just turns the water grey. The cook has washed every pot twice to check, and cannot stop wondering why.

pieces.label: Soak the Ash Side by Side
pieces.text: (Cook) sets up two jars of water, one with husk ash, one with driftwood ash, and leaves them for a whole day...

pieces.label: Test Husk Against Driftwood
pieces.text: (Cook) has two ideas: it's the fuel itself, or it's the salt in the driftwood that makes the difference. (cook.He/She) tests husk, driftwood, and a mix...

pieces.label: Ask Why the Pots Got Cleaner
pieces.text: (Cook) asks the other cooks and helpers if they've noticed anything (cook.he/she) hasn't...

pieces.label: Teach the Ash Test
pieces.text: (Cook) shows (novice) how (cook.he/she) has been running the test, so it can be done again by someone else...
The husk ash makes the water slippery every single time, and the driftwood ash never does. Nobody's sure yet what slippery water is for. The cook has ideas.
Some batches are slippery and some aren't, and the cook starts a third jar.
The more husk ash, the more slippery the water: the fuel, not the salt. And it cleans greasy pots far better than plain water ever did.
The fuel and the salt both still fit. More tests are needed, and more tests is the cook's favourite thing now.
"Why do the husk ash pots always come out cleaner?" Slippery didn't mean dirty; the slippery water was cleaning the pots.
Big hands? Small hands? Heaped or flat? An evening of arguing ends with a coconut shell measure: one half shell, level.
The novice learns to repeat the ash soak: the same jar, the same measure, the same water, the same time, and gets the same results the first time.
One jar had seawater in it, filled at the beach. The notes are revised, and now the water jars have labels too.
Every pot washed twice. Then the neighbours' pots.
Two jars of ash, with labels.
Talking about ash at dinner.

pieces.label: The Tide Clock
pieces.text: A fisher has an idea: every day, when the sun touches the top of the big rock on the point, plant a marker stick at the waterline. "If we know the tide, we know the fish." One fisher points out they already know the tide: it's "the wet bit."

pieces.label: Plant a Stick Every Day
pieces.text: Every day for a whole moon, (fisher) waits for the sun to touch the rock, and plants a stick at the water's edge...

pieces.label: Test Moon Against Wind
pieces.text: (Fisher) wonders: is the tide following the moon, or the wind? (fisher.He/She) starts noting both, beside each stick...

pieces.label: Ask Whether the Rock Moves
pieces.text: (Fisher) invites everyone to poke holes in the method...

pieces.label: Teach the Stick Line
pieces.text: (Fisher) decides to teach (novice) how to keep the stick line, so it can carry on when (fisher) is out fishing...
After a moon of sticks, a long curving line shows the waterline creeping along the beach in a steady order. Even the "wet bit" fisher plans by it.
Storms scatter the line, and some sticks get used as firewood by someone who didn't know. The fisher starts again, with heavier sticks.
The moon fits the tide far better than the wind: the highest sticks are at full and new moon, every time. The fisher is unbearably smug for a week.
The moon and the wind both seem to matter, pulling the sticks in different directions. More sticks are needed. The other fishers groan.
"Does the sun touch the rock at the same time every day? Doesn't it go up later in the winter?" A child exposes the hidden assumption in the whole method.
The bottom of the sun? The middle? Arguing what "touching the rock" means takes longer than planting the sticks.
The novice learns to keep the stick line without the rock: breaths from sunrise, shadow lengths, a knotted cord of days.
Two sticks were planted on cloudy days, when nobody could see the sun touch the rock. They were guesses, and are now ringed with shells.
"We already know the tide. It's the wet bit."
A large bundle of sticks.
Unbearably smug for a week.

pieces.label: The Sick Plant Puzzle
pieces.text: In a long, healthy row of taro, one plant right in the middle has wilted yellow and limp while the plants on either side are perfectly fine. The gardener has visited it every hour since dawn, sometimes talking to it, as if it might explain itself.

pieces.label: Dig Gently Around the Roots
pieces.text: (Gardener) kneels down and starts, very gently, to scoop the soil away from the wilted plant's roots, with (gardener.his/her) bare hands...

pieces.label: Test Water Against Bugs
pieces.text: (Gardener) has two ideas: too much water, or bugs in the soil. (gardener.He/She) takes a cutting and sets up a test...

pieces.label: Ask Whether It Is Just Old
pieces.text: (Gardener) asks everyone who works in the garden what they think...

pieces.label: Teach the Root Check
pieces.text: (Gardener) decides to show (novice) how to check a plant's roots without killing it...
The plant sits in a little hollow where water pools after rain, and its roots are drowning. Two other weak plants are in hollows too.
The roots look white, firm and normal. The gardener packs the soil back, and apologizes to the plant.
A cutting replanted in dry ground perks up, green and healthy, and no bugs are found. Soggy soil explains it, and drainage channels follow.
The cutting perks up a little, but there are some bugs too. The gardener decides not to make any more plants sick to find out.
"Wasn't that one planted first? The leftover from last season?" The plant isn't sick. It's just old, and done.
Anything touching the ground counts as a droop. The wilted plant has seven. A very satisfying number, though it doesn't help the plant.
The novice learns to check roots without harm: dig at an angle, from the side, feel, don't pull. They find two more drowning taro by the end of the day.
The sick plant is the one everyone steps on taking the shortcut across the garden. A fence goes around the taro row.
Talking to it, when nobody is watching.
Tall and green and glossy, except one.
Seven droops.

pieces.label: The Stone That Floats
pieces.text: A child found a stone near the volcano, grey, light and full of tiny holes, like a sponge made of rock, and dropped it in the water bucket to wash it. It floated. A STONE. That FLOATS.

pieces.label: Float Every Volcano Stone
pieces.text: (adult) suggests they find out if all volcano stones float. (Child) grabs a basket and drags (child.him/her) off toward the volcano at a run...

pieces.label: Test Air Against Magic
pieces.text: Half the village thinks the stone is full of air. The other half thinks it's a little bit of volcano magic. (adult) suggests a test...

pieces.label: Ask Whether It Stays Afloat
pieces.text: (adult) asks everyone: "What haven't we thought of?"...

pieces.label: Teach the Bucket Test
pieces.text: (Child) decides (novice) needs to be taught the floating test, properly, by an expert. (Child) is the expert...
Only the light, holey volcano stones float, every time; the heavy, solid black ones sink. The builders get interested in stones light enough to carry easily.
Some float, some sink, and some float for a while and then sink. The child is stumped for the first time, and seems to enjoy it.
Ground into powder, the stone sinks like sand. The trapped air in the holes explains it far better than magic, and the boat builders start wondering.
Some of the powder floats on top for a while, which nobody can explain. The child, who was rooting for magic, is delighted.
Left overnight, the stone sinks: the water slowly crept into the holes. What's true for a moment isn't always true for a day.
In the bucket? In the sea? Does bobbing halfway count? The big water jar is chosen, though the stone has already been floated in every container in the village.
The child, as the expert, teaches the novice the floating test: one stone at a time, dry stones only, same bucket.
Some stones were still wet from the last test, their holes already full of water. The child lays them out to dry in a very neat row.
A STONE. That FLOATS.
Like a sponge made of rock.
Floated in every container in the village.

pieces.label: The Breadfruit Question
pieces.text: Two breadfruit, picked the same morning from the same grove, sit side by side in the cooking hut. One has gone soft and sweet in two days. The other is still as hard as a stone: it went "tok." The cook has started talking to them.

pieces.label: Track Every Breadfruit Picked
pieces.text: From now on, (cook) decides, every breadfruit that comes into the cooking hut gets a mark: which tree, which side of the tree, and what day...

pieces.label: Test Sunny Tree Against Shady Tree
pieces.text: (Cook) has two ideas: it's how ripe the fruit was when it was picked, or it's how it was stored afterward. (cook.He/She) sets up a test...

pieces.label: Ask Whether the Basket Matters
pieces.text: (Cook) asks the other cooks if they have any ideas, and promises not to talk to the breadfruit while they think...

pieces.label: Teach the Breadfruit Tally
pieces.text: (Cook) decides (novice) should learn to keep the tally, so the cooking hut can carry on the work...
Breadfruit from the sunny side of the tree softens first, every time, so the cooks pick sunny for this week and shady for next. Nothing goes to waste.
The fruit soften in no clear order at all, and the cook asks the hard breadfruit, again, what it's playing at.
Stored exactly the same way, the sunny tree's fruit still softens first. Ripeness at picking explains it, and the pickers learn to read it by skin colour.
The results are muddled, and more breadfruit are needed. The cooks don't mind: more breadfruit means more roasted breadfruit.
"Wasn't the soft one stored next to the bananas?" It was. To ripen fruit faster, store it with bananas.
If a thumb leaves a dent, it's soft. Every breadfruit is pressed by every cook. Several are now dented.
The novice learns to keep the tally: one mark per fruit, one mark per day, a different mark for each tree, all on the same board.
Two fruit swapped places in the basket, so the marks no longer match. The cook starts carving marks directly onto the skins.
It went "tok."
"What did you do?"
The other cooks avoid the shelf.

pieces.label: The Echo in the Cave
pieces.text: Two explorers find a cave mouth in the cliffs, and one shouts "HELLO!" It comes back quickly from the left wall. Then, much later, from deep on the right: "...hello." The second one sounds slightly offended. As if it was interrupted.

pieces.label: Clap and Count Each Echo
pieces.text: (Explorer_1) decides to treat it scientifically. (explorer_1.He/She) claps once, sharply, and counts heartbeats until each echo comes back...

pieces.label: Test Distance Against Tunnels
pieces.text: (Explorer_1) thinks the right wall must just be much farther away. (Name2) thinks there must be a hidden tunnel. They light a torch and go in to find out...

pieces.label: Ask Whether It Is Really an Echo
pieces.text: Back in the village, (explorer_1) and (name2) tell the story at the fire, and ask what everyone else thinks...

pieces.label: Teach the Echo Count
pieces.text: (Explorer_1) decides (novice) should learn the clap-and-count method, so the echo can be studied properly...
The gap is always the same: two heartbeats for the left echo, eleven for the right. The researchers start using echoes to guess how deep caves go.
The counts change every time someone shifts their feet. "It's offended," comes the whisper, every time the second echo returns.
By torchlight, a narrow tunnel curves off low in the right-hand corner. The sound goes down it and comes back late. Nobody goes down the tunnel. Yet.
The right wall IS farther, and there MIGHT be a tunnel, behind some rocks. More shouting is needed, and there is a lot more shouting.
"Is the second voice an echo at all?" They go back with claps instead of words. Claps come back. It's only an echo. Probably.
They agree to shout "very" loudly for a fair test. "VERY," says the left wall. A long pause. "...very," says the right.
The novice learns the clap-and-count test at the cave mouth: the same rock, the same clap, the same heartbeats, and gets the same numbers the first time.
The tide was in for one count and out for the other, and water changes how sound bounces. The tide is recorded alongside every clap.
"HELLO!" ... "...hello."
As if it was interrupted.
Neither of them is sure whether to shout again.

pieces.label: The Person Beyond the Torchlight
pieces.text: Past the last torch on the path home, a still figure calls (subject) by a childhood pet name no one alive should know.

pieces.label: Approach the Figure
pieces.text: (Subject) swallows hard and takes one step past the torch, then another. The figure does not move. Up close, (subject.he/she) can make out a hooded wrap, a walking stick, and a face half in shadow...

pieces.label: Call for Witnesses
pieces.text: "Hey! Somebody come here, quick!" (subject) shouts toward the huts, never taking (subject.his/her) eyes off the shape in the dark. Doors bang open. Sleepy villagers come stumbling down the path with torches...

pieces.label: Ask How They Know
pieces.text: "How do you know that name?" (subject) demands, voice shaking a little more than (subject.he/she) would like...

pieces.label: Walk Away
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that whatever this is, (subject.he/she) wants no part of it. (subject.He/She) turns around and walks home very quickly, not looking back...
The figure warns of a storm that will uncover a buried stone, then vanishes behind a tree; days later the rain uncovers a carved marker.
The figure is an old traveler who knew (subject)'s family, and they laugh until dawn about toddler (subject) and the goat pen.
