The others arrive but can't see the figure; everyone hears footsteps retreating through the grass.
The figure is gone, but a warm shell necklace nobody recognizes lies in the dirt.
The figure answers with the one question (subject) never dared ask aloud, and (subject) can't sleep.
It's an old neighbor who heard (subject)'s mother shout that name across the village a hundred times.
Nothing follows (subject) home, though (subject.he/she) starts coming home earlier.
A whisper warns (subject) off the cliff path; next day that stretch of path collapses onto the rocks.
The torch leans in a wind no one else can feel.
The figure's outline wavers like a reed in a current.
(subject) hums to keep the dark at bay.
The name sounds exactly the way (subject)'s mother used to say it.

pieces.label: The Old Beggar at the Door
pieces.text: A barefoot old stranger knocks at (subject)'s door in the rain, asking for shelter, and (subject.his/her) shadow seems to move a moment late.

pieces.label: Offer Food and a Place to Rest
pieces.text: (Subject) waves the old stranger inside, wraps a dry blanket around those bony shoulders, and puts a bowl of stew into trembling hands. The stranger eats slowly, eyes closed, as if it is the best meal in the world...

pieces.label: Invite the Stranger to Stay
pieces.text: "You shouldn't be wandering about at your age," (subject) says firmly. "Stay here. Stay with us. There's always room for one more." The old stranger stares at (subject.him/her) for a long moment, then (subject.his/her) eyes fill up...

pieces.label: Refuse Politely
pieces.text: "I'm sorry," (subject) says, and means it. "We have barely enough for ourselves. The next village might be able to help." (subject.He/She) hands over a broad banana leaf to keep the rain off...

pieces.label: Drive the Stranger Away
pieces.text: "Go on! Get away from here!" (subject) snaps, waving (subject.his/her) arms. "We don't want beggars sniffing around our stores!" The old stranger flinches...
The guest leaves a bundle of speckled seeds that grow unusually well.
By dawn the latched hut is empty except for a warm polished stone on the pillow.
The stranger stays and becomes a quiet, capable elder of the tribe.
The stranger declines but teaches (subject) to seal a cracked jar with resin.
The stranger thanks (subject) anyway and plods on toward the next village.
That night the latch rattles three times in still air; nothing is missing.
A freak gust from a calm sky overturns stored grain; nobody agrees whether it's connected.
The old traveler is found exhausted by the path, and the village argues about how they treated (subject.him/her).
Rain drips from the stranger's grey hair onto the doorstep.
The ragged wrap smells of wet ashes.
The shadow on the wall shifts a heartbeat after its owner.
The stranger's hands shake around the bowl.

pieces.label: The Second Footprint
pieces.text: (subject) comes home from a solitary walk with a second, smaller set of tiptoeing footprints beside (subject.his/her) own.

pieces.label: Follow the Prints
pieces.text: (Subject) grabs a walking stick and sets off back down the path, eyes on the ground. The second set of prints stays beside (subject.his/her) own for a long way, then veers off into the trees all on its own...

pieces.label: Ask the Elders
pieces.text: (Subject) brings the whole puzzle to the elders, who listen gravely, then go look at the path themselves, muttering...

pieces.label: Wait at the Path
pieces.text: (Subject) decides to settle it once and for all. (subject.He/She) sits on a stump beside the path as the sun goes down, arms folded, watching...

pieces.label: Leave an Offering
pieces.text: Just in case, (subject) leaves a small bowl of fruit at the spot where the second prints began, and says a quiet word of thanks to whoever (or whatever) kept (subject.him/her) company...
The prints lead to a sealed clay bottle holding a red-dye map of an unknown cove.
The prints end at the tide line beside a pair of small sandals that belong to no one.
An elder recalls the same thing happening to a cousin, then refuses to say how it ended.
A giggling child with carved wooden soles on a stick has been faking prints for days.
At dusk, invisible footsteps stop beside (subject), then move on toward the village.
A light-footed traveler with bad knees admits to tiptoeing down that trail every night.
The offering is gone by morning, replaced by a fresh, cold fish.
The offering sits untouched until the rain washes it away.
The second prints are pressed only at the toes.
The mud is still soft, so the prints are very fresh.
A bird calls once from the trees and then goes silent.

pieces.label: The Crate with No Owner
pieces.text: A sealed crate of strange wood washes ashore after a calm night, and something inside taps in slow, patient threes.

pieces.label: Open It Carefully
pieces.text: (Subject) borrows a stone blade, takes a deep breath, and works the lid loose inch by inch while everyone else takes a big step back. The tapping stops. The lid creaks open...

pieces.label: Listen Before Opening
pieces.text: (Subject) kneels and presses (subject.his/her) ear against the damp wood. The others hold their breath. For a while, there's only the tapping...

pieces.label: Return It to the Sea
pieces.text: "It isn't ours," (subject) says. With a few helpers, (subject.he/she) pushes the crate back out past the breakers and watches it bob away...

pieces.label: Store It for Its Owner
pieces.text: "Somebody lost this," (subject) says. "Somebody will come looking." The crate is hauled into the storehouse and set carefully in a corner...
The crate is packed with jars of preserved fruit, all still good.
A furious crab bursts out, glares at everyone, and stomps off to the surf.
Under the tapping, something seems to count backward; inside are only broken shells.
The crate taps whenever the tide turns, even far inland, and becomes the village's tide clock.
The crate returns next morning tied with a sailor's knot no one on Isola knows.
It sinks like a stone the moment it clears the breakers.
A traveler recognizes the family mark on the rope and claims it with tears of thanks.
The wood splits in storage and ruins several baskets of dried food.
Barnacles crust one corner of the crate.
The rope is braided in a pattern no fisher knows.
Tap. Tap. Tap. A pause. Then again.

pieces.label: The Bottle of Blue Light
pieces.text: (subject) digs up a wax-sealed glass bottle that glows a soft, breathing blue, just as (subject)'s friend (friend) lies sick with a fever.

pieces.label: Unseal the Bottle
pieces.text: (Subject) breaks the wax with (subject.his/her) thumbnail and pulls the stopper. There's a soft pop, and a breath of cool, sweet-smelling mist curls out...

pieces.label: Study It Without Opening
pieces.text: (Subject) carries the bottle very, very carefully to the researchers, holding it at arm's length the whole way...

pieces.label: Offer It to a Healer
pieces.text: (Subject) brings the bottle to the healers' hut and sets it down in front of (healer), the oldest healer, who peers at it for a very long time...

pieces.label: Bury It Again
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that whatever this is, it was buried for a reason. (subject.He/She) puts it back among the roots, covers it up, and pats the earth down firmly...
A cool mist escapes, and (friend) feels better by morning.
The liquid dyes (subject)'s hands bright blue for three days, to the children's delight.
The researchers discover a mineral that glows in the dark.
The glow fades once the bottle leaves the roots, and no theory can be proven.
(healer) identifies a fever draught but refuses to guess its dose.
(healer) seals it on a high shelf, where it glows like a nightlight.
Pale blue flowers grow over the spot and close whenever anyone walks by.
Nothing happens, and the bottle becomes a fireside story.
The glow pulses slowly, like breathing.
Moths circle the bottle in a soft grey ring.
The wax seal bears a symbol no one recognizes.

pieces.label: The Woman No One Else Hears
pieces.text: At the village edge, (subject) hears a woman singing behind the trees, a song nobody else can hear.

pieces.label: Answer the Song
pieces.text: Feeling rather silly, (subject) hums back. The song pauses, as if surprised. Then it starts again, a little softer, as if inviting (subject.him/her) closer...

pieces.label: Bring a Companion
pieces.text: (Subject) grabs (friend) by the wrist. "Come with me. Please. I need to know I'm not going mad." (Friend) grumbles but comes along, and the two of them creep toward the trees...

pieces.label: Record the Melody
pieces.text: (Subject) rushes home and hums the tune over and over to anyone who will listen, trying to fix it in (subject.his/her) memory before it slips away...

pieces.label: Leave the Woods Alone
pieces.text: (Subject) turns (subject.his/her) back on the trees, sits down by the fire, and tries very hard to listen to the crickets...
The unseen singer teaches (subject) a verse in a language (subject.he/she) almost remembers.
(subject) follows the song and comes back hours later with wet sandals and sand between (subject.his/her) toes.
(friend) hears a different song, from the shore, and both songs stop at the same moment.
Behind the trees sits a basket of freshly dug roots no one gathered.
(friend), a musician, recognizes an old harvesting tune and teaches it to the gardeners.
No one can agree on the final notes, and the village ends up with eleven endings.
The song stops, and (subject) sleeps more peacefully than in months.
The song keeps returning only when (subject) is alone, never explained.
The song rises and falls like a swell over the reef.
The crickets go quiet one by one.
The others hear only insects.

pieces.label: The Mask That Changes Faces
pieces.text: A honey-coloured carved mask found under a fallen tree grins in daylight and weeps by firelight.

pieces.label: Wear It at the Festival
pieces.text: On festival night, (subject) ties the mask on with a strip of bark cloth. The drums start. The wood is warm against (subject.his/her) face, and the world looks a little different through those carved eyes...

pieces.label: Examine the Carving
pieces.text: (Subject) takes the mask to the researchers and the village carvers, who turn it over and over in the light, squinting at every groove...

pieces.label: Return It to the Forest
pieces.text: "It was under that tree for a reason," (subject) decides, and the next morning (subject.he/she) carries the mask back and lays it gently in the hollow where (subject.he/she) found it...

pieces.label: Ask Its Story
pieces.text: (Subject) carries the mask around to the oldest villagers one by one, asking each of them if they've ever seen it before...
(subject) dances wildly all festival night and discovers a love of dancing.
Through the mask, (subject) sees the crowd as it looked generations ago.
The carvers find two expressions cleverly carved over each other, one for each kind of light.
There are no tool marks anywhere, and the wood matches no nearby tree.
The mask is gone the next day, with no tracks leading away.
A child finds a second, surprised-looking mask that seems to stare at the first.
An elder remembers a traveling carver who made masks for joy and grief together.
The elders argue loudly about its age, and nobody agrees.
Moss has grown into the grooves around its eyes.
In the firelight, the mask is weeping.
The wood is warm, as if someone just took it off.

pieces.label: The Three Sealed Jars
pieces.text: In an abandoned shelter, (subject) finds three sealed jars painted with a sun, rain, and a closed eye.

pieces.label: Open the Sun Jar
pieces.text: (Subject) picks up the sun jar. It's heavy and warm from sitting in a patch of light. (subject.He/She) cracks the seal and tips it toward (subject.him/her)...

pieces.label: Open the Rain Jar
pieces.text: (Subject) picks up the rain jar. Something sloshes inside. (subject.He/She) peels back the seal...

pieces.label: Open the Closed-Eye Jar
pieces.text: The closed eye seems to be watching (subject), which is a strange thing for a closed eye to do. (subject.He/She) takes a deep breath and breaks the seal...

pieces.label: Leave the Jars Sealed
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that jars left in such a neat row belong to somebody. (subject.He/She) carries them back to the village one at a time, very carefully...
The sun jar pours out enough honey-scented grain for several meals.
A harmless swarm of shimmering green insects escapes into the grass.
The cracked rain jar keeps slowly filling with fresh water.
A damp scroll shows a forgotten way of watering fields.
(subject) dreams of a hill village and wakes knowing the path there.
A gust puts out every torch at once; the jar is empty.
The jars are stored for study, and the children dare each other to peek; the elders think the shelter was a lone healer's, long ago.
By morning the closed-eye jar's lid lies face down on the floor, and no one admits touching it.
Vines hang through the gaps in the fallen roof.
The jars sit in a neat row, as if just set down.
The closed eye seems to be watching.

pieces.label: The Stranger at the Crossroads
pieces.text: At a three-way crossroads, a salt-smelling traveler tells (subject) which path (subject.he/she) meant to take before (subject.he/she) says a word.

pieces.label: Ask for Directions
pieces.text: "Well, since you seem to know where I'm going," (subject) says slowly, "is there a better way?" The traveler taps the staff thoughtfully against a stone...

pieces.label: Ask the Stranger's Name
pieces.text: "Who are you?" (subject) asks. "How do you know where I'm going?" The traveler bows...

pieces.label: Share the Journey
pieces.text: "If we're going the same way, we may as well walk together," (subject) says. The traveler seems pleased, and they set off side by side...

pieces.label: Take Another Path
pieces.text: (Subject) doesn't like being predicted. Just to be stubborn, (subject.he/she) turns on (subject.his/her) heel and takes the right-hand path instead...
The traveler's route avoids a bridge that washes out that very morning.
The advice leads to a grove of mangoes so heavy their branches touch the ground.
The traveler gives the name of a villager who died many years ago.
The traveler is a salt trader and it was a lucky guess.
The traveler steps around a bend and vanishes, leaving no footprints in soft mud.
The traveler asks about the village and moves in that week.
(subject) takes a different path and gets home without trouble.
(subject) gets lost all night and limps home at dawn, scraped and exhausted.
The staff is wrapped in faded red cord.
The cloak smells of salt, though the sea is half a day away.
Three paths, and a smile that already knows the answer.

pieces.label: The Beggar's Empty Bowl
pieces.text: In a lean season, a tired old beggar asks (subject) for one spoonful of food in an empty, polished coconut bowl.

pieces.label: Share a Meal
pieces.text: (Subject) sighs, ladles (subject.his/her) own supper into the coconut bowl, and sits down beside the old beggar to share what's left...

pieces.label: Give the Beggar a Job
pieces.text: "We're short on food, but we're also short on hands," (subject) says. "Help us gather, and you'll eat with us tonight." The beggar nods and picks up a digging stick...

pieces.label: Offer Water but No Food
pieces.text: "I'm sorry. I can't spare food this season," (subject) says. "But you can have all the water you want." (subject.He/She) fills the coconut bowl from the jar...

pieces.label: Turn the Beggar Away
pieces.text: "We have nothing for you," (subject) says shortly. "Try somewhere else." The beggar lowers the empty bowl and turns away without a word...
The beggar teaches a smoke-drying method that stops fruit going to waste.
The beggar eats, bows, and walks on, with no mysterious reward at all.
The beggar has an uncanny nose for roots and fills every basket.
The work is too hard for the old one, and (subject) apologizes for making help conditional.
The beggar drinks and goes on down the road.
Next morning, a fresh spring bubbles up between two dry stones on the path.
A blight ruins much of the harvest, and rumours of a curse follow (subject).
Nothing happens, but (subject) searches the road for days to make it right.
The coconut bowl is polished by years of hands.
The storehouse baskets are looking thin.
The beggar's eyes are kind and very tired.

pieces.label: The Door That Was Not There
pieces.text: After a night of rain, a carved wooden door stands upright between two boulders, with no wall around it and light showing beneath.

pieces.label: Open the Door
pieces.text: (Subject) grips the carved handle, takes a deep breath, and pulls. The door swings open with a long, groaning creak...

pieces.label: Knock Three Times
pieces.text: Feeling ridiculous, (subject) raps on the door. Knock. Knock. Knock. (subject.He/She) waits...

pieces.label: Mark Its Location
pieces.text: (Subject) doesn't touch it. Instead, (subject.he/she) scratches marks on the nearby trees and hurries to fetch the researchers and their maps...

pieces.label: Carry It to the Village
pieces.text: "Good wood is good wood," (subject) declares. (subject.He/She) wraps (subject.his/her) arms around the door and heaves...
Behind the door is a narrow cave stacked with old stone tools.
The door opens onto flat darkness; when a torch is brought, the door has vanished.
Someone knocks back twice, and no one volunteers to knock again.
(name2), a prankster, leaps out from behind the boulders with a door washed down from the old hut ruins.
The door stays for days and is carefully mapped.
Next morning the boulders stand pressed together, with no room for a door.
The door becomes the village's finest tabletop.
The door is impossibly heavy, and (subject) strains (subject.his/her) back trying.
The door is carved all over with spirals.
A thin line of light shows beneath it.
From the back, it is just the back of a door.

pieces.label: The Mirror of Another Age
pieces.text: (subject) digs up a polished bronze disc that shows (subject.him/her) as a white-haired elder, though the trees behind look unchanged.

pieces.label: Look Again
pieces.text: Heart pounding, (subject) slowly raises the disc again and makes (subject.himself/herself) look...

pieces.label: Ask a Scholar
pieces.text: (Subject) brings the disc to (friend), who turns it over in (friend.his/her) hands with great interest...

pieces.label: Offer It to a Spirit
pieces.text: Unsure what else to do, (subject) carries the disc to a quiet spot under the trees, sets it on a flat stone like an altar, and says a few awkward words to whatever might be listening...

pieces.label: Hide It
pieces.text: (Subject) decides nobody should look into this thing ever again, including (subject.himself/herself)...
For an instant (subject) sees a small child in the disc, then (subject.his/her) own face again.
The bronze is just warped, and (subject) spends the afternoon pulling faces into it.
The scholar demonstrates curved reflections with a polished spoon.
The scholar sees something in it, goes quiet, and puts it away.
A gust lifts the heavy disc from the altar and carries it into the brush.
(subject) dreams of a smiling ancestor and wakes at peace with growing old.
The disc is buried where no one will find it.
(subject) sneaks back to look again and finds only the folded cloth.
The bronze is green at the edges.
The face in it has deep laugh lines.
Behind the old face, the trees look exactly the same.

pieces.label: The Guest Who Knew Tomorrow
pieces.text: A soft-spoken visitor warns (subject) that the fishing net will break at sunrise, then asks to sleep by the fire.

pieces.label: Welcome the Guest
pieces.text: (Subject) shrugs and makes up a bed by the fire. The visitor thanks (subject.him/her) and curls up without another word...

pieces.label: Ask for Another Prediction
pieces.text: "If you can see tomorrow," (subject) says, half joking, "what else is going to happen?" The visitor looks up at the sky, then at (subject), and smiles...

pieces.label: Question the Claim
pieces.text: "Nobody knows tomorrow," (subject) says, folding (subject.his/her) arms. "How could you possibly know that?" The visitor's tired eyes crinkle...

pieces.label: Send the Guest Away
pieces.text: "I don't let fortune-tellers sleep by my fire," (subject) says firmly. "Good night." The visitor bows, unoffended, and walks off into the dark...
Before dawn the visitor teaches (subject) to mend a hidden frayed seam, and the net holds.
The visitor leaves a perfectly knotted spare net, and the old one splits at sunrise.
The visitor predicts heavy rain; the sky stays clear all day.
The visitor describes a child finding a rare shell, and it comes true the next day.
The visitor admits noticing crab-chewed rope and explains how nets fail.
The visitor smiles and says some questions are better left unanswered.
The net snaps at sunrise and half the catch is lost.
The net holds, and "It will break at sunrise" becomes the village joke.
The visitor's sandals are salt-white.
The voice is so soft (subject) has to lean in.
Down on the beach, the net hangs on its poles, looking perfectly fine.

pieces.label: The Cask of Forgotten Names
pieces.text: A cask raised from a wreck is full of clay name tokens, and one of them bears (subject)'s own name.

pieces.label: Search for the Owner
pieces.text: (Subject) carries the cask from hut to hut and asks every traveler who passes through if they know where it came from...

pieces.label: Read the Names Aloud
pieces.text: (Subject) sits on the beach as the sun goes down and reads the names aloud, one by one, slowly, so that someone hears them again...

pieces.label: Burn the Tokens
pieces.text: "Names of the dead shouldn't be dragged up from the sea," (subject) says. "Let them rest." (subject.He/She) builds a fire on the beach and tips the cask into it...

pieces.label: Preserve the Records
pieces.text: (Subject) hands the whole cask over to the researchers and asks them to take good care of it...
A traveler recognizes the tokens as birth records from a village lost to the sea.
No one claims it, and after the rain there is one fresh new token in the cask.
(subject) forgets (subject.his/her) own name, as if the old tokens took it, and is now "?".
(friend), an elder, hears the name of a long-lost uncle and weeps.
The smoke smells of a garden nobody on the island has planted.
A gust scatters the tokens out of the fire, every name unburnt.
The researchers learn much about the island's former inhabitants.
The tokens are stored, but their script resists translation.
The tokens clink softly, like rain on a roof.
One name is stamped clear as day.
The cask smells of salt and old wood.

pieces.label: The Figure in the Tidal Pool
pieces.text: In an empty tidal pool, (subject) sees the reflection of a patient stranger standing where no one stands.

pieces.label: Speak to the Reflection
pieces.text: "H-hello?" (subject) whispers to the water, feeling very foolish. The face in the pool tilts, as if listening...

pieces.label: Touch the Water
pieces.text: Slowly, (subject) reaches out one finger and touches the surface of the pool, right where the reflection's face is...

pieces.label: Fetch a Witness
pieces.text: (Subject) scrambles up the rocks, grabs (friend) by the arm, and drags (friend.him/her) down to the pool. "Look! Look in there! Tell me you see it!"...

pieces.label: Leave Quietly
pieces.text: (Subject) decides not to disturb whatever is in the pool. (subject.He/She) backs away across the rocks, carefully, without turning (subject.his/her) back on it...
The reflection warns (subject) to move the fishing baskets just before a freak tide.
The reflection mouths words that no one can hear.
The image breaks up into a school of silver fish.
(subject) is struck dizzy and must be helped home.
(friend) sees only sky and accuses (subject) of a prank.
(friend) sees a different face: (friend.his/her) own dead grandmother.
The reflection fades with the changing light.
A wet, deep-sea-smelling shell with a strange symbol turns up in (subject)'s pocket.
The water is clear and ankle-deep.
Little crabs scuttle at the edges of the pool.
The face looks patient, as if it has been waiting.

pieces.label: The Potion with Two Labels
pieces.text: An old green bottle in the medicine chest has two labels: one promises healing, the other warns of forgetfulness.

pieces.label: Study the Ingredients
pieces.text: (Subject) brings the bottle to (friend), who dips a reed in it, sniffs, squints, and spreads tiny smears on leaves to watch how they dry...

pieces.label: Try a Tiny Drop
pieces.text: When no one is looking, (subject) pulls the stopper, touches a single drop to (subject.his/her) tongue, and waits...

pieces.label: Ask the Oldest Healer
pieces.text: (Subject) takes the bottle to (friend), the oldest healer in the village, who turns it slowly in (friend.his/her) wrinkled hands...

pieces.label: Seal It Away
pieces.text: (Subject) decides this is one mystery best left alone. (subject.He/She) wraps the bottle in leaves and puts it in the storehouse...
The healers identify the herbs and record their effects without anyone drinking it.
The mixture has separated into layers, and its recipe is lost.
(subject) tastes a drop and is ill for several days.
The drop tastes of nothing, which makes everyone more nervous.
The old healer recalls a draught once made to soften painful memories.
The old healer warns that no trustworthy medicine carries two stories.
The bottle is labelled UNKNOWN and shelved out of children's reach.
The bottle cracks overnight, leaving no liquid and a sweet guava smell.
One label is painted with a sun, the other scratched with a crescent moon.
The stopper is sealed with old resin.
The bottle is darker than any green in the healers' hut.

pieces.label: The Woman at the Last House
pieces.text: Every evening, a still woman in a pale wrap stands beside the village's last house, and its family insist no one has visited.

pieces.label: Invite Her Inside
pieces.text: Gathering every scrap of courage (subject.he/she) has, (subject) walks over. "You must be cold," (subject.he/she) says. "Would you like to come in and sit by a fire?"...

pieces.label: Watch from a Distance
pieces.text: (Subject) hides behind a pile of firewood across the path and watches the woman as the sun sinks lower and lower...

pieces.label: Ask Who She Seeks
pieces.text: (Subject) walks up to her slowly. "Excuse me," (subject.he/she) says, as politely as (subject.he/she) can manage. "Who are you waiting for?"...

pieces.label: Ignore the Figure
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that whatever she is, she's none of (subject.his/her) business. (subject.He/She) stops looking toward the last house in the evenings...
She tells a story by the fire about a family who once lived on that spot, then leaves.
She vanishes, leaving a steaming bowl of strangely spiced soup on the doorstep.
She turns toward (subject) without moving her feet.
(friend), an old neighbor, admits to waiting there every evening for a sister who never came home.
She names a villager who disappeared years ago.
She asks the way to a settlement no one has ever heard of.
The sightings stop after a week.
She appears in (subject)'s dream, pointing to a buried bone bracelet.
She stands very still in the long evening shadows.
The dogs never bark at her.
Her wrap is the colour of moonlight.

pieces.label: The Sealed Box of Winds
pieces.text: A small carved box hums before every storm, and its lid says 'Open when the air grows still.'

pieces.label: Open It in Calm Weather
pieces.text: On the stillest afternoon of the season, with the whole village watching from a safe distance, (subject) lifts the little lid...

pieces.label: Wait for a Storm
pieces.text: (Subject) decides the box should be watched, not opened. When the next storm rolls in, (subject.he/she) sits up with it all night, listening to it hum louder and louder...

pieces.label: Ask a Builder to Inspect It
pieces.text: (Subject) brings the box to (friend), the best builder in the village, who turns it over with clever, calloused fingers...

pieces.label: Give It to a Traveler
pieces.text: When a traveler passes through on the way to the far shore, (subject) holds out the box. "Maybe you know where this came from?"...
A burst of wind scatters the drying grain across the beach for the gulls.
A folded drawing inside shows a clever windbreak for the gardens.
The box falls silent at the storm's height, as though listening.
The box cracks, releasing storm-grey moths that sit on every roof until the rain ends.
A hidden reed chamber explains the hum, and the builders make storm warnings.
(friend) finds no opening at all for air to enter.
A traveler promises to return with news of its maker.
The traveler refuses to touch it, having seen it in a dream before a great storm.
The hum is a low drone felt in the teeth.
The carving swirls like wind patterns on sand.
The air is perfectly still, for once.

pieces.label: The Three Gifts of the Wanderer
pieces.text: A wanderer offers (subject) one of three gifts: a sack of grain, a fish-skin book of strange symbols, or a warm plain stone.

pieces.label: Choose the Grain
pieces.text: "Food is food," (subject) says practically, and picks up the heavy sack. The wanderer nods as if (subject.he/she) expected exactly that...

pieces.label: Choose the Book
pieces.text: (Subject) can't resist. (subject.He/She) picks up the book with both hands and opens it carefully. The pages are covered in neat little drawings between the strange symbols...

pieces.label: Choose the Stone
pieces.text: The plain little stone is warm in (subject)'s palm, warmer than the morning sun could make it. "This one," (subject.he/she) says, surprising (subject.himself/herself)...

pieces.label: Refuse All Three
pieces.text: (Subject) looks at the three gifts for a long time, then shakes (subject.his/her) head. "Thank you. But I don't need any of them. Give them to someone who does."...
The sack holds enough clean grain to feed several households.
The grain is spoiled beneath its clean top layer and taints the stores.
The book's drawings teach the village a better way to store water.
The symbols shift in everyone's memory, and no one agrees what they mean.
The stone keeps (child), a sick child next door, warm through a cold night.
The stone is ordinary basalt, but (subject) treasures it anyway.
The wanderer respects the refusal and walks on whistling.
"You have chosen the fourth gift," says the wanderer, and leaves without explaining.
The book is bound in fish skin.
The stone steams faintly in the cool morning.
The wanderer waits as if this choice matters very much.

pieces.label: The Bridge Keeper's Question
pieces.text: A reed-hatted stranger sits by the public bridge and asks each passerby what they will give to cross.

pieces.label: Offer a Story
pieces.text: (Subject) thinks for a moment, then sits down on the bank and tells the keeper a story, the one about (subject.his/her) grandfather and the very angry goat...

pieces.label: Challenge the Toll
pieces.text: "This bridge belongs to all of us," (subject) says, hands on hips. "Nobody pays to cross it. Not me, not anybody."...

pieces.label: Offer Food
pieces.text: (Subject) opens (subject.his/her) pack and holds out (subject.his/her) lunch, dried fruit and a lump of cold cooked yam. "Will this do?"...

pieces.label: Find Another Crossing
pieces.text: (Subject) doesn't fancy answering riddles at a bridge. (subject.He/She) turns and heads upstream to find another way over the river...
The keeper laughs at (subject)'s story and steps aside.
The keeper tells a story back that teaches a forgotten fishing knot.
The village agrees no one should pay to use a common path.
The keeper vanishes mid-argument, leaving a stick carved with tiny bridges.
The keeper shares the food with a line of hungry travelers.
(subject) finds twice as much dried fruit in (subject.his/her) pack that evening.
A long, muddy detour gets (subject) across safely.
(subject) slips on slimy stepping stones and is hurt.
The keeper's hat is woven from river reeds.
The water under the bridge runs fast and brown.
Nobody remembers appointing a keeper.

pieces.label: The Song That Opens the Cave
pieces.text: A child hums a tune learned from an unknown visitor, and at its last note a crack in the cliff seems to widen.

pieces.label: Sing the Melody Again
pieces.text: (Subject) has (child) teach (subject.him/her) the tune, and the two of them hum it together, loudly, right in front of the crack...

pieces.label: Explore the Crack
pieces.text: (Subject) sends (child) home, fetches some friends and a torch, and the group squeezes sideways into the narrow crack in the cliff...

pieces.label: Ask the Child About the Visitor
pieces.text: (Subject) sits down on a rock beside (child). "Tell me about this visitor. Everything you can remember."...

pieces.label: Leave the Cliff Undisturbed
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that a cliff with a song is best left alone. (subject.He/She) takes (child) home by the hand...
A passage opens onto a neatly wrapped cache of old tools.
Nothing happens, and the child insists the tune was never meant to be sung twice.
The group finds edible roots growing in a cool hollow.
Loose stones fall and injure (subject)'s shoulder.
The child describes a kind, tall stranger with eyes like moonlit water.
The child admits copying the wind whistling through stone, which whistles the same tune.
The melody becomes the village's favourite lullaby.
The crack closes after the next rain, leaving no trace.
The cliff is streaked with orange lichen.
A thin breath of cold air sighs out of the rock.
The child hums very seriously, eyes closed.

pieces.label: The Fisherman's Impossible Catch
pieces.text: (subject) hauls up a net holding a sealed iron-banded chest instead of fish, and something inside knocks three times.

pieces.label: Open the Chest
pieces.text: (Subject) pries at the rusty clasp with a fish knife until, with a squeal, the lid pops open...

pieces.label: Return It to the Water
pieces.text: (Subject) doesn't like the sound of that knocking one bit. (subject.He/She) drags the chest back down to the waves and shoves it out to sea...

pieces.label: Take It to the Village
pieces.text: (Subject) heaves the chest onto (subject.his/her) shoulder and staggers up the beach with it, the knocking going all the way...

pieces.label: Wait for the Knocking
pieces.text: (Subject) sits down on the sand next to the chest and waits to see what the knocking will do...
Inside are preserved hooks and a sharkskin chart of unknown fishing grounds.
A soaked letter asks whoever finds it to remember one lost name.
The chest floats away against the current.
The chest returns at dawn with a fresh knot tied around its handle.
The chest is repaired and becomes the village's sturdiest storage box.
Rotten cargo spills out and spoils nearby supplies.
The knocking stops at sunset and never resumes.
A very offended gold-eyed lizard crawls out and waddles off.
Seaweed drips from the iron bands.
The knock is slow and polite, like a guest at a door.
The chest is far too small for a person.

pieces.label: The Visitor Who Cast No Shadow
pieces.text: At high noon a traveler asks (subject) for directions, and everyone notices the traveler casts no shadow.

pieces.label: Offer Directions
pieces.text: (Subject) clears (subject.his/her) throat, tries very hard not to look at the ground, and gives the traveler directions as best (subject.he/she) can...

pieces.label: Invite the Traveler to Eat
pieces.text: "You've come a long way. Sit, eat with us," (subject) says. The traveler accepts, delighted, and joins the villagers around the cooking fire...

pieces.label: Ask About the Shadow
pieces.text: (Subject) can't help it. "Excuse me," (subject.he/she) says, pointing at the ground. "But where's your shadow?"...

pieces.label: Follow the Traveler
pieces.text: (Subject) gives the directions, then sneaks after the traveler as (subject.he/she) leaves the village, keeping well back...
By evening the traveler casts a perfectly ordinary shadow on the beach.
The traveler warns of a trail that a landslide buries two days later.
The traveler tells stories of a black-sand beach and a sea that holds the moon.
The traveler leaves a basket of unusual but edible fruit.
The traveler shows the roof's shadow was hiding (subject.his/her) own.
"I left it where I was born," says the traveler, and changes the subject.
The footprints lead to a village (subject) has never seen, where a woman waves as if expecting (subject.him/her).
The traveler disappears around a bend where no other path exists.
The dust in the square is white with heat.
Even the chickens have little puddles of shadow.
The traveler waits politely, noticing nothing.

pieces.label: The Lantern on the Empty Boat
pieces.text: An empty boat drifts into the lagoon at night, its blue lantern still burning, and bumps ashore at (subject)'s feet.

pieces.label: Bring the Boat Ashore
pieces.text: (Subject) wades into the shallows, grabs the prow, and hauls the little boat up onto the sand, the lantern swinging above (subject.his/her) head...

pieces.label: Search the Coast
pieces.text: "Someone must have been in it," (subject) says. (subject.He/She) runs to wake the fishers, and soon canoes are out on the dark water with torches, calling...

pieces.label: Extinguish the Lantern
pieces.text: Something about that steady blue flame bothers (subject). (subject.He/She) reaches up and pinches it out...

pieces.label: Keep Watch Until Dawn
pieces.text: (Subject) ties the boat to the dock post, sits down on the sand beside it, and waits for morning, the blue light flickering on (subject.his/her) face...
The boat carries dried food wrapped against the spray.
The only cargo is a child's charcoal drawing of the village, every hut in place.
A missing fisher is found alive on a sandbar after two days.
The search finds no one, and the boat's origin stays unknown.
The flame goes out, but the wick is cold and the lantern holds no oil.
The lantern relights itself once before finally going dark.
At sunrise a relieved traveler arrives to claim the boat.
The boat is gone by morning, though its rope is still tied to the dock.
The lantern hangs on a hook of carved bone.
The flame is steady and blue in the still night.
The boat bumps softly against the sand.

pieces.label: The Beggar and the Broken Cup
pieces.text: An old beggar holds out a cracked red clay cup for water, in a voice that sounds just like someone (subject) knew long ago.

pieces.label: Mend the Cup
pieces.text: "That cup won't hold anything for long," (subject) says gently. "Let me fix it first." (subject.He/She) sits down with the beggar, mixes a little wet clay, and starts pressing it into the crack...

pieces.label: Give a Better Cup
pieces.text: (Subject) runs into (subject.his/her) hut and comes back with (subject.his/her) own best cup, smooth and whole, and fills it to the brim...

pieces.label: Invite the Beggar to Rest
pieces.text: "Come and sit in the shade," (subject) says. "Rest a while. You look like you've walked a long way." The beggar sinks down gratefully beneath a breadfruit tree...

pieces.label: Send the Beggar Away
pieces.text: Something about that voice frightens (subject). "I'm sorry, I can't help you," (subject.he/she) says, and hurries off without looking back...
The beggar teaches (subject) a clay repair stronger than the pot itself.
The mended cup breaks again along the same line as the beggar walks away.
The beggar leaves a tiny carved turtle charm in exchange for a whole cup.
The beggar refuses the new cup: the cracked one belonged to someone dear.
The beggar's stories help the elders remember an old yam-planting method.
The beggar wakes with no memory of arriving, and an ordinary voice.
The beggar leaves quietly, and nothing unusual follows.
That evening the familiar voice calls (subject)'s name from an empty path.
The crack runs all the way down one side of the cup.
The voice is almost, almost someone (subject) knows.
The beggar's hands tremble around the cup.

pieces.label: The House That Dreamed
pieces.text: Several villagers dream of the same unfamiliar house with a table set for one more, where an unseen host offers a seat.

pieces.label: Draw the House
pieces.text: (Subject) gathers all the dreamers together and asks each of them to draw the house, separately, without peeking at anyone else's...

pieces.label: Visit the Ruins
pieces.text: (Subject) leads a little group of the bravest dreamers out past the hills, to where an old ruined shelter sits half swallowed by vines...

pieces.label: Accept the Dream Invitation
pieces.text: That night, (subject) goes to sleep determined. When the dream comes, and the voice invites (subject.him/her) to sit, (subject.he/she) says yes, and pulls out the empty chair...

pieces.label: Stop Discussing the Dreams
pieces.text: "It's just a dream," (subject) says firmly. "Let's stop talking about it, and maybe it'll stop." The others reluctantly agree...
The drawings match perfectly, except half show a red door and half a blue one.
A traveler recognizes the house as a ruined shelter beyond the hills.
Beneath the ruin's floor is a sealed jar of grain.
A broken chair and fresh footprints lead to a wall with no door.
(subject) dreams of an ancestor who helps with a difficult choice.
(subject) wanders endless rooms all night and wakes exhausted.
The dreams gradually fade.
(child), the youngest dreamer, keeps visiting and finds warm coconut milk waiting each night.
The house has a red door. Or was it blue?
A table is set for one more.
The smell of baking bread drifts from somewhere inside.

pieces.label: The River's Returned Gift
pieces.text: The broken tool (subject) threw into the river reappears on the bank the next morning, whole and polished.

pieces.label: Use the Returned Tool
pieces.text: (Subject) picks up the tool, weighs it in (subject.his/her) hand, and heads out to the gardens to give it a try...

pieces.label: Study the Workmanship
pieces.text: (Subject) takes the tool to (friend), the village's best craftsperson, who turns it over and over in the sunlight, muttering...

pieces.label: Leave a Thank-You Gift
pieces.text: Just to be polite, (subject) leaves a little bundle of fruit and a pretty shell on the flat stone where the tool was, and says thank you to the river, feeling slightly silly...

pieces.label: Watch the River at Night
pieces.text: (Subject) hides in the reeds by the river after dark, determined to catch whoever, or whatever, mended (subject.his/her) tool...
The tool never dulls, and the gatherers fight over whose turn it is.
The tool breaks on its first use, in exactly the same place.
(friend), the best craftsperson, learns a new polishing method from it.
No one recognizes the signature-like marks on the handle.
The gift is replaced by a perfectly round, moon-striped pebble.
The gift goes untouched and is eventually reclaimed.
A figure on the far bank raises one hand, then vanishes in the mist.
(friend), a shy old fisher, admits mending the tool as a quiet kindness.
The river is low and green and says nothing.
The tool shines as if it was just made.
Mist rises off the water after dark.

pieces.label: The Orchard of One Night
pieces.text: At dawn, (subject) finds a grove of ripe fruit trees where there was bare ground the evening before.

pieces.label: Harvest Carefully
pieces.text: (Subject) runs back to the village yelling for baskets, and soon half the village is in the grove, picking fruit as fast as they can...

pieces.label: Examine the Trees
pieces.text: (Subject) brings (friend), the most knowledgeable farmer in the village, to take a good, hard look at the mysterious grove...

pieces.label: Leave the Fruit Untouched
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that fruit which appears overnight is not fruit (subject.he/she) wants to eat. (subject.He/She) tells everyone to leave the grove alone...

pieces.label: Return at Sunset
pieces.text: (Subject) decides to wait and see whether the grove is still there at the end of the day...
The village gathers a huge, sticky harvest before the fruit spoils.
Every fruit is horribly bitter, and the harvest is thrown away.
(friend), the best farmer, finds the grove was hidden under strangler vines all along.
The trees have unfamiliar leaves and look a hundred years old.
Birds feast in the grove, and the villagers love watching them.
All the fruit falls overnight, leaving the ground carpeted in seeds.
At sunset the grove is still there, ordinary in the fading light.
The trees are gone, but fresh fruit lies scattered in the grass.
The air smells of nectar.
Bees are already working the blossoms.
Fallen fruit splits open in the grass.

pieces.label: The Name Spoken from the Well
pieces.text: While drawing water, (subject) hears (subject.his/her) own name whispered from deep in the old well.

pieces.label: Answer the Voice
pieces.text: (Subject) leans over the edge, heart pounding. "Y-yes? I'm here. What do you want?"...

pieces.label: Lower a Lantern
pieces.text: (Subject) ties a little oil lamp to the bucket rope and lowers it, slowly, hand over hand, down into the dark...

pieces.label: Ask Another Villager to Listen
pieces.text: (Subject) runs to fetch (friend). "Come and listen to the well. Please. Just listen."...

pieces.label: Cover the Well for a Night
pieces.text: (Subject) drags a big wooden lid over the well and weighs it down with stones. "Let's see you whisper through that," (subject.he/she) mutters...
The whisper gives directions to a sweet hidden spring.
The voice repeats (subject)'s words exactly, a clever echo, though not the first whisper.
The light reveals an ancient carving of reaching hands just above the waterline.
The lantern goes out before it touches the water.
(friend) hears a different name, someone (friend.he/she) lost, and turns pale.
(friend) hears nothing but believes (subject) is sincere.
The whispers stop, and the well is reopened safely.
A faint knocking begins beneath the cover, but nothing is found.
The rope creaks as the bucket goes down.
Cold air rises from the dark, smelling of wet stone.
The whisper is soft and very clear.

pieces.label: The Gift That Could Not Be Given
pieces.text: A stranger gives (subject) a seed-and-shell necklace that grows heavy whenever anyone tries to give it away.

pieces.label: Keep the Necklace
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that if it wants to stay with (subject.him/her) that badly, so be it. (subject.He/She) puts it on...

pieces.label: Give It to a Friend
pieces.text: (Subject) is determined to test it properly. (subject.He/She) takes the necklace off and holds it out to (friend). "Here. Take it. Tell me if it gets heavy."...

pieces.label: Ask Its Maker
pieces.text: (Subject) goes around the village showing the necklace to every craftsperson and every elder, hoping someone knows who made it...

pieces.label: Return It to the Stranger
pieces.text: (Subject) hurries off down the path after the stranger, the necklace light in (subject.his/her) hand, and catches up just before the trees...
(subject) grows fond of the necklace and starts loving jewelry.
Once (subject) stops worrying, the necklace feels ordinary.
It thumps to the ground like a rock when (friend) takes it, and only (subject) can lift it.
(friend) takes it easily, suggesting the weight was imagined.
(friend), the oldest craftsperson, reveals a sand-filled seed: a teaching puzzle.
No one on Isola recognizes the seeds or the shell.
The stranger thanks (subject) and disappears into the trees.
Next morning the necklace hangs swinging from (subject)'s door latch, though there is no wind.
Black seeds and a single white shell.
The stranger holds it out with both hands.
It is light, until it isn't.

pieces.label: The Shoreline Procession
pieces.text: At night, (subject) sees a silent procession of people carrying lights along the beach; at dawn there are no footprints.

pieces.label: Follow at a Distance
pieces.text: (Subject) creeps along the dunes behind the procession, keeping low, keeping quiet, following the little lights all the way to the rocky point...

pieces.label: Call the Village
pieces.text: (Subject) runs back up to the huts, banging on doors. "Come quick! Down on the beach! Bring torches!"...

pieces.label: Offer a Greeting
pieces.text: (Subject) steps out onto the open sand, raises a hand, and says, as steadily as (subject.he/she) can, "Good evening..."

pieces.label: Wait Until Morning
pieces.text: (Subject) sits down in the dunes, wraps (subject.his/her) arms around (subject.his/her) knees, and decides that whatever this is, it can be dealt with in daylight...
The procession leads (subject) to castaways who saw no one else on the beach.
The lights walk out over the waves and vanish past the horizon.
Everyone sees the lights but argues about whether anyone carried them.
The others see nothing, leaving (subject) shaken.
One figure turns and bows like an elder at a funeral.
A voice from nowhere says, "Remember us."
The shore is quiet at dawn, and work resumes.
The tide uncovers an old burial marker, and the village gathers to honour it.
Not a single footfall, not a single word.
The lights are small and yellow, held at chest height.
The line is perfectly even between the surf and the dunes.

pieces.label: The Stranger's Unfinished Story
pieces.text: A visitor's fireside tale stops just as the hero touches a forbidden box, and the visitor asks (subject) to choose the ending.

pieces.label: Open the Box in the Story
pieces.text: "The hero opens it, of course!" (subject) says. "After all that? Who wouldn't?" The children cheer. The visitor's eyes glitter in the firelight...

pieces.label: Leave the Box Closed
pieces.text: "The hero leaves it closed," (subject) says. "Some things are forbidden for a reason." The children groan in disappointment...

pieces.label: Give the Box Away
pieces.text: "The hero doesn't want it," (subject) says. "So (subject.he/she) gives the box to someone else to decide." The children look confused. The visitor laughs out loud...

pieces.label: Ask the Hero to Seek Help
pieces.text: "The hero goes back down the mountain and asks the elders what to do," (subject) says firmly. "No one should make a choice like that alone." The visitor leans back, interested...
The visitor says curiosity brings both knowledge and sorrow.
The visitor hands (subject) a real cord-bound box with no keyhole, then leaves.
The visitor warns that restraint can also become fear.
The visitor asks whether the hero ever knew what was lost.
The visitor laughs and says even giving it away is a choice with responsibility.
The visitor declares the story now belongs to the village.
The visitor teaches a riddle about solving problems together.
The visitor says the hero must choose alone, and is gone by dawn.
The fire has burned down to coals.
The children have crept close enough to listen.
The visitor's eyes glitter in the firelight.

pieces.label: The Stone That Remembered
pieces.text: A warm hearthstone seems to whisper fragments of conversations from years ago.

pieces.label: Listen Closely
pieces.text: (Subject) sits down, holds the warm stone to (subject.his/her) ear, and closes (subject.his/her) eyes, trying to catch every word...

pieces.label: Ask an Elder
pieces.text: (Subject) brings the stone to (friend), the oldest villager (subject.he/she) can find, who takes it in two wrinkled hands and listens...

pieces.label: Place It in the Sun
pieces.text: (Subject) sets the stone on a flat rock in the full blazing sun, to see what happens when it warms up properly...

pieces.label: Return It to the Hearth
pieces.text: (Subject) decides the stone belongs where it was found. (subject.He/She) sets it back in the fire pit, right where it sat for years...
(subject) hears an old planting method and it works beautifully.
The stone repeats a private argument; the pair sulk a week, then make up over stew.
(friend), the oldest villager, recognizes the stone from a grandmother's hearth and hears her laughing.
(friend) hears nothing and blames the wind in a crack.
The stone cools in the sun and falls silent.
A faint map of rivers appears on its surface.
Back in the hearth, the whispers stop and it becomes a cooking stone.
(subject) dreams of the family who once lived around that hearth.
The stone is smoothed by years of cooking pots.
The whispers come and go like voices through a wall.
It is warm, though the fire has been out for days.

pieces.label: The Two Identical Travelers
pieces.text: Two strangers with the same face, clothes and walking stick arrive from opposite directions, each insisting they have never met.

pieces.label: Invite Both to Stay
pieces.text: "Well," (subject) says, after a long pause, "you both look like you could use a meal. And a place to sleep. Stay with us, both of you, and you can sort this out at your leisure."...

pieces.label: Ask About Their Histories
pieces.text: (Subject) sits them down at opposite sides of the fire and asks each of them to tell their story, from the very beginning...

pieces.label: Let Them Meet Privately
pieces.text: "This is between the two of you," (subject) says, and shoos everyone else away. The two travelers step into an empty hut together, and the door closes...

pieces.label: Consult a Storyteller
pieces.text: (Subject) fetches (friend), the village's best storyteller, who looks from one traveler to the other with great interest...
{#made:One settles in, one camps nearby|Both settle in}, take different names and jobs, and wave the same wave each morning.
One departs overnight, leaving the other deeply unsettled.
Their stories differ in everything except a childhood lullaby.
Both describe the same storm from opposite shores.
They come out laughing and refuse to explain.
Only one emerges; one set of footprints leads west.
(friend), the storyteller, recalls a tale of a man meeting himself coming back.
(friend) says resemblance is not proof of magic, and the mystery remains.
Both wraps have the same frayed hem.
Both sticks have a notch near the top.
Both tilt their heads the same way when puzzled.

pieces.label: The Merchant's Impossible Price
pieces.text: A merchant offers (subject) a sunset-coloured bottle for "one thing you will not miss until it is gone."

pieces.label: Accept the Bargain
pieces.text: "Deal," (subject) says, before (subject.he/she) can think better of it. The merchant's smile widens. The bottle is placed in (subject.his/her) hand...

pieces.label: Ask for a Clear Price
pieces.text: "I don't trade for riddles," (subject) says firmly. "Tell me exactly what you want, or no deal."...

pieces.label: Refuse the Trade
pieces.text: "No thank you," (subject) says. "I'd rather keep whatever it is I won't miss." The crowd murmurs approvingly...

pieces.label: Offer Food Instead
pieces.text: "I can't pay in riddles," (subject) says. "But I can give you a good meal. How about that?" (subject.He/She) fetches some food from the stores...
The bottle holds rare seeds, but (subject) forgets (subject.his/her) favourite song.
The merchant takes an old broken comb, which (subject) only later misses terribly.
The merchant admits it's ordinary perfume and names a fair price.
The merchant refuses to explain and withdraws the offer.
The merchant bows and leaves without complaint.
(subject) dreams nightly of the bottle opening by itself.
The merchant eats well and maps every spring along the coast road.
The merchant refuses food: the bargain was never about hunger.
The bottle is the colour of a sunset.
The merchant's smile does not reach the merchant's eyes.
The crowd murmurs, and nobody knows what the price means.

pieces.label: The Empty Seat at the Feast
pieces.text: At a village feast, an extra place is set that no one remembers arranging, and its food slowly disappears.

pieces.label: Leave the Seat Undisturbed
pieces.text: (Subject) decides it's not (subject.his/her) place to clear someone else's seat, whoever they are. (subject.He/She) goes back to (subject.his/her) own food, trying not to stare...

pieces.label: Invite the Unseen Guest
pieces.text: (Subject) stands up, faces the empty seat, and says loudly, "Whoever you are, you're welcome at our fire. Eat, and be our guest."...

pieces.label: Watch the Plate
pieces.text: (Subject) moves to sit right across from the empty seat and fixes (subject.his/her) eyes on the leaf of food, determined not to blink...

pieces.label: Remove the Setting
pieces.text: "It's just a mistake," (subject) says, and clears the extra leaf and cup away, tipping the food into the shared pot...
The plate is empty by morning, and the next feast sets an extra place again.
(child), very small and very sticky, admits taking the food meant "for the spirits".
A warm breeze passes and every torch burns brighter.
A shy traveler steps out of the dark and takes the seat.
A fruit bat swoops down and steals a whole mango.
The food vanishes bite by bite while everyone watches.
The feast continues normally.
The next morning the leaf and cup sit folded on (subject)'s doorstep.
The extra place has a banana leaf and a cup of coconut milk.
Each time someone looks, there is a little less on the leaf.
Nobody remembers setting it.

pieces.label: The Forest's Borrowed Voice
pieces.text: While gathering wood, (subject) hears a loved one's voice calling (subject.his/her) name from deep in the forest.

pieces.label: Follow the Voice
pieces.text: (Subject) drops the firewood and plunges into the trees, calling (loved one)'s name, following the voice deeper and deeper into the green...

pieces.label: Call Back from the Path
pieces.text: (Subject) stays right where (subject.he/she) is, on the safe path, and cups (subject.his/her) hands around (subject.his/her) mouth. "(Loved one)? Is that you? What's wrong?"...

pieces.label: Bring a Companion
pieces.text: (Subject) runs back to fetch (loved_one), and the two of them creep into the forest together, listening hard...

pieces.label: Return Home
pieces.text: Something about this isn't right, and (subject) knows it. (subject.He/She) picks up (subject.his/her) firewood and walks back to the village as fast as (subject.he/she) can without running...
(subject) finds the loved one gathering herbs and returns relieved.
The voice leads to a ravine where (subject) falls and is hurt.
The voice answers in words the loved one has never spoken.
A long-tailed bird copies the call perfectly, very pleased with itself.
Both hear the voice, but each recognizes a different person.
The companion hears only wind moving through hollow trees.
The loved one is safe at home and never called.
A bundle of deep-forest herbs waits on the doorstep, tied with a strange knot.
The call has the same little lift at the end.
The voice comes from {among the strangler figs|behind a mossy trunk|somewhere just ahead}.
The forest goes very quiet between calls.

pieces.label: The Sea's Three Warnings
pieces.text: A dripping stranger walks out of the surf and warns (subject) the sea will give three signs before taking something back.

pieces.label: Watch the Tides
pieces.text: (Subject) sits up on the dunes for three days, watching the sea for signs. The other villagers think (subject.he/she) has lost (subject.his/her) mind...

pieces.label: Ask What Will Be Taken
pieces.text: "What do you mean, take something back?" (subject) demands. "Take what?"...

pieces.label: Ignore the Warning
pieces.text: "Thanks, I'll keep it in mind," (subject) says, and goes back to (subject.his/her) canoe. The stranger shrugs and wanders off down the beach...

pieces.label: Share the Warning
pieces.text: (Subject) runs to tell the fishers and the elders, and the warning spreads around the village faster than fire...
Three unusual waves arrive, but no disaster follows.
The careful watch saves the stored food from a huge wave.
"Only what was borrowed," says the stranger, and walks into the surf.
The stranger admits it's an old fisher's proverb, said for drama.
A wave carries the red-striped food basket out to sea.
Nothing happens, and the warning fades into memory.
The village prepares, and no boat is lost in the squall.
The warning becomes a rumor that frightens the children.
Seaweed is tangled in the stranger's hair.
The sea behind the stranger is calm and blue.
{A gull cries overhead|The surf hisses on the sand|A wave curls in, then pulls back}.

pieces.label: The Clay Figure in the Garden
pieces.text: A thumb-sized clay figure appears in (subject)'s garden and points a different direction every morning.

pieces.label: Follow Its Direction
pieces.text: Feeling more than a little silly, (subject) walks in a straight line in the direction the little figure is pointing, all the way to the far edge of the garden...

pieces.label: Leave It Alone
pieces.text: (Subject) decides the little figure isn't doing any harm, and goes about (subject.his/her) work, giving it a polite nod each morning...

pieces.label: Ask Who Made It
pieces.text: (Subject) carries the little figure around the village, holding it up and asking everyone, "Is this yours?"...

pieces.label: Place It in the Shrine
pieces.text: (Subject) decides the little figure deserves a proper home, and places it respectfully on the village shrine beside the offering bowls...
It points to a patch of rich soil that grows fat yams.
It points to a puddle where a clay-covered child admits hiding it.
The figure stays for weeks and becomes a familiar friend.
One morning it is gone, leaving only a round imprint.
(name2), a shy young potter, admits making it as a thank-you gift.
No one claims it, and the clay matches none on this part of the island.
The figure cracks in the heat and is lovingly repaired.
At dawn, a second figure stands beside it, offering a gift.
The soil around it is always freshly smoothed.
Today it points {toward the sea|at the yams|straight at (subject)|at the sky}.
The figure has a round body and one pointing arm.

pieces.label: The Night Visitor's Secret
pieces.text: A hooded stranger at the village boundary whispers to (subject) that a lost villager may still be alive.

pieces.label: Ask for Proof
pieces.text: "Prove it," (subject) says, voice shaking. "If you know so much, prove it."...

pieces.label: Gather a Search Party
pieces.text: (Subject) runs back into the village and wakes everyone. By dawn, a search party is setting off in the direction the stranger pointed...

pieces.label: Keep the Secret
pieces.text: (Subject) decides not to tell anyone. Not yet. Not until (subject.he/she) knows more. (subject.He/She) walks home with the secret burning inside (subject.him/her)...

pieces.label: Confront the Stranger
pieces.text: "Who are you?" (subject) demands, stepping closer. "Why tell me this? What do you want?"...
The stranger produces the lost one's bracelet but won't say where it came from.
The directions lead only to an abandoned camp.
The search finds the lost one alive, thin and sunburned, sheltering in a far valley.
The search finds only old footprints, and the fate stays uncertain.
(subject) carries the hope privately, unsure whether sharing it would be kind.
The secret weighs so heavily that (subject) confides in a friend.
The stranger admits only hearing a rumor from another settlement.
The figure steps back into the dark and cannot be found again.
The face is lost in the shadow of the hood.
The stranger smells of woodsmoke and river mud.
{An owl calls|The cane rustles|A dog whines} somewhere behind the fence.

pieces.label: The Old Woman's Three Questions
pieces.text: An old woman arrives at (subject)'s door in a storm and asks three questions about hunger, kindness and truth before asking for shelter.

pieces.label: Answer and Welcome Her
pieces.text: (Subject) thinks hard, then answers each question as honestly as (subject.he/she) can, and then steps aside. "Now come in, before you drown."...

pieces.label: Welcome Her Without Answering
pieces.text: "Never mind the questions," (subject) says, pulling her in out of the rain. "You're soaked through. Sit down and get warm."...

pieces.label: Answer but Refuse Shelter
pieces.text: (Subject) answers the three questions as best (subject.he/she) can, then shakes (subject.his/her) head. "I'm sorry. There's no room in here. You'll have to try the next hut."...

pieces.label: Turn Her Away Angrily
pieces.text: "I don't have time for riddles in the middle of a storm!" (subject) snaps. "Go away!" And (subject.he/she) slams the door...
She teaches a salt-and-smoke recipe that makes dried fish keep twice as long.
She leaves a note: "Your answers were wrong, but your door was right."
She laughs that warmth matters more than cleverness.
She says refusing a test can itself be a wise answer.
She accepts the answers and walks back into the rain.
Next morning the drying racks are overturned and grain is scattered.
A neighbor takes her in and loves her stories.
A week of dreams follows of knocking at a door no one opens.
Water streams from her grey braids.
Her walking stick is topped with a shell.
She asks each question {slowly|as if it matters very much|without blinking}.

pieces.label: The Broken Seal
pieces.text: A resin-sealed box tangled in the roots of an ancient tree says 'Do not open until the last light.'

pieces.label: Open It at Sunset
pieces.text: (Subject) waits until the very last sliver of sun slips beneath the sea, and then, with the whole village watching, breaks the seal...

pieces.label: Open It at Noon
pieces.text: "Last light, first light, who cares? Let's just open it," (subject) says impatiently, and cracks the seal in the full blaze of midday...

pieces.label: Wait Until Night
pieces.text: (Subject) decides 'last light' means the very last light of all, the end of the night. (subject.He/She) sits up with the box under the stars, waiting...

pieces.label: Leave It for Its Owner
pieces.text: (Subject) decides this box was hidden on purpose by someone, and isn't (subject.his/hers) to open. (subject.He/She) wraps it in cloth and leaves it in a safe place...
Inside is the record of an old expedition across the island.
A cloud of harmless glowing insects rises into the trees like stars.
Ordinary stones and a note asking why (subject) couldn't wait.
A bitter smell bursts out and makes (subject) ill for days.
Before dawn it opens easily, revealing a silver shell.
It stays locked, and the inscription fades.
A traveler claims the family keepsake and thanks the village.
Years pass without anyone coming for it.
The roots around it are as thick as arms.
The seal shows a sun sinking into a wave.
{The researchers argue|The children beg|The elders frown} about what "last light" means.

pieces.label: The Road of Returning Steps
pieces.text: Walking home at night, (subject) keeps arriving back at the same pale paperbark tree, whichever way (subject.he/she) turns.

pieces.label: Mark the Path
pieces.text: (Subject) pulls a strip of cloth from (subject.his/her) wrap, ties it to a branch beside the tree, and sets off again, tying strips as (subject.he/she) goes...

pieces.label: Walk with a Friend
pieces.text: (Subject) shouts for help toward the village, and after a while (friend) comes crashing through the undergrowth with a torch, grumbling...

pieces.label: Wait for Dawn
pieces.text: (Subject) gives up. (subject.He/She) sits down with (subject.his/her) back against the paperbark, wraps (subject.his/her) arms around (subject.his/her) knees, and waits for the sun...

pieces.label: Follow a Different Landmark
pieces.text: Forget the tree. (Subject) listens for the sound of running water and heads for it, hoping the stream will lead (subject.him/her) home...
The markers reveal a confusing loop of similar trails and two look-alike trees.
The marker keeps turning up on the wrong side of the tree.
Together they walk straight home; for once it's just a tree.
The friend gets lost too, and both wait out the night under the tree.
In daylight the path home is a three-minute walk.
At sunrise, (subject)'s own footprints come from a direction (subject.he/she) never walked.
(subject) follows the stream home safely.
(subject) blunders into thorny brush and comes home scratched.
The paperbark's white trunk looms up out of the dark.
The village fires are so close (subject) can smell the smoke.
{Left, right, straight|Ten steps, twenty, thirty}, and there it is again.

pieces.label: The Guest Who Left No Name
pieces.text: A silent visitor in a brown wrap spends a whole day carrying water for the village, then disappears before anyone learns their name.

pieces.label: Search for the Helper
pieces.text: (Subject) sets off down the road the visitor might have taken, asking every traveler and every neighboring village, "Have you seen someone in a plain brown wrap?"...

pieces.label: Leave a Gift at the Well
pieces.text: In case the helper comes back, (subject) leaves a basket of food and a good woven mat beside the well, with a note of thanks...

pieces.label: Tell the Story
pieces.text: That evening by the fire, (subject) tells everyone the whole story of the silent helper, from the first jar of water to the last...

pieces.label: Inspect the Work
pieces.text: (Subject) walks the whole route the visitor took, from the spring to the cooking huts, looking at everything carefully...
A neighboring village recognizes the helper and sends sweet potatoes and thanks.
No one matching the description is found anywhere.
The gift vanishes overnight and a perfect new well rope appears.
(child) returns the gift, thinking someone lost it.
The village starts a tradition of thanking unknown helpers with secret kindnesses.
Some villagers argue the visitor was just a shy traveler.
A clever bamboo channel now carries water to the cooking huts.
The repairs are sound but would have taken a week, not a day.
Jar after jar, as if it were nothing.
The visitor never says a single word.
{The cooks are delighted|The gardens are soaked|Every jar is full} by evening.

pieces.label: The Promise Beneath the Tree
pieces.text: Under an old banyan, a soft-spoken stranger offers (subject) one wish that must never be spoken aloud.

pieces.label: Wish for Abundance
pieces.text: (Subject) closes (subject.his/her) eyes and wishes, very hard, that the village will never go hungry. When (subject.he/she) opens them, the stranger is gone...

pieces.label: Wish for Knowledge
pieces.text: (Subject) closes (subject.his/her) eyes and wishes to understand things, to know how the world works. When (subject.he/she) opens them, the stranger is gone...

pieces.label: Wish for Someone's Return
pieces.text: (Subject) closes (subject.his/her) eyes and wishes, with all (subject.his/her) heart, that someone (subject.he/she) has lost would come home. When (subject.he/she) opens them, the stranger is gone...

pieces.label: Refuse the Wish
pieces.text: (Subject) shakes (subject.his/her) head. "No, thank you. I don't think I want a wish I can't talk about."...
A huge school of fish sweeps into the lagoon.
The harvest is ordinary, and (subject) wonders whether the wish did anything.
(subject) dreams of a clever new way to weave nets.
Some questions stay unanswered, even after a wish.
A long-absent traveler unexpectedly returns.
The missing person does not return, and (subject) learns to live with not knowing.
The stranger says (subject) already knows what matters.
The stranger leaves a heart-shaped black seed and no explanation.
The banyan's roots hang like curtains.
The stranger's voice is almost drowned by the leaves.
{Just think it|Never say it|Only once}, the stranger says.

pieces.label: The Boatman Who Asked for a Memory
pieces.text: At a misty crossing, a boatman in a palm hat offers (subject) passage in exchange for the memory of one happy day.

pieces.label: Pay the Price
pieces.text: (Subject) thinks about it for a long time. Then (subject.he/she) nods, steps into the boat, and chooses a memory: a festival, long ago, when (subject.he/she) was very small...

pieces.label: Offer Food Instead
pieces.text: "I'm not giving up my memories," (subject) says firmly. "But I've got food. A whole basket of it. Will that do?"...

pieces.label: Ask Where the Boat Goes
pieces.text: "Wait. Where exactly does your boat go?" (subject) asks, eyeing the grey water...

pieces.label: Turn Back
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that a boatman who wants memories is not a boatman (subject.he/she) wants to ride with. (subject.He/She) turns and walks back the way (subject.he/she) came...
(subject) is carried across but can no longer recall a childhood festival.
The boatman accepts the story instead: memories should be shared, not stolen.
The boatman takes the whole basket of food and rows (subject) across.
The boatman refuses and points (subject) to a hidden bridge.
The boatman points to a shore that vanishes as the mist clears.
He's an ordinary ferryman who likes to joke with newcomers.
(subject) returns safely, the crossing unexplained.
The mist lifts to reveal there was never a river there at all.
The water around the boat does not ripple.
The boatman's face is hidden beneath a wide palm hat.
{A heron watches|The mist curls|Something splashes far off} as (subject) decides.

pieces.label: The Old Shrine's Strange Guest
pieces.text: At the quiet memorial, (subject) finds an unfamiliar elder among the flowers, speaking softly to people no one else can see.

pieces.label: Sit Beside the Elder
pieces.text: (Subject) quietly sits down in the flowers beside the old one, not wanting to interrupt...

pieces.label: Ask Who Is Being Addressed
pieces.text: "Excuse me," (subject) says softly. "I'm sorry to interrupt. But who are you talking to?"...

pieces.label: Offer Flowers
pieces.text: (Subject) holds out the bundle of flowers (subject.he/she) brought. "For whoever you're speaking with," (subject.he/she) says...

pieces.label: Invite the Elder Home
pieces.text: "You shouldn't be out here on your own," (subject) says. "Come back to the village with me. There's food, and a fire, and people."...
The elder speaks movingly about remembering the dead without forgetting the living.
The elder says nothing, but the silence feels companionable.
The elder names ancestors whose stories have nearly been forgotten.
The elder admits talking to lost loved ones as a way of coping.
The elder adds the flowers to the memorial, saying "they thank you".
The elder vanishes, and the flowers are found arranged in a circle.
The elder joins the village and tends the memorial.
The elder declines: the journey is nearly finished.
The memorial is all stones and blossoms.
The elder nods, as if listening to an answer.
{The wind moves through the stones|A petal falls|A bird lands on the nearest stone}.

pieces.label: The Wishing Vessel
pieces.text: A painted vessel found in the collapsed hut of a long-forgotten healer bears the words 'Ask once, and listen twice.'

pieces.label: Ask for Food
pieces.text: "Food," (subject) whispers into the vessel, feeling silly. "For the village." Then (subject.he/she) listens, once, twice...

pieces.label: Ask for a Lost Answer
pieces.text: (Subject) thinks of something (subject.he/she) has forgotten: (subject.his/her) grandmother's recipe for honeyed yams, lost when she died. (subject.He/She) whispers the question into the vessel, and listens...

pieces.label: Ask for a Loved One
pieces.text: (Subject) holds the vessel close and whispers the name of someone (subject.he/she) misses terribly, someone who went away long ago. Then (subject.he/she) listens...

pieces.label: Ask for Nothing
pieces.text: (Subject) decides (subject.he/she) has everything (subject.he/she) needs. (subject.He/She) holds the vessel up and says, "Nothing, thank you. I don't need anything."...
The vessel gives a handful of seeds that grow into a healthy crop.
The vessel stays empty, but (name2), a neighbor, shares a generous meal.
A lost family recipe comes back to (subject) in the night.
The vessel only echoes the question back.
A traveler arrives with news of someone long absent.
The vessel grows warm, but the person does not return.
A faint sound of distant laughter fades from the vessel.
Nothing happens, and it becomes a jar for dried beans.
The vessel is painted with blue waves and a single eye.
Something inside settles, like sand.
{Ask once|Listen twice}, the faded paint says.

pieces.label: The Hollow Tree's Visitor
pieces.text: A child insists a tall, silver-haired person steps out of a hollow fig tree after dark, though the adults who wait see nothing.

pieces.label: Believe the Child and Listen
pieces.text: (Subject) kneels down so (subject.he/she) is eye to eye with (child). "I believe you," (subject) says. "Tell me all about it."...

pieces.label: Wait Beside the Tree
pieces.text: (Subject) sends (child) home to bed, then settles down in the long grass beside the hollow fig, alone, to keep watch through the night...

pieces.label: Leave a Lantern
pieces.text: Just in case, (subject) leaves a small lit lantern at the foot of the fig tree, so the visitor, if there is one, won't stumble in the dark...

pieces.label: Ask the Child to Draw the Visitor
pieces.text: (Subject) hands (child) a stick of charcoal and a flat piece of bark. "Can you draw them for me? Exactly how they look?"...
The child's story becomes a village song about a kind moonlight stranger.
The child admits being frightened and needs someone to walk (child.him/her) past the tree.
(subject) hears soft footsteps climbing inside the trunk, but sees no one.
A huge, disapproving owl ducks out of the hollow.
By morning, the lantern has been moved to a high, safe branch.
The lantern stays put and burns out; the child says the visitor sees in the dark.
The drawing matches an ancestor on an old, worn carving.
The drawing looks like a white-haired traveler the child saw that afternoon.
The fig is so big the visitor has to duck to come out.
(Child) stamps (child.his/her) foot: it's real!
{An owl hoots|The leaves rustle|Something creaks inside the trunk}.

pieces.label: The Sea Chest of Two Brothers
pieces.text: A chest drifts ashore holding one fine tool and two sealed letters from two brothers who each claimed it.

pieces.label: Read Both Letters
pieces.text: (Subject) breaks both seals and reads the letters aloud, one after the other, while the village listens in silence...

pieces.label: Find the Brothers
pieces.text: (Subject) sends word up and down the coast with every trader and traveler: a chest has been found, with letters from two brothers...

pieces.label: Use the Tool Temporarily
pieces.text: "It's a shame to let a tool like that sit idle," (subject) says. "We'll borrow it, look after it, and give it back if anyone comes."...

pieces.label: Keep the Chest Sealed
pieces.text: (Subject) closes the lid firmly, ties the tarred rope back around it, and puts it away. "It's not ours. It's not even ours to read."...
The letters reveal the brothers agreed to share it: "remember we are brothers".
The letters contradict each other, and the dispute stays unresolved.
One grieving brother arrives and reclaims the chest.
Both brothers were lost at sea in a storm.
The tool repairs the fishing gear in half the time, and (subject) becomes a better builder.
The tool breaks under strain, and the village frets over how to explain it.
A traveler recognizes the family mark and carries it home.
The chest stays unclaimed, a reminder of unfinished promises.
The chest is bound in tarred rope.
The note is written in two hands, each pressing harder than the last.
The adze's bronze blade gleams.

pieces.label: The Visitor at the Cradle
pieces.text: Just after a baby is born, a quiet grey-wrapped stranger appears under the family's eaves, and only (subject) can see them.

pieces.label: Invite the Stranger to Speak
