pieces.text: (Subject) steps out into the shade, heart thumping, and says softly, "You're welcome here. Is there something you'd like to say?"...

pieces.label: Ask What the Visitor Wants
pieces.text: (Subject) walks over to the grey figure and asks, as politely as (subject.he/she) can, "Excuse me. What do you want with our baby?"...

pieces.label: Keep Watch Together
pieces.text: (Subject) and the rest of the family take turns staying up through the night beside the cradle, keeping watch for the grey stranger...

pieces.label: Leave a Small Gift
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that whoever the visitor is, they're welcome. (subject.He/She) leaves a small bowl of fruit and a woven flower in the shade under the eaves...
The visitor speaks a blessing like water over stones, and is gone by dawn.
The figure turns out to be (friend), a shy old neighbor, checking on the family.
The stranger asks only that the child be taught kindness and curiosity.
The visitor whispers a name no one in the household recognizes.
No one appears, and the family enjoys a peaceful night.
(friend), (subject)'s cousin, hears pacing footsteps all night, but no one is there.
The gift stays untouched, but the gesture comforts the family.
The gift is replaced by a white shell that fits the baby's tiny palm.
The stranger stands very still in the shade of the eaves.
The baby stops crying the moment the stranger appears.
{Nobody else can see anyone there|The family look where (subject) points and see nothing}.

pieces.label: The Box of Winter in Summer
pieces.text: A traveler sells (subject) a small wooden box that stays icy cold even under the tropical sun.

pieces.label: Open the Box
pieces.text: (Subject) wedges a thumbnail under the lid and flips it open...

pieces.label: Use It to Cool Food
pieces.text: (Subject) has an idea. (subject.He/She) puts a portion of the morning's fish inside the cold box and closes the lid, to see whether it'll keep...

pieces.label: Return It to the Seller
pieces.text: (Subject) decides (subject.he/she) doesn't want a box that makes (subject.his/her) fingers ache, and goes looking for the trader to give it back...

pieces.label: Leave It in the Sun
pieces.text: (Subject) sets the box on a flat rock in the full blazing sun and waits to see what happens...
A rush of cold air spoils the fruit drying nearby.
Inside is a mineral that stays cool in the shade, fascinating the scholars.
The box keeps a small portion of fish fresh until evening.
The cold fades before anyone can test it.
The trader cheerfully refunds the trade: the box is from the cold southern mountains.
No one remembers seeing any trader enter the village.
The box warms in the sun and becomes ordinary.
Frost feathers spread across the lid at midday, then melt.
Beads of water gather on its sides in the heat.
(subject)'s fingers ache with cold.
{"Very special," the trader winks|The trader is gone before (subject) can ask why}.

pieces.label: The Voice at the Old Boundary
pieces.text: At the old lichen-crusted boundary stones, a voice tells (subject), "You are not the first to build a home here."

pieces.label: Ask About Those Before
pieces.text: (Subject) swallows hard. "Who was here before us?" (subject.he/she) asks the stones. "Tell me."...

pieces.label: Invite the Speaker to Appear
pieces.text: "Whoever you are," (subject) says, "please, show yourself. I won't hurt you."...

pieces.label: Bring an Elder
pieces.text: (Subject) runs back to fetch (friend), who comes hobbling out to the boundary stones with a walking stick and a lantern...

pieces.label: Leave Respectfully
pieces.text: (Subject) bows to the stones, as if to an elder, and says, "Thank you for telling me." Then (subject.he/she) walks away...
The voice describes a settlement whose ruins are found under the jungle.
The voice falls silent, and the stones reveal nothing.
A robed figure steps into the moonlight, bows without a name, and is gone.
A resting traveler pops up from behind the stones, apologizing.
(friend) finds a carved symbol meaning "home" beneath the lichen.
(friend) hears nothing but shares stories of earlier generations.
(subject) returns home full of new questions about the island's past.
A warm breeze smelling of cooking fires follows (subject) home.
The stones lean together like old friends.
Grey lichen crusts every surface.
The voice comes from somewhere between the stones.

pieces.label: The Three Knocks at Midnight
pieces.text: Three slow knocks at midnight bring (subject) to the door, where a soaked traveler holds out an unopened parcel.

pieces.label: Invite the Traveler In
pieces.text: (Subject) pulls the door open. "Come in, come in, before you drown!" The traveler stumbles gratefully inside and huddles by the embers...

pieces.label: Accept Only the Parcel
pieces.text: (Subject) opens the door just a crack and reaches out a hand. "I'll take that," (subject.he/she) says. The traveler hands it over without a word, and (subject) shuts the door...

pieces.label: Ask the Traveler to Wait
pieces.text: "Just a moment," (subject) calls through the door. "Wait there, please." (subject.He/She) hurries next door to wake (friend), so (subject.he/she) won't be alone...

pieces.label: Refuse to Open the Door
pieces.text: Nobody good knocks at midnight, (subject) decides. (subject.He/She) stays very still behind the door, holding (subject.his/her) breath, and doesn't answer...
The traveler warms by the fire and joins the village the next day.
The guest leaves before sunrise, leaving a parcel of dried fish.
The parcel holds a map to an abandoned orchard full of fruit.
The parcel holds a split mask and a shaky note asking forgiveness.
The traveler waits patiently and turns out to be a lost wanderer.
The traveler is gone, but the dry parcel remains on the step.
The knocking stops, and the village sleeps undisturbed.
At dawn, footprints lead from the door to the shore, and none come back.
Knock. Knock. Knock. Slow and even.
Rain drips from the traveler's hood.
The parcel is wrapped in waxed leaves and tied with string.

pieces.label: The Silent Market Stall
pieces.text: A driftwood market stall appears overnight at the village edge, laid with bottles, boxes and carved figures, and no merchant in sight.

pieces.label: Trade for a Bottle
pieces.text: (Subject) leaves a handful of shells on the red cloth, as fair payment, and picks up one of the little bottles...

pieces.label: Choose a Wooden Box
pieces.text: (Subject) leaves a few shells and picks up one of the little carved boxes. It's light. Something inside shifts as (subject.he/she) turns it...

pieces.label: Wait for the Merchant
pieces.text: (Subject) sits down beside the stall to wait. Surely the merchant will be back soon...

pieces.label: Leave the Goods Untouched
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that goods without an owner aren't goods (subject.he/she) wants to take. (subject.He/She) tells the others to leave the stall alone...
The bottle holds a fragrant oil that soothes cracked skin.
The liquid turns cloudy, and (subject) sets it aside rather than risk it.
The box holds a bundle of preserved herbs.
The box holds a note in (subject)'s own handwriting: "You already know."
An elderly traveler returns, having set up before sunrise.
The stall vanishes while (subject) is fetching water.
The stall is gone by evening, leaving no trace.
A small carved bird remains on the ground, as if left on purpose.
The wares lie on a red cloth.
A small bell hangs from the roof, without a clapper.
{Nobody wants to touch anything first|The crowd whispers|A child reaches out and is pulled back}.

pieces.label: The Person in the Rain
pieces.text: In a heavy downpour, (subject) sees a stranger beyond the village lights, standing completely dry in the rain.

pieces.label: Offer Shelter
pieces.text: (Subject) cups (subject.his/her) hands around (subject.his/her) mouth and shouts over the rain, "Come in out of that! There's room by our fire!"...

pieces.label: Ask Why They Are Waiting
pieces.text: (Subject) splashes closer, rain streaming down (subject.his/her) face. "Who are you waiting for out here?"...

pieces.label: Approach With a Lantern
pieces.text: (Subject) fetches a covered lantern from the nearest hut and walks out toward the still figure, holding the light high...

pieces.label: Leave Them Alone
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that whoever it is, they clearly want to be left alone. (subject.He/She) ducks inside and pulls the door shut...
The stranger's cloak of tightly woven leaves sheds the rain like oil.
The figure follows (subject) to the door, then vanishes.
The stranger is waiting for someone who has not yet been born.
The stranger is looking for a lost companion, found safe before dawn.
The lantern reveals an old stone statue half hidden by vines.
The figure retreats into the rain, leaving no tracks.
The figure is gone when the rain ends.
A bundle of perfectly dry firewood appears by (subject)'s home.
The rain bounces off the paths.
The stranger stands dry and still, hands folded.
{Not a drop touches the stranger|The village lights flicker|Thunder rolls far off}.

pieces.label: The Gourd That Would Not Empty
pieces.text: A wandering elder gives (subject) a drinking gourd that "will always hold exactly what is needed, never what is wanted."

pieces.label: Use It for Water
pieces.text: That afternoon, a thirsty traveler stops at the village, and (subject) tips the gourd to pour (subject.him/her) a drink...

pieces.label: Use It for Soup
pieces.text: The cooks are short on broth for supper. (Subject) has an idea, and tips the gourd over the pot...

pieces.label: Study the Gourd
pieces.text: (Subject) brings the gourd to the researchers and builders, who turn it over and over, tapping, sniffing, holding it up to the light...

pieces.label: Return It to the Elder
pieces.text: A gift like this is too much, (subject) decides. (subject.He/She) hurries down the path after the wandering elder...
The gourd pours exactly enough water for a thirsty traveler.
The gourd is bone dry when (subject) tries to pour a second cup for (subject.himself/herself).
The gourd fills the soup pot with rich broth.
The broth spills before anyone can eat it.
The builders find a clever hidden double chamber.
No seam or chamber can be found.
The elder leaves the gourd on a stone for the next person in need.
The elder has already gone, and no one knows where.
The gourd makes no sound when shaken.
Its stopper is carved wood, worn smooth.
"Exactly what is needed," the elder says. {"Never what is wanted."|"Remember that."}

pieces.label: The Old Beggar's Last Request
pieces.text: An exhausted elderly beggar arrives at the village boundary, asking only to sit beneath the flame tree until morning.

pieces.label: Offer a Bed and Food
pieces.text: "A tree is no place to sleep," (subject) says gently. "Come inside. There's a mat and a fire and a bowl of something hot." (subject.He/She) helps the old one to (subject.his/her) hut...

pieces.label: Sit and Listen
pieces.text: (Subject) helps the old one to the flame tree, brings a blanket, and sits down beside (subject.him/her) on the carpet of red blossoms. "Tell me about yourself," (subject.he/she) says...

pieces.label: Ask Someone Else to Help
pieces.text: (Subject) doesn't have room in (subject.his/her) hut, so (subject.he/she) runs to knock on the neighbors' doors. "There's an old traveler at the boundary. Can anyone help?"...

pieces.label: Send the Beggar Away
pieces.text: "We can't take in every stranger who comes along," (subject) says, not unkindly, but firmly. "You'll have to move on." The beggar nods slowly and shuffles away into the dusk...
The guest recovers and shares a long-forgotten method of storing grain.
The guest dies peacefully in the night and is buried with respect beneath the flame tree.
The stranger tells of a family left behind on another shore.
"You listened when I had nothing to give," says the stranger, leaving a wooden fish charm.
(name2), a neighbor, welcomes the guest, and the village shares the care.
No one acts quickly, and the beggar is gone before dawn.
Insects spoil the stored grain overnight; some call it a curse.
The beggar finds shelter elsewhere, and no punishment follows but shame.
The flame tree's red blossoms carpet the path.
The beggar's legs tremble, dusty from the road.
The voice is thin as paper.

pieces.label: The Mist That Called a Name
pieces.text: A thick dawn mist swallows the village, and from somewhere inside it (subject) hears the voice of a villager who went missing long ago, calling (subject.his/her) name. The elders say the lost can walk in a sea mist like this one.

pieces.label: Follow the Voice
pieces.text: (Subject) takes one careful step into the white, then another. The village disappears behind (subject.him/her) as if it had never been there. The voice keeps calling, always a little ahead, always just out of sight, leading (subject.him/her) past the last hut and toward the edge of the trees...

pieces.label: Call for Help
pieces.text: "Everyone! Wake up! There's someone out there!" (Subject) shouts, banging a cooking pot with a spoon until bleary-eyed villagers stumble out of their huts. Together they link arms and follow the sound into the mist...

pieces.label: Speak to the Mist
pieces.text: (Subject) swallows hard and answers. "I hear you," (subject.he/she) says into the white. "If it's really you... tell me something only you would know." There is a long pause. Then the voice answers.

pieces.label: Wait for the Mist to Clear
pieces.text: (Subject) presses (subject.his/her) back against the hut wall, shuts (subject.his/her) eyes, and waits. The voice calls a few more times. Then it stops. Slowly, the sun climbs and the mist begins to pull back from the village like a tide going out...
On a flat stone at the edge of the trees, (subject) finds a beaded bracelet the missing villager once wore, damp with dew. The family hangs it above their door.
(Subject) steps into the white and is never seen again. Only (subject.his/her) sandals are found, side by side at the edge of the trees.
The voice belongs to an injured traveler under the old fig tree, who has been calling every name (subject.he/she) knows. The villagers carry (subject.him/her) to the fire.
The voice stops the moment the others arrive. The search finds only wet grass and a startled pig.
The voice recalls the day the two of them stole honey as children, a story no one else knows. (Subject) weeps, and the mist lifts.
It is only an echo from a rocky hollow, which repeats everything in a softer, older voice. Almost exactly like the one from this morning.
The mist pulls back, the chickens demand breakfast, and the day goes on as if nothing happened.
Small bare footprints lead up to the well and simply stop. They match no one in the village.
The mist smells of wet stone and old rain.
Somewhere a rooster crows, then thinks better of it.
The voice is warm and patient, exactly as (subject) remembers it.
Dew drips from the thatch like slow rain.

pieces.label: The Crown of Driftwood
pieces.text: Little (subject) finds a crown of driftwood and shells on the beach, and a traveler warns that it once belonged to a ruler of the sea.

pieces.label: Let the Child Wear It
pieces.text: "It's just a crown," one of (subject)'s parents says, and plonks it onto (subject)'s head, where it promptly slides down over one ear. (Subject) straightens it with great dignity and announces that (subject.he/she) is now in charge...

pieces.label: Ask for the Crown's History
pieces.text: The villagers gather around the fire, and (subject) sits right at the front, crown in (subject.his/her) lap. "Tell us," (subject.he/she) says. "Who was the ruler of the sea?"...

pieces.label: Return It to the Sea
pieces.text: "If it belongs to the sea," (subject) says solemnly, "then the sea should have it back." The whole village follows (subject.him/her) down to the shore, where (subject.he/she) wades out to (subject.his/her) knees and lets a wave carry the crown away...

pieces.label: Preserve It
pieces.text: The villagers decide something this unusual should be kept safe. (Subject) carries the crown to the driest hut in the village, and the craftspeople set it carefully on a high shelf, out of reach of goats and children (mostly children)...
(Subject) leads a royal procession of three children, two dogs and a very confused chicken around the village.
(Subject) dreams of green halls beneath the waves and wakes demanding to learn to swim, today.
The traveler tells of a proud sea ruler who lost everything and wove a new crown from what was left.
An elder laughs: it is last year's harvest festival decoration, which blew away. The traveler leaves early, red-faced.
A wave carries the crown away and leaves a pearly spiral shell in its place.
The crown washes back to the same spot three mornings running, so (subject) is allowed to keep it.
The weavers marvel at the craftsmanship, and the crown becomes a treasured example of island work.
The crown dries out and crumbles; (subject) threads the loose shells into a necklace instead.
The crown smells powerfully of the tide.
It keeps sliding down over (subject)'s ear.
The chicken has opinions about being a royal subject.
The traveler's smile is hard to read.

pieces.label: The Sleeper Beneath the Hill
pieces.text: A traveler tells (subject) that an ancient sleeper rests beneath the village hill, and that night the ground seems to breathe.

pieces.label: Listen at the Hill
pieces.text: (Subject) kneels in the warm grass, takes a deep breath, and presses (subject.his/her) ear flat against the ground. At first there is nothing. Then, very faintly...

pieces.label: Dig a Small Test Pit
pieces.text: "If something's down there, there's only one way to find out," (subject) says, and the next morning (subject.he/she) and a couple of curious friends start digging a small pit into the side of the hill. The soil is soft and warm and comes away easily. A little too easily...

pieces.label: Leave the Hill Untouched
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that whatever is under the hill, it has been there a lot longer than (subject.he/she) has, and does not need (subject.his/her) help. (subject.He/she) goes back to bed and pulls the blanket over (subject.his/her) head...

pieces.label: Tell the Tale at the Fire
pieces.text: That evening, (subject) gathers everyone around the fire and repeats the traveler's story, adding a few dramatic pauses and one or two details the traveler definitely did not say...
The rumble is an underground stream, which the researchers trace beneath the hill.
A long, slow sigh rises through the stones. (Subject) walks around the hill from then on.
The pit uncovers a layer of fine blue clay that fires hard as stone.
The side of the pit collapses on (subject)'s legs; friends dig (subject.him/her) out and carry (subject.him/her) to the healers.
After three days of rain, the rumbling stops and the hill is just a hill again.
One warm patch of grass never cools, and the elders take their naps there.
The musicians turn the tale into a favorite song about a patient, snoring sleeper.
Half the village is delighted and half is terrified; several families move their sleeping mats.
The single palm on the hilltop leans as if listening.
The grass is warm, like the flank of a sleeping animal.
The traveler does not laugh.
Somewhere below, something seems to shift.

pieces.label: The Flower That Bloomed for the Dead
pieces.text: Overnight, a flower blooms beside the memorial stone in the exact colour a lost villager always wore.

pieces.label: Tend the Flower
pieces.text: (Subject) fetches a little water in (subject.his/her) cupped hands and pours it gently around the roots. Then (subject.he/she) pulls the weeds away, sets a ring of small stones around it to keep the goats off, and promises to come back tomorrow...

pieces.label: Ask a Botanist
pieces.text: (Subject) fetches (botanist), the village's plant expert, who arrives grumbling about being woken so early, kneels by the flower, and immediately stops grumbling...

pieces.label: Leave an Offering
pieces.text: (Subject) goes home, wraps a little cake of sweet mashed fruit in a leaf, the lost villager's favourite, and sets it gently beside the flower. "For you," (subject.he/she) whispers, feeling a little foolish and not caring...

pieces.label: Tell the Family
pieces.text: (Subject) goes straight to the lost villager's family and, as gently as (subject.he/she) can, tells them about the flower. They follow (subject.him/her) to the memorial in silence...
The flower lasts for weeks, and the family's grief softens as they water it each morning.
It fades, but its seeds ring the memorial with orange flowers the next season.
It is a dusk lily, rare and seldom seen; the researchers fill pages of notes.
The botanist has never seen anything like it, and never finds another.
The offering stays untouched all week, not even the ants go near it.
A tiny orange-tailed bird steals the cake in four trips, and (subject) laughs for the first time in days.
The family gathers and trades stories, laughing and crying until sunset.
One relative cannot bear it and walks away, but is later seen watering the flower alone at dawn.
Dew sits on the petals like tears.
The orange is exactly the right orange.
The memorial stone is warm in the morning sun.
Someone hums the lost villager's favourite song.

pieces.label: The Bargain of the Hidden Garden
pieces.text: A veiled stranger offers (subject) the way to a garden that grows food without tending, asking only that no one boast of finding it.

pieces.label: Accept and Keep Quiet
pieces.text: (Subject) nods, and the stranger leans close and whispers directions: past the split rock, down the fern gully, and left at the tree that looks like it is waving. (Subject) follows them, and finds...

pieces.label: Tell the Village
pieces.text: (Subject) thanks the stranger, then runs straight back to the village shouting about a magic garden full of food. Promise or no promise, this is too good to keep to (subject.himself/herself). Half the village grabs baskets and follows (subject.him/her) into the forest...

pieces.label: Ask Who Owns the Garden
pieces.text: "Wait," (subject) says. "If I take food from a garden, I'd like to know whose garden it is." The stranger tilts (subject.his/her) veiled head, as if no one has ever asked that before...

pieces.label: Decline the Offer
pieces.text: "Thank you," (subject) says carefully, "but I'll find my own food." The stranger bows (subject.his/her) veiled head...
The garden is real; (subject) quietly leaves baskets of greens on hungry neighbours' doorsteps.
It is ordinary wild plants and a lot of nettle, which (subject) discovers by sitting in it.
The whole village organizes a careful harvest of an enormous garden and holds a feast.
By the time everyone arrives, the garden has been trampled flat; the last bean pod hangs alone.
"It belongs to whoever cares for it," says the stranger, and (subject) spends the day weeding it.
The stranger lifts the veil: (elder), an elder who has tended the garden for years, testing who would ask.
The stranger leaves without complaint, and the village asks (subject) why on earth (subject.he/she) said no.
A green seed falls from (subject)'s pocket that night and sprouts by morning.
The veil shivers in every breeze.
The stranger's hands smell of crushed mint.
The tree that looks like it is waving is waving.
Bees hum somewhere just out of sight.

pieces.label: The Threshold Test
pieces.text: A stranger in worn sandals waits at (subject)'s door and will not step over the threshold until invited in by name.

pieces.label: Offer a Warm Welcome
pieces.text: "Well, come in then, traveler, come in, you're letting the mosquitoes in!" (Subject) says, and the stranger smiles and steps over the threshold as if crossing a river. (subject.He/she) sits by the fire, warms (subject.his/her) hands, and gratefully accepts a bowl of stew...

pieces.label: Ask for the Stranger's Name
pieces.text: "I'll gladly invite you," (subject) says, "but first, what's your name? I can't invite you by name if I don't know it." The stranger seems pleased by the question...

pieces.label: Offer Food Outside
pieces.text: (Subject) decides to be kind, but careful. (subject.He/she) does not say the words. Instead, (subject.he/she) brings a bowl of stew and a cup of water and sets them on the step outside the door...

pieces.label: Turn the Stranger Away
pieces.text: "I'm sorry," (subject) says firmly. "Not tonight." The stranger nods as though (subject.he/she) expected it, and turns to go...
The guest tells a story about a fisher who listened to the birds, and the method works.
The guest eats, snores, and is gone by dawn, leaving no footprints and a very clean bowl.
The stranger's name turns up carved on the oldest stone in the village.
It is an ordinary name and an ordinary custom from back home; the village laughs at (subject) for weeks.
The stranger eats on the step, bows and walks on, humming.
The stew is untouched, but a sunset-coloured shell sits on the doorstep.
Nothing happens at all, and (subject) wonders about the stranger for months.
"The third beam from the left," says the stranger. In the next storm, that beam splits.
The stranger's toes rest exactly at the edge of the threshold.
Mosquitoes drift in through the open door.
The cooking fire crackles as if listening.
The stranger's patience seems endless.

pieces.label: The Lost Page of the World
pieces.text: (Subject) finds a sealed bottle holding a page that describes a place on Isola that changes whenever it is visited.

pieces.label: Follow the Directions
pieces.text: (Subject) tucks the page into (subject.his/her) wrap and sets off: from the black rock, a hundred paces toward the morning sun, up the dry streambed, through a gap in the rocks that (subject.he/she) has somehow never noticed before...

pieces.label: Copy the Page
pieces.text: Worried the old page will fall apart, (subject) borrows a sheet of bark-paper and some ink from the researchers and sits down to copy every word, very carefully, letter by letter...

pieces.label: Show the Elders
pieces.text: (Subject) carries the bottle carefully to the elders' fire. The oldest of them takes out the page, holds it close to the flames, and reads it in silence...

pieces.label: Return It to the Bottle
pieces.text: Something about the page makes (subject) uneasy. (subject.He/she) rolls it up again, slides it back into the bottle, presses the wax down firmly, and takes the bottle home to a dry corner of (subject.his/her) hut...
The directions lead to a forgotten hilltop observatory with star charts carved in stone.
They lead to a familiar grove, which is quite different after dark.
(Subject)'s copy saves a map of the island's springs just before the old ink fades away.
Every copy (subject) makes comes out slightly different from the original.
An elder recognizes the handwriting of a traveler who wrote stories about impossible places.
The elders argue all night about whether it is history or fiction, and blame (subject).
The bottle goes to the research hut, where it sits waiting for someone clever enough.
The next morning the sealed bottle holds a new page describing (subject) holding the bottle.
The handwriting slopes uphill.
The wax seal is cracked with age.
The page smells of salt and old smoke.
A gull watches (subject) with great interest.

pieces.label: The Night of the Open Doors
pieces.text: At midnight every unlatched door in the village swings open at once, and villagers glimpse a cloaked figure walking between the huts.

pieces.label: Follow the Figure
pieces.text: (Subject) grabs a torch and creeps after the figure, keeping to the shadows. It does not look back. It walks to the old food store at the edge of the village, pauses at the door, and seems to look up at the roof...

pieces.label: Check the Wind
pieces.text: (Subject) is a sensible sort of person, and sensible people know that doors do not open by themselves without a reason. (subject.He/she) wets a finger, holds it up, and goes to wake the researchers...

pieces.label: Invite the Visitor to Speak
pieces.text: (Subject) steps out into the moonlight, takes a deep breath, and calls out: "Whoever you are, you are welcome here. If you have something to say, say it!" The figure stops...

pieces.label: Secure the Village
pieces.text: (Subject) does not care who or what is out there. (subject.He/she) runs from hut to hut, pulling doors shut, waking the builders and calling for rope and pegs. By the time the sky begins to grey, every door in the village has a fresh latch...
The figure leads (subject) to the old food store; (subject.he/she) saves the food just before the roof crashes in.
The figure walks behind a hut that backs onto bare rock, and is gone.
The researchers find a sudden change in the air before a storm, and the village is ready for it.
There is no wind at all; the smoke rises straight up into the still night.
A voice says "Close what you wish to keep," and the doors creak shut one by one.
It is (neighbour), a sleepwalking neighbour wearing a fishing net as a cloak, looking for (subject.his/her) own door.
New latches go on every door, and the story grows taller every time it is told.
Before dawn, only (subject)'s own door stands open, its new latch neatly undone.
The doors open together with one long sigh.
Every cooking fire leans the same way.
A dog whimpers and refuses to come out.
The figure never hurries.

pieces.label: The Hidden Companion
pieces.text: For days (subject) has been talking calmly and happily to a companion no one else can see.

pieces.label: Ask About the Companion
pieces.text: "Tell me about your friend," (friend) says. (Subject)'s face lights up, and (subject.he/she) glances at the empty air beside (subject.him/her) as if asking permission. Apparently permission is granted...

pieces.label: Listen Without Judgment
pieces.text: (Friend) decides not to argue. "All right," (subject.he/she) says simply. "I believe you." And (subject.he/she) listens as (subject) chatters on about everything the friend has said and done...

pieces.label: Invite the Companion to Join
pieces.text: That evening, (friend) sets an extra place at the family meal, with an empty seat, a bowl of stew and a cup of water. "For your friend," (subject.he/she) says. (Subject) beams...

pieces.label: Explore Other Explanations
pieces.text: (Friend) is worried. (subject.He/she) quietly asks (healer), one of the healers, to come and have a look at (subject), just to make sure (subject.he/she) is well...
(Subject) retells the companion's stories of the old island, and the village gathers every evening to listen.
The companion keeps (subject) from feeling lonely, so (friend) starts sitting with (subject.him/her) at every meal.
(Subject) is grateful to be believed, and talks about the friend less and less.
(Subject) describes the companion's face, and it matches a founder's portrait (subject.he/she) has never seen.
The family chats with the empty seat at supper, and it becomes a tradition.
A hungry traveler arrives and asks who the extra place was for. (Subject)'s friend says to let (subject.him/her) sit.
(healer) prescribes rest; the companion mostly visits when (subject) is very tired.
The healer finds nothing wrong, and the village chooses to respect (subject)'s friend.
A little food waits on a leaf beside (subject).
(Subject) laughs at something nobody else heard.
The empty air beside (subject) seems somehow attentive.
(Subject) says goodnight to two people instead of one.

pieces.label: The Box of the Last Word
pieces.text: In the old hut of a puzzle-maker who loved riddles, (subject) finds a box carved with tiny mouths that opens only for a word the speaker has never said before.

pieces.label: Invent a New Word
pieces.text: (Subject) thinks hard, screws up (subject.his/her) face, and says the most ridiculous word (subject.he/she) can come up with: "Flobbamunk!" There is a pause. Then...

pieces.label: Speak a Forgotten Language
pieces.text: (Subject) fetches (elder), the oldest elder in the village, who remembers a few words of an ancient tongue (subject.his/her) own grandmother used to speak. The elder leans close to the box and whispers one of them...

pieces.label: Break the Lock
pieces.text: "I've had enough of this," (subject) mutters, and fetches a heavy stone. (subject.He/she) brings it down hard on the lid of the box. Crack!...

pieces.label: Leave It Closed
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that a box which opens only for a word (subject.he/she) has never said is the kind of box best left alone for now. (subject.He/she) wraps it in a cloth and puts it on a high shelf in the research hut...
"Flobbamunk!" The box opens on a bundle of old seeds, which grow into a very odd crop.
The box clicks for every word but never opens; the village spends the evening shouting nonsense.
(elder)'s ancient word opens it, revealing pictured instructions for making carving tools.
The box whispers the old word back from deep inside, and (elder) asks to go home.
The box splinters and the fragile scroll inside is destroyed.
The box is empty except for one dead beetle, which was doing the rattling.
The box waits on the research hut shelf, and the village tries new words now and then.
A child's song about a turtle with three hats opens it at last.
The tiny carved mouths all seem to be listening.
Something inside rattles softly.
The lid has no hinge at all.
The click sounds like someone clearing their throat.

pieces.label: The Watcher on the Cliff
pieces.text: Every night a figure stands on the black cliff above the village holding a lantern that never moves, and every dawn both are gone.

pieces.label: Climb to the Cliff
pieces.text: (Subject) waits until the moon is high, then starts up the goat track toward the cliff top. The path is steep and crumbling, and the lantern above never flickers. The higher (subject.he/she) climbs, the colder the wind gets, until (subject.he/she) is pulling (subject.himself/herself) up the last stretch hand over hand...

pieces.label: Signal with a Torch
pieces.text: (Subject) lights a torch, walks out to the open beach where the figure can see (subject.him/her) clearly, and raises it high above (subject.his/her) head. (subject.He/she) waves it slowly: once, twice, three times...

pieces.label: Ask Who Keeps Watch
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that if anyone knows about the light, it will be the elders. (subject.He/she) sets out around the village with a basket of sweet buns as a bribe, asking everyone (subject.he/she) meets...

pieces.label: Leave a Lantern Below
pieces.text: (Subject) fills a lantern with oil, lights it, and sets it carefully at the foot of the cliff path, where anyone coming down would find it. Then (subject.he/she) goes home and lies awake, watching the two lights through the doorway...
At the top, (subject) finds a stocked lookout shelter for stranded travelers.
The ledge crumbles and (subject) falls; villagers lower a rope at dawn and carry (subject.him/her) to the healers.
The lantern blinks back three times, and late fishers steer by it ever after.
A cloud covers the moon, and the lantern is never seen again.
(elder) remembers a guardian who kept a storm lantern on the cliff for forty years.
(fisher), a shy fisher, admits to watching the sea from up there and is mortified.
The lantern below is replaced by a coil of rope no weaver can identify.
The lantern burns out untouched, and the cliff light returns every night.
The lantern never flickers, even in high wind.
The goat track is steep and crumbling.
The children refuse to go to bed.
The sea booms against the foot of the cliff.

pieces.label: The Beggar Who Returned as a King
pieces.text: An old beggar wearing a snake-shaped copper ring asks (subject) for bread, and days later a finely dressed stranger arrives wearing the very same ring.

pieces.label: Welcome the Beggar
pieces.text: (Subject) brings the beggar inside, sits (subject.him/her) by the fire and gives (subject.him/her) the best of the stew. The beggar eats every drop, thanks (subject) twice, and is gone by morning. Days later, a finely dressed stranger rides into the village on a cart, with two strong attendants walking beside it. On (subject.his/her) finger is a copper snake ring with a green stone eye. The stranger climbs down, looks around the staring crowd, and walks straight toward (subject)...

pieces.label: Offer Work and Shelter
pieces.text: "I can't spare much bread," (subject) says, "but I can give you a mat by the fire, if you'll help me with a few jobs." The beggar stays the night and is gone at dawn. Days later, a finely dressed stranger rides into the village on a cart, with two strong attendants walking beside it, wearing a copper snake ring with a green stone eye. The stranger catches sight of (subject) in the crowd and smiles in recognition...

pieces.label: Refuse the Beggar
pieces.text: "Sorry. Nothing to spare," (subject) says, and shuts the door. The beggar's slow footsteps shuffle away. Days later, a finely dressed stranger rides into the village on a cart, with two strong attendants walking beside it. On (subject.his/her) finger is a copper snake ring with a green stone eye, catching the light exactly the same way. The stranger climbs down, scans the faces in the crowd...

pieces.label: Ask About the Ring
pieces.text: "Where did you get a ring like that?" (subject) asks. The beggar only smiles, takes a heel of bread, and wanders off. Days later, a finely dressed stranger rides into the village on a cart, wearing the very same copper snake ring. (Subject) pushes to the front of the crowd. "Excuse me," (subject.he/she) says, pointing. "That ring. An old beggar came to my door wearing one exactly like it. Who are you?"...
"Kindness should be repaid with interest," says the stranger, unloading a cart of grain.
It was the stranger's old uncle, who returns in clean clothes with a carved bowl for (subject).
The beggar's clever tool binding spreads through the whole village.
The beggar slept like a stone and left at dawn; the stranger just raises a hand in thanks.
"Why did this village turn away someone hungry?" (Subject) has no answer.
The stranger never looks at (subject), and the memory sits uncomfortably for weeks.
It is a family ring; there are twenty cousins wearing them, and one likes to travel light.
"Some faces are easier to recognize than others," says the stranger, humming the beggar's tune.
The green stone eye catches the light.
The cart's wheels squeak on every turn.
Children follow the attendants, staring.
The stranger's hands are rough, like a worker's.

pieces.label: The Visitor's Final Footstep
pieces.text: A tall visitor who leaves no footprints tells (subject), "One day you will hear my final footstep," and walks silently away.

pieces.label: Follow the Visitor
pieces.text: (Subject) hurries after the tall figure, but no matter how fast (subject.he/she) walks, the visitor stays exactly the same distance ahead, gliding silently between the trees and leading (subject.him/her) deeper and deeper into the forest...

pieces.label: Ask for Meaning
pieces.text: "Wait!" (subject) calls. "What does that mean? What final footstep?" The visitor stops, and turns back slowly...

pieces.label: Tell the Village
pieces.text: (Subject) rushes home and tells everyone at the evening fire what happened, and what the visitor said. The villagers listen in silence, and then all start talking at once...

pieces.label: Forget the Encounter
pieces.text: (Subject) shakes (subject.his/her) head firmly. It was a strange person saying strange things, and that is all. (subject.He/she) goes home, eats (subject.his/her) supper and resolutely thinks about other things...
The visitor leads (subject) to a hollow log holding a bundle of fine old tools.
The visitor vanishes, and (subject) spends a frightened night lost a stone's throw from home.
"Listen when someone needs you." Villagers start coming to (subject) to talk.
The visitor is leaving Isola for good and wanted someone to know (subject.he/she) was here.
Half the village fears an omen and half stays up guessing the riddle.
(neighbour) recognizes old Pebble-Eyes, who says strange things to everyone.
Nothing happens, and (subject) genuinely forgets the whole thing.
Weeks later, one heavy footstep sounds outside an empty hut, and no other follows.
The mud on the path is smooth and unmarked.
The visitor's eyes are like wet river stones.
A bird stops singing as the visitor passes.
(Subject) checks the path for footprints again.

pieces.label: The Jar of Two Sunrises
pieces.text: (Subject) digs up a clay jar painted with two suns above a little boat, and although it was buried far inland, it smells of the sea. The elders say the sea came up to these fields long ago.

pieces.label: Open the Jar at Dawn
pieces.text: Two suns, (subject) reasons, must mean something about sunrise. So (subject.he/she) waits until dawn, sets the jar facing the first light, and as the sun breaks over the hills, lifts the lid...

pieces.label: Ask About the Painting
pieces.text: (Subject) carries the jar to the elders' fire and asks what the two suns and the little boat could mean. The elders pass it from hand to hand, squinting...

pieces.label: Carry It to the Shore
pieces.text: The jar smells of the sea, so (subject) decides it should see the sea. (subject.He/she) walks the half-day to the beach with the jar cradled in (subject.his/her) arms like a baby...

pieces.label: Keep It Sealed
pieces.text: (Subject) presses the lid firmly back on. Whatever is inside has waited this long; it can wait a bit longer. (subject.He/she) gives the jar to the elders, who place it with the village's collection of old things...
The jar is packed with perfectly preserved salted fish, shared out at a feast.
Inside is a map of an old coastal route to fishing grounds nobody knew.
(elder) says two suns in one boat means a parent and child sailing together.
(storyteller) spins an all-night tale involving a talking turtle and an argument with a volcano.
At the water's edge the jar grows warm, then cools, as if glad to be home.
A traveler on the beach recognizes it as a jar from (subject.his/her) faraway island.
The sealed jar becomes a treasured relic that the children tell stories about.
The jar cracks overnight and spills fine white beach sand across the floor.
The painted suns still glow orange.
Tiny shells are crusted on the clay.
The smell of the sea drifts across the dry field.
A gull circles overhead, far from the shore.

pieces.label: The Dreamer's Stranger
pieces.text: (Subject) dreams night after night of a stranger beneath a crooked guava tree who asks, "What did you leave unfinished?"

pieces.label: Visit the Tree
pieces.text: (Subject) walks out past the old fields, and there it is, exactly as in the dream: the same crooked trunk, the same heavy branches, the same patch of shade beneath. (subject.He/she) approaches slowly...

pieces.label: Answer the Question
pieces.text: That night, when the stranger asks the question again, (subject) does not wake up. (subject.He/she) sits down under the dream tree, and thinks. And thinks. And finally, (subject.he/she) knows...

pieces.label: Ask a Healer
pieces.text: (Subject) is worried that something might be wrong with (subject.him/her). (subject.He/she) goes to the healers' hut and describes the dream in every detail to (healer)...

pieces.label: Ignore the Dream
pieces.text: (Subject) decides it is just a silly dream, and (subject.he/she) is not going to let it ruin (subject.his/her) day. (subject.He/she) works extra hard, eats a large supper, and goes to bed determined to dream about something else...
An ordinary traveler is resting under the real tree, and is alarmed to have been dreamed of.
In the roots lies the knife (subject) lost two seasons ago, (subject.his/her) father's knife.
(Subject) knocks on the door of an old friend (subject.he/she) fell out with years ago.
(Subject) finishes the canoe (subject.he/she) abandoned years ago, and the village cheers.
(healer) explains how worry shapes dreams, and the stranger stops coming.
(Subject) knows details of a tree (subject.he/she) has never seen, and (healer) cannot explain it.
The dreams fade slowly until (subject) dreams of fishing instead.
The stranger smiles one last time and never returns.
The guava's fruit hangs heavy on one side.
The stranger's open hands rest on (subject.his/her) knees.
(Subject) yawns all through breakfast.
The question lingers long after waking.

pieces.label: The Old Man at the Storm Gate
pieces.text: In the middle of a howling storm, a bent old man with a lightning-carved walking stick asks to wait beneath the village's roof.

pieces.label: Invite Him In
pieces.text: "Come in, come in, quickly!" (Subject) dashes out into the rain, takes the old man's arm and hurries him under the communal roof, where the villagers make room for him by the fire...

pieces.label: Offer a Blanket Outside
pieces.text: (Subject) is not comfortable letting a stranger in, but cannot leave him out in the wind with nothing. (subject.He/she) runs out with a thick blanket and wraps it around the old man's shoulders...

pieces.label: Demand He Leave
pieces.text: "We've no room for strangers!" (subject) shouts over the wind. "Go on, find somewhere else!" The old man looks at (subject.him/her) for a long moment, then nods, and turns away into the rain...

pieces.label: Ask About the Stick
pieces.text: Before (subject) decides anything, (subject.his/her) curiosity gets the better of (subject.him/her). "That carving on your stick," (subject.he/she) shouts through the rain. "What is it?" The old man lifts the stick, and lightning flashes behind him as if on cue...
The old man climbs the ladder like a youngster and lashes the roof down before it is lost.
He leaves at dawn, and where he sat is a bundle of dried food he could never have carried.
He shelters under the fig tree, and the blanket comes back folded and perfectly dry.
Lightning splits the stump by the gate, and the old man is nowhere to be seen.
The moment he leaves, a gust tears the food store roof away and ruins the stores.
A trader later says he fixed the next village's roof and told them stories all night.
He carved the stick after a storm sank his canoe, the day he met his wife.
"It was there before I was born," he says, and the carving seems to flash with the lightning.
The palms thrash and howl.
His white hair blows straight back.
Thunder rolls right over the huts.
The fire leans away from the door.

pieces.label: The Stone Boat
pieces.text: (Subject) finds a tiny stone boat tangled in a fishing net, and when set on the water it floats.

pieces.label: Test the Boat
pieces.text: (Subject) brings the boat back to the village and the researchers get very excited. They float it in a bowl, then a bucket, then the stream, prodding it, weighing it and arguing loudly...

pieces.label: Keep It as a Charm
pieces.text: Bad luck or no bad luck, (subject) likes the little boat. (subject.He/she) threads a cord through a gap under its mast and wears it around (subject.his/her) neck...

pieces.label: Return It to the Sea
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that something which floats when it should not probably belongs where it came from. (subject.He/she) wades out to the end of the reef, kisses the little boat for luck, and sets it on the water...

pieces.label: Ask a Traveler
pieces.text: A trader from another island is staying in the village, so (subject) brings the little boat to show (subject.him/her). The trader takes one look and claps (subject.his/her) hands...
A hidden air chamber explains it, and the builders seal chambers into their canoes.
It glides upstream against the current, then sinks as if tugged from below.
(Subject) wears it on a cord and grows fond of boats and the shore.
The cord snaps on an ordinary day, and (subject) misses it more than expected.
It drifts steadily out to sea, the little paddler facing forward.
It washes back the next morning with a fresh arrow scratched on it, pointing out to sea.
A trader laughs: it is a children's toy from (subject.his/her) island, made of bubbly volcanic stone.
The trader says such boats once carried messages to those lost at sea.
The little stone paddler faces forward.
Someone mutters about bad luck.
It bobs as happily as driftwood.
The fish in the net seem to avoid it.

pieces.label: The Voice Behind the Curtain
pieces.text: In the noise of an evening gathering, (subject) hears a soft, sad voice speaking from behind a hanging curtain where nobody is standing.

pieces.label: Answer the Voice
pieces.text: (Subject) leans close to the curtain, keeping (subject.his/her) voice low so that no one will think (subject.he/she) has lost (subject.his/her) mind. "I'm listening," (subject.he/she) whispers. "What is it?"...

pieces.label: Search the Room
pieces.text: (Subject) is not having any of this. (subject.He/she) rips the curtain aside, throws the old mats around, taps the walls, and peers into every corner of the hut while the gathering carries on noisily behind (subject.him/her)...

pieces.label: Ask Others to Listen
pieces.text: (Subject) waves over two of (subject.his/her) friends and pulls them close to the curtain. "Shh. Listen," (subject.he/she) whispers. The three of them stand there, ears straining, while the gathering roars on around them...

pieces.label: Leave the Curtain Closed
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that whatever is behind the curtain, it can stay there. (subject.He/she) moves to the other side of the hut, sits down with (subject.his/her) friends, and joins loudly in the singing...
The voice warns of spoiling food, and (subject) finds a basket of rotting yams just in time.
The voice asks (subject) to remember a forgotten healer, whose name is spoken at the memorial again.
A child hiding behind the wall has been practising (subject.his/her) sad voice for an hour.
There is no gap, no passage, and nowhere anyone could hide.
Three friends hear the same words, but cannot agree whether it was an old woman or a boy.
No one hears anything, but the curtain sways in the still, hot air.
The singing drowns everything out, and the evening goes on happily.
The next morning the curtain is found folded on the floor, its knots still tied.
The voice is soft, polite and rather sad.
A single moth circles the corner.
Someone is attempting to sing, badly.
The curtain hangs perfectly still.

pieces.label: The Gift from the Unseen Fisher
pieces.text: For three mornings, a basket of fresh fish tied with red cord appears on (subject)'s doorstep, and no one sees who leaves it.

pieces.label: Share the Fish
pieces.text: Whoever the fish are from, there are far too many for one household. (Subject) loads the baskets onto (subject.his/her) hip and sets off to share them...

pieces.label: Keep Watch
pieces.text: (Subject) is determined to find out. That night, (subject.he/she) hides behind a woodpile across from (subject.his/her) own doorway, with a blanket and a great deal of stubbornness, and waits. Very late, as the stars are fading, there is movement on the path...

pieces.label: Leave a Thank-You Note
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that whoever is leaving the fish deserves to be thanked. (subject.He/she) scratches a careful message on a flat piece of bark ("Thank you for the fish. They are delicious. Who are you?") and leaves it on the step that night...

pieces.label: Follow the Trail
pieces.text: At first light, (subject) kneels by (subject.his/her) doorstep and examines the ground. There are footprints, faint ones, leading away toward the shore. (subject.He/she) follows them, step by step, down the path and onto the sand...
The baskets keep coming for a week, and the whole village eats like a chief's household.
The fish go to a struggling family, who weep and then invite half the street to supper.
(Subject) catches (fisher), a mortified shy fisher who wanted to say thank you.
A dripping shadow leaves the basket, turns toward (subject)'s hiding spot, and vanishes.
The last basket holds a shell carved with a fish chasing its tail.
The note vanishes and the baskets simply stop.
The trail leads to a fisher from down the coast, asleep in a boat hidden in the reeds.
The footprints stop in the middle of the dry sand, well above the tide.
The fish are still cold from the sea.
A single strand of red cord ties each basket.
The neighbours peer over, jealous.
There is a faint smell of salt on the step.

pieces.label: The Forest's Unclaimed Box
pieces.text: Deep in the forest, (subject) finds a box wrapped in fresh leaves on a stump, with a note: "For the one who is willing to ask."

pieces.label: Ask Who Left It
pieces.text: The note says to ask, so (subject) asks. "Hello?" (subject.he/she) calls into the trees, feeling foolish. "Who left this? Who is it for?" (subject.His/her) voice echoes among the trunks...

pieces.label: Open It
pieces.text: (Subject) peels away the wet leaves. The box underneath is plain dark wood, with a simple latch. (subject.He/she) takes a breath and lifts the lid...

pieces.label: Take It to the Village
pieces.text: (Subject) tucks the box under (subject.his/her) arm, leaves and all, and carries it back to the village to let someone wiser deal with it...

pieces.label: Leave It Untouched
pieces.text: (Subject) decides this gift is meant for someone else. (subject.He/she) leaves the box exactly where it is, on its stump in its wet green leaves, and walks home...
A traveler steps out: the box is for a missing friend, and (subject) helps find the friend's old camp.
No one answers, but slow footsteps crunch away through the leaves.
Inside are labelled seeds and a drawing of a garden, which the farmers plant.
Inside are a broken amulet and a list of names nobody knows.
(crafter) cracks its puzzle lock and teaches the whole village how it works.
The box seals itself shut in the village and opens only back on the stump.
The box is gone the next day, with no sign it was ever there.
A second note on (subject)'s door says, "You asked by leaving."
The leaves are still wet with dew.
The thorn pinning the note is fresh.
The forest is very quiet.
Something watches from between the trunks.

pieces.label: The Guest Who Ate No Food
pieces.text: A traveler invited to (subject)'s family supper does not touch the food, but watches the family with deep longing.

pieces.label: Ask If Something Is Wrong
pieces.text: (Subject) leans over and speaks gently, so the children will not hear. "Forgive me. Is something wrong? Is the food not to your liking?" The guest looks down at the full bowl as if only now noticing it...

pieces.label: Offer a Quiet Place
pieces.text: Seeing how tired the guest looks, (subject) does not press. Instead, (subject.he/she) lays out a clean mat and a blanket in the quiet corner of the hut. "Rest here tonight, if you like. Eat when you're ready, or not at all."...

pieces.label: Invite Them to Tell a Story
pieces.text: "Perhaps you'd rather talk than eat," (subject) says with a smile. "Our children love stories. Would you tell us one?" The children immediately stop squabbling and look up, hopeful...

pieces.label: Respect Their Silence
pieces.text: (Subject) catches (subject.his/her) family's eyes and gives a tiny shake of the head. Nobody says anything. The meal simply goes on: the chatter, the squabbles, the passing of bowls, with the quiet guest sitting in the middle of it all...
The guest lost a son at sea; a small child climbs into (subject.his/her) lap, and (subject.he/she) finally eats.
"I remember meals like this," the guest says, and explains no further.
The guest sleeps soundly and wolfs down cold stew at dawn.
By morning the guest is gone, the bed made, and the dog never barked.
The guest tells a tale of a family reunited, and then eats at last.
The guest's story is about (subject)'s own family, in details no stranger should know.
No one presses, and the guest leaves looking as if (subject.he/she) has been fed.
A child gives the guest a crumpled yellow hibiscus, and (subject.he/she) smiles for the first time.
The guest sits very straight.
The stew is going cold.
The children squabble over the last fish.
The guest's eyes follow every passing bowl.

pieces.label: The Silver Thread
pieces.text: (Subject) walks into a silver thread stretched between two trees, which hums in the wind and seems to lead farther than the forest goes.

pieces.label: Follow the Thread
pieces.text: (Subject) takes hold of the thread with one hand and begins to walk. It runs on and on, from tree to tree, humming under (subject.his/her) fingers, deeper into the forest than (subject.he/she) has ever been...

pieces.label: Cut the Thread
pieces.text: Whatever it is, (subject) does not want anyone else walking into it in the dark. (subject.He/she) draws (subject.his/her) knife and slices through it...

pieces.label: Wind It Onto a Spool
pieces.text: (Subject) has never seen a thread so fine and so strong. (subject.He/she) fetches a stick from the ground and begins carefully winding the thread around it, tree by tree, along the path...

pieces.label: Leave It Alone
pieces.text: (Subject) ducks carefully under the thread and walks on, leaving it humming quietly in the breeze behind (subject.him/her). (subject.He/she) tells (subject.himself/herself) not to think about it...
The thread leads to a lost village child by a stream, who followed it hoping to get home.
It ends at a forgotten mossy shrine laid with fresh flowers.
Cut, it rings a sweet note and dissolves into the air.
It is spider silk, and a hand-sized spider glares down from the branches.
The weavers study its twist and learn a stronger, finer way to spin.
In the sunlight it turns brittle and breaks into melting silver flakes.
By morning there is only an ordinary spider's web between ordinary trees.
A tiny shell bell hangs where the thread began, ringing like rain on a pond.
The thread hums when the wind touches it.
The trees seem farther apart the longer (subject) looks.
Silver glints between the leaves.
The forest is hushed, as if listening.

pieces.label: The Cave of Returned Words
pieces.text: A small cave does not echo what (subject) says, but repeats words someone else once said there.

pieces.label: Listen to the Echo
pieces.text: (Subject) holds very still and listens. The cave is quiet for a long moment. Then, faintly, the voices begin to come back...

pieces.label: Speak a Question
pieces.text: (Subject) takes a breath. "Who are you?" (subject.he/she) asks the dark. The question rolls away into the back of the cave, and (subject) waits...

pieces.label: Bring a Scholar
pieces.text: (Subject) runs back to the village and drags (researcher), the village's most learned researcher, protesting, up the hill and into the little cave. (researcher) squeezes in, knees up to (subject.his/her) chin, and listens...

pieces.label: Seal the Cave
pieces.text: (Subject) wants nothing to do with a cave full of other people's words. (subject.He/she) tells the elders, who agree that a cave which talks back is not a safe place for curious children, and the builders haul stones up the hill...
An old voice warns someone named Taro about a cracked rock, which the builders then prop up.
The cave speaks the name of a long-dead villager, and the family finally says it aloud again.
The answer comes in (subject)'s own voice, older, saying words (subject.he/she) has never said.
It is an ordinary echo that repeats every word back faithfully.
(researcher) finds tiny tunnels that carry distant voices through the hill.
(researcher) hears what sounds like a conversation from centuries ago, about a war no one knows.
The cave is sealed, grass grows over it, and it becomes a fireside story.
Faint whispers still murmur behind the stones, so villagers say hello as they pass.
Every sound comes back a little too late.
The walls are slick and dark.
Water drips somewhere in the back.
The cave seems to hold its breath.

pieces.label: The Traveler's Lost Star
pieces.text: A desperate traveler asks (subject) where the red star has gone, and when (subject) looks, the familiar star is missing from the sky.

pieces.label: Study the Sky
pieces.text: (Subject) wakes the researchers, who grumble, wrap themselves in blankets, and come out to the beach with the traveler, where they lie on their backs on the sand staring at the sky...

pieces.label: Offer Shelter
pieces.text: "Whatever's happened to the star, you'll not find it tonight," (subject) says kindly. "Come in and rest." The traveler hesitates, then follows (subject.him/her) inside to the fire...

pieces.label: Ask Why the Star Matters
pieces.text: "Forgive me," (subject) says, "but why does it matter so much? It's just one star." The traveler looks at (subject.him/her) as though (subject.he/she) has said something terrible, then sighs and sits down heavily on a log...

pieces.label: Search the Horizon
pieces.text: (Subject) and the traveler climb to the highest point above the village, and a few curious villagers tag along. They stand on the hilltop in the wind, scanning the dark horizon in every direction...
A week of watching shows the stars move with the seasons; the star was just setting early.
The clouds part, and the star is right where it should be; everyone laughs on the cold sand.
The traveler spends the night telling the fishers how to sail by stars and swells.
The traveler leaves a star chart of knots on sailcloth; the red knot has no star.
The star always led the traveler home to the one (subject.he/she) loves.
An ancestor promised the family would never be lost while it shone.
A signal fire on a distant headland reveals another settlement.
The traveler leaves at dawn, and the star is back that night and every night after.
The patch of sky is empty and black.
The sand is cold under (subject)'s back.
The traveler keeps pointing at the horizon.
A shooting star streaks past, which does not help.

pieces.label: The Beggar with the Golden Seed
pieces.text: An old beggar offers (subject) a single golden seed, far too heavy for its size, in exchange for one hot meal.

pieces.label: Feed the Beggar
pieces.text: "Fair trade," (subject) agrees, and ladles out the biggest bowl of stew (subject.he/she) can manage. The beggar eats it all, every drop, licks the bowl, and hobbles off down the road whistling. (Subject) plants the seed by (subject.his/her) door that evening...

pieces.label: Offer Shelter Instead
pieces.text: (Subject) hands the seed back. "Keep your seed," (subject.he/she) says. "You look like you need a roof more than I need a seed. Come and sit by the fire tonight."...

pieces.label: Demand Proof of the Seed
pieces.text: "A golden seed?" (subject) says suspiciously. "Prove it. Show me it's something special, and you can have the whole pot."...

pieces.label: Refuse the Bargain
pieces.text: "I'm sorry," (subject) says, handing the seed back. "We've barely enough for ourselves." The beggar nods, as if (subject.he/she) had expected that, and closes (subject.his/her) hand...
The seed grows into a silver-leaved plant whose fruit tastes of honey and lime.
The seed is a piece of amber, but the beggar's happy whistling was worth the stew.
The beggar tells of a rice pot that never emptied, and leaves the seed on the hearth.
The beggar sends (subject) to a young traveler under the fig tree who needs it more.
Tapped, the seed rings like a tiny bell, and the children carry it everywhere.
"Everyone wants proof," says the beggar, walking away for good.
Nothing happens at all, which is a little anticlimactic.
The next morning the warm, heavy seed sits on the doorstep with no footprints.
The seed shines like a drop of honey.
The beggar's eyes are bright and amused.
The stew bubbles hopefully in the pot.
The seed is faintly warm in the palm.

pieces.label: The Unseen Guide
pieces.text: Lost in the dark forest as a storm rolls in, (subject) hears a calm, invisible voice giving directions toward home.

pieces.label: Follow the Directions
pieces.text: (Subject) does not have a better idea. (subject.He/she) turns left at the big rock, then walks straight on, the voice murmuring encouragement now and then: "Mind the root. Duck. Good. Keep going."...

pieces.label: Ask Who Is Speaking
pieces.text: "Wait," (subject) whispers, voice trembling. "Who are you? Where are you?" The rain patters. For a while, the voice says nothing...

pieces.label: Call for a Friend
pieces.text: (Subject) cups (subject.his/her) hands to (subject.his/her) mouth and shouts as loud as (subject.he/she) can: "HELP! I'M LOST! OVER HERE!" Far off, through the rain, someone shouts back...

pieces.label: Ignore the Voice
pieces.text: (Subject) has heard stories about voices in the forest that lead people away. (subject.He/she) clamps (subject.his/her) hands over (subject.his/her) ears, hunkers down under a tree, and decides to wait for daylight...
The voice leads (subject) home just as the storm hits.
The voice leads (subject) to a dry cave to wait out the storm; the usual path was blocked by a fallen tree.
"Someone who was once lost here too." An elder tells of a hunter who vanished in that forest.
The voice falls silent, and (subject) has to scramble home alone.
A search party finds (subject), but they never said anything about the big rock.
The searchers heard two voices, though (subject) insists (subject.he/she) was alone.
After a miserable night, sunrise shows the village smoke just over the ridge.
(Subject) blunders into a thornbush thicket and the healers clean the scratches all evening.
Every path looks the same in the dark.
Rain drips from every leaf.
The voice is calm and close.
Thunder rolls somewhere beyond the trees.

pieces.label: The Box of Little Storms
pieces.text: Little (subject) finds a painted box full of tiny spinning storm clouds that vanish whenever an adult looks inside.

pieces.label: Let the Child Describe It
pieces.text: (Friend) sits down on the floor beside (subject). "All right. Tell me exactly what you see." (Subject) peers into the box, tongue poking out in concentration...

pieces.label: Examine the Box
pieces.text: (Friend) borrows the box (over loud protests) and takes it to the researchers, who turn it over and over, tapping and prodding and sniffing it...

pieces.label: Open It Outdoors
pieces.text: "If there are storms in there," (friend) says, "they'd probably like some fresh air." They carry the box out into the middle of the square, and (subject) solemnly lifts the lid all the way open...

pieces.label: Store It Safely
pieces.text: (Friend) decides that a box of storms, real or not, is not a toy. (subject.He/she) promises (subject) it will be kept safe, and puts it up on the highest shelf in the hut...
(Subject)'s vivid description spreads, and every child in the village claims to have seen a tiny storm.
On second thought, they are dust swirling in a sunbeam, but they look like storms.
A hidden drawer of fine powder makes the clouds, visible only from a child's height.
The researchers find nothing, and the storms come back the moment (subject) looks.
A sudden gust sweeps the square, knocking a hat off an elder and sending a chicken tumbling.
A sweet, rain-scented mist drifts out, and everyone it touches smiles.
Years later, grown-up (subject) looks in and sees nothing, and keeps it for (subject.his/her) own child.
The box vanishes from the shelf, leaving a cold wet ring that smells of rain.
Painted lightning zigzags across the lid.
(Subject) keeps saying "There! See?"
A tiny flash, maybe, out of the corner of an eye.
The box smells faintly of rain.

pieces.label: The Last Lamp in the Ruins
pieces.text: In the ruins of an abandoned settlement, (subject) finds a lamp still burning beside a bowl of rice that is still steaming.

pieces.label: Examine the Lamp
pieces.text: (Subject) creeps closer and lifts the lamp carefully. It is heavier than it looks. (subject.He/she) turns it over, peering at it from every angle...

pieces.label: Eat the Food
pieces.text: (Subject) is very hungry, and the rice smells very good. "Sorry," (subject.he/she) says to nobody, and picks up the bowl...

pieces.label: Wait for the Owner
pieces.text: It seems rude to touch someone's dinner. (Subject) sits down on the floor across from the lamp, and waits for whoever lives here to come home...

pieces.label: Leave an Offering
pieces.text: Whoever this belongs to, they deserve respect. (Subject) takes a little packet of dried fruit from (subject.his/her) bag and sets it on the shelf beside the bowl. Then (subject.he/she) leaves the house, and sleeps in the shelter of the ruined wall outside...
A hidden oil reservoir keeps the lamp burning for a month, and the village copies the design.
The lamp is bone dry, yet burns until dawn and then goes out.
The rice is delicious, and the bowl keeps refilling; (subject) carries a bundle home.
The rice is spoiled, and (subject) spends days in the healers' care with stomach cramps.
A muddy traveler living in the ruins comes home, shrieks, then shares the rice.
(Subject) falls asleep, and wakes with the lamp burning on the floor right beside (subject.him/her).
The offering stays untouched beside the cold rice.
The bowl is scraped clean, and the only footprints in the dust are (subject)'s own.
Moss hangs from the fallen roof.
The flame does not flicker.
The rice still steams.
Somewhere a bird calls, then stops.

pieces.label: The Old Woman Who Asked for Nothing
pieces.text: A bright-eyed old woman on (subject)'s doorstep insists she needs nothing, and asks only whether the household has room for one more story.

pieces.label: Invite Her to Tell It
pieces.text: "There's always room for a story," (subject) says, and the old woman beams and settles herself by the fire. The family gathers round, the children elbowing each other for the best spots...

pieces.label: Offer Her Supper
pieces.text: "Nothing at all? Not even a little supper?" (subject) asks. "We've plenty. Please, sit down." The old woman hesitates, then sits...

pieces.label: Ask Why She Came
pieces.text: "Forgive me," (subject) says, "but why come all this way just to tell a story?" The old woman's eyes twinkle...

pieces.label: Send Her Away
pieces.text: "I'm sorry," (subject) says, "it's late, and we're tired. Perhaps another time." The old woman nods kindly...
Her story teaches a way to dry and wrap herbs so they keep twice as long.
She tells of two sisters parted by the sea, and the family sits quietly together long after.
She eats heartily and shares wickedly funny gossip from every village.
She cannot eat, but treasures the place at the table, and is suddenly gone.
Someone who remembered (subject)'s kindness sent her, but she will not say who.
She lives alone and missed laughter; she becomes a weekly supper guest.
She leaves without anger, and the evening is just a little quieter.
A note in the doorframe thanks (subject) for listening, though (subject.he/she) did not.
The shawl is patterned like fish scales.
The evening insects begin their song.
Her eyes twinkle in the firelight.
She smells faintly of the sea.

pieces.label: The Hidden Name of the Mountain
pieces.text: A traveler tells (subject) the mountain has a secret name, and that speaking it on the slopes changes the path beneath one's feet.

pieces.label: Ask for the Name
pieces.text: "Tell me the name," (subject) says. The traveler studies (subject.him/her) for a long moment, then beckons (subject.him/her) to follow, up to the foot of the mountain where the mist begins...

pieces.label: Try a Name of Their Own
pieces.text: (Subject) does not see why the mountain cannot have a new name. (subject.He/she) marches up to the first slope, takes a deep breath, and shouts the grandest name (subject.he/she) can think of up into the clouds...

pieces.label: Study the Trails
pieces.text: Secret names or not, (subject) thinks the mountain could do with a proper map. (subject.He/she) gathers a few of the bravest villagers, and they spend weeks walking the slopes, marking every path, stream and landslide...

pieces.label: Leave the Mountain Alone
pieces.text: (Subject) thinks about it and decides some secrets are best left with the mountain. (subject.He/she) thanks the traveler for the story, and goes home...
The traveler whispers the name and a hidden trail appears in the mist, never found again.
"Names are earned by listening," and (subject) comes to know the mountain better than anyone.
The mountain echoes (subject)'s new name back in a voice like grinding stone.
Nothing happens, and the children name it "The Big Pointy One."
The mappers chart a safer route around unstable ground, and nobody gets hurt that season.
The paths keep changing, and the map is all gaps and question marks.
(Subject) lets the mountain keep its secrets, and is content.
At sunset, the mountain's shadow forms a doorway across the valley.
The peak is wrapped in its cloak of cloud.
The traveler glances up as if the mountain were listening.
Wind moans along the high ridges.
A stone clatters down a slope somewhere.

pieces.label: The Stranger Who Counted the Stars
pieces.text: A figure in a pale cloak sits outside the village counting stars aloud, though the count never matches the stars anyone can see.

pieces.label: Count Along
pieces.text: (Subject) sits down on the rock beside the stranger, squints up at the sky, and says, "Four hundred and fifteen?" The stranger chuckles, and points, and they count on together...

pieces.label: Ask Why They Count
pieces.text: "Excuse me," (subject) says politely, "but why are you counting stars no one can see?" The stranger lowers (subject.his/her) finger...

pieces.label: Offer a Place to Sleep
pieces.text: "It's cold out here," (subject) says. "You're welcome to sleep in my hut tonight, if you'd like. The stars will still be there tomorrow."...

pieces.label: Return the Next Night
pieces.text: (Subject) decides not to disturb the stranger tonight, and goes home to bed. But (subject.he/she) cannot stop thinking about it, and the next night, (subject.he/she) walks back out to the flat rock...
The stranger shows (subject) three stars that always point south, and the fishers learn it.
The count ends at a number later found carved on an ancient stone.
Each star is a promise, the stranger says, and (subject) goes home to keep one.
They used to count with someone they miss; (subject) counts the next one with them.
The stranger sleeps by the fire, murmuring numbers, and leaves one scratched in the floor.
"I haven't finished counting." By morning, only a folded blanket remains.
The stranger is gone, but the last number is written in the sand.
A grieving neighbour sits on the rock instead, and they count together.
The voice is like dry leaves.
Clouds hide most of the sky.
One long finger points upward.
An owl hoots, as if losing count.

pieces.label: The Hungry Stranger's Blessing
pieces.text: A hungry traveler with a stick carved all over with tiny fish asks (subject) for a bowl of food in a lean season.

pieces.label: Share a Full Meal
pieces.text: Lean season or not, (subject) sits the traveler down and fills (subject.his/her) bowl to the brim, then fills it again. The traveler eats like someone who has not eaten in days, which (subject.he/she) probably has not...

pieces.label: Share What Is Available
pieces.text: (Subject) explains, a little embarrassed, that it has been a lean season, and offers what (subject.he/she) can: half a bowl of thin stew and a couple of roasted roots. The traveler takes it gratefully...

pieces.label: Ask for Work in Exchange
pieces.text: "There's food," (subject) says, "but everyone here works for it. Would you help me in the field this afternoon?" The traveler nods...

pieces.label: Refuse the Request
pieces.text: "I'm sorry," (subject) says. "We have barely enough for ourselves this season." The traveler nods, sighs, and limps off down the path...
The traveler draws the way to a violet-water fishing ground packed with fish.
No magic gift, just a full traveler and a washed bowl, and (subject) does not mind.
The traveler shows (subject) where to dig, and they fill three baskets of roots.
The traveler mends (subject)'s cracked basket in five minutes, weaving in a little fish.
The traveler teaches a faster way to harvest that the whole village copies.
The traveler is too weak to work, and (subject) feeds (subject.him/her) anyway.
A sudden storm spoils the drying fish right after the traveler leaves.
The traveler finds help next door, and no misfortune follows.
The carved fish seem to swim on the stick.
The traveler's lips are cracked from the sun.
The pot is thinner than usual this season.
A gull eyes the cooking fire hopefully.

pieces.label: The Unfinished Statue
pieces.text: The villagers uncover an ancient half-carved statue beneath the vines whose face is exactly (subject)'s.

pieces.label: Study the Statue
pieces.text: The village carvers gather around the statue, running their hands over the stone, peering at the chisel marks, muttering to each other...

pieces.label: Finish the Carving
pieces.text: "Someone started it," (subject) says. "Someone should finish it." (carver), the best carver in the village, agrees, and with (subject) sitting as a model, (subject.he/she) picks up the chisel...

pieces.label: Ask the Elders
pieces.text: (Subject) brings the eldest villagers up the hill to see the statue. They stand before it in silence for a very long time...

pieces.label: Leave It Untouched
pieces.text: (Subject) has seen quite enough of (subject.his/her) own stone face. "Leave it," (subject.he/she) says. "It's been there this long. It's not hurting anyone." The others agree, and they let the vines fall back over it...
The carvers learn to split stone with wedges along its grain.
The rough face looks a bit like everyone, which is a relief and a slight disappointment.
Finished with (subject) as model, it becomes the symbol of this generation.
A crack splits the face in two, and (carver) refuses to touch it again.
An elder says faces come back, when the island wants to keep someone.
It is the work of the long-dead Old Carver, perhaps (subject)'s ancestor.
Moss and ferns reclaim the statue, and it becomes a quiet old friend.
A fresh chisel mark appears overnight, making the smile exactly as crooked as (subject)'s.
Vines wrap the statue's shoulders like a shawl.
The moss is centuries thick.
The crooked smile is unmistakable.
Someone suggests they got (subject)'s good side.

pieces.label: The Silent Stranger at the Well
pieces.text: At midnight, a stranger waiting by the well asks (subject) whether (subject.he/she) would share water with someone who can offer nothing in return.

pieces.label: Offer Water Freely
pieces.text: "Of course," (subject) says at once, and lowers the bucket, and hauls it up brimming, and fills the stranger's cupped hands. The stranger drinks slowly, as though it were the finest thing (subject.he/she) has ever tasted...

pieces.label: Ask Why They Need It
pieces.text: "Why ask like that?" (subject) says carefully. "Anyone can drink from our well. Why do you need to ask?"...

pieces.label: Call for Others
pieces.text: (Subject) is not sure about this alone. "Wait here," (subject.he/she) says, and runs to wake the neighbours...

pieces.label: Refuse the Request
pieces.text: "I don't know you," (subject) says, stepping back. "Come back in daylight, and ask the elders." The stranger lowers (subject.his/her) empty hands...
The stranger leaves a carved cup at the well that never chips, no matter what.
It is a tired young traveler, embarrassed by (subject.his/her) dramatic question.
The stranger has lost everything; (subject) takes (subject.him/her) in for as long as needed.
"To know what kind of village this is," and the stranger is gone.
Neighbours bring blankets and stew, and an exhausted old traveler is taken in.
