The stranger is gone, but the bucket on the rim is full, and the water is sweet.
After a storm, the well runs muddy and some stored food is spoiled.
The stranger finds water at the stream, and nothing supernatural follows.
The frogs have gone quiet.
Moonlight silvers the well's rim.
Two empty hands, palms up.
The bucket rope creaks.

pieces.label: The Ancient Bottle's Warning
pieces.text: (Subject) digs up an old bottle holding a hurried warning that the great tree on the bend must never be cut down, the day before the builders mean to cut it.

pieces.label: Protect the Tree
pieces.text: (Subject) runs to the builders, waving the bottle, and tells them the tree has to stay. After a great deal of arguing, and some sulking, the builders agree to route the path around it instead. That afternoon, (subject) goes to look at the tree properly for the first time...

pieces.label: Study the Roots
pieces.text: Before anyone touches an axe, (subject) insists the researchers take a look. They spend a day crawling around the base of the tree, digging and poking at the enormous roots...

pieces.label: Ask a Storyteller
pieces.text: (Subject) takes the bottle to (storyteller), the oldest storyteller in the village, who reads the warning by firelight, then sits back with a long, slow "Ahhhh..."...

pieces.label: Ignore the Warning
pieces.text: (Subject) shrugs. It is an old bottle with an old note, and the path needs widening. (subject.He/she) tucks the note in (subject.his/her) wrap and joins the builders the next morning, axe in hand...
Behind the leaves, the tree is laden with purple fruit nobody had ever noticed.
Nothing is found, but the children call it the Never Tree and climb it every day.
The roots are holding the whole slope together above the huts.
A small carved figure is found wedged deep in the roots, its purpose unknown.
The storyteller tells of a guardian who asked to be bound into the tree.
"Warnings outlive their reasons," says the storyteller, and (subject) decides to listen.
A falling limb pins (subject), who is carried to the healers; the note is never found again.
The tree falls safely and its wood builds three huts.
The handwriting shakes as if in a hurry.
The old tree creaks in the wind.
Roots knot the path like knuckles.
The builders sharpen their axes.

pieces.label: The Shore's Unseen Companion
pieces.text: Collecting shells on the empty beach at low tide, (subject) hears footsteps keeping pace beside (subject.him/her), stopping whenever (subject.he/she) stops.

pieces.label: Speak to the Companion
pieces.text: (Subject) swallows, and says to the empty air beside (subject.him/her), as casually as (subject.he/she) can manage: "Nice day for shells, isn't it?"...

pieces.label: Look for Footprints
pieces.text: (Subject) turns slowly and looks down at the wet, smooth sand beside (subject.his/her) own feet...

pieces.label: Walk Toward the Village
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that whatever it is, (subject.he/she) would rather be among people. (subject.He/she) turns and walks briskly up the beach toward the village, and the footsteps crunch along beside (subject.him/her) all the way...

pieces.label: Leave a Shell Behind
pieces.text: (Subject) picks out the prettiest shell in (subject.his/her) basket, a pink spiral one, and sets it gently on a flat rock above the tideline. "For you," (subject.he/she) says to the empty air, feeling rather silly, and walks home...
A soft voice says, "I used to walk here," and fades with the tide.
(friend), (subject)'s best friend, has been crunching shells behind the dunes and ends up in the sea.
A second set of bare footprints walks beside (subject)'s, until a wave erases only them.
Only (subject)'s own prints are on the sand, but the footsteps keep pace.
The footsteps walk (subject) to the first house and then go back to the beach.
They follow (subject) all the way home, and shells are on the doorstep in the morning.
The shell is replaced by a warm white pebble, every time.
The shell is still there, and (subject) laughs at (subject.himself/herself). Probably the wind.
The wet sand reflects the sky like glass.
Shells crunch softly underfoot.
A gull lands, looks around, and leaves.
The tide whispers along the beach.

pieces.label: The Basket of Unknown Fruit
pieces.text: A covered basket of unfamiliar velvet-skinned fruit appears outside the food store with a note: "For those who dare to taste."

pieces.label: Identify the Fruit
pieces.text: "Nobody eats anything," (subject) says firmly, "until someone who knows plants has a look." (subject.He/she) fetches (botanist), the village botanist, who arrives with a magnifying shell and a great deal of self-importance...

pieces.label: Try a Small Portion
pieces.text: "Fine," (subject) says, with the air of a hero going into battle. (subject.He/she) cuts a tiny sliver of the fruit, holds it up to the crowd, and pops it in (subject.his/her) mouth. Everyone holds their breath...

pieces.label: Search for the Giver
pieces.text: (Subject) wants to know who leaves mysterious fruit outside food stores in the middle of the night. (subject.He/she) sets off around the village, basket on (subject.his/her) hip, asking everyone (subject.he/she) meets...

pieces.label: Plant the Seeds
pieces.text: Rather than risk eating them, (subject) suggests planting them. (subject.He/she) cuts the fruits open, carefully takes out the big glossy seeds, and plants a row of them along the edge of the garden...
(botanist) identifies a safe, delicious velvet pear, and an expedition finds more.
(botanist) cannot identify it, and the fruit wrinkles untouched.
(Subject) runs a fever for days after one sliver, and the rest goes in the sea.
It is delicious, and (subject) can never get enough fruit after that.
(farmer), a farmer, has been growing the trees in secret and thought the note was funny.
Nobody claims it, though the leaves were packed only hours ago.
The seeds sprout into a row of young trees that (subject) names one by one.
Nothing grows; the seeds vanish from the soil, leaving only a smell of honey.
The fruit smells of honey and cut grass.
Nobody wants to be first.
The skins are like purple velvet.
A child reaches for one and is swiftly stopped.

pieces.label: The Old Traveler's Shadow
pieces.text: An elderly traveler asks (subject) for shelter, and by the hearth the traveler's shadow on the wall stands straight and moves like a much younger person.

pieces.label: Welcome the Traveler
pieces.text: Shadow or no shadow, a guest is a guest. (Subject) fetches a blanket and a bowl of stew, and the old traveler smiles a toothless smile of thanks...

pieces.label: Ask About the Shadow
pieces.text: (Subject) cannot help it. "Forgive me," (subject.he/she) says, pointing at the wall, "but your shadow... it doesn't look like you." The traveler turns slowly to look at it...

pieces.label: Offer a Meal Outside
pieces.text: (Subject) decides (subject.he/she) would rather not have that shadow on (subject.his/her) walls. Politely, (subject.he/she) suggests they eat outside in the cool evening air, and brings out a bowl and a mat...

pieces.label: Turn the Traveler Away
pieces.text: (Subject) does not like it. "I'm sorry," (subject.he/she) says, "on second thought, we haven't room tonight." The traveler nods slowly, and shuffles back out of the door...
The traveler stays through a three-day storm telling stories older than anyone remembers.
At dawn the traveler leaves a packet of fast-growing seeds.
"Perhaps shadows remember us differently," and the shadow seems to bow.
A child shows how the low fire and curved wall stretch everyone's shadow tall.
Outside in the evening light, the traveler casts an ordinary shadow and goes on, humming.
The traveler visits the old memorial, where (subject.his/her) moonlit shadow is young and weeping.
The traveler leaves without complaint, and (subject) regrets it all night.
The hearth fire goes out the instant the traveler leaves.
The shadow steps lightly.
The old stick taps on the floor.
The fire throws long shapes on the wall.
The traveler groans as (subject.he/she) sits.

pieces.label: The Book That Wrote Back
pieces.text: A blank sealskin book from a washed-up crate fills with new handwriting whenever (subject) leaves it alone, the ink still wet.

pieces.label: Read the New Pages
pieces.text: (Subject) sits down with the book in (subject.his/her) lap, takes a deep breath, and begins to read...

pieces.label: Watch the Book
pieces.text: (Subject) is determined to catch whoever, or whatever, is writing in it. That night, (subject.he/she) leaves the book open on the table, blows out the lamp, and hides behind a basket in the corner, wide awake...

pieces.label: Write a Question
pieces.text: (Subject) borrows a little ink from the researchers, and on a fresh blank page writes, in (subject.his/her) best hand: "Who are you?" Then (subject.he/she) closes the book, and waits until morning...

pieces.label: Store It Safely
pieces.text: Whatever this book is, it should not be left lying around. (Subject) wraps it in oiled cloth, ties it shut with a cord, and takes it to the researchers' hut for safekeeping...
The pages teach how to measure rainfall, and the farmers plant at exactly the right time.
The pages tell a story about a villager named (subject), accurate down to (subject.his/her) sleeping mat.
A village child has been sneaking in to write tales of a heroic pig.
Nothing happens all night, until (subject) blinks once at dawn and the page fills.
The book answers with a riddle that nobody in the village can solve.
The reply says "You already know," in (subject)'s own handwriting.
The book sits tied shut on the research hut shelf, waiting for someone braver.
It is found open on the floor to a new page describing its own untying.
The ink is still slightly damp.
The sealskin smells of salt and dust.
The handwriting is small and neat.
A page turns, though there is no breeze.

pieces.label: The Stranger at the Funeral Path
pieces.text: As the village carries flowers along the cliff path to the memorial, (subject) notices a barefoot stranger in grey walking with the procession whom no one else seems to see.

pieces.label: Offer a Flower
pieces.text: (Subject) separates one flower from (subject.his/her) armful, a bright red one, and quietly holds it out to the stranger as they walk...

pieces.label: Ask Whom They Mourn
pieces.text: (Subject) falls into step beside the stranger, and whispers, so as not to disturb the silence: "Who are you mourning?"...

pieces.label: Tell a Companion
pieces.text: (Subject) leans over to (friend), walking beside (subject.him/her), and whispers: "Who's that? In grey, walking with us?" (Friend) looks where (subject) is pointing...

pieces.label: Leave the Stranger Alone
pieces.text: Whoever the stranger is, this is a day for mourning, not for questions. (Subject) lowers (subject.his/her) eyes and keeps walking in silence...
The stranger takes the flower, bows, and vanishes; it is later found on a nameless old grave.
The stranger's hand passes through the flower like smoke.
The stranger mourns someone buried on a distant shore, and walks to the village's graves instead.
"Everyone who was loved," says the stranger, standing at the back with head bowed.
(Friend) sees no one, but holds (subject)'s hand tightly the rest of the way.
(Friend) recognizes the stranger from a painting of (subject.his/her) great-grandmother.
The procession reaches the memorial peacefully, and the stranger seemed to belong.
An extra white flower that grows nowhere on the island lies among the offerings.
The sea whispers below the cliff.
Bright flowers fill every arm.
The stranger's feet are bare on the stones.
Nobody speaks.

pieces.label: The Hidden Cup of Rain
pieces.text: In a bone-dry cave, (subject) finds a cracked cup full of fresh water, inscribed "Fills each night. Share it."

pieces.label: Share the Water
pieces.text: (Subject) carries the cup carefully back to the path, where a group of thirsty travelers have stopped to rest in the heat. "Here," (subject.he/she) says. "It's not much, but drink."...

pieces.label: Study the Cave
pieces.text: (Subject) wants to understand how a dry cave can fill a cup. (subject.He/she) fetches the researchers, and they spend a day and a night in the cave, lamps lit, examining every crack in the stone...

pieces.label: Keep the Cup Secret
pieces.text: (Subject) thinks of (subject.his/her) own family and how dry the season has been. (subject.He/she) tells no one about the cup, and goes back to the cave each morning to fill (subject.his/her) water skin...

pieces.label: Return It to the Cave
pieces.text: (Subject) decides the cup belongs where it is. (subject.He/she) sets it back on the ledge exactly as (subject.he/she) found it, drinks one careful sip from it, and goes home...
Seven thirsty travelers drink from one cup, and each says it tastes like home.
It is one ordinary cupful, gone in a swallow, and never fills outside the cave.
A hair-thin carved channel catches the night dew, and the village builds dew-catchers.
The researchers watch all night, and the cup fills anyway without anyone seeing it.
(Subject)'s family never goes thirsty, but the words "Share it" keep (subject.him/her) awake.
On the third morning, the cup is bone dry and never fills again.
The cave becomes a place for one quiet sip on hot days, and it fills every night.
The cup is gone, leaving a cool damp circle that dries under (subject)'s fingertip.
The cave is dry as bone.
The water trembles in the lamplight.
The village wells are low this season.
The smell of old smoke lingers.

pieces.label: The Stranger's Two Faces
pieces.text: A visitor passing through appears to (subject) as an old woman in a faded shawl, but (friend) saw the very same visitor as a tall, laughing young man.

pieces.label: Ask the Visitor Directly
pieces.text: (Subject) marches down to the river, determined to settle this once and for all. The visitor is sitting on a rock, dangling (subject.his/her) feet in the water. To (subject), it is very clearly an old woman...

pieces.label: Invite Both Witnesses
pieces.text: (Subject) grabs (friend) by the arm. "Right. We're going together, and we're both going to look at the same time." The two of them hurry down to the river, side by side...

pieces.label: Offer Hospitality
pieces.text: Whoever the visitor is, they are a guest on the island. (Subject) goes down to the river and invites them up to the village for a meal, and the visitor accepts with a smile...

pieces.label: Let the Mystery Rest
pieces.text: "It doesn't matter," (subject) says at last, giving up. "Old, young, man, woman, whoever it was, they asked for directions and they've gone." (Friend) reluctantly agrees, and they go back to work...
"People see what they expect," says the visitor, and (subject) comes away unsure of the pronoun.
They are a grandmother and grandson traveling together, who laugh until a fish falls in the river.
Together they see an ordinary traveler, and afterward neither can remember the face.
They look at the same moment and still disagree, once a season for life.
The visitor shares news of a village where everyone swaps hats, and leaves in (subject)'s.
The visitor leaves a shell charm with two faces carved back to back.
The argument fades, though (subject) looks twice at strangers ever after.
A child draws both faces side by side: "Both, of course."
The visitor {dangles (subject.his/her) feet in the river|hums by the water|waves from the far bank}.
(Subject) and (friend) {argue through lunch|glare at each other|each insist they are right}.
A laugh like a drum echoes from the river, or maybe a cackle.
The fishers {saw an old woman|saw a young man|did not look closely}.

pieces.label: The Traveler Who Never Arrived
pieces.text: A dusty messenger warns that a traveler is coming with an important red-wrapped gift for the village, but days pass and no one arrives.

pieces.label: Search the Road
pieces.text: (Subject) gathers a few strong villagers and sets off down the long road out of the village, calling out and searching the ditches and the trees on either side...

pieces.label: Wait at the Gate
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that if the traveler is coming, someone should be there to greet (subject.him/her) properly. (subject.He/she) sits down at the village gate with a jug of water and waits, all day...

pieces.label: Ask the Messenger Again
pieces.text: (Subject) sits down beside the messenger, who is eating (subject.his/her) fifth free meal in four days. "Tell me again," (subject) says, "exactly where you met this traveler."...

pieces.label: Leave a Light Burning
pieces.text: (Subject) thinks the traveler might have got lost in the dark. (subject.He/she) hangs a lantern on a pole at the village gate, fills it with oil, and keeps it burning through the night...
The traveler is found pinned and injured under a fallen tree, still clutching the red gift.
An abandoned pack holds labelled seeds and a scrap of red cloth, never claimed.
At dusk a quiet stranger hands over a map of forgotten paths and leaves without a name.
No one comes, and the messenger has vanished too, cup still half full.
The messenger admits it was a dream, and stays on as a very good cook.
The messenger insists they met by the black rocks, but nothing is ever found.
A traveler lost for three days in the hills stumbles in, following the lantern.
The lantern burns every night for a week, and the road stays empty.
The messenger {eats a fifth free meal|keeps watching the road|insists it will be any moment now}.
Dust hangs over the empty road.
Someone wonders aloud what is in the red cloth.
The gate creaks in the {wind|dusk|rain}.

pieces.label: The Little God of the Garden
pieces.text: Little (subject) insists a tiny guardian lives under the garden leaves, and one morning fingertip-sized footprints appear between the bean rows.

pieces.label: Watch Quietly
pieces.text: That evening, (friend) and little (subject) lie on their stomachs at the edge of the garden, hidden behind the squash leaves, and wait, as still and quiet as two people can be when one of them is very excited...

pieces.label: Leave a Small Offering
pieces.text: "Well," (friend) says, "if there is a little god looking after our garden, we should say thank you." (Subject) is thrilled. Together they set a single berry, a crumb of honey cake and a flower petal on a leaf at the end of the bean row...

pieces.label: Ask the Child to Explain
pieces.text: (Friend) sits (subject) down on an upturned bucket. "All right. Tell me everything. Who is this little god, and what does (subject.he/she) do?"...

pieces.label: Protect the Garden
pieces.text: Little god or no little god, the footprints have reminded (friend) that the garden fence is falling apart. The next morning, (subject.he/she) and (subject) start fixing it, post by post...
A long-toed brown frog makes the prints and glares at being discovered.
The prints end beside a thumbnail-sized clay cup full of water.
The offering vanishes, and the garden grows better than ever with no slugs all season.
The offering stays, and (friend) explains that knowing can be enough.
(Subject) describes a thumb-sized guardian in a beetle-shell hat who sings to the seeds.
(Subject) confesses to making the prints with a carved twig, so someone would believe (subject.him/her).
The mended fence keeps out wild pigs and saves the next crop.
No more mystery, but grown-up (subject) still leaves a berry each harvest.
The footprints always lead toward the water barrel.
(Subject) looks {extremely smug|very patient|ready to say "I told you so"}.
The bean leaves rustle with no wind.
The cat refuses to go near the bean rows.

pieces.label: The Jar of Silent Thunder
pieces.text: In the old stone circle, (subject) finds a jar sealed with a strange knot that trembles during storms without making a sound.

pieces.label: Untie the Knot
pieces.text: (Subject) kneels by the jar, and very carefully, loop by loop, begins to work at the strange knot, while the thunder rolls overhead and the jar trembles under (subject.his/her) fingers...

pieces.label: Study the Jar
pieces.text: (Subject) brings the researchers up to the stone circle during the next storm, and they crouch around the jar in the pouring rain, watching it dance, and arguing loudly over the thunder...

pieces.label: Carry It Home
pieces.text: (Subject) decides the jar would be safer in the village. (subject.He/she) wraps it in a cloth, hefts it into (subject.his/her) arms, and starts down the hill...

pieces.label: Leave It at the Circle
pieces.text: (Subject) decides that whatever this jar is, it belongs to the stone circle, not to the village. (subject.He/she) leaves it exactly where it is and heads home through the rain...
A warm breath of storm air rushes out, and the jar becomes ordinary.
The knot unravels into a thread of red beads, one for every stone in the circle.
The clay responds to tremors in the ground, and the researchers make jars of their own.
The jar keeps trembling for a day after the storm, in perfect calm.
The jar cracks on the way home and spills glittering powder no one can identify.
It grows too heavy to carry, and is found back in the circle.
Watching the jar dance in storms becomes a quiet village tradition.
A second, smaller jar with the same knot appears beside it.
The jar {shivers|rattles|dances} without a sound.
Thunder rolls over the standing stones.
The knot makes (subject)'s eyes hurt to follow.
Rain {hammers|patters|streams} down the stones.

pieces.label: The Ferryman's Empty Boat
pieces.text: At dawn, a small ferry glides across the misty lagoon with no rower, then returns and waits at (subject)'s feet.

pieces.label: Board the Ferry
pieces.text: Every sensible bone in (subject)'s body says no. (Subject) steps in anyway. The boat dips under (subject.his/her) weight, then, without anyone touching the paddle, pulls smoothly away from the shore, out into the mist...

pieces.label: Call to the Rower
pieces.text: "Hello?" (subject) calls, peering at the empty boat. "Is anyone there? Who's rowing?" The mist muffles (subject.his/her) voice. For a moment there is only the soft lap of water against the hull...

pieces.label: Watch from Shore
pieces.text: (Subject) does not go near it. (subject.He/she) sits down on a rock, wraps (subject.his/her) arms around (subject.his/her) knees, and watches the empty ferry very carefully as it pulls away again across the lagoon...

pieces.label: Leave the Boat Alone
pieces.text: (Subject) backs slowly up the beach, turns around, and goes home for breakfast, trying very hard not to look back...
The ferry carries (subject) through a hidden channel to a bay full of striped fish.
The ferry heads out to deep water, and (subject) must swim ashore exhausted.
A voice from the empty stern asks, "Where do you wish to go?"
A rumpled fisher sits up from under the canvas, having dozed off mid-crossing.
A submerged rope and a hidden winch explain it, and the builders copy the idea.
The empty ferry crosses all day, and at sunset is gone from both shores.
The ferry drifts back into the mist and is never seen again.
A flustered traveler asks after a missing boat, which sits perfectly still in the lagoon.
The lagoon is {flat as glass|silver in the dawn|wrapped in mist}.
The paddle rests in the bottom of the boat.
Not a single ripple follows the ferry.
A heron watches from the reeds.

pieces.label: The Old Woman's Empty Hands
pieces.text: An old woman smelling of jasmine asks (subject) for food, then refuses everything offered, saying she came to learn whether anyone would offer.

pieces.label: Ask What She Needs
pieces.text: (Subject) puts down the bowl. "All right," (subject.he/she) says gently. "Then what is it you need?" The old woman's smile softens...

pieces.label: Offer a Meal Anyway
pieces.text: (Subject) ignores the refusal completely, sets the bowl in her hands, puts a spoon in it, and says, "Eat. I insist. Nobody leaves my door hungry." The old woman looks at the bowl for a long moment...

pieces.label: Invite Her to Tell Her Story
pieces.text: "If you won't eat," (subject) says, "then at least come and sit by the fire and tell me who you are." The old woman considers this, then nods and steps inside...

pieces.label: Dismiss Her
pieces.text: (Subject) has had enough. "Look, if you don't want anything, then I have work to do." The old woman nods, unoffended...
She is lonely, and sits on the step with (subject) until the stars come out.
(Subject) walks her over the hills to the grandson she lost track of.
She laughs, eats every bite, and leaves seeds tied in blue cloth: "You passed."
She gently hands the bowl back: "That's all I needed to know."
She tells of a ruler who walked her lands each year as a beggar.
She tells of a secret neighbour who fed her family through the hard years.
She leaves unoffended, and (subject) wishes (subject.he/she) had asked her name.
(Subject) dreams the same question all night, and starts leaving food at the gate.
Her hands are thin and empty.
The scent of jasmine drifts from the coast road.
She shakes her head at {the fish|the fruit|the blanket|the bread}, smiling.
Her eyes are bright and patient.

pieces.label: The Circle of Unseen Dancers
pieces.text: At dusk, (subject) hears laughter and a drumbeat from an empty clearing, where the grass is flattened in a faintly glowing ring.

pieces.label: Join the Dance
pieces.text: The drumbeat is impossible to resist. Before (subject) has quite decided, (subject.his/her) feet are already moving, and (subject.he/she) steps into the glowing ring, and begins to dance...

pieces.label: Bring Musicians
pieces.text: (Subject) runs back to the village and rounds up every musician (subject.he/she) can find, with drums, flutes and rattles. "Come on! There's a party in the woods and no one invited us!" They follow (subject.him/her) to the clearing...

pieces.label: Examine the Clearing
pieces.text: (Subject) waits until the music has faded and the light has gone, then creeps into the clearing with a torch to have a proper look at the flattened ring...

pieces.label: Leave an Offering
pieces.text: (Subject) does not dare step into the ring. Instead, (subject.he/she) takes the little sweet cake (subject.he/she) was saving for later and sets it carefully at the edge of the circle, as a thank-you for the music...
(Subject) dances alone, feels hands brush (subject.his/hers), and comes home grinning, seeds in (subject.his/her) hair.
(Subject) dances what feels like minutes, and returns after sunrise to a search party.
The village joins in, seen and unseen, and the clearing becomes the festival ground.
The laughter stops at the first drumbeat and never returns.
A herd of small playful animals has worn the ring with drumming hooves.
The ring has no tracks at all and stays perfectly smooth through a week of rain.
The cake is replaced by a wildflower wreath that blooms for a month.
The cake stays, and the music never comes again.
The drumbeat is felt more than heard.
Laughter rises, {light|many-voiced|just out of sight}.
The ring of grass glows faintly in the dusk.
Fireflies drift above the clearing.

pieces.label: The Wanderer's Three Doors
pieces.text: A wandering traveler tells (subject) of three doors hidden in the forest: one to food, one to knowledge, and one the traveler refuses to name.

pieces.label: Seek the Door of Food
pieces.text: Following the traveler's directions, (subject) searches the forest for a day and a half, until (subject.he/she) finds it: an old wooden door standing alone among the trees, carved with a fish, with nothing but forest on either side. (subject.He/she) takes a breath, and pulls it open...

pieces.label: Seek the Door of Knowledge
pieces.text: (Subject) wants to know things more than (subject.he/she) wants to eat them. (subject.He/she) follows the traveler's directions deep into the forest, until (subject.he/she) finds an old stone doorway standing alone among the trees, carved with an eye...

pieces.label: Seek the Unnamed Door
pieces.text: (Subject) cannot stop thinking about the door with nothing on it. Against the traveler's quiet warning, (subject.he/she) goes looking for it, and after a long, strange day of walking, finds it: a plain grey door standing alone among the trees, with no marks at all...

pieces.label: Refuse the Search
pieces.text: (Subject) looks at the three doors drawn in the dirt for a long time, and then shakes (subject.his/her) head. "No thanks," (subject.he/she) says. "I'd rather stay here." The traveler looks up, surprised...
The fish door opens on a forgotten storehouse of sealed grain.
An empty hut, but the path back is lined with wild food.
The eye door opens on walls carved with a forgotten carving craft.
A room of blank tablets, "waiting for you," says the traveler.
The plain door opens on a quiet memorial to people with no names.
(Subject) steps through and is never seen again; the door stands open on ordinary forest.
"Good answer," says the traveler, and they share a meal and stories instead.
"Then you've found the fourth door, the one you already walked through."
Three doors drawn in the dirt: {a fish|an eye|nothing at all}.
The embers crackle under the traveler's stick.
The forest beyond the fire is very dark.
The traveler will not meet (subject)'s eye when (subject.he/she) mentions the third door.

pieces.label: The Beggar and the Stolen Sunlight
pieces.text: On a strangely dim afternoon, an old beggar asks (subject) for shelter, saying the sun has forgotten the village.

pieces.label: Welcome the Beggar
pieces.text: "Come in, come in," (subject) says, and sits the beggar down with a cup of tea and a bowl of whatever is in the pot. The beggar beams, and settles in as though (subject.he/she) owns the place...

pieces.label: Offer a Place by the Fire
pieces.text: (Subject) waves the beggar inside to warm up by the hearth, since the dim afternoon has turned the air chilly. The beggar holds (subject.his/her) hands to the flames with a grateful sigh...

pieces.label: Ask Why the Sun Is Dim
pieces.text: "What do you mean, forgotten?" (subject) asks. "Why is the sun so dim?" The beggar tilts (subject.his/her) head and looks up at the brassy sky...

pieces.label: Chase the Beggar Away
pieces.text: "We've no room," (subject) snaps. "Go on, get away from my door." The beggar looks up at the dim sky, then back at (subject), and shuffles off without a word...
The clouds part at sunset and the beggar is gone, leaving a big basket of ripe fruit.
The beggar tells a story about a goat, a canoe and a surprised fisherman that is retold for years.
The beggar reads the smoke and birds and warns of rain, and the farmers cover their racks in time.
The beggar sleeps soundly and leaves at a perfectly ordinary dawn.
The dimness is smoke from a wildfire across the strait.
"Some lights return when remembered," and a sunbeam falls on (subject)'s doorstep.
Damp clouds linger for days and mould spoils some of the stores.
The sky clears the next morning, and no curse follows.
The sky is the dull yellow of old brass.
Birds roost {in the middle of the day|on every roof|in silence}.
The beggar's eyes are startlingly bright.
The cooking fires look strange in the gloom.

pieces.label: The Stranger Who Spoke to the Tree
pieces.text: (Subject) finds a hooded stranger whispering to the oldest tree in the village, who says the tree has been waiting a long time for an answer.

pieces.label: Ask What Was Said
pieces.text: "What did you ask it?" (subject) says. "And... what did it say?" The stranger takes (subject.his/her) hands from the bark and smiles...

pieces.label: Listen to the Tree
pieces.text: (Subject) steps in among the hanging roots, feeling very silly, and presses (subject.his/her) own ear to the great trunk. The stranger watches in silence...

pieces.label: Offer to Help
pieces.text: "If the tree needs something," (subject) says, "I'll help." The stranger looks genuinely delighted...

pieces.label: Send the Stranger Away
pieces.text: (Subject) does not like strangers whispering to the village's trees. "That tree belongs to the village," (subject.he/she) says firmly. "Please leave it alone, and move along."...
The tree answered with a riddle about patience and seasons that half the village puzzles over.
The tree asked for someone to care for its choking roots, so (subject) fetches a rake.
The wind through the canopy sounds almost like a slow voice in an unknown tongue.
A hidden hollow whispers words back, and the researchers learn how sound travels.
A dozen villagers clear the roots, and the old tree puts out new leaves.
The stranger leaves a packet of seeds "from the tree," which grow into sweet yams.
The stranger leaves quietly, and the tree stays as it always was.
A great branch falls in the windless night across (subject)'s morning path.
Roots hang from the branches like ropes.
The stranger's hands rest flat on the bark.
The canopy {creaks|sighs|rustles} far above.
A bird in the banyan stops singing to listen.

pieces.label: The Returned Lost Child
pieces.text: A child who vanished from the village years ago appears at the edge of the grass, not a day older, wearing the same shell necklace.

pieces.label: Welcome the Child Home
pieces.text: (Subject) does not stop to think. (subject.He/she) runs to the child, kneels, and takes (subject.his/her) small hands. "Come home," (subject.he/she) says, voice shaking. "Come on, everyone will want to see you." The child lets (subject.him/her) lead the way...

pieces.label: Ask Where They Have Been
pieces.text: (Subject) kneels down in the grass, slowly, so as not to frighten the child. "Where have you been all this time?" (subject.he/she) asks softly. The child thinks about it seriously...

pieces.label: Seek an Explanation
pieces.text: Before letting anyone get their hopes up, (subject) fetches the elders. They come out to the grass and look the child over carefully, and ask (subject.him/her) a great many questions...

pieces.label: Give the Child Time
pieces.text: (Subject) decides not to overwhelm the child. The village offers (subject.him/her) a quiet hut to rest in, food and a blanket, and leaves (subject.him/her) be, without demanding a single answer...
The family hold the child for a long time; many questions remain, but (subject.he/she) stays.
The child recognizes no one and is reunited with another family in the next village.
The child lived with kind strangers beyond the hills, but the valley is found empty.
The child speaks of a place where the seasons never changed.
The elders decide it is a relative with a striking resemblance, and a coastal family raises (subject.him/her).
The child answers questions only the missing child could know.
The village shelters the child without asking, and after a week (subject.he/she) takes the mother's hand.
The child is gone before dawn, leaving a carved turtle that is still warm.
The little shell necklace is exactly the same.
The grass sways around the child.
An old mother {drops her basket|cannot speak|whispers a name}.
The child waits calmly, as if this is all quite ordinary.

pieces.label: The Wandering Herbalist's Box
pieces.text: A traveling herbalist leaves a lacquered medicine box with (subject) to keep until the full moon, and then (friend) falls sick with a fever no one can break.

pieces.label: Open the Box for an Emergency
pieces.text: (Subject) hesitates for a long time, then decides a promise is worth less than a life. (subject.He/she) carries the box to the healers' hut and opens it. Inside, packed in tiny compartments, are dozens of dried herbs, powders and roots...

pieces.label: Keep It Sealed
pieces.text: (Subject) made a promise. (subject.He/she) keeps the box closed on the shelf, and helps the healers care for (friend) in the ordinary way, with cool cloths and broth, through the long nights...

pieces.label: Study the Labels
pieces.text: (Subject) does not open the remedies, but (subject.he/she) does take the box to the healers so they can look at the tiny painted labels on each compartment, in case any of them might help...

pieces.label: Search for the Herbalist
pieces.text: (Subject) decides the best thing to do is find the herbalist and bring (subject.him/her) back. (subject.He/she) sets off up the road the herbalist took, box in (subject.his/her) bag, asking at every village (subject.he/she) passes...
A careful tea from one herb breaks (friend)'s fever overnight.
An unknown powder makes (friend) dizzy and sick for days, and is put away for good.
The herbalist returns at the full moon and mixes the right remedy.
The full moon passes, and the herbalist never comes back.
The labels teach the healers a faster, safer way to sort their remedies.
The labels are in a looping script no one can read.
The herbalist is found nursing another village through a fever, and sends a remedy home.
The trail ends at a cold, abandoned camp with no sign of the traveler.
The box smells of camphor and dried ginger.
Tiny white flowers are painted on the black lacquer.
The moon is {nearly full|swelling each night|almost round}.
(Friend)'s fever {climbs|holds|will not break}.

pieces.label: The Guest with the Old Song
pieces.text: A visitor sings the village's oldest song with (subject), and keeps going past where the song has always ended, into a verse no one has ever heard.

pieces.label: Sing Together
pieces.text: (Subject) catches the tune, stumbles over the unfamiliar words, then finds them, and sings along with the visitor into the new verse, while the whole fire listens...

pieces.label: Ask Where They Learned It
pieces.text: When the last note fades, (subject) asks, quietly, "Where did you learn that verse? Nobody here knows it." The visitor looks into the fire...

pieces.label: Offer Hospitality
pieces.text: "You must stay with us," (subject) says. "Please. At least for a few days." The visitor hesitates, then accepts with a little bow...

pieces.label: Refuse to Sing
pieces.text: (Subject) stops singing, uneasy. "I'm sorry," (subject.he/she) says, "I don't think I want to sing any more tonight." The visitor nods, unoffended...
The lost verse tells of the first canoe to reach Isola, and the song is whole again.
The visitor weeps: the song was (subject.his/her) family's, and (subject.he/she) thought it was lost.
A grandfather from this village taught it, and the oldest elder remembers him.
"I heard it sung before there was a village here."
The visitor stays a season teaching the children every forgotten song, including one about a crab.
The visitor leaves at dawn, and no one can remember (subject.his/her) face.
The visitor leaves, and the song's ending is never learned.
The visitor hums the lost verse walking away, and it becomes the village lullaby.
The visitor's voice is old and clear.
The fire {crackles|pops|sinks low} in the silence.
Everyone has stopped singing but the visitor.
An elder mouths along, then stops.

pieces.label: The Garden of the Vanished
pieces.text: (Subject) finds a hidden garden ringed with stones carved with the names of people who disappeared from Isola, and someone is still tending it.

pieces.label: Read the Names
pieces.text: (Subject) walks slowly around the ring of stones, reading every name aloud, softly, one at a time. Some (subject.he/she) knows. Many (subject.he/she) does not. And then (subject.he/she) comes to one that stops (subject.him/her) short...

pieces.label: Tend the Garden
pieces.text: (Subject) kneels and begins to pull the weeds from between the stones, gently, and brings water from a nearby stream for the swaying red and white flowers. When (subject.he/she) comes back the next day, (subject.he/she) brings friends...

pieces.label: Search for Its Keeper
pieces.text: Someone made this garden. Someone is keeping it. (Subject) is determined to find out who. (subject.He/she) searches the paths and thickets around the garden...

pieces.label: Leave It Undisturbed
pieces.text: (Subject) decides this is not a place for strangers. (subject.He/she) bows to the stones, backs out of the thicket, and tells only the elders what (subject.he/she) found...
Many names match the old records, and the researchers fill long-missing gaps.
One name belongs to a living villager, once lost for three days as a child.
The villagers take over the garden, and families finally have a place to grieve.
Every flower blooms out of season, and some call it a blessing.
(elder), a solitary old villager, has tended it alone for sixty years, and weeps when (subject) offers to help.
No keeper can be found, but the paths are always freshly swept.
It stays a quiet, half-secret place of remembrance.
A new stone appears, carved with a name no one knows.
Red and white flowers sway with no wind.
The stones are low and grey.
A name catches (subject)'s eye: {a fisher|a child|a traveler}, long gone.
The thicket closes softly behind (subject).

pieces.label: The Stranger Who Offered a Choice
pieces.text: At midnight, a cloaked stranger sets three gifts before (subject), a sealed green bottle, an iron-bound chest and a plain bowl, and says to choose only one.

pieces.label: Take the Bottle
pieces.text: (Subject) reaches for the green bottle. It is cool and heavy in (subject.his/her) hand. The stranger nods once, gathers up the chest and the bowl, and is gone. (Subject) works the wax seal loose, and pulls out the stopper...

pieces.label: Take the Chest
pieces.text: (Subject) chooses the iron-bound chest. It is heavy, and something shifts inside it. The stranger nods, gathers up the other two gifts, and is gone. (Subject) drags the chest inside and pries open the lid...

pieces.label: Take the Bowl
pieces.text: (Subject) looks at the gleaming bottle and the heavy chest, and then picks up the plain bowl. The stranger seems to smile under the hood, gathers the other two gifts, and is gone into the dark...

pieces.label: Refuse All Gifts
pieces.text: (Subject) looks at the three gifts for a long time. Then (subject.he/she) shakes (subject.his/her) head. "Thank you," (subject.he/she) says. "But I don't want any of them."...
The bottle holds a golden oil that soothes aching joints for years.
A sweet mist bursts out and leaves (subject) feverish in bed for days.
The chest holds fine old tools with drawings showing how to use them.
The chest holds spoiled grain whose weevils spread into the stores.
Left beneath a tree, the bowl fills with fresh fruit once a day.
The bowl stays empty, so (subject) gives it to a family with nothing to eat from.
The stranger smiles, bows and departs, and (subject) sleeps well.
"Then your choice is your own," and everything vanishes.
The moon is very bright.
The bottle is {dark green|cool and heavy|sealed with old wax}.
The plain bowl seems to vanish in the moonlight.
The stranger's hood hides everything but a smile.

pieces.label: The Last Stranger of the Season
pieces.text: On the last evening before the rains, a solitary traveler asks (subject) for shelter, and asks after villagers who died long before (subject) was born.

pieces.label: Invite the Traveler In
pieces.text: (Subject) swallows and steps aside. "Come in," (subject.he/she) says. "The rain's coming." The traveler smiles, and sits down by the fire, and the wind howls outside as the first heavy drops begin to fall...

pieces.label: Ask How They Know the Names
pieces.text: "Forgive me," (subject) says carefully, "but how do you know those names? (grave1) and (grave2) died long ago. Long before I was born."...

pieces.label: Offer a Meal Outside
pieces.text: (Subject) is uneasy about letting this traveler in. Instead, (subject.he/she) brings out a bowl of hot stew and a cup of water, and sets them on the bench beside the door, out of the wind...

pieces.label: Send the Traveler Away
pieces.text: Something about this traveler makes (subject)'s skin crawl. "I'm sorry," (subject.he/she) says, "we can't take anyone tonight." The traveler nods, and turns, and walks away into the wind...
All night the traveler tells stories of the village's dead, and the elders fill in the details.
At dawn the traveler is gone, leaving rare seeds "from (grave1)'s garden."
The traveler lived nearby long ago, and sits by the old memorial stones talking to them.
"Some names are carried by the wind," and the traveler hums (grave2)'s song through the storm.
The traveler eats gratefully and goes on toward the shore as the rain begins.
The traveler asks for a candle instead, and it burns all night at the memorial in the rain.
The traveler goes, the rains come, and the season changes as usual.
At dawn a familiar old voice calls from the empty, muddy path, and leaves no footprints.
The sky is heavy and purple with storm clouds.
The air smells of {coming rain|wet earth|the sea}.
The traveler's cloak snaps in the wind.
The memorial stones darken with the first drops.

pieces.label: The Undertow
pieces.text: (Swimmer) has swum out past the reef, where the water turns deep and cold, and the current takes hold of (swimmer.his/her) legs while (fisher), the head fisher, mends nets on the beach.

pieces.label: Swim Across the Current
pieces.text: (Swimmer) stops fighting the pull and turns sideways, swimming along the beach instead of towards it, the way the old fishers always said. (swimmer.His/Her) arms burn. A wave slaps (swimmer.him/her) in the face, and then another...

pieces.label: Wave and Shout for Help
pieces.text: (Swimmer) throws an arm up and yells (fisher)'s name as loud as (swimmer.his/her) aching lungs will let (swimmer.him/her). The wind takes most of it. On the beach, (fisher) stops mending, and lifts (friend.his/her) head...

pieces.label: Float and Wait
pieces.text: Float and Wait.

pieces.label: Swim Straight for Shore
pieces.text: Swim Straight for Shore.
The canoes search until dark and again at first light. The sea has kept (swimmer).
(Swimmer) crawls up far down the beach, and never loves swimming again.
(Fisher) paddles along the edge of the current and hauls (swimmer) in like the biggest catch of (friend.his/her) life.
By the time (fisher) reaches the place, the water is empty. The fishers bring (swimmer) home the next morning.
(Swimmer) lies back and floats until the current lets go, then drifts in on the evening waves, freezing and furious with (swimmer.himself/herself).
Past the reef the water turns from green to a deep, cold blue.
(Fisher) has said twice already that the tide is turning.
The shore is getting smaller.

pieces.label: The Three-Day Fever
pieces.text: (Patient) has had a fever for three days and is talking to people who aren't there. (healer) has one thing left to try: a bitter red root from the cliff that breaks fevers and can take other things with it.

pieces.label: Use the Red Root
pieces.text: (healer) grinds the root into a paste that smells like rust and wet stone, and spoons it between (patient)'s teeth. (Patient) swallows, makes a face like (patient.he/she) has bitten a beetle, and falls straight asleep...

pieces.label: Keep (Him/Her) Cool and Wait
pieces.text: (healer) puts the root away. (healer.He/She) sits by the mat all night with a bowl of cool water and a cloth, wiping (patient)'s face, listening to (patient) argue with the fish on the roof...

pieces.label: Use Half a Dose
pieces.text: Use Half a Dose.

pieces.label: Call in Every Healer
pieces.text: Call in Every Healer.
The fever breaks by morning, and the root takes (patient)'s name with it. Everyone calls (patient.him/her) "?" now.
The fever breaks before dawn, and the smell of the healers' hut, which (patient) always hated, has become a comfort.
A long night with a cool cloth. In the morning (patient) is weak, grumpy and fine.
The fever hangs on. The healers take turns sitting up. Recovery is slow when it comes.
(Patient) asks why the roof is full of fish.
The root smells like rust and wet stone.
A bowl of cool water and a cloth by the mat.

pieces.label: The Basket in the Mangroves
pieces.text: Among the mangrove roots, (finder) finds a well-made woven basket with a baby inside, and a canoe track in the mud leading out to the channel.

pieces.label: Take the Baby Home
pieces.text: (Finder) tucks the basket against (finder.his/her) chest and wades back through the roots, talking to the baby the whole way about crabs, and mud, and how they're nearly home...

pieces.label: Wait for Someone to Come Back
pieces.text: (Finder) sits down on a dry root with the basket on (finder.his/her) knees and waits, watching the channel, rocking the baby whenever (finder.he/she) starts to fuss. The tide comes in. The sun starts to drop...

pieces.label: Follow the Canoe Track
pieces.text: Follow the Canoe Track.

pieces.label: Call for the Healers
pieces.text: Call for the Healers.
No one comes looking. "I found you, so I'll take care of you." And (finder) does, every night and day.
Six people crowd into the hut with opinions, and by nightfall the baby is asleep on (finder)'s chest. "We'll take turns."
At dusk a canoe comes back with two exhausted parents who got lost in the channels. They decide to stay.
Nobody comes. A couple who have hoped for a child for years take the baby in, and (finder) is the favourite visitor.
The basket is tightly plaited, the kind of thing someone makes with care.
The baby grabs (finder)'s thumb and stops crying.
The canoe track in the mud is already filling with water.

pieces.label: The Pool Under the Moon Rock
pieces.text: On a dare, (looker) climbs to the Moon Pool, where dust from a pale rock that fell from the sky is said to make the water "remember" whoever looks into it.

pieces.label: Touch the Water
pieces.text: (Looker) dips one finger in. The water is warm, warmer than skin. The milky light gathers around (looker.his/her) finger and climbs up (looker.his/her) hand like a glove...

pieces.label: Drop a Stone In
pieces.text: (Looker) picks up a pebble and drops it into the middle of the pool. The ripples don't spread like ripples should. They gather, and fold, and take a shape...

pieces.label: Call the Friends Up
pieces.text: Call the Friends Up.

pieces.label: Walk Back Down
pieces.text: Walk Back Down.
{#made:One person climbs|Two people climb|Three people climb} out, exactly (looker). The village gives {#made:the newcomer a name|them names|them names} of {#made:its|their|their} own.
One more (looker) rises out of the pool, and the two of them finish each other's sentences.
Something with (looker)'s face climbs out, but it remembered only the outside. It becomes (made1).
The light fades and the pool is just a pool. (Looker) never goes up the hill again.
The water shines with a faint, milky light even in the shade.
The reflection is too sharp, like a carving rather than a picture.
The friends are waiting at the bottom of the hill.

pieces.label: The Blessing Stones
pieces.text: (Hopeful_parent) and (friend) have hoped for a baby for a long time, and the oldest healer presses two warm river stones into their hands with a promise of leaf tea.

pieces.label: Try the Stones and the Tea
pieces.text: The tea tastes of grass and something sweet. The stones go under the mat. (Hopeful_parent) and (friend) lie awake for a long time that night, holding hands, feeling a little silly and a little hopeful...

pieces.label: Let Things Happen in Their Own Time
pieces.text: They thank (healer) the next day, and give the stones back. "We'd like to just see what happens," (hopeful_parent) says. (healer) nods as if (healer.he/she) expected nothing else...

pieces.label: Ask the Healer What It Means
pieces.text: Ask the Healer What It Means.

pieces.label: Put the Stones on the Shelf
pieces.text: Put the Stones on the Shelf.
A few weeks later (hopeful_parent) can't stand the smell of fish. A baby is expected.

The healer listens to (hopeful_parent)'s belly and starts counting on (hopeful_parent.his/her) fingers. {#babies:"Just the one"|"Two, you'll want a bigger sleeping mat"|"Three, you'll want a much bigger sleeping mat"}
They stop counting the days, and a few months later a baby is expected. "No stones. Just us."
No baby comes that season, and every child in the village runs to their hut anyway. Their life is already full.
The stones are smooth, and warm from the healer's pocket.
The tea tastes of grass and something sweet.
Everyone knows, the way everyone in a small village knows everything.

pieces.label: The Struck Tree
pieces.text: Lightning split the big banyan last night while (first) and (second) sheltered under it, and the wood inside still glows faintly blue and hums like a hive.

pieces.label: Touch the Glowing Wood Together
pieces.text: They count to three and each lay a hand on the blue wood. It buzzes up their arms like a swarm of bees under the skin. The ringing in their ears gets louder and louder...

pieces.label: Leave It Be
pieces.text: (First) grabs (second)'s arm and walks (friend.him/her) firmly away. They go home and try to forget about it. That night, both of them have the same dream, of standing under the tree, looking out of the other one's eyes...

pieces.label: Ask the Elders
pieces.text: Ask the Elders.

pieces.label: Sleep Under the Tree Again
pieces.text: Sleep Under the Tree Again.
When the buzzing stops, (first) is looking at (second)'s hands. The tree stays dark ever after.
A crack, a smell of singed hair, and their hair doesn't lie flat for a week.
They wake up in each other's huts. "Your back hurts." "I know. I did tell you."
At breakfast they act out the shared dream as each other, and the whole village cries with laughter.
The two halves of the banyan are still smoking a little.
A ringing in their ears sounds a lot like each other's voices.
Their hair is still standing on end.

pieces.label: The Night of the Big Wind
pieces.text: A storm screams over the village after dark. (builder) checks roof poles hut to hut, and old (elder)'s roof is sagging badly, but (elder.he/she) won't leave the hut (elder.he/she) was born in.

pieces.label: Prop the Roofs Now
pieces.text: (builder) shouts for every pair of hands that can hold a pole. In the howling dark, the villagers stagger from hut to hut, wedging posts under the worst roofs while the rain comes sideways...

pieces.label: Everyone into the Storehouse
pieces.text: The storehouse has thick walls and a low, heavy roof. (builder) bangs on every door and herds the whole village inside, children and elders and dogs, and even old (elder), grumbling, carried the last few steps...

pieces.label: Carry (Name) Out
pieces.text: Carry (Elder) Out.

pieces.label: Wait It Out at Home
pieces.text: Wait It Out at Home.
They work all night, and every hut is still standing by morning.
The middle beam of (elder)'s hut gives way, and the neighbours dig (elder.him/her) out too late.
Forty people and three dogs in one room. Everyone is there in the morning, and the huts go back up stronger.
A palm crashes across the storehouse and soaks the village's notes and carvings.
Every few minutes something cracks out in the dark.
"The roof has held for sixty years."
The rain comes sideways.

pieces.label: The Mirror Shell
pieces.text: A shell as big as a cooking pot washes up, polished inside like a mirror, and the face in it keeps flickering younger and older. A fisher says deep-water shells "keep" a little of every face they've seen.

pieces.label: Keep Looking
pieces.text: (Finder) sits cross-legged in front of the shell and stares. The face in the mirror flickers faster and faster, young, old, young, old, like a fish flashing in a stream...

pieces.label: Wrap It Up and Put It Away
pieces.text: (Finder) sends the queue home, wraps the shell in an old mat and shoves it under (finder.his/her) sleeping shelf. That night, (finder.he/she) wakes up to a faint silver light leaking out from under the mat...

pieces.label: Let Everyone Look
pieces.text: Let Everyone Look.

pieces.label: Throw It Back in the Sea
pieces.text: Throw It Back in the Sea.
The flickering stops on a younger face, and it's (finder)'s own. "I look like I slept."
The shell stops on an old, kind face. "I look like my grandmother. She was the best person I ever knew."
In the morning (finder)'s face is different, as if the shell lent (finder.him/her) one.
The light fades, and the shell ends up as a bowl for fish scraps.
Half the village is queuing outside (finder)'s hut.
A faint silver light leaks out from under the mat.
The face in the shell flashes like a fish in a stream.

pieces.label: The Cliff Path
pieces.text: Halfway along the narrow cliff path with a full basket of eggs, (gatherer) is slapped against the rock by a gust, and a chunk of the ledge drops into the sea.

pieces.label: Keep Going
pieces.text: (Gatherer) presses (gatherer.his/her) back to the rock and shuffles forward, one heel at a time, the basket held tight against (gatherer.his/her) chest. The wide part is ten steps away. Then eight. Then five...

pieces.label: Drop the Eggs and Go Back
pieces.text: (Gatherer) lets the basket go. It tumbles down the cliff, and the eggs burst on the rocks like little yellow suns. (gatherer.He/She) edges backwards, inch by inch, (gatherer.his/her) cheek pressed to the stone...

pieces.label: Wait for the Wind to Drop
pieces.text: Wait for the Wind to Drop.

pieces.label: Call to the Other Gatherers
pieces.text: Call to the Other Gatherers.
The ledge gives way three steps from safety. (Gatherer)'s leg mends crooked, and the builders make (gatherer.him/her) a strong ironwood cane.
(Gatherer) cracks (gatherer.his/her) head on an overhang. Every egg is unbroken. The name never comes back.
(Gatherer) edges back and sits down hard on the grass. "The cliff will still be there next spring. So will you."
The wind comes again, harder. The gatherers bring (gatherer) home the long way, round by the beach.
The sea booms on the rocks far below.
The rock takes a very long time to hit the water.
The eggs burst on the rocks like little yellow suns.

pieces.label: The Cook Who Hated Cooking
pieces.text: (Helper) loves cooking, but (cook), the head cook, has had (helper.him/her) scraping pots and peeling taro for a month, and today something in (helper) snaps.

pieces.label: Speak Up
pieces.text: "I came here to cook," (helper) says, a lot louder than (helper.he/she) meant to. The whole cooking area goes quiet. Someone drops a ladle. (cook) looks up from the fire...

pieces.label: Keep Peeling
pieces.text: (Helper) picks the basket back up and peels. Thin. Then thinner. (helper.He/She) peels until (helper.his/her) fingers ache and the taro is as fine as paper...

pieces.label: Cook Something in Secret
pieces.text: Cook Something in Secret.

pieces.label: Ask Another Cook for Advice
pieces.text: Ask Another Cook for Advice.
"Then cook somewhere else." (Helper) walks out, and the smell of the fire just reminds (helper.him/her) of that day.
"Finally. A cook who won't stand up for the food isn't a cook." (Helper) gets the fish stew that night.
A peel so thin the light shows through it, and "Tomorrow you cook." (Helper) no longer minds the gritty feel of soil.
"I forgot you liked cooking. You're so good at peeling."
"Peel. Thin. Not like last time."
Someone drops a ladle.
(Helper) hasn't touched a spice in a month.

pieces.label: The Fog from the Vents
pieces.text: The hot vents breathe out a yellow, egg-smelling fog that the elders say "takes impressions" like wet clay, and (wood_gatherer) is caught in it, with footsteps beside (wood_gatherer.him/her) that move only when (wood_gatherer.he/she) moves.

pieces.label: Call Out
pieces.text: "Who's there?" (wood_gatherer) calls. From the fog, in (wood_gatherer.his/her) own voice, something answers: "Who's there?"...

pieces.label: Feel the Way Home Quietly
pieces.text: (Wood_gatherer) holds (wood_gatherer.his/her) breath and puts one foot in front of the other, feeling for the path with (wood_gatherer.his/her) toes. The footsteps beside (wood_gatherer.him/her) do the same, every step, all the way down the valley...

pieces.label: Stand Still Until It Lifts
pieces.text: Stand Still Until It Lifts.

pieces.label: Run
pieces.text: Run.
Out of the murk steps (wood_gatherer), looking at the trees as if it has never seen one. It becomes (made1).
(Wood_gatherer) follows (wood_gatherer.his/her) own voice deeper into the fog. Two sets of footprints lead towards the vents.
At the edge of the village there's a second (wood_gatherer) behind (wood_gatherer.him/her), scared of chickens and in love with the rain.
(Wood_gatherer) turns at the first huts and there's nobody there. Only the fog going out like a tide.
The fog smells of eggs.
Once the fog left a pair of identical goats.
(Wood_gatherer) can barely see (wood_gatherer.his/her) own hands.

pieces.label: The Canoe from the North
pieces.text: A patched canoe comes in from the north with a tired, sunburnt family aboard. Their island had a terrible year, and they ask politely for a few days' rest. Some villagers mutter about the food.

pieces.label: Invite Them In
pieces.text: (First_to_see_them) walks down the beach and holds out (first_to_see_them.his/her) hand. "You won't rest on the sand," (first_to_see_them.he/she) says. "Come up to the fire." Behind (first_to_see_them.him/her), a few of the mutterers go quiet...

pieces.label: Give Them Supplies for the Journey
pieces.text: (First_to_see_them) fetches dried fish, water gourds and a basket of fruit and carries it down to the canoe. The family thanks (first_to_see_them.him/her) over and over...

pieces.label: Ask the Elders
pieces.text: Ask the Elders.

pieces.label: Bring Them Food on the Beach
pieces.text: Bring Them Food on the Beach.
Under the sail cloth there's a baby. A week becomes a month, and nobody remembers deciding they should stay.
A grandparent with arms like rope, a gangly teen and a sleepy child. The grandparent is annoyingly right about the gardens.
They push off on the evening tide and wave until they're a dot.
The hidden baby cries as they push off, and the mutterers are first down the beach. "There's room."
The canoe sits low in the water, patched with bark.
They sit very close together.
A voice hoarse from the sea.

pieces.label: The Spotted Sickness
pieces.text: A sickness of red spots and a barking cough has three villagers down, and (healer), the best healer, remembers an old steam of sea-grape and smoke-root that might help, or might spread it to the healer.

pieces.label: Try the Steam
pieces.text: (Healer) sets the pot boiling in the middle of the healers' hut and holds the mat over each patient in turn, breathing the same steam (healer.himself/herself) to keep the pot right...

pieces.label: Keep the Sick Apart
pieces.text: (Healer) moves the sick into a hut of their own at the edge of the village. Only two healers go in, with cloths over their faces, and the rest of the village leaves food at the door...

pieces.label: Ask the Elders for Remedies
pieces.text: Ask the Elders for Remedies.

pieces.label: Try the Steam on Yourself First
pieces.text: Try the Steam on Yourself First.
The coughs soften and the spots fade. Every healer writes down the recipe and argues about it.
The steam works, but (healer) catches the cough and dies among the empty mats of the people (healer.he/she) saved.
Two slow, miserable weeks, but nobody else catches it. Someone leaves (healer) a basket of fruit.
It was already in the village. Three more wake up spotted and coughing.
A cough like a barking dog.
The steam smells like a swamp.
Food is left at the door of the hut at the edge of the village.

pieces.label: The Naming Stone
pieces.text: Once a year at the full moon, anyone may scratch their name off the village's naming stone and carve a new one. (Namer) has never liked (namer.his/her) great-uncle's name.

pieces.label: Carve a New Name
pieces.text: (Namer) scratches out the old name with three careful strokes. Then (namer.he/she) stands there with the knife over the empty stone, and realises (namer.he/she) has no idea what to carve...

pieces.label: Keep the Old One
pieces.text: (Namer) puts the knife down. (namer.He/She) runs (namer.his/her) fingers over the old carving, worn smooth at the edges, and sits by the stone until the moon is high...

pieces.label: Ask the Children
pieces.text: Ask the Children.

pieces.label: Ask an Elder About the Name
pieces.text: Ask an Elder About the Name.
A child says "(renamed). Like the brave one in the old stories." (Namer) carves it in big, clear letters.
(Namer) carves the first name that comes to mind. "That'll do."
(Namer) decides (namer.he/she) doesn't need to be like (namer.his/her) great-uncle, and gives up climbing.
"He fell out of trees fetching the children's lost balls." (Namer) carves the old name deeper.
The stone is covered in names carved by every generation.
The old carving is worn smooth at the edges.
The great-uncle was a very loud man who fell out of trees.

pieces.label: The Night Moths
pieces.text: On the one night the moon-vine blooms, (sleeper) falls asleep on the hill and wakes covered in great grey moths whose silver dust is said to "make you forget."

pieces.label: Lie Still
pieces.text: (Sleeper) holds (sleeper.his/her) breath. The moths shift their wings, slow and soft, like breathing. One by one, as the sky starts to grey, they lift off and drift away towards the vines...

pieces.label: Brush Them Off and Run
pieces.text: (Sleeper) leaps up, flapping and spluttering, and a great silver cloud bursts up into the dark. (sleeper.He/She) runs downhill through the glittering air, dust in (sleeper.his/her) mouth and eyes...

pieces.label: Blow on Them Gently
pieces.text: Blow on Them Gently.

pieces.label: Call for Help
pieces.text: Call for Help.
The name has gone, carried off on grey wings. The village calls (sleeper.him/her) "?" from then on.
The moths take away (sleeper)'s hatred of the cold shock of deep water. "Vine night."
The next day (sleeper)'s love of leaping in the dance is simply gone. The moths took the loving of it.
Nothing is missing, only silver dust that glitters in (sleeper.his/her) hair for a week.
Moths as big as a hand, with wings like breathing.
The moon-vine blooms for a single night.
Silver dust glitters on everything.

pieces.label: The Grandchild's Spell
pieces.text: (young) has been learning charms from the wise-woman and wants to try a "feeling young" charm on (elder), (young.his/her) grandparent. (Elder) remembers what happened to the goat.

pieces.label: Let (Young Name) Try
pieces.text: (young) waves the bundle over (elder)'s head three times, mutters the words, gets one of them wrong, says "Sorry, sorry," and starts again. The herbs start to smoke without being lit...

pieces.label: Tell (Young Name) to Practise on the Goat Again
pieces.text: "Goat first," (elder) says firmly. (young) sighs and goes to find the goat. A few minutes later there is a strange popping noise from behind the huts, and a startled bleat...

pieces.label: Ask the Wise-Woman to Watch
pieces.text: Ask the Wise-Woman to Watch.

pieces.label: Try It on Yourself First
pieces.text: Try It on Yourself First.
The grey goes from (elder.his/her) hair, and (elder.his/her) knees make no noise at all. "That's more than I meant."
The charm gives (elder) the face (elder.he/she) had at twenty-five, and nothing else. "At least I'm handsome while it hurts."
The goat sneezes the charm straight at (elder), whose face ages ten years.
The goat leaps onto a roof it couldn't reach for years, and lives there for a week.
A bundle of herbs tied with red thread.
"I'm nearly sure."
The herbs start to smoke without being lit.

pieces.label: The Child Who Followed the Parrot
pieces.text: (Lost_child) was chasing a red parrot at the edge of the jungle at noon and hasn't been seen since. It's late afternoon, and (search_leader) has gathered everyone who can walk.

pieces.label: Spread Out and Search
pieces.text: The villagers go into the trees in a long line, an arm's length apart, calling and calling, banging pots, shaking rattles, until the whole jungle rings with (lost_child)'s name...

pieces.label: Follow the Parrot
pieces.text: At sunset the red parrot comes back to its tree, right on time. When it flies off, (search_leader) and a few others follow it, crashing through the undergrowth, trying not to lose sight of the flash of red...

pieces.label: Light Fires on the Hill
pieces.text: Light Fires on the Hill.

pieces.label: Check Every Hut First
pieces.text: Check Every Hut First.
At dusk a small voice calls back from a dry gully. The village has a feast, and (lost_child) sleeps with a mango in each hand.
They search for a month and find a sandal and some red feathers. The village still calls (lost_child.his/her) name in the trees.
(Lost_child) is up a fig tree by the parrot's nest, and a slip and a bump have taken (lost_child.his/her) name.
The parrot lands on (lost_child)'s own hut, and (lost_child) is asleep inside.
The red parrot keeps landing just out of reach.
The whole jungle rings with (lost_child)'s name.
The shadows under the trees are getting long.

pieces.label: The Night the Whales Sang
pieces.text: Late one night (listener) wakes to a deep, slow moaning through the hut floor, and out past the reef, great dark backs are rolling in the moonlight. The whales are singing.

pieces.label: Wake the Whole Village
pieces.text: (Listener) runs hut to hut, shaking people awake, and soon the whole village is on the beach in its sleeping wraps, babies and elders and all, standing silent in the moonlight...

pieces.label: Listen Alone
pieces.text: (Listener) sits down on the cool sand and wraps (listener.his/her) arms around (listener.his/her) knees. It's just (listener.him/her), the moon, and the great slow voices out past the reef...

pieces.label: Paddle Out to See
pieces.text: Paddle Out to See.

pieces.label: Fetch the Elders
pieces.text: Fetch the Elders.
The whole village listens until the sky turns grey. "Do you remember the night the whales sang?"
The slow rhythm gets into everyone's hands. "It's in our bones now."
(Listener) listens until dawn and finds (listener.he/she) can sit still at last.
Nobody believes (listener) about the whales. (listener.He/She) keeps the night for (listener.himself/herself).
A sound like wind in a hollow log, but sadder and much bigger.
Great dark backs roll in the moonlight.
The elders cry a little without being sad.

pieces.label: The Mudslide
pieces.text: After a week of rain, a tongue of red mud has slid between the huts, knocking two off their posts, and (builder), the best builder, sees a long crack opening below the ridge.

pieces.label: Rebuild the Huts First
pieces.text: (Builder) gets every builder to work, digging posts out of the mud, straightening walls, re-tying thatch. People need somewhere dry to sleep tonight...

pieces.label: Drain the Hillside
pieces.text: (Builder) takes three villagers up the hill with digging sticks and baskets, and they start cutting a channel along the slope, just above the crack, to carry the water away to the stream...

pieces.label: Move Everyone Out of the Way
pieces.text: Move Everyone Out of the Way.

pieces.label: Build a Wall of Logs
pieces.text: Build a Wall of Logs.
Both huts are on their posts by nightfall, and the hill holds. "Lucky."
A second slide pins (helper), whose hip mends badly. (friend.He/She) becomes the one who tells the builders where to put their posts.
Two days of digging, and the water runs to the stream. The three diggers will tell anyone all about mud.
A week in the storehouse, where the food is. The cooks count the baskets with a pained look.
Everything smells of wet earth and broken roots.
A long crack has opened just below the ridge.
The builders stand ankle-deep in red mud.

pieces.label: The Cave of Echoes
pieces.text: (First) and (friend) have dared each other into the north-shore cave, where a wise-woman once went in to talk to herself and came out as two people, and halfway in the echoes start answering before they speak.

pieces.label: Shout
pieces.text: (First) takes a deep breath and shouts (first.his/her) own name at the dark. It comes back, and back, and back, and then, very close, it says it again in a voice that isn't an echo at all...

pieces.label: Whisper
pieces.text: (First) and (friend) whisper their names at the same time. The whispers slide off into the dark, and come back mixed up together, (first)'s voice saying (friend)'s name, (friend)'s voice saying (first)'s...

pieces.label: Sing
pieces.text: Sing.

pieces.label: Turn Back
pieces.text: Turn Back.
{#made:One more (first) walks|Two more (first)s walk|Three more (first)s walk} out of the dark, and they all agree about everything.
The last echo walks out with (first)'s face and a stranger behind it, and asks where the food is.
The whispers come back mixed, and so do they. "At least it's someone I like."
Something giggles deep in the cave, and they run all the way to the beach.
Each echo comes back a little different.
The cave has been "full of voices" ever since.
Cold air breathes out of the dark.

pieces.label: The Hundred-Year Lotus
pieces.text: The lotus the first villagers planted, said to bloom once a century and "give the village something it needs," has bloomed, and (finder) finds a baby asleep in the heart of the flower.

pieces.label: Lift the Baby Out
pieces.text: (Finder) slides (finder.his/her) hands under the petal and lifts. The baby is warm and smells of honey too. As soon as it is out of the flower, the great lotus begins, very slowly, to close...

pieces.label: Fetch the Elders
pieces.text: (Finder) wades back and runs for the elders. By the time they arrive, half the village is standing round the pond, and the lotus has begun to close, petal by petal, around the sleeping baby...

pieces.label: Sing to the Baby
pieces.text: Sing to the Baby.

pieces.label: Call (Name2)
pieces.text: Call (Friend).
"It seems it chose who to give it to." (Finder) carries the baby home in the petal.
(Friend) wades in clothes and all, takes the baby's other foot, and that's that.
The flower closes and sinks. "Another hundred years."
The closing flower breathes honey over the village, and for days nobody fights.
The lotus is as big as a canoe, pink at the edges and white in the middle.
The whole pond smells of honey.
The baby is wrapped in a petal like a blanket.

pieces.label: The Old Fisher's Last Voyage
pieces.text: (Old_fisher) has fished for sixty years, and now (old_fisher.his/her) hands shake. This morning (old_fisher.he/she) wants to sail past the far reef alone, "to see what's on the other side of the morning."

pieces.label: Let (Him/Her) Go
pieces.text: The young fishers help (old_fisher) push the canoe out through the surf. (old_fisher.He/She) raises the sail, waves once without turning round, and heads straight out towards the sunrise...

pieces.label: Talk (Him/Her) into Staying
pieces.text: "Stay," says the youngest fisher. "Teach us instead. Nobody knows these waters like you." (Old_fisher) looks out to sea for a long time, then at the young faces, and sighs...

pieces.label: Go with (Him/Her)
pieces.text: Go with (old_fisher.Him/Her).

pieces.label: Ask (Him/Her) to Wait a Day
pieces.text: Ask (old_fisher.Him/Her) to Wait a Day.
The sail becomes a white speck, and then nothing. The young fishers touch (old_fisher.his/her) spear for luck every morning.
At sunset (old_fisher) steers in a fish that takes four people to lift.
(Old_fisher) stays, and suddenly looks every one of (old_fisher.his/her) years. "I'm fine."
(Old_fisher) stays and teaches, and is "too old to be cross" anymore.
The young fishers carry (old_fisher.his/her) catch whether (old_fisher.he/she) asks or not.
(old_fisher.He/She) waves once without turning round.
The old canoe sits waiting at the top of the beach.

pieces.label: The Rivals at the Spirit Rock
pieces.text: (First_rival) and (second_rival) have quarrelled for a year about a fishing spot and a borrowed pot, and have come to the warm, handprinted spirit rock, where a quarrel "has to end one way or another."

pieces.label: Put Their Hands on the Rock
pieces.text: They glare at each other, and slap their hands down on the warm stone at the same moment. The rock thrums like a struck drum. The world turns over...

pieces.label: Walk Away Still Arguing
pieces.text: "This is silly," says (first_rival). "You're silly," says (second_rival). They turn their backs on the rock and stomp off in different directions. Behind them, the rock goes on thrumming, very quietly, as if it isn't finished...

pieces.label: Let the Elder Judge
pieces.text: Let the Elder Judge.

pieces.label: Shout at the Rock
pieces.text: Shout at the Rock.
The rock ends it the simplest way: now each lives the other's life.
The anger drains out like water from a cracked pot. "I don't even like that fishing spot."
They wake in each other's huts. "It has to end one way or another."
The village gives them a new pot and a new spot, and they argue about the weather instead.
The rock is warm and covered in faded handprints.
The rock thrums like a struck drum.
By now they mostly argue about who started it.

pieces.label: The Hot Spring in the Hills
pieces.text: A landslip has uncovered a cloudy hot spring. An elder's grandmother bathed in one and came out "looking like her own daughter"; her sister came out looking like their grandmother.

pieces.label: Get All the Way In
pieces.text: (Bather) sinks into the cloudy water up to (bather.his/her) chin and groans. The heat goes straight into (bather.his/her) bones. The steam is so thick (bather.he/she) can't see the rocks at the edge...

pieces.label: Just Soak the Feet
pieces.text: (Bather) sits on the black rock and lowers (bather.his/her) feet into the water. It's like being hugged by the ground. A cool breeze blows the steam into (bather.his/her) face...

pieces.label: Splash Water on the Face
pieces.text: Splash Water on the Face.

pieces.label: Bring the Healers
pieces.text: Bring the Healers.
An older face looks back from the still water. "Well, my back's better."
(Bather) climbs out looking years younger, and the next day there are two queues.
The steam does it. "It was only ever my feet."
A cough of weeks loosens in the steam, and the healers start bottling the water.
The water is cloudy white and smells faintly of eggs.
Steam rises from a hollow of black rock.
It's like being hugged by the ground.

pieces.label: The Fire in the Weaving Hut
pieces.text: A spark has caught the weaving hut's thatch. Inside is the great loom and the sail cloth (weaver) has been weaving for three months, and the fire is spreading to the next roof.

pieces.label: Go In for the Cloth
pieces.text: (Weaver) wraps a wet mat round (weaver.his/her) arms and ducks inside, into the heat and the roar. (weaver.He/She) can't see. (weaver.He/She) feels for the loom...

pieces.label: Help Stop the Fire Spreading
pieces.text: (Weaver) turns away from the door, and it is the hardest thing (weaver.he/she) has ever done. (weaver.He/She) grabs a bucket and runs for the next roof, where the thatch has just started to smoke...

pieces.label: Cut the Cloth Free from Outside
pieces.text: Cut the Cloth Free from Outside.

pieces.label: Pull Down the Burning Roof
pieces.text: Pull Down the Burning Roof.
(Weaver) comes out with the cloth, and (weaver.his/her) hands are badly burned. (weaver.He/She) teaches the young weavers instead.
Out a heartbeat before the roof comes down. The new weaving hut goes far from the cooking fire.
They lose the loom and save every other roof, and build a better one together.
The scholars' notes are burned and soaked. "At least we're all here."
Smoke pours past (weaver) in the doorway.
The great loom the whole village helped build.
The bucket chain is already forming.

pieces.label: The Sleepwalker
pieces.text: (Sleepwalker) has been sleepwalking to the headland all week. Tonight (neighbour) finds (sleepwalker.him/her) at the very edge, toes over the drop, looking out to sea.
