pieces.text: For three nights a wordless song has carried in from the reef, where (listener) glimpses a long-haired figure with what looks like a fish's tail. The old stories say it "gives back years to those who listen, and takes those who answer."

pieces.label: Answer It
pieces.text: (Listener) wades into the shallows and sings back, the first song that comes into (listener.his/her) head. Out on the reef the figure goes still, and turns, and holds out a hand...

pieces.label: Just Listen
pieces.text: (Listener) sits down on the sand and listens, hugging (listener.his/her) knees, while the song rolls over the water. It's so beautiful it hurts...

pieces.label: Paddle Out
pieces.text: Paddle Out.

pieces.label: Wake the Fishers
pieces.text: Wake the Fishers.
Footprints lead into the water and don't come out. A white shell comb is wedged in the coral.
The figure laughs like water over stones, and (listener) walks home years younger.
"Gives back years to those who listen." (Listener)'s face is years younger at dawn.
(Listener) goes back every night, and on the fourth night only a folded wrap is left on the sand.
The song is wordless and beautiful.
A comb carved from white shell.
It's so beautiful it hurts.

pieces.label: The Old Healer Steps Down
pieces.text: After forty years, (old_healer)'s healing hands shake, and (old_healer.he/she) wants to pass on what (old_healer.he/she) knows, but the young person with the best hands for it, (young), goes pale at the sight of a scraped knee.

pieces.label: Teach All the Healers
pieces.text: Every healer in the village crowds into the healers' hut, and (old_healer) teaches from dawn to dark, three days running, every remedy (old_healer.he/she) knows...

pieces.label: Take (Young Name) Aside
pieces.text: (Old_healer) finds (young) at the stream and sits down beside (young.him/her). "You've got good hands," (old_healer.he/she) says. "Steady. Healer's hands." (young) looks horrified...

pieces.label: Write It All Down
pieces.text: Write It All Down.

pieces.label: Teach by Stories
pieces.text: Teach by Stories.
Three days from dawn to dark, and every healer is better at the work.
(young) listens at the door and stops feeling sick at the thought of it.
"Good hands are good for lots of things." (young) becomes the best net-maker in years.
"Just hold the bowl." The child grins at (young), and something changes.
Forty years of remedies.
(young) goes pale at the sight of a scraped knee.
"Steady. Healer's hands."

pieces.label: The Double Rainbow
pieces.text: A double rainbow touches down just beyond the gardens, and the elders say where it lands "everything is twice as much." (First_there) is closest.

pieces.label: Step into It
pieces.text: (First_there) steps into the shimmer. The air is full of colours, red and gold and violet, warm on (first_there.his/her) skin, and everything seems to blur, as if (first_there.he/she) is seeing double...

pieces.label: Call the Whole Village
pieces.text: "Come and see!" (first_there) shouts, and the whole village comes running, and crowds round the shimmering end of the rainbow, elbowing for a look...

pieces.label: Throw a Shell In
pieces.text: Throw a Shell In.

pieces.label: Run Round It
pieces.text: Run Round It.
There are two of (first_there) in the wet grass. "Everything is twice as much. We did say."
The colours paint (first_there)'s face again, and (first_there.he/she) likes the new paint.
Nobody dares step in, and the day turns into a festival of berry-juice stripes.
The rainbow has moved over the sea. The children believe (first_there) anyway.
Red and gold and violet, warm on the skin.
One end touches the ground just beyond the gardens.
The children are already running for it.

pieces.label: The Shell Swap
pieces.text: (First_friend) and (second_friend) each wear half of a rare double shell, and an old carver warns that friends who swapped such shells "swapped a little of themselves" too.

pieces.label: Swap the Shells
pieces.text: They hang the shells round each other's necks. The two halves click softly against their chests, as if trying to fit back together...

pieces.label: Keep Their Own Halves
pieces.text: They look at the carver's face, and at each other, and hang their own shells back round their own necks. The carver nods, relieved...

pieces.label: Fit the Halves Together
pieces.text: Fit the Halves Together.

pieces.label: Ask the Carver to Swap Them
pieces.text: Ask the Carver to Swap Them.
Each sees (first_friend.himself/herself) wearing the other's shell. "I did say it was for weddings."
(First_friend)'s name feels as if it went with the shell, and (first_friend.he/she) chooses a new one.
Friends for life, and nobody has to swap anything.
(First_friend) starts coming to every gathering, because the shells click when they find each other.
Two halves that fit together perfectly.
The shells click softly.
The carver is watching, frowning.

pieces.label: The Leaking Roofs
pieces.text: The rains have come early and half the roofs are leaking. (Builder), who loves the rain and is already soaked from dancing in it, is handed a bundle of thatch. "You're wet anyway. Up you go."

pieces.label: Climb Up and Patch
pieces.text: (Builder) scrambles up onto the first roof. The rain hammers down, the thatch is slippery, and the wind keeps trying to snatch the bundle out of (builder.his/her) hands...

pieces.label: Go Round with Buckets
pieces.text: (Builder) grabs every bowl and bucket in the village and goes hut to hut, setting them under the drips. The huts fill with the plink and plonk of water...

pieces.label: Get Everyone on the Roofs
pieces.text: Get Everyone on the Roofs.

pieces.label: Wait for a Break in the Rain
pieces.text: Wait for a Break in the Rain.
Roof after roof until every hut is dry, and then (builder) goes back out to dance in the puddles.
By the twelfth roof (builder) never wants to feel another drop.
The buckets save the mats, and every roof is patched in a single bright morning.
Not enough buckets, and the food store drips for hours.
The plink and plonk of water in the bowls.
The thatch is slippery and the wind snatches at the bundle.
"You're wet anyway."

pieces.label: The Baby from the Waves
pieces.text: At the lowest tide of the year, a long-haired figure with what might be a tail sets a baby wrapped in seaweed on a flat rock, looks at (finder), and is gone. The grandmothers told of children "given by the sea."

pieces.label: Take the Baby
pieces.text: (Finder) scoops the baby off the rock just as the first wave washes over it. The baby smells of salt, and grabs (finder.his/her) hair, and laughs...

pieces.label: Wait for the Figure
pieces.text: (Finder) stands on the beach, the water lapping round the rock, watching the waves for long hair and a tail. The baby gurgles happily...

pieces.label: Call (Name2)
pieces.text: Call (Friend).

pieces.label: Sing to the Sea
pieces.text: Sing to the Sea.
The sea chose who was on the beach. Every year they leave a shell on the flat rock.
(Friend)'s grandmother told that story too. The three of them leave a shell every year.
The figure lifts the baby back into the waves. A test, the fishers say.
The figure doesn't come back, and (finder) snatches the baby up as the water reaches the wrapping.
Wrapped in woven seaweed, perfectly dry.
The baby smells of salt.
Always at the lowest tide.

pieces.label: The Hourglass Shell
pieces.text: (Finder) has found a spiral shell of fine white sand that runs back and forth on its own. The old tales call it "the keeper of hours": whoever turns it by hand will "turn their own time with it."

pieces.label: Turn It Over
pieces.text: (Finder) flips the shell. The sand stops, hangs in the air inside the spiral, and then begins to fall the other way, faster...

pieces.label: Let It Run
pieces.text: (Finder) sets the shell down and watches the sand run. Down, and back, and down again, steady as breathing...

pieces.label: Give It to the Scholars
pieces.text: Give It to the Scholars.

pieces.label: Bury It
pieces.text: Bury It.
Ten years settle into (finder)'s bones at once. "At least now I know what it does."
The sand rushes back, and (finder)'s face is years younger. Creaky knees, though.
(Finder)'s face ages quietly while (finder.he/she) watches. "Time passes when you watch it."
The sand moves with the tides, not with time. The scholars are disappointed.
Fine white sand runs back and forth on its own.
Steady as breathing.
Wrapped in three layers of cloth.

pieces.label: The Storm at the Lookout
pieces.text: A sudden squall catches (lookout) on watch at the lookout rock, with lightning hitting the ridge closer each time.

pieces.label: Shelter in the Lean-To
pieces.text: (Lookout) crawls under the palm leaves and curls up small. The rain roars on the leaves. Then the whole world goes white...

pieces.label: Run for the Village
pieces.text: (Lookout) runs down through the long grass, rain in (lookout.his/her) eyes, the thunder right on top of (lookout.him/her)...

pieces.label: Lie Flat in the Grass
pieces.text: Lie Flat in the Grass.

pieces.label: Climb Down the Rocks
pieces.text: Climb Down the Rocks.
Lightning strikes a body length away, and the flash burns (lookout)'s name away.
The lean-to holds, and (lookout) guides a squall-caught canoe in by shouting.
(Lookout) always loved the rain. Not anymore.
"That was the best run of my life."
A little lean-to of palm leaves.
The whole world goes white.
The lightning walks across the hill.

pieces.label: The Bark Boat Race
pieces.text: In the summer bark-boat race, (runner), the fastest runner, has won three years running. At the split rock both (runner.his/her) boat and a younger villager's boat are stuck.

pieces.label: Free (His/Her) Own Boat
pieces.text: (Runner) splashes in and pushes (runner.his/her) boat free, and races alongside it, faster than ever, down to the lagoon...

pieces.label: Free the Younger One's Boat
pieces.text: (Runner) reaches across the rock and gives the younger one's boat a push. It spins free and shoots off downstream. (Runner)'s own boat stays stuck...

pieces.label: Free Both
pieces.text: Free Both.

pieces.label: Stop and Watch
pieces.text: Stop and Watch.
Four years running, and from then on (runner) throws (runner.himself/herself) into everything with the same speed.
The cheer sounds thin, and the joy of running goes out of (runner).
The younger one wins, and it's the best race anyone can remember.
(Runner)'s boat drifts in last to a big cheer. "Next year."
Little boats of folded bark.
The stream splits around a rock.
The younger one is crying with excitement.

pieces.label: The Flood
pieces.text: The river has burst its banks in the night and brown water runs knee-deep between the huts, still rising. (builder) wants a wall of logs; others want to carry everything to the hill.

pieces.label: Build the Wall
pieces.text: (Helper) hauls logs with (builder) and a dozen others, waist-deep in brown water, wedging them into a line across the flow...

pieces.label: Carry Everything to the Hill
pieces.text: (Helper) carries baskets, mats, children and an outraged pig up the hill, trip after trip, while the water rises behind...

pieces.label: Get the Children Out First
pieces.text: Get the Children Out First.

pieces.label: Dig a Channel
pieces.text: Dig a Channel.
By evening the flood is draining back to the river. The wall becomes a proper bank.
The wall bursts with (helper) in the gap. The new bank carries (helper.his/her) name.
Everything safe on the hill, and every hut rebuilt on raised floors.
On the last trip, for an elder's carving box, (helper) is pulled under.
Baskets, mats and squawking chickens float past.
An outraged pig carried up the hill.
Waist-deep in brown water.

pieces.label: The Moon Tree
pieces.text: Asleep under the glowing moon tree, which "dreams of whoever sleeps under it," (sleeper) wakes at midnight to (sleeper.his/her) own voice humming in the branches.

pieces.label: Climb Up to Look
pieces.text: (Sleeper) climbs into the glowing branches. Near the top, sitting on a bough with (sleeper.his/her) back to the trunk, humming, is someone who turns round...

pieces.label: Lie Still and Pretend to Sleep
pieces.text: (Sleeper) closes (sleeper.his/her) eyes and breathes slowly. The humming comes closer, down the trunk, and (sleeper) feels someone lie down in the grass beside (sleeper.him/her)...

pieces.label: Call Out
pieces.text: Call Out.

pieces.label: Run Home
pieces.text: Run Home.
The tree's dream of (sleeper) climbs down at dawn, likes different things and laughs much more.
(Sleeper) as a child touches (sleeper.his/her) face, and in the morning it's younger.
{#made:One more (sleeper)|Two more (sleeper)s|Three more (sleeper)s} curled up in the grass. "It does that."
Only a hollow in the grass, as if someone got up early.
It glows faintly, like a lamp turned low.
(sleeper.His/Her) own voice humming in the branches.
A wise-woman planted it long ago.

pieces.label: The Elder Who Wants to Stop
pieces.text: (Elder) has worked every day of (elder.his/her) life and never taken a day off. This morning (elder.he/she) sits on (elder.his/her) doorstep and says, quite calmly, "I think I'd like to stop now."

pieces.label: Let (Him/Her) Rest
pieces.text: The village brings (elder) a soft mat and a cup of something warm, and leaves (elder.him/her) alone on (elder.his/her) doorstep in the sun...

pieces.label: Ask (Him/Her) to Teach Instead
pieces.text: "Teach us," says one of the young ones. "Just sit there and tell us what we're doing wrong." (Elder)'s eyes light up...

pieces.label: Throw a Feast for (Him/Her)
pieces.text: Throw a Feast for (elder.Him/Her).

pieces.label: Ask What (He/She) Wants
pieces.text: Ask What (elder.He/She) Wants.
The love of work has gone, like a fire that has burned everything it needed to. (Elder) feeds the birds, clearly happy.
"I should have tried this sixty years ago." (Elder) takes the afternoons off.
(Elder) tells everyone what they're doing wrong, and is right every time.
Teaching suits (elder) so well (elder.he/she) looks twenty years younger.
From before dawn to after dark.
A soft mat and a cup of something warm.
(elder.He/She) sits on (elder.his/her) doorstep and doesn't get up.

pieces.label: The Carved Cradle
pieces.text: (Hopeful_parent) and (friend) want a child, and (friend) has started carving a cradle before there's a baby. The old carvers say that's bad luck; the old healers say good luck.

pieces.label: Finish It Now
pieces.text: (Friend) carves every evening by the fire, with (hopeful_parent) sitting beside (friend.him/her), sanding the edges smooth with a piece of coral...

pieces.label: Put It Away for Now
pieces.text: (Friend) wraps the half-carved cradle in a mat and puts it up in the roof beams. "When it's time," (friend.he/she) says...

pieces.label: Ask the Healers
pieces.text: Ask the Healers.

pieces.label: Ask the Carvers
pieces.text: Ask the Carvers.
The cradle is finished on a full-moon night, and a month later a baby is expected.
{#babies:"Just the one, and the cradle is just right"|"Two, you'll need a wider cradle"|"Three, you'll need a much wider cradle"}
A few months later it's time, and the cradle is finished in three evenings.
The half-carved cradle goes to a neighbour's early baby. "Ours can have the next one."
Sanding the edges smooth with a piece of coral.
Everyone has an opinion.
Wrapped in a mat in the roof beams.

pieces.label: The Great Bird's Egg
pieces.text: On the cliff top (finder) finds a nest as wide as a canoe with a huge cracked egg and a tiny fist poking out, while a great white bird, said to "carry lost children home," circles overhead.

pieces.label: Help the Baby Out
pieces.text: (Finder) peels the shell away, piece by piece, as gently as (finder.he/she) can. Inside, curled up and blinking at the light, is a baby, warm and wet and furious about the whole business...

pieces.label: Leave It for the Bird
pieces.text: (Finder) backs away from the nest. The great bird drops down out of the sky, lands on the edge of the nest and looks at (finder) for a long time with one gold eye...

pieces.label: Call (Name2)
pieces.text: Call (Friend).

pieces.label: Bow to the Bird
pieces.text: Bow to the Bird.
"It carries lost children home. And this one was coming to you."
(Friend) holds out (friend.his/her) arms at the bottom of the cliff path.
The bird sets the baby down at (finder)'s feet. "I suppose this is home now."
The bird flies off with the egg towards another island. A white feather lies on the path.
An egg as big as a water jar.
One gold eye.
The wind of its wings.

pieces.label: The Cracking Cliff
pieces.text: A crack wide enough for a hand has opened along the cliff top above the eastern huts, and stones are pattering onto the roofs. (builder) wants to wedge it; others want everyone away now.

pieces.label: Help Wedge the Crack
pieces.text: (Subject) climbs up with (builder) and starts hammering logs into the crack with a stone. The cliff groans under them...

pieces.label: Get Everyone Away
pieces.text: (Subject) runs from hut to hut, shouting, herding families and children and goats out from under the cliff and across to the far side of the village...

pieces.label: Prop the Huts
pieces.text: Prop the Huts.

pieces.label: Ask the Elders
pieces.text: Ask the Elders.
The cliff comes down before they've wedged half. They plant a tree where it stood.
The edge breaks under (subject)'s feet. The families bring (subject.him/her) meals for a year.
The cliff comes down that night on empty huts, which are rebuilt in the open.
The cliff holds. The builders tell the doubters to be quiet.
Little stones patter onto the roofs.
The cliff groans.
A roar like the end of the world.

pieces.label: The Race to the Far Reef
pieces.text: In the yearly race to the far reef, a stranger in a carved canoe and a face-hiding hat turns for the open sea and calls to (paddler), "Race me further!"

pieces.label: Follow the Stranger
pieces.text: (Paddler) swings (paddler.his/her) canoe after the carved one, out past the reef, into the long blue swells, paddling harder than (paddler.he/she) has ever paddled...

pieces.label: Turn for Home
pieces.text: (Paddler) shakes (paddler.his/her) head and swings for home. Behind (paddler.him/her), the stranger laughs, and the carved canoe heads out to sea...

pieces.label: Shout to the Others
pieces.text: Shout to the Others.

pieces.label: Ask Who They Are
pieces.text: Ask Who They Are.
Two canoes over the curve of the sea, and only one ever comes back. Not (paddler).
The stranger tips their hat. "You'll do." (Paddler) comes home with a new sureness.
Everyone else was watching the stranger, and (paddler) wins by a canoe length.
The young paddler behind (paddler) keeps going after the carved canoe, and never comes back.
An old, beautiful canoe, carved all over.
A hat that hides their face.
The long blue swells past the reef.

pieces.label: The Second Shadow
pieces.text: For three days (subject) has had a second shadow, late and to the left, that sometimes waves. The elders say it is "trying to become someone" and will at the full moon, unless it's sent back to the cave pool.

pieces.label: Let It Happen
pieces.text: (Subject) sits by the fire as the full moon rises, and watches the second shadow stretch out across the ground, and thicken, and stand up...

pieces.label: Take It to the Cave Pool
pieces.text: (Subject) walks into the cave with a torch, and the second shadow follows, late and to the left, all the way down to the black, still pool...

pieces.label: Talk to It
pieces.text: Talk to It.

pieces.label: Stand in the Dark
pieces.text: Stand in the Dark.
The shadow becomes (subject) exactly, with opinions about the last three days.
A person with (subject)'s face who is very excited about being able to eat.
The shadow sinks and takes some of (subject)'s face with it. A fair trade.
One shadow, right where it should be. (Subject) keeps checking.
A little late, and a little to the left.
The black, still pool where shadows sink.
Sometimes it waves.

pieces.label: The Sleeping Sickness
pieces.text: (Patient) has the sleeping fever, which passes on its own but sometimes takes a little of the sleeper with it. (healer) can wake (patient.him/her) with harsh pepper-leaf smoke, or let (patient.him/her) sleep it off.

pieces.label: Use the Smoke
pieces.text: (healer) lights a pepper-leaf and holds the smoke under (patient)'s nose. (Patient) coughs, and sneezes, and sits bolt upright, eyes streaming...

pieces.label: Let (Him/Her) Sleep It Off
pieces.text: (healer) puts the pepper-leaf away and keeps watch instead, cooling (patient)'s face, giving (patient.him/her) water whenever (patient.he/she) stirs...

pieces.label: Sing to (Him/Her)
pieces.text: Sing to (patient.Him/Her).

pieces.label: Try a Milder Remedy
pieces.text: Try a Milder Remedy.
Awake, and the fever breaks. "This time," underlined.
Awake, but the fever took (patient)'s name with it. (patient.He/She) is "?" now, and cheerful about it.
On the ninth day (patient) wakes years younger in the face. "Best sleep of my life."
Weeks later (patient) wakes, weak but alive, having dreamed the whole time.
The taste of pepper stays for a week.
Woken only to drink.
Cooling (patient)'s face through the night.

pieces.label: The Festival Masks
pieces.text: (Sun_dancer) and (moon_dancer) have drawn the Sun and Moon masks for the festival, which are traded halfway through the dance, and the elders say the masks "remember the story" of two people who traded places.

pieces.label: Trade the Masks
pieces.text: They meet in the middle of the circle and trade masks, as the drums crash. When (sun_dancer) ties on the Moon, (sun_dancer.he/she) feels it settle, like a hand on the back of the neck...

pieces.label: Keep Their Own
pieces.text: They meet in the middle and, instead of trading, bow to each other and dance on in their own masks. Some of the elders mutter. The masks feel heavier...

pieces.label: Trade Them Twice
pieces.text: Trade Them Twice.

pieces.label: Take Them Off
pieces.text: Take Them Off.
The masks remember the story too well, and each looks out of the other's face.
The best festival anyone can remember, and everyone hums the drums for days.
They trade in a dream, and wake in each other's bodies.
"Two people who stayed themselves and danced together anyway. That's a good story too."
An old carving from the first village, painted fresh every year.
Like a hand on the back of the neck.
The drums crash.

pieces.label: The Fire at the Children's Hut
pieces.text: The thatch of the hut where the youngest children nap has caught fire, and they're still asleep inside. (Rescuer) is the first to see the smoke.

pieces.label: Go In Through the Smoke
pieces.text: (Rescuer) pulls (rescuer.his/her) wrap over (rescuer.his/her) face and plunges into the smoke, feeling along the floor for small warm bodies...

pieces.label: Tear Open the Back Wall
pieces.text: (Rescuer) runs round the back and rips at the woven wall with (rescuer.his/her) bare hands, pulling it open strip by strip...

pieces.label: Shout Them Awake
pieces.text: Shout Them Awake.

pieces.label: Pull Down the Roof
pieces.text: Pull Down the Roof.
Every child out, and (rescuer)'s arms and back badly burned. The children never forget whose arms carried them.
Every child out, singed and unhurt. The new hut has a wide door at each end.
The children tumble out through the hole, and the new back door is "(rescuer)'s door."
Torn hands bound for a month, and more food than (rescuer) can eat.
Small warm bodies on the floor.
The bucket chain is forming.
The children help by carrying things the wrong way.

pieces.label: The Washing Stones
pieces.text: (Washer) loves washing day, and everyone else lets (washer.him/her) do far more than (washer.his/her) share. (washer.His/Her) hands are raw, and a friend offers to take over.

pieces.label: Keep Washing
pieces.text: (Washer) waves the friend away and picks up the next wrap. The stream is cold, the stones are hard, the pile doesn't seem to get any smaller...

pieces.label: Swap with the Friend
pieces.text: (Washer) hands over the washing and sits down with the nets. The friend scrubs, and grumbles, and scrubs...

pieces.label: Wash Together
pieces.text: Wash Together.

pieces.label: Ask the Village to Take Turns
pieces.text: Ask the Village to Take Turns.
By sunset (washer) never wants to see a washing stone again. The love of it is just gone.
The whole village's washing flapping in the sun. The most satisfying thing (washer) has ever seen.
"It's not so bad, with the stream so cold and the sun so hot."
The patient hands that washed a thousand wraps make perfect knots.
The slap of wet cloth on the stones.
Clean wraps drying in the sun.
The pile is taller than (washer.he/she) is.

pieces.label: The Spring of First Light
pieces.text: High on the mountain, a spring runs for an hour at dawn, and the water "remembers the morning": whoever washes in it looks as they did in the morning of their life. (Climber) has climbed all night to reach it.

pieces.label: Wash Now
pieces.text: (Climber) cups the cold water in (climber.his/her) hands and splashes it over (climber.his/her) face. It's colder than snow-melt, and tastes of stone...

pieces.label: Wait for the First Light
pieces.text: (Climber) kneels by the spring and waits. The sky goes from grey to pink to gold. The first ray of sun touches the water, and it lights up like a lamp...

pieces.label: Drink It Instead
pieces.text: Drink It Instead.

pieces.label: Fill a Gourd to Take Home
pieces.text: Fill a Gourd to Take Home.
(Climber)'s face is younger: maybe the late morning of (climber.his/her) life. "Good enough."
Just cold water. Watching it glow was enough.
The face in the golden pool is (climber.his/hers) from long ago. The village doesn't recognise (climber.him/her) until (climber.he/she) laughs.
Clouds, thin light, and nothing happens. Halfway down, (climber) starts laughing at (climber.himself/herself).
Colder than snow-melt, tasting of stone.
The water lights up like a lamp.
The path is long and the hour is short.

pieces.label: The Lagoon Mirror
pieces.text: On a still morning the lagoon is as flat as polished shell, and (stander) has stood still in it longer than anyone ever has, until (stander.his/her) reflection starts looking back up very attentively. "The lagoon gets ideas."

pieces.label: Step Out
pieces.text: (Stander) lifts one foot. The ripples run out from it in perfect circles. The reflection doesn't break up. It lifts its own foot, too, and steps up...

pieces.label: Keep Standing
pieces.text: (Stander) keeps very, very still. The reflection does too. They look at each other for a long time, and the whole lagoon seems to hold its breath...

pieces.label: Wave at It
pieces.text: Wave at It.

pieces.label: Call the Children Closer
pieces.text: Call the Children Closer.
Someone steps up out of the lagoon with (stander)'s face and a whole new person inside.
The reflection breaks into a hundred pieces of sky. "I won. That's enough of that game."
The reflection blinks first, stands up and bows. "You win."
(Stander) is champion forever, carried up the beach on the children's shoulders.
Flat as a sheet of polished shell.
The reflection, upside down, at (stander.his/her) feet.
The whole lagoon seems to hold its breath.

pieces.label: The Contest of Hands
pieces.text: In a slow, snappish season, (organiser) suggests a contest of hands where everyone shows what they do best. The cooks want to know who'll judge cooking.

pieces.label: Judges and Prizes
pieces.text: The elders appoint judges. Everyone practises for a week. On the day, the clearing is full of stalls and shouting and smoke from a dozen cooking fires...

pieces.label: Show and Teach
pieces.text: No judges. No prizes. Everyone sets up in the clearing and shows what they do, and anyone who wants to can sit down and learn...

pieces.label: Let the Children Judge
pieces.text: Let the Children Judge.

pieces.label: Make It a Feast
pieces.text: Make It a Feast.
Everyone has practised so hard the whole village is better at its work.
The losers sulk, and half the village isn't speaking to the other half.
Three villagers find teachers who change everything for them.
Nobody learns much, but the boredom and snappishness are gone.
Smoke from a dozen cooking fires.
The cooks still say the cooking judge was wrong.
A slow season.

pieces.label: The Night Fishers' Lamp
pieces.text: Night fishing past the reef, (first_fisher) and (second_fisher) see a pale blue light rise under the water with thousands of fish following it. It "leads to the richest fishing in the world," and some who followed it never came back.

pieces.label: Follow the Light
pieces.text: They paddle after the blue glow, further and further out, the fish thick as rain around the canoe, the reef far behind...

pieces.label: Head for Home
pieces.text: (First_fisher) grabs (second_fisher)'s arm and shakes (friend.his/her) head, and they turn the canoe round and paddle hard for the reef, with the blue light glowing behind them...

pieces.label: Wait Where They Are
pieces.text: Wait Where They Are.

pieces.label: Cast a Net After It
pieces.text: Cast a Net After It.
(Second_fisher) leans over, says "Oh," very softly, and slips into the sea as the light goes out.
The fish jump into the canoe by themselves, and the whole village eats fish for a week.
With no wind and no stars, the canoe hits the reef. A blue lamp is carved on (first_fisher)'s grave post.
Home by the sound of the surf. "There won't be a next time."
Like a lamp carried just under the surface.
The fish thick as rain around the canoe.
The wind drops completely.

pieces.label: The Grandmother's Memory Charm
pieces.text: (elder) has made a charm of knotted string and shells to forget bad memories, but warns it "can't tell a bad memory from a good one if you aren't clear," and often takes a name instead.

pieces.label: Tie the Last Knot
pieces.text: (Subject) thinks of the bad year, as hard as (subject.he/she) can, and ties the last knot. The shells click. Something in (subject.his/her) head goes quiet...

pieces.label: Throw It on the Fire
pieces.text: (Subject) looks at the charm for a long time, and then throws it on the fire. The string burns blue. The shells crack in the heat...

pieces.label: Give It Back
pieces.text: Give It Back.

pieces.label: Wear It Untied
pieces.text: Wear It Untied.
The charm takes the nearest thing to hand: (subject)'s name.
The bad year goes soft and far away, and (subject) wants a new name to go with it.
"I'll keep my memories. Even that one." They talk until late.
The smoke takes (subject)'s love of learning instead. "At least I know what's left."
Knotted string and shells.
The string burns blue.
The shells click.

pieces.label: The Typhoon
pieces.text: The worst storm in living memory screams in under a green sky, the sea coming over the beach in great grey walls. (Last_out), last to leave for the hill cave, hears the goats bleating in their shore pen.

pieces.label: Free the Goats
pieces.text: (Last_out) runs down to the shore, waist-deep in surging water, and wrestles the pen gate open. The goats explode out of it and run for the hill...

pieces.label: Run for the Cave
pieces.text: (Last_out) turns and runs uphill, the wind trying to lift (last_out.him/her) off (last_out.his/her) feet, the goats' bleating fading behind...

pieces.label: Shout for Help
pieces.text: Shout for Help.

pieces.label: Climb Onto a Roof
pieces.text: Climb onto a Roof.
The goats make it. (Last_out) doesn't. The goats always graze near the grave.
(Last_out) staggers into the cave with a goat under each arm, and everyone is alive.
The village is wrecked but everyone is alive, and everyone learns something about building.
The goats and much of the food store are gone. A hungry season.
The sky has been green all afternoon.
Great grey walls of water.
Two goats turn up a week later, looking smug.

pieces.label: The Twin Pools
pieces.text: Two pools side by side in the hills, one warm and one cold, made by two sisters: the warm one "takes off years," the cold one "puts them on, with what they taught you."

pieces.label: The Warm Pool
pieces.text: (Bather) slides into the warm pool. It's like sinking into a bath of honey. (bather.His/Her) aches melt away one by one...

pieces.label: The Cold Pool
pieces.text: (Bather) steps into the cold pool and gasps. It's like ice. (bather.He/She) sinks under, and for a moment hears voices, very far away, telling (bather.him/her) things...

pieces.label: Try Both Pools
pieces.text: Try Both Pools.

pieces.label: Neither
pieces.text: Neither.
Ten years younger, knees silent, and (bather) runs all the way home.
A younger face, and the aches come back. "She didn't say anything about knees."
Ten years older, and knowing how to do it all better. "Fair."
Older, and nothing else. "The cold sister must have been in a bad mood."
Like sinking into a bath of honey.
Voices, very far away.
One warm and one cold.

pieces.label: The Leaping Contest
pieces.text: At the harvest leaping contest over a fire pit, (leaper), who loves jumping more than anything, takes a run up and sees at the last moment how much wider the pit has been dug.

pieces.label: Jump Anyway
pieces.text: (Leaper) leaps. For a long moment (leaper.he/she) is flying over the flames, the heat on (leaper.his/her) feet...

pieces.label: Pull Up
pieces.text: (Leaper) skids to a stop at the edge of the pit, arms windmilling. The crowd groans...

pieces.label: Ask Who Dug It
pieces.text: Ask Who Dug It.

pieces.label: Jump It Twice
pieces.text: Jump It Twice.
(Leaper) clears it by a hand's width. Champion again, and fearless all year.
A singed heel, and the joy of leaping is gone.
"Too wide." The pit is filled in, and (leaper) wins on the third leap.
The elders dug it wider "to make it more exciting." The whole village laughs.
The heat on (leaper.his/her) feet.
The crowd is chanting.
Arms windmilling at the edge.

pieces.label: The Sunken Statue
pieces.text: On the lagoon bottom the divers have found a sea-worn stone figure with open palms, like the old carver's "statue that makes company for the lonely," and up close its face looks very like (diver)'s.

pieces.label: Touch the Palm
pieces.text: (Diver) presses (diver.his/her) palm against the cold stone one. The water around them shivers, and the sand at the statue's feet starts to stir...

pieces.label: Swim Up
pieces.text: (Diver) kicks for the surface, and doesn't look back, though (diver.he/she) has the strangest feeling the statue's head turned to watch (diver.him/her) go...

pieces.label: Bring the Elders
pieces.text: Bring the Elders.

pieces.label: Dig It Out
pieces.text: Dig It Out.
{#made:Another head comes up|Two more heads come up|Three more heads come up}, all (diver) exactly.
Someone with (diver)'s face and nothing else of (diver.his/hers): "Hello. Are you lonely?"
The statue is gone the next day, the sand smooth.
(Diver)'s face is reshaped like stone worn by the sea. A calm face.
Arms out, palms up, worn smooth by the sea.
The sand at the statue's feet stirs.
The statue's head seems to turn.

pieces.label: The Coughing Season
pieces.text: A dry cough has gone through the children and three adults, and the healers are run off their feet. (Helper) can build an old-style steam hut over the hot spring, or go hut to hut with honey and leaf tea.

pieces.label: Build the Steam Hut
pieces.text: (Helper) and the healers build a little hut of woven leaves over the hot spring in a single day, and fill it with the sick, coughing and grumbling and sweating...

pieces.label: Go Hut to Hut
pieces.text: (Helper) goes from hut to hut with a pot of honey and a basket of leaves, day after day, making tea and sitting with the sick...

pieces.label: Ask the Elders for Old Remedies
pieces.text: Ask the Elders for Old Remedies.

pieces.label: Send the Children to the Beach
pieces.text: Send the Children to the Beach.
Three days in the steam and the coughs are fading. The steam hut becomes everyone's favourite place.
The steam is too much. An elder faints, and (helper) is teased for a month.
Two weeks hut to hut, and the children call (helper) "the honey one."
Two weeks with coughing children, and (helper) isn't squeamish around the sick anymore.
Coughing and grumbling and sweating.
A pot of honey and a basket of leaves.
The healers are run off their feet.

pieces.label: The Last Night of the Year
pieces.text: On the last night of the year, the village sits up until dawn while the eldest, (eldest), tells the story of the year: every birth, every loss, every storm and every good catch.

pieces.label: The Old Way
pieces.text: (Eldest) tells it slowly, solemnly, by the firelight, every name and every day, and the village sits in silence, listening...

pieces.label: With the Funny Parts
pieces.text: (Eldest) tells the hard parts gently, and then tells about the fish that jumped into the wrong canoe, and the night the pigs got into the stores, and the village starts to laugh...

pieces.label: Let Everyone Tell a Part
pieces.text: Let Everyone Tell a Part.

pieces.label: Sing It
pieces.text: Sing It.
The year is put down gently somewhere safe, and they watch the first sunrise in silence.
The long night settles into (eldest)'s face. "Worth it."
Tears and laughter together, the way the year really was.
A night of laughing washes the years out of (eldest)'s face.
Every birth, every loss, every storm and every good catch.
A moment of silence for each person lost.
The first sunrise of the new year.

pieces.label: The Fever Tea
pieces.text: In the middle of a fever that won't leave, (brewer) finds a purple spoon-leafed herb by the healers' hut that (healer)'s grandmother brewed "for fevers, or possibly for warts."

pieces.label: Brew the Tea
pieces.text: (Brewer) drops the leaves into the pot. The water turns the colour of a bruise and starts to hum, very faintly, like a bee trapped in a gourd. (brewer.He/She) pours out a cup for (patient), then, after a moment's thought, takes a sip first...

pieces.label: Wait for (Healer Name) to Remember
pieces.text: (Brewer) sets the leaves down carefully on a flat stone. "Think," (brewer.he/she) says. "Fevers or warts?" (healer) sits down, closes (brewer.his/her) eyes, and thinks for so long that (brewer) wonders if (brewer.he/she) has fallen asleep...

pieces.label: Taste It First
pieces.text: Taste It First.

pieces.label: Ask the Other Healers
pieces.text: Ask the Other Healers.
(Patient) drinks it, pulls a face like a child eating a lemon, and wakes up well. The healers write it all down. "It was definitely fevers."
The tea cures (patient), and gives (brewer) a fever-dream of a village with no names. (Brewer) wakes well, and nameless.
(healer) hums (brewer.his/her) grandmother's song: two handfuls, boil it twice, cool it under the moon. The fever leaves every hut.
By the time (healer) remembers, the leaves are black and slimy. (Patient) gets better the slow way.
(Brewer) tastes it and goes pale. It tastes like pepper, wet stone and regret. Nobody else is brave enough.
The leaves are shaped like little spoons.
The water turns the colour of a bruise and hums like a bee in a gourd.
"Or possibly for warts. One or the other."
Every blanket in the hut is soaked through.

pieces.label: The Night the Roofs Flew
pieces.text: A night wind lifts the thatch off half the village's huts, and at dawn everyone turns to (builder), the best builder, to decide what to do.

pieces.label: Rebuild Together Today
pieces.text: (Builder) climbs onto the nearest bare roof frame and shouts until everyone is listening. Children are sent for fronds, the strongest villagers to the grove with knives, and everyone else is handed a coil of rope and told to hold on to it and not let go...

pieces.label: Fetch Back the Old Thatch
pieces.text: "Our old thatch is out there drying in the sun," (builder) says. "No sense cutting new." The village spreads out into the jungle in a long line, picking up armfuls of thatch from bushes and branches and the tops of trees...

pieces.label: Send Only the Builders
pieces.text: Send Only the Builders.

pieces.label: Wait for the Weather
pieces.text: Wait for the Weather.
Everyone on a roof, or under one. By sunset every hut is roofed, greener and more crooked. "They'll do."
A cracked beam gives way under (builder). The roofs are finished, and (builder) walks with a stick from now on.
Whole roofs are found in the clearings like blown-off hats, and carried home four people to a roof.
The thatch is in shreds, it rains twice onto everyone's beds, and the food store gets wet.
The builders work through the night on their own, and the huts are roofed by dawn, but nobody can stay awake the next day.
People stand in their huts looking straight up at the sky.
Thatch hangs from every branch like washing.
Someone finds the chief's sandal in a tree.
"Hold on to the rope and don't let go."

pieces.label: The Still Pool Above the Falls
pieces.text: Kneeling at the still pool above the falls, which the elders say remembers everyone, (looker) sees (looker.his/her) reflection looking back at (looker.him/her) as (looker.he/she) was twenty years ago.

pieces.label: Reach Into the Pool
pieces.text: (Looker) pushes (looker.his/her) hand into the water. It is so cold it burns. The young reflection reaches up from below and takes (looker.his/her) fingers, firmly, the way a parent takes a child's hand to cross a stream...

pieces.label: Leave It Alone
pieces.text: (Looker) sits back on (looker.his/her) heels. There is something about the way the reflection is smiling that (looker.he/she) doesn't like, as if it wants something too. (looker.He/She) fills (looker.his/her) gourd from the stream below instead, and gets up to go...

pieces.label: Ask the Reflection
pieces.text: Ask the Reflection.

pieces.label: Splash the Water
pieces.text: Splash the Water.
The young reflection takes (looker)'s hand, and (looker) walks down the hill ten years younger.
The pool gives back the face, and only the face. "Everything else still feels fifty."
A cold drop from the gourd falls back in, and the pool takes it as a gift. (Looker) comes home with grey temples.
(Looker) dreams of being pulled into the pool by (looker.his/her) own young hands, and never runs down to the water again.
The reflection only says, "Not yet," and fades.
The pool looks like a hole in the ground filled with sky.
The water is so cold it burns.
The real (looker) touches (looker.his/her) face. The reflection doesn't.
The waterfall roars just out of sight below.

pieces.label: The Name Stone
pieces.text: (Namer) stands before the old Name Stone with a sharp shell, ready to scratch out a name that everyone connects with (namer.his/her) great-uncle falling out of a tree at a wedding.

pieces.label: Scratch a New Name
pieces.text: (Namer) kneels and scratches carefully into the stone, tongue between (namer.his/her) teeth. At sunset (namer.he/she) lies down beside it on a mat, feeling a little silly, and watches the first stars come out over the names of everyone who did the same before...

pieces.label: Keep the Old Name
pieces.text: (Namer) looks at all the names on the stone, all the people who wanted to be someone else, and puts the shell down. "It's just a name," (namer.he/she) says, and goes home. That evening, by the fire, someone mentions the wedding again...

pieces.label: Ask the Elders About the Stone
pieces.text: Ask the Elders About the Stone.

pieces.label: Scratch Two Names
pieces.text: Scratch Two Names.
In the morning the old name is neatly scratched out, and everyone already calls (namer.him/her) Tonga.
The new name on the stone is in someone else's loopy handwriting: (made1). It suits (namer.him/her) better.
(Namer) hears the whole story: the great-uncle fell climbing for a child's kite. Some old grudges come undone.
(Namer) climbs a palm for a coconut to honour the name, and the village makes it a festival.
The stone can't decide between two names, and scratches out both. (Namer) keeps the old one, slightly annoyed.
Hundreds of names, some nearly washed away by rain.
(namer.He/She) scratches with (namer.his/her) tongue between (namer.his/her) teeth.
"The stone sometimes knows better."
Somebody mentions the wedding again.

pieces.label: The Blessing Shell
pieces.text: A huge pink spiral shell that hums with children's laughter washes up, and it hums only in the hands of (hopeful_parent), who has been hoping for a baby with (friend) for a long time.

pieces.label: Take the Shell Home
pieces.text: They carry the shell between them like a full pot of water, and set it by the door of their hut. All night it hums, very softly, a tune that (friend) swears (friend.his/her) mother used to sing...

pieces.label: Give It Back to the Whales
pieces.text: "It's not ours," says (hopeful_parent). "If the whales want us to have a baby, they'll find a way." They paddle out past the reef at dawn with the shell between them in the canoe, and lower it into the deep blue water...

pieces.label: Ask the Fishers
pieces.text: Ask the Fishers.

pieces.label: Keep It Secret
pieces.text: Keep It Secret.
The shell goes quiet with one small laugh left in it, and (hopeful_parent) is pregnant with one baby.
The shell hums louder and louder, then stops. "{#babies:Just the one|Two|Three}. I'd start weaving {#babies:a cradle|two cradles|three cradles}."
On the way back from the reef, they tow in a young couple and their crying baby. The couple stay.
A whale sings right under the canoe, and that is all, and it is enough.
The fishers say it's just a big shell. It stops humming the moment they touch it.
The shell is pink inside and smooth as skin.
Held to the ear, it sounds like children laughing.
The paddles buzz in their hands.
"Whales leave these shells for people they like."

pieces.label: The Hollow Log
pieces.text: (Shouter) shouts "Hello!" into the great hollow log in the jungle, and the echo answers in (shouter.his/her) own voice: "Hello yourself. Are you coming through, or shall I?"

pieces.label: Walk Through the Log
pieces.text: (Shouter) ducks inside. It smells of moss and wet bark and something like a cooking fire a long way off. Halfway through, in the dark, (shouter.he/she) bumps shoulders with someone coming the other way, who says "Sorry," in exactly (shouter.his/her) voice...

pieces.label: Wait at This End
pieces.text: (Shouter) steps back from the log, very slowly, and sits down on a root to watch. For a long time nothing happens. A bird lands on the log and walks along it. Then, deep inside, there is a rustle, and then footsteps...

pieces.label: Shout Again
pieces.text: Shout Again.

pieces.label: Run Home
pieces.text: Run Home.
Someone comes out of the other end with (shouter)'s face and none of (shouter)'s tastes, and follows (shouter.him/her) home as (made1).
Two more (shouter)s step out of the log. "Sorry, I was behind you."
An exact (shouter) comes out, chewing its lip, and carries the basket home because it knows (shouter)'s back is sore.
"Your turn," says the dark. Only the basket is found, and footprints going in.
(Shouter) runs home and doesn't look back, and that night someone outside the hut says "Goodnight" in (shouter.his/her) voice.
The light comes down green.
The log smells of moss, wet bark and a far-off cooking fire.
The echo always comes back a little wrong.
A bird walks the length of the log and leaves.

pieces.label: The Festival Masks
pieces.text: Cleaning the old festival masks for the harvest dance, (wearer1) and (wearer2) each try on the other family's mask, which the rule forbids, just as (carver), the mask-carver, comes back up the path.

pieces.label: Keep Them On
pieces.text: The masks are warm, warmer than wood should be, and they smell of old smoke and coconut oil. (Wearer1) looks across at (wearer2), and through the shell eyes, (wearer2) looks very strange, and very familiar...

pieces.label: Put Them Back Quickly
pieces.text: They snatch the masks off and throw them back onto the mat just as (carver) comes round the corner. Two masks land face up and two face down. (carver) looks at the mat, then at them, and raises one eyebrow very high...

pieces.label: Dance in Them
pieces.text: Dance in Them.

pieces.label: Confess to (Carver Name)
pieces.text: Confess to (Carver).
They pull off the masks in each other's bodies. "That's why the rule."
Swapped, and each of them is better at both jobs than ever. "A better deal than I expected."
The old paint has come off on their faces, red and white, and won't wash off. Everyone loves it.
The family quarrel behind the rule was about a pig nobody remembers. They laugh their old grudges away.
(carver) is so pleased they told the truth that (wearer1.he/she) lets them carve the next masks.
Wooden faces with shell eyes and grass hair.
The masks are warmer than wood should be.
They smell of old smoke and coconut oil.
One eyebrow goes up very high.

pieces.label: The Goat Path
pieces.text: Late for the fruit gathering, (climber) stands at the start of the goat path, a foot-wide ledge along a sea cliff, while a goat watches (climber.him/her) chewing.

pieces.label: Take the Goat Path
pieces.text: (Climber) puts (climber.his/her) back to the cliff and shuffles out along the ledge, one foot, then the other. The wind pulls at (climber.his/her) clothes. Far below, the waves boom on the rocks. Halfway along, the ledge crumbles a little under (climber.his/her) heel...

pieces.label: Go the Long Way
pieces.text: (Climber) looks at the goat. The goat looks at (climber). "Not today," says (climber), and sets off the long way round through the jungle, at a jog, to make up the time...

pieces.label: Follow the Goat
pieces.text: Follow the Goat.

pieces.label: Wait for Tomorrow
pieces.text: Wait for Tomorrow.
The ledge gives way. (Climber) is laid to rest under the fruit trees, and a safe path is cut with (climber.his/her) name on it.
(Climber) lands on a lower ledge and hits (climber.his/her) head. (climber.He/She) knows the goats' names, but not (climber.his/her) own.
Jogging the long way, (climber) twists an ankle on a root, and walks with a stick from now on.
(Climber) walks the long way with old (elder), and learns more about (climber.his/her) work than in five years.
The goat walks the path in front of (climber) the whole way, and (climber) makes it, shaking. The goat looks bored.
The ledge is as wide as a foot.
The waves boom on the rocks far below.
The goat looks at (climber) as if (climber.he/she) is a very slow goat.
The wind pulls at (climber.his/her) clothes.

pieces.label: The Weaver's Last Mat
pieces.text: (weaver), the oldest weaver, with fingers knotted like old roots, has one more mat left in (student.him/her), and offers to teach (student) while making it, or to make (student) something to wear instead.

pieces.label: Ask to Be Taught
pieces.text: (weaver) puts (student)'s hands on the reeds and covers them with (student.his/her) own. "Not with your eyes," (student.he/she) says. "Feel it. Over, under, over. The reed tells you." They weave until the light goes...

pieces.label: Ask for Something to Wear
pieces.text: (Student) asks shyly for something to wear. (weaver) laughs, delighted. "Everyone always asks to be taught. Nobody's asked me for a present in years." (student.He/She) starts at once, (student.his/her) knotted fingers flying...

pieces.label: Ask for Both
pieces.text: Ask for Both.

pieces.label: Ask for a Story
pieces.text: Ask for a Story.
Over, under, over. The lumpy mat is the best first mat (weaver) ever felt, and (student)'s own work goes better after.
(weaver) ties the last knot, lies down for a nap, and doesn't wake. (Student) loses (student.his/her) heart for work.
A whole set of clothes in (weaver)'s mother's pattern, soft as feathers. "Don't sit in the mud."
While weaving a wrap, (weaver) talks about the small things (student.he/she) wishes (student.he/she) hadn't fussed over. (Student) stops fussing too.
Fingers knotted like old roots.
"Not with your eyes. Feel it."
A pattern along the hem that nobody has seen before.
The reeds whisper over and under.

pieces.label: The Raft at Dawn
pieces.text: At first light, (rescuer) sees a badly made raft out past the reef, low in the water, drifting towards the rocks, and (fisher), the best fisher, is already pushing out a canoe.

pieces.label: Jump Into the Canoe
pieces.text: (Rescuer) splashes out and throws (rescuer.himself/herself) into the canoe. They paddle so hard their arms burn, out through the gap in the reef, where the waves stand up tall and green and slam down again...

pieces.label: Run for Help
pieces.text: (Rescuer) runs up the beach shouting, and the whole village comes pouring down to the shore with canoes and ropes and paddles, while (fisher) goes out alone...

pieces.label: Swim Out
pieces.text: Swim Out.

pieces.label: Throw a Rope from the Rocks
pieces.text: Throw a Rope from the Rocks.
A tired adult, a teen with a split lip and a small child wrapped in a sail. They bail all the way home, and stay.
On the raft is only a screaming baby in a fold of sail. It stops crying only for (rescuer).
Five canoes bring in a young couple and their baby, six days adrift. They eat everything and stay.
The raft people are saved, but (fisher)'s canoe goes round the point and is never seen again.
The rope falls short twice, and lands on the third throw. Everyone gets ashore, scraped and coughing. They rest a week and sail home.
Three logs and a lot of rope.
A shirt waved on a stick.
The waves stand up tall and green and slam down again.
The raft breaks up on the rocks that afternoon.

pieces.label: The Knock After Midnight
pieces.text: Three soft knocks after midnight, and on (finder)'s doorstep in the rain is a baby wrapped in dry leaves, with a carved fish tied to its wrist and small bare footprints leading away.

pieces.label: Take the Baby In
pieces.text: (Finder) scoops the bundle up and kicks the door shut behind (finder.him/her). The baby is cold but not crying. It grips (finder)'s thumb with a surprisingly strong little fist, and holds on...

pieces.label: Follow the Footprints
pieces.text: (Finder) tucks the baby inside (finder.his/her) shirt and runs out into the rain after the footprints. They lead to the edge of the jungle and then, strangely, up the trunk of a tall tree, and stop...

pieces.label: Wake the Neighbours
pieces.text: Wake the Neighbours.

pieces.label: Wait on the Doorstep
pieces.text: Wait on the Doorstep.
(Finder) sits up all night with the baby on (finder.his/her) chest. "They picked my door."
(Friend) wakes, sits down, and takes one of the baby's feet in (friend.his/her) hand. They raise it together.
Up the tree is a soaked twelve-year-old who couldn't feed her baby brother. She goes home; the baby stays with (finder).
The footprints end at an empty tree. (healer), who has milk to spare, takes the baby in.
The neighbours come out, argue in the rain about whose turn it is, and the baby falls asleep through all of it.
Three knocks, soft and polite.
A little carved fish tied to the baby's wrist.
The footprints fill with rain.
The baby grips (finder)'s thumb and holds on.

pieces.label: The Builders' Wager
pieces.text: After a hard rainy season, (builder1) and (builder2), the two best builders, argue about how to fix the village's damaged huts, until (builder2) proposes a wager.

pieces.label: Take the Wager
pieces.text: By sunrise the village has been divided down the middle with a line of shells. Everyone on (builder1)'s side gets new posts and careful thatch, slowly. Everyone on (builder2)'s side gets patched up by lunchtime and sits about looking smug...

pieces.label: Work Together
pieces.text: "No wager," says (builder1). "We'll do it your way on the roofs and my way on the posts." (Builder2) opens (friend.his/her) mouth to argue, closes it, and holds out a hand...

pieces.label: Ask the Chief to Decide
pieces.text: Ask the Chief to Decide.

pieces.label: Let the Families Choose
pieces.text: Let the Families Choose.
Neither side falls down. Each builder learns from the other, and the line of shells gets kicked away.
The first storm tears off every patch, and (builder2) redoes them all properly, out of pure embarrassment.
One on the roof, one on the posts, trading cheerful insults. The crawling family walks in the front door again.
A rotten post brings down a roof and (builder1) with it. (Builder1) supervises from under a tree.
The chief decides they should both do it the chief's way, which is worse than either.
A doorway so slumped the family has to crawl in.
A line of shells down the middle of the village.
Cheerful insults shouted from roof to post.
"Fine. A wager."

pieces.label: The Grey Mist
pieces.text: A silvery mist that smells of ash and old flowers rolls down from the mountain and turns everything it touches grey, and (early_riser) remembers that it "borrows years from whoever it finds outside."

pieces.label: Wake Everyone
pieces.text: (Early_riser) runs from hut to hut, banging on doorposts, shouting at people to stay in and cover their heads. Most of them listen. Some of them come outside to see what the shouting is about...

pieces.label: Climb the Mountain
pieces.text: (Early_riser) wraps (early_riser.his/her) head in a cloth and climbs up into the mist. The higher (early_riser.he/she) goes, the thicker and colder it gets, until (early_riser.he/she) can hardly see (early_riser.his/her) own hands. Near the top, (early_riser.he/she) hears someone crying...

pieces.label: Stay Inside
pieces.text: Stay Inside.

pieces.label: Light the Fires
pieces.text: Light the Fires.
Three people who came out to complain about the shouting go grey from crown to chin.
(Early_riser) stays out longest and goes silver. The village makes (early_riser.him/her) a crown of white flowers.
At the top, (early_riser) sits with a grieving grey spirit and tells it about (early_riser.his/her) grandmother.
(Early_riser) leaves a flower, the crying stops, and the mist gives back what it borrowed, and then some.
The fires burn the mist off by noon, and only the leaves stay grey.
The mist settles over the huts like a cobweb.
A child's eyebrows have gone white.
Leaves turn grey at the tips.
It smells of ash and old flowers.

pieces.label: The Kite Hill Wish
pieces.text: A child's runaway kite lands in (wisher)'s garden, and (child) explains the rule: whoever sends it back up must make a wish for the sky spirits.

pieces.label: Make the Wish
pieces.text: (Wisher) closes (wisher.his/her) eyes and whispers the wish into the leaves of the kite. Then (wisher.he/she) lets go of the string. The kite jumps up into the wind as if someone has pulled it, higher than any kite has gone all day...

pieces.label: Just Give the Kite Back
pieces.text: (Wisher) feels silly. Wishes are for children. (wisher.He/She) hands the string back to (child), who looks a little disappointed in (wisher.him/her), and runs back up the hill...

pieces.label: Wish for Someone Else
pieces.text: Wish for Someone Else.

pieces.label: Fly It Together
pieces.text: Fly It Together.
The sky spirits take the wish literally, and (wisher) is twenty-five again. "I told you it was the rule."
(Wisher)'s face is young again, and the rest of (wisher.him/her) isn't. "I said LOOK."
(child) wishes for (wisher), and adds a wish of her own. Now she's fourteen.
(Wisher) realises children just don't sit still, gives up napping and works like (wisher.he/she) is young.
They fly it together until dark and forget to wish at all.
Kites made of leaves and string and stubbornness.
The kite tugs at the string, eager to go.
"That's the rule."
The kite jumps higher than any kite has gone all day.

pieces.label: The Healers' Moon
pieces.text: Under the rare mango-orange Healers' Moon, with half the village coughing and the baskets empty, (healer) must choose between climbing the cliff for night-flowers and brewing everything at the hut.

pieces.label: Climb for the Night-Flowers
pieces.text: (Healer) climbs by moonlight, which is bright enough to read by. Halfway up the cliff, the flowers start to open all around (healer.him/her), pale and glowing, with a sound like a hundred tiny breaths...

pieces.label: Brew at the Hut
pieces.text: (Healer) empties every basket onto the floor of the hut: old roots, dried leaves, bits of bark nobody can name. The healers sit in a circle in the moonlight and start brewing everything, one pot after another...

pieces.label: Bring the Sick Outside
pieces.text: Bring the Sick Outside.

pieces.label: Pray to the Moon
pieces.text: Pray to the Moon.
Two baskets of glowing flowers, a night of brewing and singing, and the cough is gone from every hut.
(Healer) slides down the cliff on (healer.his/her) back, still holding the baskets. Everyone is cured except (healer).
Under the orange moon even the old herbs work twice as well, and the village wakes up hungry and loud.
One odd pot cures the two sickest, and nobody wrote down what was in it. "Definitely bark."
The sick lie in the moonlight all night, and feel a little better, and catch a chill.
The moon rises the colour of a ripe mango.
The flowers open with a sound like tiny breaths.
Moonlight bright enough to read by.
"It had bark in it. Definitely bark."

pieces.label: The Mimic Bird
pieces.text: The Mimic, the jungle bird that copies sounds, is sitting on (copied)'s roof in plain sight, and it is copying (copied) itself, its outline stretching into a small, feathery (copied).

pieces.label: Catch the Bird
pieces.text: (Copied) climbs onto the roof very slowly, making soft cooing noises. The bird watches (copied.him/her) with its gold eyes and makes exactly the same noises back, in exactly the same voice...

pieces.label: Leave It Alone
pieces.text: (Copied) decides that whatever the bird is doing, (copied.he/she) doesn't want to be part of it. (copied.He/She) goes inside and shuts the door. On the roof, (copied.his/her) own voice starts to sing...

pieces.label: Shoo It Away
pieces.text: Shoo It Away.

pieces.label: Copy It Back
pieces.text: Copy It Back.
The bird turns into a whole second (copied) in (copied.his/her) hands. It whistles better. It stays as (made1).
The bird splits in mid-air into two perfect (copied)s. Now there are three.
A half-finished copy sits on the doorstep, (copied) outside and bird inside. "I wasn't finished."
The bird sings all of (copied)'s songs in (copied)'s voice, wrong notes and all, and (copied) goes quiet for good.
(Copied) waves a broom, and the bird flies off doing the chief's cough.
Small and brown, with bright gold eyes.
It does the cooking drum so well the cooks come running.
A feather stuck in (copied.his/her) hair.
The outline wobbles, and stretches.

pieces.label: The Red Fish Supper
pieces.text: (Catcher) has caught a once-in-a-generation red fish with blue spots and a sulky face, which is either very lucky or very unlucky to eat, and (fisher)'s grandmother woke up with a fever and a different name after eating one.

pieces.label: Eat the Fish
pieces.text: (Catcher) eats the whole fish, every bite, with a little salt. It tastes like nothing (catcher.he/she) has ever eaten, sweet and smoky and a little bit like lightning. By the time (catcher.he/she) has licked (catcher.his/her) fingers, (catcher.his/her) cheeks are burning...

pieces.label: Throw It Back
pieces.text: (Catcher) carries the red fish down to the water and lets it go. It swims a little way, then turns round and looks at (catcher.him/her), sulkily, with one eye...

pieces.label: Share It
pieces.text: Share It.

pieces.label: Ask the Fish
pieces.text: Ask the Fish.
(Catcher) dreams of chasing (catcher.his/her) own name into the deep, and wakes with the fever gone and the name gone too.
After a night of fever, (catcher) sits up sure that (catcher.his/her) name is (made1). "My grandmother was the same."
The fish traps fill up every morning for a week. That's what comes of being polite to the red fish.
The fish stares at (catcher) for a long time and sinks. (Catcher) eats cold breadfruit.
Everyone gets one bite, and everyone gets a mild fever and a funny dream, and nobody's name changes.
Fins like little fans and a sulky expression.
It tastes a little bit like lightning.
(catcher.His/her) feet in a bucket of cold water until dawn.
"Depends on who's asking."

pieces.label: The Old Fisher's Last Trip
pieces.text: (fisher), an old fisher with shaking hands and cloudy eyes, drags (companion.his/her) canoe to the water to see the yearly shoal of silverfish one more time, and (companion) runs down to stop (companion.him/her).

pieces.label: Go With (Him/Her)
pieces.text: (Companion) climbs into the front of the canoe and takes the paddle. (fisher) sits in the back, steering with one hand and pointing with the other, calling out the names of rocks nobody has used in years...

pieces.label: Talk (Him/Her) Out of It
pieces.text: (Companion) sits down on the edge of the canoe so it can't move. "You can't see," (companion.he/she) says. "You'll go straight onto the rocks." (fisher) glares at (companion.him/her), then at the sea, then back at (companion.him/her)...

pieces.label: Bring the Whole Village
pieces.text: Bring the Whole Village.

pieces.label: Paddle for (Him/Her)
pieces.text: Paddle for (companion.Him/Her).
A river of silver past the far rocks, and (fisher) teaches (companion) everything (companion.he/she) knows about the sea.
(fisher) watches the shoal, smiling, trails a hand in the water, and closes (companion.his/her) eyes for good.
That night the canoe and (fisher) are gone, and never found. Each year the food left on the beach is gone by morning.
Furious, (fisher) tells every fisher what they've done wrong for ten years. They catch more than ever.
Ten canoes follow (fisher) out, and the shoal scatters at the noise. (fisher) laughs all the way home anyway.
A whole river of silver under the water.
(fisher) calls out the names of rocks nobody has used in years.
Hands that shake, eyes gone cloudy.
"I'm going whether you come or not."

pieces.label: The Bitter Berry Week
pieces.text: A new bush with fat yellow berries spreads along the paths after the rains, from seeds a passing trader dropped, and the children who ate the berries no longer like their favourite things.

pieces.label: Dig Up Every Bush
pieces.text: (Investigator) gets the strongest villagers together with digging sticks, and they work their way along every path, pulling the yellow bushes up by the roots and piling them on the fire. The smoke smells sweet and sour at the same time...

pieces.label: Try a Berry
pieces.text: (Investigator) picks one fat yellow berry and eats it, while (healer) watches with (investigator.his/her) arms folded. It tastes like nothing. Then it tastes like everything (investigator) has ever disliked, all at once...

pieces.label: Burn Them
pieces.text: Burn Them.

pieces.label: Feed Them to the Pigs
pieces.text: Feed Them to the Pigs.
Three diggers get a faceful of the smoke and each go off something they loved.
The bushes are gone, and the children stop hating what they used to hate. A little feast.
The berry takes away whatever a person holds on to hardest: (investigator)'s love of food, and one old dislike.
The berry burns away (investigator)'s month-old cough, and now (investigator.he/she) can't stand lying in the shade.
The pigs eat every berry and go off mud for a week. Then they're fine.
Fat yellow berries that taste of nothing, then everything.
The smoke smells sweet and sour at once.
(child) eats a whole plate of greens.
"It just takes away whatever you hold on to hardest."

pieces.label: The Two Canoes
pieces.text: Two canoes tied together come in at sunset, loaded with everything their people own and a very unhappy goat, because the spring on their island has dried up.

pieces.label: Welcome Them All
pieces.text: (Greeter) holds out both hands, the old way, and says the words of welcome (greeter.his/her) grandmother taught (greeter.him/her). The old man starts to cry. The small boy lets go of the goat, and it runs off immediately...

pieces.label: Send for the Chief
pieces.text: (Greeter) runs to fetch the chief, who comes down the beach very slowly, looking at the canoes, the people, the goat. (greeter.He/She) asks a lot of questions. The strangers answer every one...

pieces.label: Offer Food First
pieces.text: Offer Food First.

pieces.label: Help Them Find Water
pieces.text: Help Them Find Water.
The couple and their baby stay, and the old man too, who can find water where nobody else would look.
The second canoe stays: a young woman, her teenage cousin from under the mats, and the boy with the goat.
The chief says yes, there's a welcome feast, and the husband turns out to be a very good cook.
The chief allows a week. The strangers slip away before dawn, leaving a cooking pot as thanks.
(Greeter) helps them find a spring on their own island's map, and they sail home with hope.
A goat that is very unhappy about the whole thing.
The old way of welcome, both hands held out.
The small boy will not let go of the goat.
Everything their people own, tied in two canoes.

pieces.label: The Lightning Tree
pieces.text: Caught on the hill by a sudden storm, (sheltering1) and (sheltering2) can run through the open grass or shelter under the black lightning tree, whose victims "come down from the hill a little mixed up."

pieces.label: Shelter Under the Tree
pieces.text: They huddle together against the black trunk. It is warm, which it should not be, and it hums under their backs. (Sheltering2) starts to say, "I don't like this," and doesn't get to finish...

pieces.label: Run for the Village
pieces.text: "Run!" shouts (sheltering1), and they go, slipping and splashing down through the long grass with their heads down. Behind them, the lightning finds its tree...

pieces.label: Lie Flat in the Grass
pieces.text: Lie Flat in the Grass.

pieces.label: Climb Down to the Stream
pieces.text: Climb Down to the Stream.
A white flash, and each of them is looking at their own face. "That's what they meant."
The lightning jumps. (Sheltering1) lives, weak on one side, white-haired where it came out.
Twenty steps away is close enough for the lightning tree. "Even from here?"
They reach the village pouring water from their sleeves, and the elders say they were lucky.
They lie flat in the grass while lightning hits all around, and walk home with their hair standing on end for a day.
The trunk is black, twisted and shiny as a cooking pot.
The tree is warm and hums under their backs.
Water pours out of their sleeves.
"A little mixed up."

pieces.label: The Fig That Fruits Once
pieces.text: The seven-year fig tree has one fat purple fig, and whoever shares it will have a baby, but (farmer) has watered that tree every day for seven years, hoping.

pieces.label: Pick the Fig
pieces.text: (Hopeful_parent) reaches up and twists the fig off the branch. It comes away with a soft pop, and the whole tree seems to sigh. They split it in two right there in the garden, and eat it...

pieces.label: Leave It for (Farmer Name)
pieces.text: They walk away from the tree without touching it, and tell (farmer) about the fig. (farmer) runs out of (hopeful_parent.his/her) hut so fast (hopeful_parent.he/she) forgets (hopeful_parent.his/her) sandals...

pieces.label: Split It Four Ways
pieces.text: Split It Four Ways.

pieces.label: Ask the Tree
pieces.text: Ask the Tree.
The fig works, and (hopeful_parent) is pregnant, and a little guilty walking past (farmer)'s hut.
They confess. "It was never going to be for me." All four work the garden together after that.
(farmer) eats the fig, and two more grow overnight for (hopeful_parent) and (friend). "The tree pays its debts."
(farmer) is expecting at last, and promises (hopeful_parent) and (friend) the next fig, in seven years.
Four bites of one fig is not enough for anybody. It was delicious, though.
The fig is so heavy it bends the branch.
It comes away with a soft pop, and the tree sighs.
(farmer) forgets (hopeful_parent.his/her) sandals.
"Seven years I've watered that tree."

pieces.label: Too Many Babies
pieces.text: (Tired_parent), who had twins a month ago and hasn't slept since, sits on (helper)'s doorstep with both babies yelling and begs (helper) to take one, "just for a while."

pieces.label: Take One of the Twins
pieces.text: (Helper) holds out (helper.his/her) arms. (Tired_parent) hands over the louder one, which immediately goes silent and stares at (helper) with enormous, astonished eyes...

pieces.label: Help Some Other Way
pieces.text: (Helper) sits down beside (tired_parent) on the doorstep and takes one of the babies on (helper.his/her) knee, just to hold. "Go to sleep," (helper.he/she) says. "Here. Now. I'll wake you when they're hungry." (Tired_parent) is asleep before (helper) has finished the sentence...

pieces.label: Fetch the Healers
pieces.text: Fetch the Healers.

pieces.label: Start a Village Rota
pieces.text: Start a Village Rota.
"Just for a while" becomes a year, and the twins grow up with two homes.
The other twin won't settle without its sister. The village makes a rota with shells.
(Tired_parent) sleeps all afternoon on the doorstep with (friend.his/her) mouth open, and wakes up able to face anything.
The twins sleep, (tired_parent) sleeps, and the stew burns to a black crust. Worth it.
The healers say the twins are fine and the parent isn't, and send (tired_parent) to bed with a stern look.
One baby on each hip.
Asleep standing up, spoon in hand.
The louder twin goes silent and stares.
A rota, with shells, by the cooking fire.

pieces.label: The Painter's Pot
pieces.text: A visiting painter, (painter), wants to paint (sitter)'s "interesting face" with squid ink that is "very long-lasting."

pieces.label: Sit for the Portrait
pieces.text: (Sitter) sits on a rock in the sun while (painter) paints, humming, glancing up and down. The colours on the stone glisten. As the face takes shape, (sitter) starts to feel very odd, as if (sitter.he/she) is being looked at from two directions...

pieces.label: Ask to Be Painted Instead
pieces.text: "Paint ME," says (sitter). "On my face. Not on a stone." (painter) looks at (sitter.him/her), thinks about it, and then dips the brush...

pieces.label: Ask to Paint the Painter
pieces.text: Ask to Paint the Painter.

pieces.label: Refuse Politely
pieces.text: Refuse Politely.
The painted (sitter) blinks and sits up out of the stone. "That's never happened before. Well. Twice."
The portrait climbs out and says, "I don't like your clothes." The painter did the inside from imagination.
Blue and gold swirls across (sitter)'s face that no scrubbing brush can shift.
(painter) paints everything in the village, runs out of paint, and stays. "People sit still here."
(Sitter)'s painting of the painter is so bad the painter laughs for an hour and gives (sitter.him/her) a brush anyway.
A brush made of the painter's own hair.
Paint made from crushed shells and deep-sea squid ink.
"You have an interesting face."
The colours on the stone glisten.

pieces.label: The Rope Bridge
pieces.text: The rope bridge across the gorge is older than the oldest elder, furry with moss and sagging like a hammock, and (builder) said last week that it needs new ropes before anyone crosses.

pieces.label: Cross the Bridge
pieces.text: (Crosser) puts one foot on the first plank. It creaks. (crosser.He/She) puts the other foot on the second plank. It creaks louder. Halfway across, the whole bridge begins to swing...

pieces.label: Take the Long Way
pieces.text: (Crosser) sighs and starts walking. The long way is long, hot and uphill, and full of biting flies. Halfway round, (crosser.he/she) comes across (builder), cutting new rope in the forest...

pieces.label: Test It with a Rock
pieces.text: Test It with a Rock.

pieces.label: Cross on Hands and Knees
pieces.text: Cross on Hands and Knees.
The old rope gives way. (builder) builds a new bridge and never says "I told you so" again.
A plank snaps and (crosser)'s leg goes through. (crosser.He/She) limps from then on and can't stand heights.
(Crosser) helps (builder) cut new rope and learns everything about knots, weight and wind.
By the time (crosser) gets round, the fruit is gone. "It held. Creaked a lot."
The rock goes straight through the third plank. (Crosser) goes the long way, very quickly.
Ropes furry with moss.
The river far below looks like a piece of string.
It sags in the middle like a hammock.
Every plank creaks louder than the last.

pieces.label: The Cave That Keeps Names
pieces.text: At low tide, (caller) goes into the sea cave where the island keeps the names of everyone who ever lived, and finds (caller.his/her) own name written in shells under the water at the back.

pieces.label: Call Out
pieces.text: (Caller) calls (caller.his/her) own name into the dark. The cave takes it, and turns it over, and passes it back and forth between the walls, softer and softer, until (caller) can hardly hear it...

pieces.label: Leave Quietly
pieces.text: (Caller) backs away from the pool. Some things are better left unheard. On the way out (caller.he/she) passes a long row of names written in shells on the wall, and stops, and touches one...

pieces.label: Call an Ancestor's Name
pieces.text: Call an Ancestor's Name.

pieces.label: Take One of the Shells
pieces.text: Take One of the Shells.
The echo never comes back, and the cave keeps (caller)'s name. The village calls (caller.him/her) "?".
The echo comes back calling "Ponui," a great-great-grandparent's name. "The cave thought you should have it back."
(Caller) finds (caller.his/her) grandmother's name, and her lost brother's, and the family talks late into the night.
The tide comes in fast and throws (caller) against the shell wall.
Walls covered in tiny white shells.
Footsteps echo for a long time.
A name written in shells under the water.
The sea coming in, softly.

pieces.label: The Children's Spring
pieces.text: (child) leads (guide), (guide.his/her) favourite grown-up with a bad back, to a secret spring in the jungle that tastes like sugarcane and makes the children feel like running all day.

pieces.label: Drink
pieces.text: (Guide) kneels, which hurts, and drinks from (guide.his/her) cupped hands. The water is sweet, and fizzy, and makes (guide.his/her) teeth tingle. (child) watches (guide.him/her) very hard, waiting...

pieces.label: Just Wash (His/Her) Face
pieces.text: (Guide) doesn't trust water that makes children run all day. (guide.He/She) cups a little and splashes it on (guide.his/her) face, then sits back on (guide.his/her) heels and lets it drip...

pieces.label: Fill a Gourd for Later
pieces.text: Fill a Gourd for Later.

pieces.label: Tell the Elders
pieces.text: Tell the Elders.
(Guide)'s back stops hurting and (guide.his/her) hair falls over (guide.his/her) eyes, thick and luscious. "I TOLD you."
(Guide) drinks too much and is fifteen. "You're not a grown-up now. You're just BIG."
A splash on the face gives (guide.him/her) a young face, and the same bad back. "You're meant to drink it."
Nothing happens but a clean face, and an hour of the children's secrets, some of them alarming.
The elders go to see, and the spring has dried up overnight. (child) won't speak to (guide) for a week.
Water sweet and fizzy, tingling on the teeth.
A ring of very small footprints round the spring.
A nest of roots under a fig tree.
"It'll fix your back. I promise."

pieces.label: The Termite Year
pieces.text: Half the posts in the village have been hollowed out by termites, and (decider) must choose between smoking them out with bitter herbs or replacing every post.

pieces.label: Smoke Them Out
