pieces.text: "It's beautiful," says (wearer), "but I like my own face." (carver) looks hurt, and then thoughtful, and takes the mask away. That night (wearer.he/she) can't stop looking at it...
When the mask comes off, (wearer)'s face has changed, like a cousin nobody has met. "Told you."
A name is scratched on the back of the mask, and (wearer) answers to nothing else.
(carver) tries it on in the night and wakes up with a new face.
The mask is left on the beach, and later bobs out by the reef, facing the island.
The mask is warmer than wood should be.
It smells of salt and smoke.
A carver's hands sometimes know things the carver doesn't.

pieces.label: The Grey Shark in the Shallows
pieces.text: Halfway to the reef on (swimmer.his/her) morning swim, (swimmer) sees a big shark with a torn fin gliding along the sand beneath (swimmer.him/her), the one that once bit a canoe in half.

pieces.label: Keep Very Still
pieces.text: (Swimmer) floats, barely moving, as the shark circles beneath (swimmer.him/her) once, twice. Its eye rolls up to look at (swimmer.him/her)...

pieces.label: Swim for the Shore
pieces.text: (Swimmer) turns and swims for the beach as hard as (swimmer.he/she) can, kicking and splashing. Behind (swimmer.him/her), the grey shape turns too...
The shark gets bored and leaves, and the joy goes out of swimming for (swimmer) for good.
The shark nudges (swimmer) like a dog, and (swimmer), who never liked fishing, goes out with the fishers the next morning.
The shark catches (swimmer)'s leg in the shallows, and it never works properly again.
(Swimmer) scrambles out just in time. A crab walks across (swimmer.his/her) chest. "Not now."
A long grey shape glides along the sand.
The fishers say it once bit a canoe clean in half.
Its eye rolls up to look at (swimmer).

pieces.label: The Festival of Floating Lanterns
pieces.text: (chief) asks (organiser) to organise the longest-night festival, when the village floats a leaf lantern on the lagoon for every person who has ever lived there.

pieces.label: The Old Way
pieces.text: Each family sits in its own doorway in the evening, folding leaves and filling them with oil, saying the names of the people the lanterns are for...

pieces.label: All Together
pieces.text: All Together.

pieces.label: With Music
pieces.text: With Music.
Hundreds of little lights drift out to the reef, and nobody speaks. The village is gentle with each other for days.
Saying (organiser.his/her) grandparent's name, (organiser) lets a small child climb into (organiser.his/her) lap, and the noise isn't so bad.
Everyone teaches everyone something in the hot, loud hall.
The oil pot spills onto the food, and for (organiser), food never quite tastes right again.
Lanterns are made of leaves and candlenut oil.
One lantern for every person who has ever lived in the village.
The children fold lanterns badly and the elders fold them beautifully.

pieces.label: The Polished Shell Mirror
pieces.text: (polisher) has polished a giant clam shell into the best mirror the village has ever seen, from an old song about a clam that kept faces, and (looker)'s reflection blinks a moment too late.

pieces.label: Keep Looking
pieces.text: (Looker) leans closer. The face in the shell leans closer too, and then a little further, until its nose is right at the surface, as if it is pressing on a window...

pieces.label: Turn It Face-Down
pieces.text: (Looker) flips the shell over quickly. There's a soft thump from underneath, as if something has bumped into the inside of a door. (polisher) looks at the shell, then at (looker)...
Someone with (looker)'s face and none of (looker)'s manners climbs out and eats (polisher)'s breakfast.
An exact copy climbs out, and they both scratch their ears at once. "The song was right."
(polisher) takes one last look in the night, and the second (polisher) goes fishing.
The shell becomes a soup bowl, and a face looks up from the bottom of the soup.
The clam shell shines like still water.
The face in the shell presses on the surface like a window.
A soft thump comes from under the shell.

pieces.label: The Coconut Climb
pieces.text: (Climber) has looked at the biggest coconuts on the island every day for a month, and today (climber.he/she) is going to climb the tall leaning palm on the point to get them.

pieces.label: Climb to the Top
pieces.text: (Climber) loops the belt around the trunk and starts climbing, hand over hand. The palm sways more the higher (climber.he/she) goes. The crowd below goes quiet...

pieces.label: Halfway
pieces.text: Halfway.

pieces.label: With a Stick
pieces.text: With a Stick.
A gust at the top, a slide, the rocks. (Climber) wakes without a syllable of (climber.his/her) own name.
The bark belt snaps on the way down, and (climber)'s back never mends.
A coconut drops straight onto (climber)'s head. "Who's asking? And who's answering?"
Three big sweet coconuts roll to the cheering crowd.
The palm leans out over the rocks.
The top sways gently against the clouds.
"Don't," says someone. "Do," says someone else.

pieces.label: The Elders' Anniversary Wish
pieces.text: On the anniversary of the night they met, (elder) and (friend), elders who have been together longer than most of the village has been alive, see a falling star and get one shared wish.

pieces.label: Wish to Be Young Again
pieces.text: They both close their eyes and wish, as hard as they can, to be as young as they were the night they met. The sand under them grows warm...

pieces.label: Wish for Another Good Year
pieces.text: "Another good year," says (elder). "That's all." (Friend) smiles and nods, and they wish it together, quietly. The star burns out over the sea...
Their faces are the ones they had that night, though their backs still creak. "You've still got the nose."
Fifteen years younger, and worn out by sunset. "Same as last time."
The best year of all, and on the next anniversary (elder) falls asleep on (friend)'s shoulder and doesn't wake.
Good years, one after another, and two elders who never had patience for games join the children's races.
They met on this beach under a falling star.
The sand under them grows warm.
The star burns out over the sea.

pieces.label: The Hammock Built for Two
pieces.text: (Friend) has secretly woven a huge, lopsided, creaking double hammock for (mother) and strings it between the shadiest palms by the lagoon. One knot looks loose.

pieces.label: Climb Straight In
pieces.text: (Mother) climbs in, (friend) climbs in after her, and the hammock swings out over the sand, creaking happily. The loose knot holds. They lie there listening to the lagoon...

pieces.label: Check the Knots First
pieces.text: (Mother) tugs at the loose knot. It slips, and the whole hammock drops to the sand with a soft thump. (Friend) looks heartbroken...
Lazy afternoons, and (friend) starts weaving a tiny hammock to hang underneath.
The healers hear {#babies:one strong heartbeat|twins|triplets}. "I'll need more fibre."
They retie it together all afternoon, and the fiddly knots of building stop bothering (friend).
Nine children claim the hammock while they argue about the knot.
The hammock is beautiful, slightly lopsided, and creaks.
They lie there listening to the lagoon.
"For lazy afternoons."

pieces.label: The Lights on the Reef
pieces.text: For three nights, small green lights have bobbed on the reef after dark, lanterns of the drowned, the elders say. Tonight (rower) is pushing a canoe into the water.

pieces.label: Go With (Name2)
pieces.text: The two of them paddle out across the black lagoon towards the reef. The green lights drift apart as they get closer, as if making room for them...

pieces.label: Talk (Him/Her) Out of It
pieces.text: (Watcher) grabs the side of the canoe. "The elders said never," (watcher.he/she) says. "Never means never." (Rower) rolls (watcher.his/her) eyes, but stops pushing...
The canoe comes back dry, paddles laid neatly across it, and two more lights burn on the reef.
(Rower) topples in reaching for a light, and (watcher) brings (watcher.him/her) home too late.
In the morning (rower)'s mat is cold and the canoe is gone. One more light on the reef.
The lights were cousins night-fishing with glowing fungus lanterns. (Rower) is furious.
The lights are too steady for fireflies and too low for stars.
The green lights drift apart as if making room.
"Never means never."

pieces.label: The Swamp Fever
pieces.text: The swamp fever has come with the mosquitoes, and (sick) is burning up and talking to people who aren't there. (Healer), the healer, must choose between the fever-tree bark across the swamp and cool cloths at home.

pieces.label: Go for the Bark
pieces.text: (Healer) wraps (healer.himself/herself) in cloth from head to foot, smears mud on every bit of skin left over, and wades into the swamp. The mosquitoes find (healer.him/her) anyway...

pieces.label: Stay and Nurse
pieces.text: (Healer) stays. (healer.He/She) brings bucket after bucket of cool river water and lays wet cloths on (sick)'s head, day and night, and doesn't sleep...
Enough bark for every sick villager, and every healer learns to brew it.
(sick) is well in two days, but the fever takes (healer). A fever tree grows on (healer.his/her) grave.
On the third night the fever breaks, and (sick) puts a blanket over the sleeping healer.
On the third night (sick) goes still, and the healers cut a path to the fever trees.
The swamp grows warm and still.
(Healer) smears mud on every bit of skin left over.
The fever-tree tea is so bitter that (sick) yells.

pieces.label: The Name Carved in the Banyan
pieces.text: Sheltering under the old banyan, planted by a woman who could see the future, (sheltering) finds a name half grown over with bark, and (sheltering.his/her) own face carved beneath it, freckle for freckle.

pieces.label: Scrape the Bark Away
pieces.text: (Sheltering) picks at the bark with (sheltering.his/her) fingernails until the whole name is clear. (sheltering.He/She) reads it out loud, without meaning to...

pieces.label: Leave It Alone
pieces.text: (Sheltering) decides that a face carved before (sheltering.he/she) was born is none of (sheltering.his/her) business. (sheltering.He/She) waits out the rain on the far side of the trunk...
The name sounds more right than (sheltering.his/her) own ever did, and from then on (sheltering.he/she) is (made1).
Only the first half of the carved name is left, and the children think it's (sheltering.his/her) new name.
Curious about the woman who carved (sheltering.him/her), (sheltering) spends a day in the scroll hut (sheltering.he/she) always found dull.
The bark has grown back smooth by morning. (Sheltering) nods to the banyan ever after.
The name is half grown over with bark.
(Sheltering)'s face is carved freckle for freckle.
Beetles have eaten the rest away.

pieces.label: The Cook Who Lost (His/Her) Taste
pieces.text: (cook), the head cook, burned (taster.his/her) tongue a week ago and can't taste a thing, and after the chilli stew that made two fishers lie down, (taster.he/she) asks (taster) to taste everything.

pieces.label: Be the Taster
pieces.text: (Taster) stands beside (cook) at the fire all day, tasting every pot, every sauce, every half-cooked yam, and saying "more salt" or "less chilli" or "what is this?"...

pieces.label: Do the Cooking Instead
pieces.text: "Sit down," says (taster). "I'll cook. You can watch." (cook) sits on a log beside the fire, arms folded, looking deeply suspicious...
A week of half-cooked, over-salted food, and (taster) loses all interest in eating. "I've eaten enough for the rest of my life."
A secret handful of red chillies. (Taster) lies in the river for an hour and never enjoys food again.
(cook) shouts from the log, "STIR IT!", and the heat and smoke of the fire stop bothering (taster).
Burnt yams, a dropped pot, and a week of raw fruit.
Two fishers had to lie down after the chilli stew.
"More salt." "Less chilli." "What is this?"
(cook) watches in silence, which is worse than shouting.

pieces.label: The Hermit's Children
pieces.text: (hermit), who has lived alone on the far side of the island for years, hears that (subject.his/her) grown children are coming back to find (subject.him/her), and asks (subject) whether (subject.he/she) should want them to.

pieces.label: Tell (Him/Her) to Welcome Them
pieces.text: "They're coming all this way," says (subject). "Let them come." (hermit) nods slowly, and goes home to sweep (subject.his/her) hut for the first time in years...

pieces.label: Meet Them First
pieces.text: (Subject) waits on the beach every morning for a week. On the eighth morning, a canoe comes in around the point, and (subject) wades out to meet it...
A grown child, a partner, and a baby with (hermit)'s exact frown. They stay.
One grown child and two grandchildren. "Much better than the last island."
(Subject) tells the young family all about (hermit) on the walk, and the meeting goes better than anyone hoped.
Just a trader, and a rumour from somebody else's cousin. (hermit) leaves (subject.his/her) hut swept anyway.
(hermit) trades dried fish for salt twice a year.
(hermit) sweeps (subject.his/her) hut for the first time in years.
The canoe comes in around the point on the eighth morning.

pieces.label: The Two Carved Totems
pieces.text: The two old carved posts at the village entrance hold the spirits of two friends, the elders say, and if two people touch them at once, the spirits trade places to say hello. (First) and (second) are about to prove it's nonsense.

pieces.label: Touch the Posts
pieces.text: "On three," says (first). "One. Two. Three." They both slap their hands against the old wood at exactly the same moment. A cold wind blows straight down the path between them...

pieces.label: Let the Story Be
pieces.text: (Second) takes (first.his/her) hand off the post. "Leave it," (first.he/she) says. "Just in case." (First) shrugs. They walk away. That night, two little children sneak out to the posts...
(First) is standing on the wrong side of the path, in (second)'s body. The spirits only say hello once.
They swap and swap back, and neither can stand picking fruit or berries afterwards.
Two children sneak out in the night and wake in each other's bodies, and become best friends.
(First) repaints the posts in red and white, the way they used to look.
A cold wind blows straight down the path between them.
"One. Two. Three."
The posts look, people say, a little smug.

pieces.label: The Lotus That Opened at Dawn
pieces.text: A giant lotus bud in the pond behind the gardens opens at dawn with a sigh, and in the middle, on yellow petals, lies a yawning baby, sent by the Lotus Mother of the old story.

pieces.label: (Name) Takes the Baby
pieces.text: (Finder) wades into the pond, lifts the baby out of the flower, and holds it close. It smells of pollen. The lotus closes slowly behind (finder.him/her)...

pieces.label: Let (Name2) Take the Baby
pieces.text: (Finder) steps back. "You go," (finder.he/she) says. (Other) wades in and lifts the baby out, very carefully, like carrying a full bowl of water...
(Finder) carries the baby home with petals stuck to its head, and every spring the child says thank you to the pond.
(Finder) and (partner) spend the first night just looking at the baby.
(Other) raises the lotus child, and (finder), who never had patience for babies, walks it up and down at night.
The baby cries, and the lotus closes over it and sinks. The Lotus Mother will try again.
The bud is the size of a sleeping pig.
The baby smells of pollen.
The children clear the weeds out of the pond every week.

pieces.label: The Grey Fog Off the Mountain
pieces.text: The Old Breath, a thick grey fog that smells of ash, rolls down off the mountain, and (walker) is caught out in it halfway home with a basket of yams on (walker.his/her) head.

pieces.label: Keep Walking
pieces.text: (Walker) walks on, step by step, feeling for the path with (walker.his/her) toes. The fog presses against (walker.his/her) face like a damp cloth...

pieces.label: Sit Down and Wait
pieces.text: (Walker) sits down right there in the middle of the path, puts the yams in (walker.his/her) lap and pulls (walker.his/her) wrap over (walker.his/her) head. The fog swirls around (walker.him/her), cold and patient...
(Walker)'s hair is streaked with grey, though (walker.his/her) age hasn't changed. "The mountain only breathed on your face."
Ten years older in one walk. "At least I didn't drop the yams."
A few grey hairs that won't wash out. "It suits you," everyone says.
The fog flows around (walker) like a rock in a stream, and a lizard falls asleep on (walker.his/her) knee.
The fog smells faintly of ash.
It presses against (walker)'s face like a damp cloth.
The elders call it the Old Breath.

pieces.label: The Warm Lake in the Crater
pieces.text: In the old crater, (climber) finds the warm lake where, the elders say, the mountain spirit leaves a little of her youth each year, and a very old frog watches from a rock.

pieces.label: Bathe in the Lake
pieces.text: (Climber) slips into the warm water up to (climber.his/her) chin. It fizzes faintly against (climber.his/her) skin, like the sea after a storm...

pieces.label: Just Splash (His/Her) Face
pieces.text: (Climber) kneels at the edge, cups the warm water in (climber.his/her) hands and splashes it on (climber.his/her) face. It fizzes on (climber.his/her) skin...
(Climber) climbs out ten years younger and runs most of the way down the mountain.
The old frog hops onto (climber)'s foot, and (climber) comes home young-faced, and floats in the lagoon like a frog.
A much younger face, and the same aching knees. "Frogs," says (climber), mysteriously.
Just warm water. (Climber) and the frog watch the steam rise together.
The water fizzes like the sea after a storm.
The lake steams on cold mornings.
The frogs up there live very long lives.

pieces.label: The Shadow That Stood Up
pieces.text: At midday on the longest day of the year, when shadows shrink to puddles, (gardener)'s shadow is long, pointing the wrong way, and peeling up off the ground.

pieces.label: Stamp on It
pieces.text: (Gardener) stamps down hard on the corner of the shadow with both feet. It wriggles. It pulls. It is surprisingly strong...

pieces.label: Let It Get Up
pieces.text: (Gardener) steps back and lets it go. The shadow peels off the ground and stands up in front of (gardener.him/her), flat and dark, and then it begins to fill in...
It tears free and fills in with (gardener)'s face, hates gardening, loves fishing, and calls itself (made1).
The shadow slumps back down, sulking, and follows a moment late for the rest of the day.
It fills in as (gardener) exactly and weeds beside (gardener.him/her), humming the same hum.
It looks just like (gardener), says "I'm going for a swim," and argues about everything from then on.
Shadows shrink to puddles at people's feet.
The shadow peels up like a mat lifted at one corner.
It tears free with a sound like ripping cloth.

pieces.label: The Masks of the Harvest Dance
pieces.text: At the harvest dance, the moon is rising and (dancer) and (dancer) still have the old spirit masks on, which, the elders say, start to become the face underneath if left on too long.

pieces.label: Take It Off Now
pieces.text: (Dancer) stops in the middle of the dance and pulls at the mask. It doesn't want to come. It clings to (dancer.his/her) cheeks, warm as skin. (dancer.He/She) pulls harder...

pieces.label: Finish the Dance
pieces.text: The drums are too good to stop. (Dancer) dances on under the rising moon, and the mask gets warmer and warmer against (dancer.his/her) face...
The mask comes away with a soft sucking sound, and (dancer)'s face is a little more like the spirit's.
(dancer)'s mask stays on past moonrise, and (dancer.his/her) own mother needs a moment to recognise (dancer.him/her).
The grandmother of the mountain's face. The children bring (dancer) flowers, just in case.
The youngest spirit's face, young and bright. "The young spirit always was a show-off."
The masks are kept wrapped in bark cloth all year.
The mask clings to (dancer)'s cheeks, warm as skin.
The moon comes up over the trees.

pieces.label: The Rockfall at the Quarry
pieces.text: Cutting a grinding stone at the quarry, (quarrier) hears a crack from high above as the soft grey cliff begins to let go.

pieces.label: Run for Open Ground
pieces.text: (Quarrier) drops (quarrier.his/her) tools and runs. Behind (quarrier.him/her), the roar of the falling rock grows louder and louder...

pieces.label: Press Against the Cliff
pieces.text: (Quarrier) throws (quarrier.himself/herself) against the cliff face under the overhang, arms over (quarrier.his/her) head. The world goes dark with dust and noise...
A single bouncing stone catches (quarrier)'s head. (quarrier.He/She) wakes without a syllable of (quarrier.his/her) name.
The rocks catch (quarrier)'s leg at the edge of the slide, and it never bends properly again.
The overhang gives way. The finished grinding stone is set at the head of (quarrier)'s grave.
The overhang holds, and (quarrier) comes out of a pocket in the rubble holding the stone. "I finished it. In the dark."
Pebbles patter down onto (quarrier)'s shoulders.
The world goes dark with dust and noise.
The rock is soft and grey.

pieces.label: The Fever That Burns Away Names
pieces.text: (Patient) has the white fever, which burns so hot that, (healer) warns, it sometimes takes a memory, a habit or even a name with it when it goes.

pieces.label: The Cold Plunge
pieces.text: (healer) and two strong helpers carry (patient) down to the river at midnight and lower (patient.him/her) into the black water. (Patient) gasps, shudders, and goes rigid...

pieces.label: The Slow Week
pieces.text: (healer) settles in for a long week. Tea every hour, cool cloths, quiet voices. (Patient) burns and mutters and sleeps...
The fever breaks with a hiss and takes (patient)'s name with it. "Who's asking? And who am I?"
(Patient) climbs out of the river and says a name that isn't (patient.his/hers), and answers to it from then on.
The fever slips away like a guest leaving early, and everything is kept, even the jokes.
On the fifth night (patient) goes quiet, and (healer) sits with (patient.him/her) until dawn.
People in the white fever talk about things they've never seen.
The river is black at midnight.
Tea every hour, cool cloths, quiet voices.

pieces.label: The Laziest Summer
pieces.text: (Idler) has spent the whole hot summer in a hammock, and this morning the other villagers have left a pile of baskets, a broken spear and a staring goat at its foot.

pieces.label: Get Up and Do Them
pieces.text: (Idler) groans, swings (idler.his/her) legs out of the hammock and starts on the pile. The baskets first, then the spear, then the goat, which turns out to need milking...

pieces.label: Roll Over
pieces.text: (Idler) rolls over to face the other way. The goat walks around the hammock and looks at (idler.him/her) from the other side...
(Idler) finds (idler.he/she) likes being busy, and the goat moves into the hammock.
The goat kicks the bucket, kicks (idler), and sits on (idler.him/her). "I got up once. Look where it got me."
The goat stares all night until (idler) cracks and finds the worst part of work was thinking about it.
The goat chews through the rope, and (idler) can never relax without listening for chewing.
The hammock has worn a groove in each palm.
The goat is looking at (idler).
The goat chews slowly, staring.

pieces.label: The Huts on Stilts
pieces.text: The king tides have soaked the beach huts for the third time this season, and (builder), a builder, wants to lift them on ironwood stilts like the ones a trader described.

pieces.label: Build the Stilts
pieces.text: (Builder) leads every builder in the village up into the hills to cut ironwood. It's hard work. The wood is so dense it blunts every axe twice a day...

pieces.label: Just Patch
pieces.text: "Patch it is," says (builder), a little disappointed. The builders replace the rotten doorposts and stuff the gaps with clay...
The beach huts stand on ironwood stilts, and the children make a den underneath.
Dry huts, but with every hand cutting ironwood, half the crop rots in the ground.
The tides calm down, and (builder) keeps the stilt drawings rolled up, just in case.
The clay washes out on the next tide. "Stilts. Fine."
Ironwood blunts every axe twice a day.
The king tides came early this year.
Little ladders lead up to the doors.

pieces.label: The Sleepwalker on the Cliffs
pieces.text: For a week (sleepwalker) has been sleepwalking along the sea cliffs at night with empty eyes, humming the song of a singer who once lived up there, and tonight (sleepwalker.he/she) is getting up again.

pieces.label: Wake (Him/Her)
pieces.text: (Watcher) grabs (sleepwalker)'s shoulders and shakes (sleepwalker.him/her), calling (sleepwalker.his/her) name. (Sleepwalker)'s eyes stay empty for a long moment...

pieces.label: Follow Quietly
pieces.text: (Watcher) follows a few steps behind as (sleepwalker) walks out of the village, up the path and onto the cliffs, humming. The wind off the sea is cold. Far below, the waves crash on the rocks...
(Sleepwalker) blinks awake, never sleepwalks again, and hums the song at bedtime and sleeps like a stone.
(Sleepwalker) wakes screaming and falls onto the rocks, and the hip never heals right.
(Sleepwalker) walks into a sea mist, humming, and is never seen again. Now two voices hum on misty nights.
Every night (sleepwalker) turns at the cliff edge and walks home asleep, until one night (sleepwalker.he/she) doesn't get up.
(Sleepwalker)'s eyes are wide open and empty.
The wind off the sea is cold.
A song nobody in the village knows.

pieces.label: The Night of Two Sunrises
pieces.text: (Mother) wakes in the dark to see the False Dawn, a glow on the horizon that babies conceived that night are said to arrive early, kick hard and laugh loud.

pieces.label: Wake (Name2)
pieces.text: (Mother) shakes (friend) gently. (mother.He/She) grumbles, then sees the glow and sits up. They wrap themselves in one blanket and sit in the doorway, watching the strange light...

pieces.label: Watch It Alone
pieces.text: (Mother) slips out without waking (friend) and sits on the beach, watching the false sunrise glow and fade. The sea is very still...
A baby who kicks so early the healers raise their eyebrows. "False Dawn," say the elders.
The healers count {#babies:one very strong kicker|two sets of kicks|three sets of kicks}, and (friend) sits down on the floor.
A tiny canoe drifts in with a baby wrapped in a mat. "Look what the False Dawn brought."
Just a light, and (friend) is very annoyed to have missed it.
A second sunrise that changes its mind and fades away.
They sit wrapped in one blanket in the doorway.
The fishers say it's the light of a far-off fire mountain.

pieces.label: The Smoke From the Next Island
pieces.text: Black smoke has risen for two days from the little island across the strait, and today it has stopped.

pieces.label: Cross the Strait
pieces.text: (Paddler) loads the canoe with water, dried fish and blankets, and paddles out into the chop. Halfway across, the wind turns against (paddler.him/her)...

pieces.label: Light a Signal Fire
pieces.text: (Paddler) builds a great fire on the point, piling it with green palm fronds until the smoke goes up thick and white. Then (paddler.he/she) waits...
A young couple and their baby, left on the burned beach, come home in (paddler)'s canoe.
A (paddler.man/woman), a teenager, a small child and a pet chicken, which lays an egg in (paddler)'s lap.
A battered canoe crosses the strait. "We took your smoke for a welcome." It was.
The families had already left. The smoke was dry grass burning itself out.
The water between the islands is rough.
The smoke goes up thick and white from green palm fronds.
The baby sleeps in a fish basket.

pieces.label: The Potter's Clay Figures
pieces.text: (potter) has found red river clay that, the old potters said, remembers what it was shaped into, and has made a little figure of (model) so lifelike it's unsettling.

pieces.label: Fire It in the Kiln
pieces.text: (potter) slides the little figure into the kiln with the evening's pots and banks up the fire. All night the kiln glows and ticks and sighs...

pieces.label: Squash It
pieces.text: "Squash it," says (model). (potter) sighs, picks up the figure and squeezes it in (model.his/her) fist. The clay is warm. It squirms...
A full-sized (model) climbs out of the kiln and catches the pot (potter) drops.
Someone with (model)'s face and (potter)'s tastes climbs out, and the two of them complain about the potter together.
The clay squirts out and grows into {#made:a copy|two copies} of (model). "That hurt."
Just clay, made into a bowl that has a faint look of (model) about the rim.
The red river clay is very smooth.
The kiln glows and ticks and sighs all night.
The clay is warm. It squirms.

pieces.label: The Eel of the Twin Pools
pieces.text: In two hill pools joined by a tunnel lives a silver eel the children say can swim through people, and (first) and (second) have come to catch it.

pieces.label: Both Dive In
pieces.text: "Now!" They dive into their pools at the same moment. Underwater, the silver eel flashes out of the tunnel and straight through (first)'s chest, and out the other side, and through (second)'s...

pieces.label: Wait for It
pieces.text: They crouch at the edges of the pools and wait. The eel takes its time. The sun moves across the sky...
The eel swims through them both, and they surface in each other's bodies. The children were right.
Swapped and tangled in each other's nets. "I've been swum through. Once is enough."
An eel as long as a person, carried home on a pole, singing.
The eel slides through (first)'s hand like cold water from the inside, and fish loses its appeal for good.
The two pools are joined underneath by a tunnel.
Silver eel is the best eating on the island.
It feels like cold water from the inside.

pieces.label: The Ash That Fell Like Snow
pieces.text: The fire mountain on the next island sends a soft grey ash drifting over the village, ash the elders say carries time in it, and (fisher) is out on the reef with nothing but a fish basket to cover (fisher.his/her) head.

pieces.label: Paddle Home at Once
pieces.text: (Fisher) paddles hard for the beach, the ash settling on (fisher.his/her) shoulders and in (fisher.his/her) hair, grey on everything...

pieces.label: Basket On
pieces.text: Basket On.

pieces.label: Keep Fishing
pieces.text: Keep Fishing.
The ash washes out, but the grey doesn't. "The mountain's time."
All the years at once. "I always did want the good sitting stone."
Salt spray scrubs (fisher)'s face younger. "The sea takes the mountain's time back."
The fish rise to nibble the ash, and (fisher) comes home with a full basket.
The ash drifts down like feathers.
The ash piles up on the basket like a little grey hat.
The mountain has grumbled for a week.

pieces.label: The Spirit Who Wanted a Name
pieces.text: For a month a nameless little forest spirit has followed (subject), whispering (subject.his/her) name, and tonight it is outside the door: "Just borrow it. I'll give it back."

pieces.label: Lend It (His/Her) Name
pieces.text: (Subject) opens the door and says (subject.his/her) own name, slowly and clearly, into the dark. Something warm brushes past (subject.his/her) face, like a breath...

pieces.label: Offer It a Different Name
pieces.text: "Not mine," says (subject) through the door. "But you can have a name of your own. How about..." (subject.He/She) thinks hard...
The spirit never gives it back. (Subject) is "?", and someone in the trees tries the name out at night.
A pebble on the doorstep, scratched with a new name, and (subject) is (made1) from then on.
"Ginger," says (subject), and then, flustered, gives (subject.himself/herself) the same name, or "Gin" if a man.
The spirit takes the name of a tree and goes away delighted.
Soft footsteps behind (subject) on the path.
The spirit laughs like rain on leaves.
A sigh at the window.

pieces.label: The Wedding Nobody Expected
pieces.text: At breakfast, (friend) stands up red to the ears and announces that (bride.he/she) and (bride) are getting joined at sunset under the big banyan. (Bride) didn't know either.

pieces.label: Yes
pieces.text: Yes.

pieces.label: At Sunset
pieces.text: at Sunset.

pieces.label: Put It Off
pieces.text: "Not like this," says (bride). "Let's do it properly. Next full moon." (Friend) deflates a little, but agrees. The village gets a month to prepare...
Flowers on the banyan and dripping drummers by sunset. The goat is never explained.
A few weeks later (bride) waits until (friend) has a mouthful of soup to tell (bride.him/her) she's pregnant.
A month of everyone trying something new, and several hidden talents.
A quiet wedding under the banyan, and (bride), already pregnant, asleep before the feast.
(Bride) is still holding her spoon.
People run in every direction carrying flowers, food and a confused goat.
The drummers are out fishing.

pieces.label: The Crocodile in the River Mouth
pieces.text: A crocodile the length of two canoes has moved into the river mouth where the village washes and fetches water, and (fetcher) has a basket of washing and a thirsty family.

pieces.label: Go to the River Carefully
pieces.text: (Fetcher) creeps down to the water's edge, well upstream of the sandbank, and kneels to fill the water jar, keeping one eye on the crocodile. It isn't on the sandbank...

pieces.label: Walk to the Hill Spring
pieces.text: (Fetcher) sighs, hoists the washing onto (fetcher.his/her) head and the jar onto (fetcher.his/her) hip, and sets off on the long walk up to the spring in the hills...
The water bulges, and the fishers come running too late. They carry (fetcher) home.
(Fetcher) hits the crocodile on the nose with the water jar, and the healers save (fetcher.his/her) life but not (fetcher.his/her) arm.
A month of hauling jars up the hill, and (fetcher) never wants to carry anything again.
The hill spring is lovely, and the crocodile seems almost offended.
Teeth that could crack a boulder.
The crocodile lies on the sandbank with its mouth open.
The hill spring is shaded by ferns.

pieces.label: The Oldest Hut Falls Down
pieces.text: The oldest hut in the village, standing since the first people came, sighs and lies down on a still afternoon, bringing down the walls of the huts on either side.

pieces.label: Rebuild It as It Was
pieces.text: (Subject) and (builder) sort through the wreckage, setting aside every old post that's still sound. The elders come to help, telling stories about every one...

pieces.label: Build New Ones
pieces.text: The village clears the old hut away, carefully, and (builder) marks out three new huts in the dirt with a stick...
The elders remember every post and knot, and learn a thing or two about building themselves.
The old posts crack, and building loses all its pleasure for (subject). "It's just wood now."
Three new huts, and an old post carved into a bench for the elders.
A stone box under the floor full of the first people's tablets.
The hut simply sighs and lies down.
The elders tell stories about every post.
(builder) marks out three huts in the dirt with a stick.

pieces.label: The Stranger With (Name)'s Face
pieces.text: A trader comes in on the morning tide with (subject)'s exact face, and has been looking for years for the one other person who wears it.

pieces.label: Invite (Him/Her) to Stay
pieces.text: (Subject) holds out (subject.his/her) hand. The trader takes it. Their hands are exactly the same size. The whole village lets out its breath at once...

pieces.label: Send (Him/Her) On
pieces.text: "I'm glad you found me," says (subject), "but this is my island." The trader nods, as if (subject.he/she) expected that, and pushes the canoe back out...
The trader stays as (made1), nothing like (subject) except in the face, and they argue happily about everything.
Both are gone by morning. "Gone to see what (subject.he/she) has seen."
"We should be good at the same things, with the same face." A morning's lesson.
The canoe becomes a speck, and (subject) checks every new face for years.
Their hands are exactly the same size.
The whole village lets out its breath at once.
The trader squints into the sun the same way.

pieces.label: The Wrong Jar
pieces.text: (Healer) reaches for the bitterleaf to settle (sick)'s stomach and finds two unmarked jars that look and smell the same: one bitterleaf, one nightshade.

pieces.label: Guess
pieces.text: (Healer) picks the jar on the left, the one that feels right, and brews a strong cup. (sick) drinks it, makes a face, and lies back...

pieces.label: Wait for the Head Healer
pieces.text: (Healer) makes (sick) as comfortable as (healer.he/she) can with cool water and a warm stone for (healer.his/her) belly, and waits. The afternoon drags...
It's bitterleaf. (Healer) scratches NIGHTSHADE on the other lid in letters as big as (healer.his/her) thumb.
It's nightshade. (sick) sleeps for two days and wakes with hands and legs that never fully come back.
The head healer sniffs once and points, and teaches every healer about the grey hairs on the nightshade leaf.
A long night and three teas. "A long night is better than the wrong jar."
Somebody forgot to scratch the mark on the lid.
A warm stone for the belly.
Tiny grey hairs on the leaf that only show in sunlight.

pieces.label: The Bird That Steals Words
pieces.text: A black-and-gold word-thief bird from the old stories has been sitting above (subject)'s door for a week saying (subject)'s name in (subject)'s own voice, and each time it sounds less like (subject)'s.

pieces.label: Chase It Off
pieces.text: (Subject) climbs the palm with a stick, yelling. The bird looks at (subject.him/her) with one bright eye, and says (subject.his/her) name one last time, very clearly...

pieces.label: Leave It a Gift
pieces.text: (Subject) leaves a ripe mango on the windowsill. The bird drops down, eats every bit of it, and looks at (subject) thoughtfully...
The bird says (subject)'s name one last time and flies away with it. The village calls (subject.him/her) "?".
The nest is lined with whispering bark scraps, and one of them is (subject)'s name.
For a mango, the bird trades (subject) a new name.
The bird decides it likes "mango" better, and says it at dawn every day, loudly.
The bird talks in other people's voices.
It looks at (subject) with one bright eye.
Black-and-gold feathers.

pieces.label: The Echo Valley
pieces.text: In the valley over the ridge every shout comes back three times, and the elders say that long ago, someone's third echo came walking back up the path.

pieces.label: Shout (His/Her) Name
pieces.text: (Traveller) cups (traveller.his/her) hands and shouts (traveller.his/her) own name as loud as (traveller.he/she) can. It comes back once. Twice. The third echo doesn't come back. Instead, there are footsteps on the path...

pieces.label: Just Whistle
pieces.text: (Traveller) whistles a little tune. It comes back once, twice, three times, each one slightly out of tune...
The third echo walks up the path humming: (traveller), exactly. "You called?"
The echo bounced off too many rocks: (traveller)'s face and nothing else.
A bird whistles the tune back perfectly and moves into the palm by (traveller)'s hut.
Someone with (traveller)'s face walks up whistling, "waiting for someone to pick a decent tune."
Any shout comes back three times.
The valley is very quiet.
Each echo is slightly out of tune.

pieces.label: The Waterfall of Two Rivers
pieces.text: Where two rivers, one warm and one cold, fall together over a cliff in the hills, the elders say two friends standing under the falls will see through each other's eyes for a moment.

pieces.label: Stand Under It Together
pieces.text: They wade in, holding hands, and step under the falling water. It hits them like a slap, warm on one side and cold on the other...

pieces.label: Take Turns
pieces.text: (First) goes first, alone, while (second) waits on the rocks. Under the water, (first) feels the cold side and the warm side pulling in two directions. Then (second), impatient, wades in after (first.him/her)...
The moment goes on, and on. "The elders said a moment!"
One dizzy moment through each other's eyes, and each comes out knowing the other's best work.
Swapped in the spray like two stones passed between hands. The rivers think once was plenty.
(First) slips on the cold side and never enjoys swimming again.
The water hits like a slap, warm on one side and cold on the other.
The two rivers swap everything they touch.
It's very loud.

pieces.label: The Coconut That Cried
pieces.text: Gathering storm-washed coconuts on the beach, (finder) picks one up that cries: a cradle carved from half a giant shell, with a wet, cross baby inside.

pieces.label: Straight to the Healers
pieces.text: (Finder) runs all the way to the healers' hut with the coconut cradle in (finder.his/her) arms. The healers wrap the baby in warm cloths and rub its hands and feet...

pieces.label: Carry It Home
pieces.text: (Finder) tucks the baby inside (finder.his/her) wrap, against (finder.his/her) chest, and walks home slowly, talking to it the whole way...
The baby won't let go of the head healer's finger. "I suppose I'd better."
"It's been looking at you the whole time." (Finder) learns fast.
(partner) says nothing at all for a while, then puts water on to warm.
The baby's parents, shipwrecked and bruised, sit down in the sand when they see it. They stay.
The beach is covered with driftwood, kelp and coconuts.
The cradle has a carved lid.
The baby is wet and very cross.

pieces.label: The Pale Blossoms of the Ridge
pieces.text: The pale creeper on the high ridge, planted by the island's first mothers, has bloomed, and (child) has climbed the whole ridge to bring (wearer) a crown of blossoms that, the elders say, give back a young face.

pieces.label: Put It On
pieces.text: (Wearer) bends down and lets (child) settle the crown on (wearer.his/her) head. The blossoms are cool and soft and smell of milk...

pieces.label: Put It in Water
pieces.text: (Wearer) thanks (child) with a hug and puts the crown in a bowl of water on the windowsill, where the evening breeze carries the smell all through the hut...
The face under the wilted crown is the one (wearer) had at twenty. "Technically, I did it," says (child).
Nothing happens, except (child) smells of honey and is followed by bees.
All night breathing the smell, and in the morning (wearer)'s face is young. "They just needed to be near."
(parent) borrows the crown in the night and turns up for breakfast young-faced and sheepish.
The blossoms smell like milk and honey.
(child) is out of breath, holding up the crown.
The evening breeze carries the smell through the hut.

pieces.label: The Burial Cave
pieces.text: A rockslide has opened a crack into the cave where the first people buried their dead, and (curious) wants to go in while (careful) thinks it's a terrible idea.

pieces.label: Go In Together
pieces.text: They squeeze through the crack one after the other with a torch. Inside, the cave opens out into a long, low hall, lined on both sides with stone shelves. Something at the far end is glowing faintly...

pieces.label: Block the Crack
pieces.text: (Careful) starts piling stones in the crack. (Curious) argues, and then, grumbling, starts helping. The cold air stops breathing out. The cave goes quiet...
(Curious) steps into the glow at the end of the hall and isn't there. The elders block the crack that evening.
The roof comes down between them, and (careful) is buried among the first people, which is an honour.
The crack is filled and plastered. "The first people sleep, and they like the dark."
Three slow knocks from the other side, and (curious) loses all interest in finding things out.
Cold air breathes out of the crack, smelling of old stone.
The hall is lined with stone shelves.
Something at the far end is glowing faintly.

pieces.label: The Moon-Shell Necklace
pieces.text: (Friend) has found a round white moon shell on the reef, the kind the sea spirit gives to women she favours, which worn for a full moon brings a child, and sometimes more than one.

pieces.label: Wear It
pieces.text: (Mother) ties the cord around her neck. The shell is cool against her skin, and for the whole month it never once gets warm, even in the midday sun...

pieces.label: Hang It in the Doorway
pieces.text: (Mother) hangs the moon shell in the doorway, where it turns slowly in the breeze and catches the light every evening...
The midwives grin: {#babies:one strong baby|twins|triplets}. "I thought that was just the stories."
One baby, and the moon shell is given back to the sea with a thank-you.
"Everyone walks through a doorway." Pregnant anyway.
The neighbour who walked past the doorway every day is suddenly pregnant.
The shell never once gets warm, even in the midday sun.
The shell turns slowly in the breeze.
The white shell sinks into the blue.

pieces.label: The Rope Bridge Over the Ravine
pieces.text: A third of the way across the old rope bridge over the ravine, with a basket of seedlings, (crosser) hears one rope go "tick," then another, and the bridge sags.

pieces.label: Hurry Forward
pieces.text: (Crosser) runs, the bridge swinging wildly under (crosser.his/her) feet, seedlings flying out of the basket into the ravine. The ticks come faster and faster...

pieces.label: Edge Back
pieces.text: (Crosser) turns very, very slowly and starts edging back, one step at a time, holding both ropes. The bridge creaks. Halfway back, another rope goes "tick"...
(Crosser) reaches the far side and cracks (crosser.his/her) head on a rock, and loses (crosser.his/her) name.
The bridge breaks with the far side in reach, and (crosser)'s legs never work properly again.
Back on the rock as the bridge drops, and the love of growing things falls into the ravine with it.
A builder throws a rope and hauls (crosser) back.
"Tick." Then another "tick."
Seedlings fly out of the basket into the ravine.
The bridge sags a hand's width.

pieces.label: The Carver's Masks of the Ancestors
pieces.text: The mask of a long-dead fisher has fallen off its peg in the meeting hut twice, right at (chosen)'s feet, and (laugher) laughs that it has obviously chosen (chosen.him/her).

pieces.label: Try It On
pieces.text: (Chosen) holds the mask to (chosen.his/her) face. It fits perfectly, as if carved for (chosen.him/her). There is a smell of salt and fish oil, and the sound of oars, very far away...

pieces.label: Hang It Back
pieces.text: (Chosen) hangs the mask carefully back on its peg and steps away. Behind (chosen.him/her), there is a soft clatter...
(Chosen) takes the mask off with a fisher's face from long ago. It doesn't fall again.
Held up to (laugher)'s face as a joke, the mask sticks. "It chose the one who laughed."
It falls a third time, damp inside, and (chosen) wakes with the fisher's weathered face.
Just a loose peg. But the mask always seems turned towards (chosen)'s seat.
The wood is warm.
A smell of salt and fish oil, and the sound of oars far away.
The ancestor masks hang in the meeting hut.

pieces.label: The Raft at the River Mouth
pieces.text: After three days of rain in the hills, a raft of lashed bamboo comes spinning down the flooded river with people clinging to it, heading for the churning river mouth.

pieces.label: Throw the Rope From the Bank
pieces.text: (Rescuer) coils the rope, swings it twice, and throws as hard as (rescuer.he/she) can as the raft spins past...

pieces.label: Wade Out to the Sandbar
pieces.text: (Rescuer) wades out into the brown water, up to (rescuer.his/her) waist, then (rescuer.his/her) chest, bracing against the current, and holds out the long fishing pole...
The rope is caught, and two adults and a baby who sleeps through anything stay.
The current drags (rescuer) in, and the teenager on the raft pulls (rescuer.him/her) out. The family stays.
(Rescuer) swings the raft in like a big fish. "We hoped we'd make it this far."
The raft spins past and comes ashore safe at a beach up the coast.
The river comes down brown and fast.
The river mouth churns like a cooking pot.
The raft spins slowly in the current.

pieces.label: The Apprentice's First Roof
pieces.text: After a year of learning, (apprentice) asks to fix the leaking healers' roof alone, and (teacher) remembers (teacher.his/her) own first roof falling in during the first storm.

pieces.label: Let (Him/Her) Do It Alone
pieces.text: (Teacher) sits on a log across the path with (teacher.his/her) arms folded, and watches without saying a word, which is the hardest thing (teacher.he/she) has done in a year...

pieces.label: Work Alongside
pieces.text: "We'll do it together," says (teacher). (apprentice) looks disappointed, but climbs up beside (teacher.him/her)...
Tight, neat, even, and better than the teacher's first roof. The healers ask for every other roof too.
(apprentice) slides off the roof, and the shoulder never works quite right again.
Done by midday, and not a damp mat in the village by evening.
"Not like that. Like this." The roof is perfect, and (apprentice) never asks to build again.
The healers' roof has leaked onto the sleeping mats for a month.
"I've watched you a hundred times."
(Teacher) sits on a log with (teacher.his/her) arms folded.

pieces.label: The Day of Small Kindnesses
pieces.text: (chief) declares a Day of Small Kindnesses to cure the village's grumpiness, and puts (organiser) in charge of making sure everyone does one kind thing.

pieces.label: Gently Remind Everyone
pieces.text: (Organiser) walks from hut to hut all morning, quietly reminding people. "Just one kind thing. Anyone. It doesn't have to be big..."

pieces.label: Set a Loud Example
pieces.text: (Organiser) starts the morning by carrying water for three different huts, singing, and then fixes a neighbour's broken stool in the middle of the path where everyone can see...
By noon it has caught on, and (chief) declares it a yearly event.
The adults forget, but every child follows someone all day and learns something new.
"We get it." (Organiser) is too tired and embarrassed to join the games at the fire, ever again.
Three small children fall asleep on (organiser), who never could stand the noise of little ones.
Two shouting matches in one week.
"Just one kind thing. It doesn't have to be big."
Half the village rolls its eyes.

pieces.label: The Flood in the Scroll Hut
pieces.text: The stream behind the scroll hut has burst its banks, and water is pouring in under the door onto generations of records while (keeper) sleeps on the other side of the village.

pieces.label: Start Carrying Them Out
pieces.text: (Subject) wades in up to (subject.his/her) ankles and starts grabbing armfuls of scrolls from the lowest shelves, running them up to the dry ground and back again...

pieces.label: Wake (Keeper Name)
pieces.text: (Subject) runs across the village and shakes (keeper) awake. (keeper) comes out at a stumbling run in (subject.his/her) sleeping wrap...
Old fish-debt lists saved, and (keeper) copies the smeared scrolls by lamplight until (subject.he/she) falls ill.
Every scroll saved, and (subject) reads them all while they dry.
The elders recite the lost scrolls for a week and are sharper for it.
(keeper) saves every one that matters, and hides copies in a dry cave.
Water pours in under the door.
Recipes, building tricks and healing teas on bark and leaf.
(keeper) runs out in (subject.his/her) sleeping wrap.

pieces.label: The Storm Gourd
pieces.text: (First) and (second) find a trader's wax-sealed gourd that holds a bottled thunderstorm, never to be opened indoors, and the wax is cracking in the heat.

pieces.label: Open It Outside Together
pieces.text: They carry it out onto the beach, both holding it, and (first) picks the last of the wax off with a fingernail. The gourd hums...

pieces.label: Put It Down and Get the Elders
pieces.text: They set it down on the floor of the meeting hut, very gently, and back away. They're halfway to the elders' hut when they hear a muffled crack behind them...
A tiny cloud cracks a bolt between their hands, and each holds the gourd with the other's.
A warm, perfect rain for the gardens, and wet clay at last for the builders.
It bursts indoors, and a bolt leaps out of the doorway. "He said not indoors."
The meeting-hut floor becomes a pond, and they dry it together for a week.
The gourd crackles faintly when shaken.
A storm cloud no bigger than a basket.
The mats are floating.

pieces.label: The Grandmother Tree
pieces.text: The Grandmother Tree, a huge fig that was once the island's first healer, gives sleepers in her shade some of her years or some of her youth, depending on her mood, and (walker) is very tired.

pieces.label: Lie Down and Rest
pieces.text: (Walker) lies down among the roots. The bark creaks above (walker.him/her) like an old woman settling into a chair. (walker.He/She) falls asleep at once...

pieces.label: Greet Her and Keep Walking
pieces.text: (Walker) stops, bows a little, and says good afternoon to the Grandmother Tree. A breeze stirs the leaves, though the rest of the clearing is still...
She was in a good mood: five years younger, and a flower at her roots every morning after.
She was in a bad mood: grey hair and lines like bark. Apologising doesn't help.
An old woman with leaves in her hair pats (walker)'s cheek in a dream. "Good manners."
Nothing happens, and (walker) waves anyway.
The bark creaks like an old woman settling into a chair.
Nobody cuts her, nobody climbs her, everybody greets her.
A breeze stirs her leaves while the clearing is still.

pieces.label: The Visitor at the Door at Night
pieces.text: Late at night a figure in a cloak of woven grass knocks at (host)'s door and asks, in a voice like wind in dry leaves, for someone to walk with it to the end of the beach and back.

pieces.label: Walk With It
pieces.text: (Host) takes a torch and walks beside the cloaked figure down to the beach, and along it, under the stars. It doesn't speak. At the end of the beach, where the rocks begin, it stops...

pieces.label: Offer It the Fire
pieces.text: "Come in and sit by the fire instead," says (host). "It's not dark in here." The figure hesitates, and then steps over the threshold...
"Just a little further." Two sets of footprints lead to the water's edge, and stop.
The hood comes down on (host)'s grandparent's smiling face. "It's time."
It warms its driftwood hands by the fire until dawn and leaves behind a bundle of old, fine tools.
"Not in. Never in." A line of grey stones across the doorway in the morning.
A voice like wind in dry leaves.
"I'm afraid of the dark."
Night walkers come once in a generation.

pieces.label: The Twin Statues on the Headland
pieces.text: Beside the two ancient statues of a sculptor and her sister on the headland, a third, rough, half-carved statue has appeared with (sitter)'s face.

pieces.label: Knock It Down
pieces.text: (Sitter) puts (sitter.his/her) shoulder to the rough statue and pushes. It rocks, tips, and falls over in the grass with a thud. A crack runs right down the middle of it...

pieces.label: Finish Carving It
pieces.text: (Sitter) borrows a chisel and a mallet and goes up to the headland every day for a month, finishing the face that is (sitter.his/her) own...
The stone cracks like a shell and someone with (sitter)'s face sits up. "Couldn't you have waited?"
Just stone, and the twins seem to turn away from each other towards the empty spot.
The finished statue blinks and steps down, {#made:alone|and one of the old twins follows}.
A very fine statue that belongs there, and a month's lesson in stone.
The statues are worn smooth by centuries of wind.
They forgot which was which.
A chisel and a mallet, every day for a month.

pieces.label: The Slippery Rocks by the Waterfall
pieces.text: Balancing on one foot on a slime-covered rock at the foot of the waterfall, reaching for a fat shrimp, (shrimper) feels the rock tip, just slightly.

pieces.label: Jump for the Bank
pieces.text: (Shrimper) leaps. For a moment (shrimper.he/she) is in the air over the pool, arms windmilling...

pieces.label: Stay Still
pieces.text: (Shrimper) freezes, arms out, perfectly still. The rock wobbles. Water roars past. Slowly, very slowly, the rock settles...
(Shrimper) slips on the bank and cracks (shrimper.his/her) head, and (shrimper.his/her) own name is simply gone.
Face-first in the mud, with the shrimp sitting on (shrimper.his/her) nose.
The rock rolls and pins (shrimper)'s foot underwater. It heals crooked.
So still the shrimp walk into the net a dozen at a time.
The rocks are covered in green slime.
The spray makes everything wet.
Water roars past.

pieces.label: The Little Sister of the Hills
pieces.text: A barefoot child with leaves woven in (weeder.his/her) hair, one of the hills' own children, steps out of the trees at dusk and holds out (weeder.his/her) hand to (weeder).

pieces.label: Take (His/Her) Hand
pieces.text: (Weeder) wipes the dirt off (weeder.his/her) palm and takes the small cold hand. The child smiles, and starts to walk back towards the trees, pulling (weeder) gently after (weeder.him/her)...

pieces.label: Call (Him/Her) to Supper
pieces.text: "Come and eat," says (weeder), pointing to the smoke of the cooking fire. The child looks at the smoke for a long time...
(Weeder) steps into the trees with the child, smiling. Two figures are seen on a ridge at dusk.
At the trees, the child becomes a baby with leaves in its hair. The hills have decided.
(Other_weeder) runs after the laughing child, and laughs in the hills on still evenings.
The child eats, sleeps against (weeder)'s arm, and leaves a ring of leaves; (weeder) starts minding the little ones.
The child never comes closer than the last garden row.
A small, cold hand.
The smoke of the cooking fire.

pieces.label: The Healers' Week of Lessons
pieces.text: (Head healer name) announces a week of dawn lessons for every healer, starting with cutting, and (student) has been hiding that (student.he/she) faints at the sight of blood.

pieces.label: Confess
pieces.text: (Student) puts (student.his/her) hand up. "I faint," (student.he/she) says. "At blood. I'm sorry." The other healers stare. (Head healer name) puts down the knife...

pieces.label: Grit (His/Her) Teeth
pieces.text: (Student) says nothing, fixes (student.his/her) eyes on the far wall, and holds very still while (head healer name) starts cutting...
"Half of healing has no blood in it." Every healer learns teas, splints and fevers.
"I fainted for three years." (Student) learns to breathe, and the hut stops being dreaded.
Green, grey, then yellow, but still standing all week. "I saw. Well done."
Down like a felled tree on the third cut, with a tray of jars.
A fresh fish and a sharp shell knife.
Dawn, every day, at the healers' hut.
(Student) fixes (student.his/her) eyes on the far wall.

pieces.label: The Sky Lantern That Came Down
pieces.text: (Maker)'s sky lantern flies beautifully over the new moon festival, then the wind changes and brings it down, still burning, onto the dry thatch by the cooking fire.

pieces.label: Climb Up With a Wet Mat
pieces.text: (Maker) soaks a sleeping mat in the water jar, scrambles up the side of the nearest hut and onto the smouldering roof...

pieces.label: Shout for Water
pieces.text: "FIRE!" (maker) shouts. "WATER! NOW!" People drop everything and come running with jars, gourds, cooking pots, anything that will hold water...
The roof gives way and (maker) falls into the smoke. The huts mend; (maker)'s scars never do.
Smothered in time, and every builder learns the old fire-resistant thatch.
A bucket chain from the stream, and several villagers learn to lay a roof.
(Maker)'s wish was for the village to do something together. "Not like this." It counts.
Bamboo and bark paper, with a little dish of oil.
A lantern that flies high carries a wish to the stars.
Jars, gourds and cooking pots full of water.

pieces.label: The Cousins From Across the Sea
pieces.text: A trader brings word that (subject)'s cousin, who left as a child, wants to come home after three bad harvests in the south.

pieces.label: Send Word to Come
pieces.text: (Subject) sends back a carved shell with the trader: a fish, which in the old way means "come home." Then (subject.he/she) waits, watching the south every morning...

pieces.label: Go and Fetch Them
pieces.text: (Subject) loads a canoe with dried fish, water and two strong paddlers, and sets out south. The journey takes nine days...
The cousin wades ashore with a partner and a baby, holding the carved shell.
The cousin comes with a long-legged teenager and a seasick child.
Nine days there, nine back, and (subject) steers them home by the stars.
The family left a week ago for nobody knows where.
A carved shell fish means "come home."
(Subject) watches the south every morning.
They were small enough to share a sleeping mat.

pieces.label: The Hollow-Log Drum
pieces.text: (drummer)'s new hollow-log drum must be woken by someone who has never danced dancing to its first beat, and everyone looks at (dancer).

pieces.label: Dance
pieces.text: (drummer) raises the sticks. BOOM. The sound goes through (dancer)'s feet and up (dancer.his/her) legs, and before (dancer.he/she) can think about it, (dancer.his/her) feet are moving...

pieces.label: Refuse
pieces.text: "No," says (dancer). "Get someone else." The crowd groans. (drummer) shrugs and looks for another first-time dancer...
The worst dancing ever seen and the best first beat a drum ever had. (Dancer) dances at every festival after.
(Dancer) lands on the side of (dancer.his/her) foot. "The drum can go back to sleep."
(eldest) dances one slow circle, and everyone cries. (dancer.His/her) face stays young in the morning.
The drum sounds like a wet log, and becomes a pig trough.
BOOM. The sound goes through (dancer)'s feet.
A new drum must be woken properly, or it sulks forever.
(Dancer) would rather swim to the next island.

pieces.label: The Old Woman of the Reef
pieces.text: At the lowest tide of the year, the Reef Grandmother, a rock that trades in years, shows above the water, and (visitor) has walked all the way out to see her up close.

pieces.label: Leave Her a Gift
pieces.text: (Visitor) unwinds (visitor.his/her) best shell necklace and lays it in a hollow of the rock, at the Grandmother's feet. The tide sighs on the reef...

pieces.label: Tell Her What (He/She) Thinks
pieces.text: "You're a rock," says (visitor). "You don't take anything. People get old on their own." (visitor.He/She) turns to go. The tide turns at the same moment...
A younger face in a still pool. "She always did like shells."
Five years younger, and a new gift at every low tide.
A lined, greying face by the time (visitor) gets home, and an apology at the next low tide.
The tide comes in faster than any tide should.
She sits with her knees drawn up.
The tide sighs on the reef.
Most people just wave at her from the beach.

pieces.label: The Double Banana
pieces.text: (Finder) has found a double banana on the plant behind the healers' hut, and the old saying goes: "eat it alone and you'll never be alone again."

pieces.label: Eat It Alone
pieces.text: (Finder) peels it, sits down behind the healers' hut where nobody can see, and eats both halves, one after the other...

pieces.label: Share It
pieces.text: (Finder) breaks the double banana in two and offers half to the nearest person: (sharer), who happens to be walking past with a basket...
Someone stands up beside (finder) with banana on (finder.his/her) chin. "That was delicious."
A copy who complains the banana was too ripe and never eats another.
{#made:Three|Four} of them behind the healers' hut. "We're never alone again."
Just a banana, and two good friends.
Two fruits joined in one skin.
The healers' grandmother planted it.
Very ripe, very sweet-smelling.

pieces.label: The Fall From the Festival Tower
pieces.text: It's (climber)'s turn to climb the swaying bamboo festival tower at sunset and hang the first fruit of the harvest, and halfway up, a lashing creaks.

pieces.label: Keep Climbing
pieces.text: (Climber) keeps going, hand over hand, the fruit tied to (climber.his/her) waist. The tower sways more with every rung...

pieces.label: Come Down
pieces.text: (Climber) climbs back down, carefully. The crowd mutters. The builders swarm up the tower to check the lashings...
The fruit is hung, then the lashing gives and (climber)'s head smacks the ground. (climber.He/She) is "?" until the name comes back.
The top folds over, and (climber)'s legs never fully heal.
The builders fix the tower and every sagging roof in the village. The cheer is louder for the wait.
Everyone makes the same joke, and (climber) keeps to the edges at festivals ever after.
A tower of bamboo poles taller than the meeting hut.
The tower sways in the evening breeze.
The village holds its breath.

pieces.label: The Naming Stone at the Spring
pieces.text: After a hard year, (seeker) climbs to the naming stone at the hill spring, where anyone who scratches their name and washes in the spring walks away with a new one.

pieces.label: Scratch (His/Her) Name
pieces.text: (Seeker) scratches (seeker.his/her) name into an empty corner of the stone, letter by letter. Then (seeker.he/she) kneels and washes (seeker.his/her) hands in the cold spring...

pieces.label: Just Wash
pieces.text: (Seeker) puts the shell back in (seeker.his/her) pocket and kneels to wash (seeker.his/her) face in the spring instead. The water is so cold it makes (seeker.his/her) teeth ache...
A new name rises as clear as speech, and the hard year belongs to someone else.
No name comes, so (seeker) takes the oldest name on the stone.
The spring washes the old name away and leaves none.
Just cold water, and the hard year is over; (seeker) goes to work without dreading it.
Names so old they are almost worn away.
The water makes (seeker)'s teeth ache.
A sharp shell in (seeker.his/her) hand.

pieces.label: The Elder's Last Story
pieces.text: (Storyteller), the oldest villager and the best storyteller anyone remembers, asks to be carried to the fire to tell the longest story, of how the first people found the island.

pieces.label: Carry (Him/Her) to the Fire
pieces.text: Four young villagers carry (storyteller) to the cooking fire on (storyteller.his/her) sleeping mat. The whole village gathers. The children sit closest. (Storyteller) clears (storyteller.his/her) throat...

pieces.label: Keep (Him/Her) in Bed
pieces.text: "Tomorrow," the healers say. (Storyteller) sighs, and lies back, and asks for (storyteller.his/her) grandchild to sit with (storyteller.him/her) instead...
"And that's how we got here." (Storyteller) closes (storyteller.his/her) eyes at dawn, and the children remember every word.
"Come back tomorrow." A month of nights at the fire.
Told in a whisper to (grandchild), who becomes the village's storyteller.
"I could have told it." Two more years and never all the way through.
The great turtle guided the first canoes in.
The children sit closest.
Four young villagers carry the sleeping mat.

pieces.label: The Tunnel Under the Headland
pieces.text: At the lowest tide in years, the sea tunnel under the headland opens, and (swimmer), the fastest swimmer in the village, stands at its mouth with cold air blowing out.

pieces.label: Swim Through
pieces.text: (Swimmer) takes three deep breaths and dives into the dark. The tunnel is narrow and cold, and the water pulls (swimmer.him/her) along faster than (swimmer.he/she) can swim...

pieces.label: Shout and Listen
pieces.text: (Swimmer) cups (swimmer.his/her) hands and shouts into the tunnel. The sound rolls away into the dark. For a long moment, nothing. Then, very faintly, something shouts back...
(Swimmer) never comes out, and the tunnel mouth gets a ring of white stones.
(Swimmer) shoots out into sunlight, the first ever, with a face the rock has reshaped.
(Swimmer)'s own head bobs up out of the dark. "Took you long enough."
The tide roars back, and the water loses its pull on (swimmer).
Cold air blows out of the tunnel.
The tide only stays out long enough for someone very fast.
Some fishers say the tunnel goes down, not through.

pieces.label: The Basket on the Turtle's Back
pieces.text: On the night the sea turtles come up the beach to lay their eggs, one of them carries a small woven basket on her shell, and a thin cry comes out of it.

pieces.label: Untie It Now
pieces.text: (Watcher) creeps out of the dunes and kneels beside the huge turtle, which stops and looks at (watcher.him/her) with one old, wet eye. (watcher.He/She) unties the kelp with trembling fingers...

pieces.label: Wait for the Eggs
pieces.text: (Watcher) stays still in the dunes while the turtle digs her nest, lays her eggs, and covers them. The cry from the basket goes quiet. When she turns to go back to the sea, (watcher) runs down...
A damp, calm baby, and every year one old turtle stops to look at them.
(partner) followed (watcher.him/her) out of the dunes. "We'd better go home."
The turtle waits at the water's edge, and the night becomes a yearly feast.
The turtle slips into the waves with the basket still on her back.
The village watches from the dunes in silence.
One old, wet eye.
A strip of kelp ties the basket on.

pieces.label: The Silver Web at Dawn
pieces.text: (Walker) walks face first into the oldest spider on the island's dew-silver web, which, the children say, she weaves faces into so she won't forget them.

pieces.label: Tear It Off
pieces.text: (Walker) claws at (walker.his/her) face, spluttering, tearing the silver threads away in handfuls. Above (walker.him/her), the spider scuttles to the edge of the ruined web...

pieces.label: Peel It Away Gently
pieces.text: (Walker) stands perfectly still and lifts the threads away one at a time, apologising to the spider under (walker.his/her) breath. It takes a very long time...
The web takes something with it: a lined, greying face, as if in revenge.
The next morning, someone with (walker)'s face untangles (walker.himself/herself) from the rebuilt web.
(Walker)'s young face shines in the web, and an older one looks back from the stream.
The spider drops down to look (walker.him/her) in the eye, and (walker)'s hands are steadier for it.
The web shines like a sheet of silver.
The spider is as big as a hand.
Cool and sticky.

pieces.label: The Two Who Looked Alike
pieces.text: (First) and (second), who everyone mixes up, swap clothes, jobs and huts for a day, and (elder) warns them the island likes a good joke and sometimes keeps one.

pieces.label: Swap Back at Once
pieces.text: They laugh, but they go straight back to their own huts, change back into their own clothes, and lie down on their own mats...

pieces.label: One More Day
pieces.text: "One more day," says (second). "It's too good." They go to bed in each other's huts again, giggling...
(First) wakes on (first.his/her) own mat in (second)'s body. "I did say."
The village gives (first) a new name to tell them apart, and it sticks.
The island decides they might as well do it properly.
A small child sees through it, and gets an extra sweet potato.
They both whistle through their teeth.
Nobody notices.
"The island likes a good joke."

pieces.label: The Fever Ward
pieces.text: The fever ward is overflowing, and (healer), the youngest healer, two days without sleep, hears of a traveller's way: move the sick into the shade where the breeze blows the fever away.

pieces.label: Move Them Outside
pieces.text: (Healer) wakes the other healers and, one by one, they carry the sick out on their mats into the shade of the big trees behind the hut, where the sea breeze blows...

pieces.label: Keep Them Inside
pieces.text: (Healer) decides the elders are right, and keeps working, bringing water and cool cloths from mat to mat in the heat...
The cool breeze breaks the fevers one after another, and every healer learns the traveller's way.
Cold rain, and (healer) hates the sound of it on a roof forever after.
A long week inside, and a nod from the head healer that means more than words.
Everyone recovers except (sick), who was sickest from the start.
People lying in the doorway.
The head healer has fallen asleep sitting up.
The sea breeze blows through the big trees.

pieces.label: The Ghost Crabs of the Night Beach
pieces.text: On a moonless night the beach crawls with ghost crabs, each carrying something someone lost, and one stops in front of (walker) and raises its claws.

pieces.label: Grab It
pieces.text: (Walker) lunges and catches the crab in both hands. It's cold, colder than the night, and it nips (walker.his/her) thumb hard...

pieces.label: Step Around It
pieces.text: (Walker) steps carefully around the crab, and another, and another. The whole beach seems to shift around (walker.him/her), clicking softly...
A cold nip goes up into (walker)'s head, and the crab takes (walker.his/her) name down into the sand.
The crab crumbles into sand, and (walker) wakes with a face the island lost long ago.
Home without touching one, and an empty pale shell on the doorstep.
A crab sits outside the door all night and leaves (walker) a new name.
Pale, see-through things that scuttle sideways.
The beach clicks softly.
Colder than the night.

pieces.label: The Lazy River
pieces.text: (Floater) has floated down the slow river on a banana-log raft every afternoon for a month, and today the farmers have asked for help with the harvest before the rains.

pieces.label: Float Down the River
pieces.text: (Floater) pushes off on (floater.his/her) raft and lies back. The sun is warm, the water is slow, the birds are singing...

pieces.label: Help With the Harvest
pieces.text: (Floater) sighs, ties up the raft and walks across the village to the gardens, where the farmers hand (floater.him/her) a basket without a word...
A submerged log tips (floater) into the snag, and doing nothing never feels as good again.
The most perfect afternoon of the summer, and half the harvest still in the ground.
A hundred-verse harvest song, and the river loses its pull.
A laugh like a waterfall in the next row, and by the next rains, a baby on the way.
Rafts of banana logs.
The gardens are hot and dusty.
The rains are coming.

pieces.label: The Hut in the Deep Jungle
pieces.text: Deep in the jungle, (finder) finds an old overgrown hut with a tree through the roof, with smoke coming from it and a baby crying inside.

pieces.label: Knock on the Door
pieces.text: (Finder) pushes through the vines and knocks. The crying stops. The door creaks open on its own...

pieces.label: Bring the Elders
pieces.text: (Finder) hurries home through the jungle and brings back three elders and two builders. It's nearly dark when they reach the hut...
A baby by a low fire and nobody else. Next week the hut has fallen in as if empty a hundred years.
A frightened young family who ran from a quarrel. Nobody asks about it.
The builders bring the family home and mend every leaking roof too.
The hut is cold, with leaves that have lain for years. "I heard it."
Vines through the walls.
The door creaks open on its own.
A basket of wild yams.

pieces.label: The Storm Season
pieces.text: After four big storms in a month, every hut has lost thatch, a post or a wall, and (chief) asks (builder), the most stubborn builder, what to do.

pieces.label: A Little Everywhere
pieces.text: (Builder) splits the builders into pairs and sends them to every hut in the village, patching and propping and tying...

pieces.label: The Worst Ones Properly
pieces.text: (Builder) picks the six worst huts and the builders work on them one at a time, slowly, properly, while everyone else squeezes in with neighbours...
Every hut is dry by nightfall, and the builders fall asleep at the cooking fire.
The fifth storm tears off the patches, and (builder) never wants to see thatch again.
Worst first, built to last, and the next storm doesn't move a bundle.
Three families to a hut, stories until dawn, and people almost sorry to go home.
Four big storms in a month.
Patching, propping and tying.
Children sleeping in heaps.

pieces.label: The Grey Heron at the Pool
pieces.text: The grey heron of the pool below the waterfall, a spirit who trades in time, stands right where (fetcher) fills the water jars and doesn't move.

pieces.label: Bow to Her
pieces.text: (Fetcher) puts down the jars and bows, feeling silly. The heron tilts her head and looks at (fetcher.him/her) with one yellow eye for a long moment...

pieces.label: Splash Her Away
pieces.text: (Fetcher) kicks water at the heron. "Shoo!" The heron opens her wings and rises out of the pool with a slow, offended croak...
A single drop flicked onto (fetcher)'s cheek, and a younger face in the pool.
She keeps (fetcher) company, and (fetcher), who never liked water, wades in to stand where she stands.
An older face in the water, and the heron never comes back.
She lands on the other side, unbothered. It seems simplest to fill the jars from there.
Perfectly still, watching.
One yellow eye.
A slow, offended croak.

pieces.label: The Shell That Doubles
pieces.text: (keeper), the spell-keeper, has made a pink shell that doubles whatever is put under it, and asks (sitter) to sit under the big one, to see if it works on a person.

pieces.label: Agree
pieces.text: (Sitter) sits down cross-legged. (keeper) lowers a huge pink shell over (sitter.him/her), and everything goes dark and smells of the sea...

pieces.label: Say No
pieces.text: "Not a chance," says (sitter). (keeper) sighs and puts the big shell down on the mat. Then (sitter.his/her) apprentice, (apprentice), wanders in, and sits down on it to rest...
Two of (sitter), blinking in the light. (keeper) is told to stick to coconuts.
"The outside doubles. The inside comes out different."
(apprentice) sits on the shell to rest, and there's a soft pop.
Two baskets of yams, then four, and a full food store.
One coconut under the shell, two when it lifts.
Everything goes dark and smells of the sea.
"Just for a moment."

pieces.label: The Octopus in the Fish Trap
pieces.text: The last fish trap holds an octopus as big as a sleeping dog, and it has wrapped one arm around each of (first) and (second)'s wrists. The elders say the reef's old octopus can change anyone's shape if annoyed.

pieces.label: Let It Go
pieces.text: They tip the trap over the side. The octopus doesn't let go at once. It holds both their wrists a moment longer, its skin rippling through every colour of the reef...

pieces.label: Bring It Home
pieces.text: They lash the trap shut and paddle for the beach as fast as they can. The octopus squeezes harder, and harder, and its skin turns black...
Full traps for a week, and (first) always knows where to set them.
Sucker marks on their wrists and flashes of red and gold all day.
One hard squeeze, stars, and (first) is looking out of (second)'s eyes.
A cloud of ink in (second)'s face, and fish tastes of ink ever after.
Eyes that look far too clever.
Its skin ripples through every colour of the reef.
It pours itself through a gap no bigger than a coconut.

pieces.label: The Golden Moths
pieces.text: On the first warm night of the year, a cloud of golden moths drifts over the village, shedding gold dust the elders say changes faces, and (subject) is outside finishing the washing.

pieces.label: Cover Up and Run Inside
pieces.text: (Subject) throws the wet washing over (subject.his/her) head and runs for the door. Moths bump against the cloth like soft raindrops...

pieces.label: Stand and Watch
